19949-autographs-for-freedom-volume-2-of:
Autographs for Freedom was an abolitionist gift book sold to fund the cause. Volume two of two is dated 1854. Its editor praises the contributors' ripe judgment and earnest purpose. Their generous sympathies win her warm thanks here. She hopes to meet many of them in future numbers. Julia Griffiths edited the volumes in Rochester, New York. Frederick Douglass's circle stood behind the enterprise.

Gift books gathered famous names between pretty covers. Here the names wrote against slavery itself. Essays, poems, and letters fill the autograph pages. Sales supported Douglass's newspaper and antislavery work. The volume is a who's who of the movement in 1854. Its literary quality served a fundraising purpose.
afr-200-2-ufo-reporting-1954:
The Air Force gave its UFO hunt a rule book on August 12, 1954. Regulation 200-2 names the things UFOBs, sets the reporting chain for the whole service, and clamps the press line on hard cases. Chief of Staff Nathan Twining signed the order himself.

Each sighting of weight was to move up the chain in set form, with care and speed. Only a small desk in Washington could speak in public on the cases that stayed unsolved. The rule was Blue Book's spine for its whole life. It turned saucer reports into office routine across the whole force.
arxiv-2509-00154:
Silvia A. Popa and Selma E. de Mink ask in 2025 how the giant, fast-spinning black holes in event GW231123 could form in a close pair. The event is the most massive black hole merger yet seen among more than two hundred detections, with extreme spins. Its origin is debated, with paths from repeated mergers to early stars each facing hurdles.

The pair focus on chemically homogeneous evolution, where rapid spin mixes a star fully so it stays compact. They compute detailed models of very massive pairs above the pair-instability gap, a mass range where stars should blow apart. The work tests if that mixed path can yield massive, fast-spinning helium stars that collapse to the observed holes.
arxiv-2509-00454:
Filip Szatkowski leads a team of eight authors who study activation sparsity in large language models in 2025. Sparsity here means that, for a given input, most neurons in a layer stay near zero. That trait is prized, since it can bring gains in speed, robustness, and clarity about how a model works. Old studies leaned on exact zeros from ReLU units, a feature modern models lack.

The team builds one shared frame to test sparsity robustness across models in use today. Their tests focus on feedforward layers, where much of each model's bulk sits. Shared traits of the phenomenon show up across model families and scales. The room for useful sparsity grows as models grow, in their results. Such shared laws could guide faster inference in the next wave of larger models.
arxiv-2509-00654:
Ashwin Nagarajan and one co-author, Hao-Wen Dong, study stylistic control in text-to-music generation when artist names are banned by policy. Models capture broad traits such as mood or instruments, but fine style is hard to steer, and methods that need retraining complicate reproducibility and compliance.

Nagarajan and Dong test whether short, human-readable modifiers sampled from a large language model can steer MusicGen-small toward two artists' styles, vocal pop and instrumental piano. Artist names prove the strongest signal, but name-free descriptors recover much of the effect, a difference they call the name-free gap. Cross-artist transfers weaken alignment, showing descriptors carry targeted cues, and safeguards based only on blocking names may not prevent imitation.
arxiv-2509-00854:
Gubio G de Lima, with three co-authors, assesses quantum neural networks in regression tasks. Quantum networks attract attention for possibly surpassing classical models. Yet the conditions for a concrete benefit remain unclear. The team compares classical and quantum models both ways. They use qualitative and quantitative analyses side by side.

Two target functions with contrasting properties drive the tests. Quantum networks show a distinct advantage in one context. They approximated a sinusoidal function far better than classical models. Their errors were up to seven orders of magnitude lower. In other cases their performance was limited, though. The pattern fits the No Free Lunch principle. No single model outperforms all others across every problem. Fair comparison methods are also explored.
arxiv-2509-01354:
Chinese medical language models need careful data handling, yet open pipelines have focused on training tricks and neglected how data are prepared. Wei Huang, Anda Cheng, Zhao Zhang, and Yinggui Wang present DPF-CM, a full data processing framework for training and deploying such models. It covers both building the training set and guarding privacy once the model is live.

For training, a chained examples strategy creates question-focused instructions where content was lacking, and an ensemble filter averages several reward models to drop noisy preference samples. For deployment, a privacy-preserving vector database searches model memory for high-risk content that could leak training data. Huang and the team argue that data processing, treated as a first-class stage, is central to safe and capable medical language models.
arxiv-2509-01454:
Chemical reactions can proceed by quantum tunneling, where a system passes through a barrier it lacks the energy to cross. Jindra Dusek, Joseph E. Lawrence, and Jeremy O. Richardson improve instanton rate theory, a semiclassical method that follows the best tunneling path. The standard ring-polymer version of that theory ignores anharmonicity, the uneven shape of the energy surface, sideways to the path.

Their corrected method, RPI+PC, uses third and fourth derivatives of the potential along the same tunneling path to capture those uneven effects. No global energy surface is needed, so the method pairs readily with first-principles electronic calculations. The derivation, done in a flux-correlation frame, yields a rate that does not depend on the chosen dividing surface. Tests in the paper show the correction captures anharmonicity and deep tunneling with rigorous support.
arxiv-2509-01654:
Words that sound alike can reveal the sound structure of a language, and measuring that likeness at scale takes computing power. Dominic Plein presents a method to score word similarity from phonetic transcriptions, written records of pronunciation, using the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm, a classic sequence alignment method from biology. The implementation is written in Rust and runs in parallel on both standard processors and graphics cards.

The graphics version uses the CUDA platform through a Rust library, gaining large speed improvements for big data sets. To validate the approach, Plein builds a fully connected graph whose nodes are words and whose edge weights are their similarities. Clustering that graph groups phonetically similar words, showing the method works. The author notes it could be extended to other languages with ease.
arxiv-2509-01854:
Jin-Li Zhang studies the inner structure of kaons when the particle sits slightly off its energy shell. Kaons are mesons, particles made of a quark and an antiquark, with one strange quark. Two distribution types map how quarks share momentum inside: one for varied probes, one for sideways motion. His counts use an effective quark model with a timing rule to keep results finite.

Off-shell shifts change the main distributions by a notable share, similar in size to the pion case. Missing symmetry in this setup creates new form factors, values that encode shape, with odd powers in their averages. Links among those factors mirror links known from electric probes. Sideways distributions also lean more on momentum share when off-shell.
arxiv-2509-02154:
Aymene Mohammed Bouayed leads three co-authors in fixing latent bias in generative models for long-tailed data. Variational autoencoders with one global prior underrepresent rare classes when training data are imbalanced. A heavy tailed prior helps robustness but still allocates mass by class frequency. Their C-t3VAE assigns each class its own heavy tailed joint prior over latent and output variables.

Uniform prior mass across class components counters the geometric bias directly. A closed form objective from a power divergence family drives optimization. An equal weight latent mixture supports balanced generation. On three imbalanced image sets, generation quality beats heavy tailed and Gaussian rivals under severe imbalance. Per class scores also lead in highly imbalanced settings.
arxiv-2509-02754:
Mingyi Wang and four co-authors wrote a 2025 autonomous driving paper testing whether components of large language models transfer to motion generation, the task of predicting how traffic agents will move. Both fields model sequences token by token with context, which invites reuse.

Five modules are evaluated: tokeniser design, positional embedding, pretraining style, post-training strategy, and test-time computation. Experiments run on the Waymo Sim Agents benchmark. With suitable adaptation, the transferred modules significantly improved motion generation results, and the combined method stayed competitive on the task. The authors separate which techniques transfer cleanly, which fail, and why, plus the adaptations driving scenarios demand. The study gives builders a map for borrowing language model machinery without blind copying.
arxiv-2509-02854:
Eden Ketchum wrote a 2025 algebra paper about almost simple groups, which are building blocks in the classification of finite groups. The question is narrow: for such a group, when are its Sylow 3-subgroups made from just two generators? A Sylow subgroup is a largest subgroup whose size is a power of a chosen prime.

Ketchum shows, by an algorithm, that a group's character table can answer that question. A character table is a grid summarizing how a group acts in simplified form. The two-generator property turns out to match a condition about how certain symmetries act on characters in one key block. That link would follow from a major open guess called the Alperin-McKay-Navarro conjecture.
arxiv-2509-03254:
Minwoo Yu and 8 co-authors studied magnetic resonances driven by sound waves in a nickel hybrid device in 2025. Surface acoustic waves are ripples that travel along a solid's surface; here they shake the magnetization of a thin nickel film grown on a lithium niobate crystal. Such spin-acoustic devices could route signals in future electronics.

Absorption of the waves depended strongly on the direction of an applied magnetic field lying in the film's plane. Light-based measurements of the film revealed both one-axis and two-axis preferences in its magnetic alignment. Adding a long-range dipolar interaction, the mutual pull between distant magnetic moments, let the authors explain the directional absorption pattern. Their message is that substrate-induced preferences and dipolar effects must be engineered together when optimizing these devices.
arxiv-2509-03854:
Joshua J. Sanchez and five co-authors' 2025 research paper is about switching a two-dimensional material's topological state with uniaxial strain, a one-directional stretch. Topological materials carry protected edge currents that ignore local defects, thanks to their inverted bulk band structure. Turning that protection off on demand would let engineers write conducting channels where they want them.

The authors argue large uniaxial strain can flip a two-dimensional Chern insulator into a topologically trivial state. The seam between strained and unstrained regions could then serve as a fresh edge for dissipationless current flow. Density functional theory calculations demonstrate the effect in monolayer MnBi2S2Te2, whose band structure and Chern number both switch under strain. Combining uniaxial and biaxial results maps a full phase diagram of topology against strain. The work points toward strain-written circuitry in topological materials, where stretching a sample redraws its conducting paths.
arxiv-2509-04054:
Giacomo Cordoni and two co-authors report the first search for close double stars in the outskirts of the star cluster 47 Tucanae in a 2025 paper. Earlier work relied on Hubble telescope images of crowded cluster centers. The team instead used early data from the Rubin Observatory, which scans wide areas of sky with sharp measurements of star brightness and color.

Past the cluster's half-light edge, the team picked out paired stars too close to separate visually. Pairs with fairly matched masses appear slightly more often there than in the center, based on Hubble results. The finding tests ideas about how double stars form and change inside clusters.
arxiv-2509-04254:
Meisam Jamshidi Seikavandi and four co-authors read emotions and personality from body signals in a 2025 research paper. Their system, MuMTAffect, watches pupil size, eye gaze, facial muscle units, and skin conductance, the sweat-linked electrical signal used in lie detectors. Separate transformer encoders, a modern pattern-reading design, handle each signal type. A fusion stage then mixes what they found. Personality prediction runs as a side task, sharpening the personal patterns used for emotion reading.

Design follows the theory of constructed emotion, splitting raw feeling signals from higher-level interpretation. On the AFFEC data set, skin signals and stimulus cues helped judge arousal, meaning intensity. Pupil and gaze cues helped judge valence, meaning pleasantness.
arxiv-2509-04754:
Information lost to the environment makes tracked quantum states impure, but looking back over the full record can recover some of it. Shota Yokoyama, lead author with eight co-authors, demonstrate quantum state smoothing in a lab test in a 2025 paper. Their setup uses an optical parametric oscillator and two independent detectors for observed and unobserved channels.

Compared with conventional causal filtering, smoothing improved state purification and restored squeezing in their measurements. The smoothed states were also better estimates of the hidden true states. The authors present the technique as promising for quantum technologies where lost information degrades control and sensing.
arxiv-2509-05054:
Lattices acting on geometric buildings were long expected to be residually finite, a property linking groups to finite quotients. Thomas Titz Mite and one co-author give the first counterexamples for irreducible buildings in a 2025 group theory paper. Their lattices are of a specific two-dimensional type.

The examples contain the first known simple CAT(0) groups with property (T), and the first CAT(0) groups not quasi-isometric to a direct product. The authors also classify certain vertex-regular lattices on another building type at thickness three. They discover an arithmetic example not commensurable with previously studied lattices, widening the known landscape.
arxiv-2509-05154:
Vision-language models can segment medical images from text prompts, but their accuracy still trails specialist architectures. Julia Dietlmeier, lead author with four co-authors, close part of that gap by ensembling in a 2025 paper. Instead of engineering prompts, they combine CLIP-based segmentation models with a low-complexity convolutional network.

On a polyp dataset, the ensembled biomedical model gains a substantial overlap score improvement. Other radiology and non-radiology datasets show smaller gains. Results vary by dataset, sometimes beating and sometimes trailing a leading specialist model. The authors release their code and flag the dataset dependence as a topic for future investigation.
arxiv-2509-05254:
Why do speakers sometimes drop the word that before a clause? Hailin Hao and Elsi Kaiser revisit that choice in a 2025 linguistics paper on English sentence building. A leading idea, uniform information density, says speakers smooth out the flow of information so it stays fairly even.

Using a large modern corpus of conversation, plus machine learning and neural language models, the authors refine how information density is measured. Their results confirm that low density, meaning a more predictable clause, favours dropping that. Older measures tied to the main verb hide a lot of word-specific variation. Measures from word embeddings in context explain more of the pattern.
arxiv-2509-05654:
A fractional equation that sits between diffusion and wave motion is given a solution theory by Bruno de Andrade and Naldisson Santos in a 2025 analysis paper. Fractional derivatives measure change with memory of the past, so the equation spreads like heat and oscillates like a wave at once.

The authors estimate the families of linear operators behind the problem, working in Lebesgue spaces and a scale of fractional powers of the Laplace operator. They prove existence and uniqueness of local mild solutions, weaker solutions defined through the operator families. Continuation to a maximal interval, spatial regularity, and continuous dependence on initial data are also treated. The theory sets basic ground rules for models of this mixed type.
arxiv-2509-05854:
When is a topology fully determined by testing sets against a chosen family of subsets? Ziqin Feng and Paul Gartside explore that question in a 2025 paper on generating families. Familiar cases include k-spaces, determined by their compact subsets, and sequential spaces, determined by convergent sequences. The authors compare such determination relations under the Tukey order, a ranking of complexity.

For separable metrizable spaces, spaces with a countable dense set and a distance, they pin down the opening structure of the k-space case completely and show its cofinal part is highly complex. The sequential case resolves in full. A consequence counts the possible Tukey types: the number can range from countably infinite up to the continuum, with exact values tied to set-theoretic assumptions about the continuum and the aleph hierarchy.
arxiv-2509-06154:
Graph-based simulators beat neural operators when training data are scarce, argue Dibyajyoti Nayak and Somdatta Goswami in a 2025 paper. Surrogate models for time-dependent partial differential equations promise fast stand-ins for expensive solvers, but neural operators hunger for data and generalize weakly without it. The authors trace that weakness to global processing that ignores a system's local, discretized structure.

Graph neural simulators instead pass messages between neighboring points and step time like a traditional solver, learning instantaneous rates of change. On five canonical systems, from Burgers' equations to flow past a cylinder, they reach under one percent error with only three percent of the trajectories. They also accumulate far less error over long rollouts than leading operators. A principal-component clustering trick picks the training trajectories.
arxiv-2509-06454:
Keeping factory clocks in step across a mobile network is the problem tackled by Julia Caleya-Sanchez and six co-authors in a 2025 engineering paper. Time-sensitive networking, which schedules data so it arrives on time, must work over 5G. One 5G option, the transparent clock, had never been tested in this setting, the authors say.

The team built the clock on commercial switches, measured how long messages spend inside the 5G link, and restored the clock signal at the receiving node. Their testbed used real equipment and varied how often timing messages were sent. The best settings held devices within about five hundred nanoseconds of each other, peak to peak. That beats the one-microsecond limit industry requires, with only small offsets at certain message rates.
arxiv-2509-06554:
Untrustworthy raters in image quality tests are hunted with deliberate attacks in a solo 2025 paper by Dietmar Saupe. When people score picture quality, bad ratings must be flagged as outliers before average scores are computed. Standard detection methods are usually tested only on simple fakes like random clicking, which may hide their worst failures.

Saupe builds a general stress-test framework that searches for the ratings most damaging to the final average. Attack generators use optimization to push the estimated score as far as possible from the truth, for both category scales and sliding scales. Applied to several hard and soft detection methods, the tests reveal large differences in worst-case accuracy. He also proposes a few simple detectors that hold up remarkably well under these attacks, offering practical options for quality labs.
arxiv-2509-06654:
Many kinds of music analysis are unified in one graph-based system by Emmanouil Karystinaios and three co-authors in a 2025 music technology paper. Computational tools for analyzing scores usually each serve a single task, such as finding chords or key. Datasets for different tasks are annotated in different ways, which blocks combined training.

AnalysisGNN represents a score as a graph and learns from shuffled, mixed datasets using a custom weighted multi-task loss. Outputs from task-specific classifiers are fused at the logit level, the raw scores before a final choice. A separate module flags non-chord tones, passing notes that do not belong to the harmony, and removes them from every task to clean up labels. Performance matches systems trained on single static datasets, and the model resists shifts between collections and annotation styles better.
arxiv-2509-06754:
Scrambling images with a new hyper-chaotic map is proposed by Yiqi Tang in a solo 2025 cryptography paper. Encryption protects images from unauthorized viewing, and chaotic systems are popular building blocks because tiny changes in input explode into completely different output. Tang designs a two-dimensional map by blending the Rastrigin and Ackley functions, two bumpy test surfaces from optimization.

Standard chaos tests, including bifurcation diagrams, Lyapunov exponents, and entropy measures, rate the new map above existing advanced chaotic functions. A self-adaptive diffusion step then evens out the brightness distribution of the encrypted image. Judged on a series of indicators, the full scheme outperformed leading image encryption techniques, the author reports. Code is published openly. Such schemes aim at secure image sharing, though independent testing usually decides whether laboratory scores survive real attacks.
arxiv-2509-06954:
A planned far-infrared space mission's view of dusty galaxy growth is simulated by Juan Antonio Fernández-Ontiveros and two co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. Most ultraviolet and optical light from young stars and feeding black holes is absorbed by dust and reradiated in the infrared, where diagnostic lines reveal accretion, star formation, and chemistry.

The PRIMA mission will run blind spectroscopic surveys reaching back to when galaxies were a few billion years old, measuring how star formation and black hole growth evolved together. The authors simulate a survey with its FIRESS instrument covering hundreds of galaxies at cosmic noon, plus follow-ups measuring nitrogen-to-oxygen ratios and metallicities. High-resolution spectra will expose feedback through outflow signatures. PRIMA will also open rest-frame mid-infrared spectroscopy of galaxies in the reionization era, probing the first galaxies and black holes.
arxiv-2509-07054:
Edgar Dobriban, writing alone in a 2025 paper, reviews what statistics can do for generative AI. Such AI is set to change many fields, yet it works by sampling from chance-based models. By itself, it gives no pledge that its output is right, safe, or fair.

Statistics, the author argues, offers tools to make these systems more sound. It can help check how good a model is, plan tests and trials, and design steps that fix flaws. The paper walks through past work on each of these themes, in plain terms first and then in AI use. It also notes where the tools fall short and where fresh work is most needed. The upshot is a call to treat stats as a base for trust in generative AI.
arxiv-2509-07354:
James R. Beattie, writing alone in 2025, traces how supernovae stir turbulence across our Galaxy. Turbulence is chaotic, swirling motion, and core-collapse supernovae, the explosions of massive stars, supply enough energy to keep galactic turbulence going at the observed level. The open question is the mechanism that turns blast energy into swirls on large scales.

Working with high-resolution simulations of a galactic disk patch, Beattie isolates individual supernova remnants and studies their shells. Instabilities on the shell surface wrinkle and fold the contact boundary, generating baroclinic vorticity, swirl born where pressure and density gradients cross. A derived formula for the resulting spectrum matches the simulations, and a timescale rule shows young remnants near their cooling radius shed turbulence most efficiently. The picture connects small shell ripples to galaxy-wide stirring.
arxiv-2509-07954:
Wenqian Zhang explains how to find every extremal graph for a forbidden family, in a solo 2025 combinatorics paper. Extremal graphs pack the most edges possible on a given number of vertices while avoiding every graph in a banned family as a subgraph. The famous Turán graph, split into equal parts, is often the unique champion.

Building on Simonovits's idea of symmetric subgraphs, Zhang works under conditions where a banned graph nearly fits inside a Turán-like template. The method aims to list all graphs that achieve the maximum, not just exhibit one. Complete lists of extremal graphs settle stability questions: they show whether near-maximal graphs must also look like the template, a theme across modern extremal combinatorics.
arxiv-2509-08054:
A loud gravitational-wave signal, GW250114, tests two pillars of black hole physics in a 2025 paper by the LIGO Scientific Collaboration, the Virgo Collaboration, and the KAGRA Collaboration. Two near-equal black holes, each around thirty-three solar masses with small spins, merged almost circularly. The signal stands far above the noise, giving unusually clean post-merger data.

The ringdown, the fading vibration of the newborn black hole, matches the dominant mode of a spinning Kerr black hole and its first overtone, with frequencies constrained close to the Kerr spectrum. Such checks test Hawking's area law and whether real black holes are truly the Kerr objects Einstein's theory describes. A single clean event can carry rare weight.
arxiv-2509-08454:
Whisper, a leading speech model, can be adapted to recognize emotions with a light technique called LoRA, but nobody knew what LoRA changes inside. Yujian Ma and 4 co-authors open that black box in a 2025 research paper. LoRA fine-tunes a model by training two small matrices instead of the whole network. The authors apply probing tools to the adapted Whisper encoder.

Their tools include layer contribution probing, logit-lens inspection, and similarity measures between representations. Two mechanisms stood out. First, specialization arrives late: early layers keep general features while later ones gather task-specific information. Second, the two LoRA matrices play opposite roles, one aligning representations forward, the other differentiating them backward. Understanding these dynamics helps engineers design cheaper, more interpretable adaptations of large speech models.
arxiv-2509-08954:
When is the optimization curve of a first order method convex? Le Duc Hieu studies that question in a 2025 paper. The curve lists function values over iterations. Convex here means each step gains less than the step before.

For gradient descent on convex smooth functions, the curve is convex for step sizes up to a sharp threshold. The author proves that threshold is tight, so larger steps can break the property. Gradient norms also fall up to a slightly larger step limit. In continuous time, gradient flow always gives a convex curve. The results refine classic tools and link discrete and continuous dynamics.
arxiv-2509-09154:
Bui Duc Manh and 8 co-authors rethink agentic spatial intelligence from a neuroscience inspired view in a 2025 paper. AI agents can reason with language, but their spatial reasoning stays limited and largely symbolic. Human spatial skill, by contrast, rests on senses, memory, and cognitive maps.

Six computation modules map biological functions to agent design: sensing, integration, coordinate conversion, a cognitive map, spatial memory, and spatial reasoning. Recent methods are judged against each module, revealing gaps that block grounded spatial skill. Benchmarks, datasets, and application domains from virtual systems to robotics are examined. Future directions aim at flexible reasoning in dynamic, unstructured environments.
arxiv-2509-09554:
Joseph Jabbour and 2 co-authors design a faster decoder for non-binary polar codes in a 2025 communications paper. Polar codes protect data in modern links, and their non-binary versions promise gains at a cost of heavier decoding work. The team's idea is to study each decoder kernel offline and tailor it to the polarisation level of its inputs, cutting effort where the signal is already strongly sorted.

Called FSC-PA, the scheme trims the load at parity-check nodes that share a polarisation level. Versions handle two modulation styles, BPSK and CCSK. Against a leading extended min-sum method, field additions fell by about three fifths and real additions by about a third, with performance loss kept under a fifth of a decibel.
arxiv-2509-10054:
Hailong Yang and 4 co-authors organise teams of language model agents around explicit rules and a living task graph in a 2025 systems paper. Multi-agent setups promise help with messy real jobs, yet their planning wobbles when a task is complex and uncertain, and one agent's confident error can poison the chain. Their framework, XAgents, attacks both faults at the structural level rather than by better prompting alone.

Work is laid out on a multipolar task processing graph that can be replanned as events unfold. During each subtask, domain rules written as if-then statements fence agent behaviour, while global rules keep collaboration orderly between agents. On three data sets spanning knowledge and logic questions, the system beat leading single-agent and multi-agent rivals throughout the reported tests.
arxiv-2509-10354:
Mithun Kumar Acharjee and AKM Fazlur Rahman build a Bayesian model for patients whose illnesses keep returning in this 2025 biostatistics paper. Events such as stroke and heart failure recur in several types and often end with death, and doctors need to know how the recurrences and the final event depend on each other.

Their joint model works on the gaps between events and ties all event types together through a shared frailty, an unmeasured patient-level risk. Flexible gamma-process priors shape each baseline hazard while keeping familiar effect measures. Computation uses a simple sampling algorithm that scales almost linearly with sample size and avoids heavy matrix work. Simulations favor their approach over a frequentist version, and they demonstrate it on the ALLHAT trial, modeling cardiovascular recurrences and death together.
arxiv-2509-11054:
Thomas Y. Chen is the sole author of this 2025 information theory paper. It asks a basic question about search systems that mix text and images. How much information must each query carry for retrieval to stay accurate?

Chen treats ranking as a form of lossy compression. He derives a rate-distortion limit for a ranking-based error measure. He then proves that no system can beat that limit. The bound splits into two parts. One part is balanced across data types. The other is a penalty for lopsided information. He also builds a coding scheme that nearly reaches the limit. Tests on image-caption data keep it close to the best possible result. Common baselines fall well behind.
arxiv-2509-11354:
Surajit Das and Pavel Zun present image analysis software built for laboratories with almost no budget in this 2025 paper. Brightfield microscopes are cheap and common, but their images of living cells are noisy and low in contrast. Existing strong tools assume graphics cards, labeled training data, or programming skill, all scarce in the labs the authors target.

Their Python program runs on an ordinary desktop processor and needs no hand-labeled data or training phase. A friendly graphical interface covers segmentation of stained-free cells, feature extraction, evaluation, and automatic reports, while a scripting mode serves developers. On public live-cell data the authors report accuracy and repeatability above two well-known tools, at competitive speed, which they pitch to basic research and cell therapy work.
arxiv-2509-12054:
Valentin Skvortsov's 2025 mathematics paper defines new versions of familiar tools for measuring rough sets. The setting is the Cantor dyadic group, a mathematical group built from endless binary sequences. On it, he introduces analogues of Riesz s-potential and s-energy, quantities that describe how a mass distribution spreads out.

Skvortsov links those quantities to Hausdorff dimension, a measure that can assign fractional size to highly irregular sets. He proves that if a set carries a distribution with finite s-energy, then its Hausdorff dimension is at least s. The same condition can be stated through Fourier coefficients, the components of the distribution in the Walsh system of functions on the group. The result extends classical potential theory into this dyadic setting.
arxiv-2509-12354:
Which products of two graphs can be drawn on a donut without crossings? Elizabeth Badgett and two co-authors answer a sharp case in 2025: take the Cartesian product of a 3-connected graph with any other graph, and ask when the result embeds on the torus.

The answer is narrow. The product fits exactly when the 3-connected factor is outer-cylindrical, a special layered shape, and the other factor is just a two-vertex path. Almost every pairing fails the test. As a side result, the product of the complete graph on four vertices with a three-vertex path is shown to need a surface of genus two.
arxiv-2509-12854:
Matthieu Heller describes the design of a next-generation telescope camera in a 2025 paper. The AdvCam is being developed by an international collaboration of Italian, Japanese, Spanish, and Swiss institutes for the Large-Sized Telescopes of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory. These telescopes image faint flashes produced when high-energy particles hit the atmosphere.

The camera uses silicon photomultipliers and a fully digital readout system. It will feature four times more pixels for the same field of view as the current camera, enabling finer resolution, better angular precision, and improved background rejection. That increase brings challenges in low-power, high-speed chip design and real-time handling on hardware accelerators. The technological leap should lower the energy threshold and give brighter images for observations.
arxiv-2509-13454:
Nelson R. F. Braga and William S. Cunha study the Hawking-Page transition in massive gravity in a 2025 physics paper. Under the gauge-gravity duality, that transition stands for a change between confined and deconfined phases. Consider a space that is anti-de Sitter far away, with a flat spatial edge. In such a space the transition never happens. Something extra must set an infrared energy scale first.

Theories of massive gravity have found a home in holography, where they stand in for systems that lose momentum. Braga and Cunha study the transition for massive gravity in an anti-de Sitter space of a mixed kind. Its boundary joins flat directions with a circle. They show that the term giving the graviton its mass does the needed job. It creates a Hawking-Page transition at a definite, finite critical temperature.
arxiv-2509-13654:
P. Diego-Palazuelos and E. Komatsu measure cosmic birefringence in a 2025 cosmology paper, a possible uniform rotation of polarized light from the cosmic microwave background as it crosses the universe. Such a rotation would break parity symmetry and could signal interaction with dark matter or dark energy fields.

Using polarization data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope's sixth data release, the pair run a Bayesian analysis of parity-violating correlations, accounting for telescope miscalibration and signal leakage. They find a rotation of roughly a fifth of a degree, nonzero at just under three sigma of statistical significance. Unresolved systematics bar strong conclusions, but the sign and size match earlier WMAP and Planck results.
arxiv-2509-13854:
Jack McKinlay, Marina De Vos, Janina Hoffmann, and Andreas Theodorou review the value alignment literature in a 2025 paper. Computer scientists use the phrase for making AI systems act in line with human values. The team find the term is used loosely across the field. Usage also shifts from paper to paper.

They analyzed over one hundred seventy recent research articles in a systematic way. The material grouped into six themes. Themes covered drivers and approaches, and challenges in the work. They also covered which values are at stake, and how humans and AI think. Human-agent teaming and system design complete the list. From that synthesis they propose a sharper definition. Alignment is an ongoing process between humans and autonomous agents. It expresses abstract values in concrete contexts, within the cognitive limits of both sides.
arxiv-2509-15454:
Boris Ginzburg models how voters learn facts through their social ties. A voter can spend effort to check a claim that matters for a vote. If the check works, the news spreads through the voter's network. Ginzburg asks how the shape of that network changes what the crowd ends up knowing. He also asks how split the crowd is to start with.

His model shows a split result. More links help voters learn basic facts, since news travels far. Yet more links leave them worse on hard issues, where checks are costly and free riding pays. Being split into camps makes voters less informed overall. The paper is a theory piece on facts, effort, and networks.
arxiv-2509-15954:
Volkan Erol, writing alone, measures how strongly entanglement boosts precision sensing. Quantum sensors can beat classical limits, and entanglement is the fuel. He studies twenty thousand random two qubit states by simulation. For each, he computes how much measurement precision the state could give at best, and compares it with three entanglement scores.

Tuning each state with local operations first makes the link far more predictable. Curve fits then match the data closely: exponential fits score near perfect, and polynomial fits closer still. The patterns show a saturation in the sensing gain. They back key claims of quantum resource theory. The bounds guide how to spend entanglement in real sensors.
arxiv-2509-16154:
A massive galaxy can bend light from a farther galaxy into a ring, and stars inside that far galaxy may flare as they cross bright zones. Sung Kei Li and twelve co-authors predict what the Webb telescope would see in one such system, nicknamed the Cosmic Horseshoe. The far galaxy forms stars at a very high rate, so many bright young stars should be present.

The team expects roughly sixty flaring stars per deep pointing. Their spread could test the nature of dark matter, and their counts could probe how top-heavy star birth is at cosmic noon. Repeat Webb visits would turn this lens into a sharp tool.
arxiv-2509-16354:
Table data still rule much of real-world prediction, yet deep networks trail tree ensembles on most table benchmarks. Sivan Sarafian and Yehudit Aperstein design RuleNet, a transformer built just for tables. It learns rule-like embeddings, projects numbers through a bent scale, and masks features in ensembles to gain robustness and honest doubt estimates.

On eight benchmark sets, the network matched or beat top tree methods in most cases while staying cheap to run. That makes it a practical neural option for table tasks. The design shows deep learning can close the table gap without giving up speed.
arxiv-2509-16454:
Exploring biomedical data through charts is faster when the charts build themselves from plain questions. Devin Lange and six co-authors prototype a system where several AI agents draft chart specifications and filters from natural language, then link the charts into a dashboard that grows step by step. Users can still steer with familiar interface parts and with generated widgets that adjust the views.

The design pairs the ease of language with the control of classic interfaces. A case study shows the system's promise for biomedical discovery work. Grammar-based charts keep each view precise and shareable, even as the dashboard assembles itself.
arxiv-2509-16754:
Franco Flandoli and Yassine Tahraoui study a plasma equation in a closed region in a 2025 math paper. The equation, named for Hasegawa and Mima, models drift waves in plasma. Here the region has firm edges, and the density has a sharp singular part. The pair ask when the setup has sound solutions.

Their proof joins three tools: a smoothed fourth-order form, a spectral method, and a tamed density. Each tool handles one snag in the problem. Results hold under varied assumptions on the starting data. Sound math for such equations backs fusion and space plasma models, where edges and sharp density jumps are common.
arxiv-2509-17154:
Yasamin Jalalian, Mostafa Samir, Boumediene Hamzi, Peyman Tavallali, and Houman Owhadi wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on learning physical systems from data. Many systems follow Hamiltonian rules, which govern how energy shapes motion over time. Learning such a system from a few recorded paths could speed up science and engineering work, if the learned model stays true to the rules.

The team offers two kernel-based routes. One rebuilds the paths first and then learns the energy rule, while the other learns both at once. On test systems such as a mass on a spring, a swinging pendulum, and the Hénon-Heiles system, their frame beat older kernel baselines. The gains were largest when data was scarce. They also prove error bounds in advance, and give a broader frame that can learn other kinds of systems too.
arxiv-2509-17254:
Ehsan Roohi and Amirmehran Mahdavi wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on fast stand-ins for costly gas flow simulations. The flows are rarefied, the thin-gas regime found at high altitude and in micro devices, here over a small step. The gold-standard particle method is too slow for many-run tasks.

Their stand-in is a DeepONet, an operator network trained to map settings to full flow fields. A new loss function guides training, with extra weight on the recirculation zone behind the step, where swirling flow is easy to get wrong. Two tasks are shown. In one, the network learns the velocity field from the Knudsen number. In the other, it learns the full solution from the step height. Outputs match the costly reference data closely, and new settings resolve fast. A global score alone would hide the gain, so the authors stress local checks.
arxiv-2509-17854:
Duong Le puts forward tiny magnetic carriers as a new way to treat brain aneurysms. His 2025 paper notes that a bulge in a brain vessel hits a small share of folk, and a burst can kill or disable. Clip surgery, coils, and flow tubes each have flaws, such as poor fit in bent vessels.

Le proposes BioBots: soft gel carriers with magnetic grains, coated with vessel-lining cells. A magnet field would steer them through a thin tube to the bulge. There they could form a patch that fits the shape and helps the wall heal. The plan is a proposal, not a proven cure.
arxiv-2509-17954:
Jonathan Biteau takes stock of all the faint glow that fills space from far-off sources. His 2025 paper builds an open database of measures of that sky glow. Data come from tools on the ground, at sea, in ice, in orbit, and at the edge of the solar system.

Photons, neutrinos, and cosmic rays are all logged across a huge range of energies. Pooling them lets him pin the energy held in most glow parts to fair precision. He checks that stock against the past of star birth and growth of huge black holes. The set is the most full of its kind to date.
arxiv-2509-18054:
Nikhil N S and 3 co-authors help a planner pick the right solver for a plant layout task. Their 2025 paper deals with the Facility Layout Problem, where units must be placed well under many goals and limits. Which solver works best rests on task traits, so picking one needs deep expert facts.

Their frame builds a knowledge graph from past papers on the task. Three search styles pull facts from that graph: exact graph search, loose vector search, and cluster search. A language model then turns those facts into a solver pick with stated grounds. Tests on six hard cases beat a plain chatbot baseline.
arxiv-2509-18254:
Vikram Manikantan and Vasileios Paschalidis show small disks around paired black holes can turn magnetically arrested. Their 2025 paper uses full curved-space sims of gas flow onto two equal, non-spinning black holes. Each hole hosts a minidisk, fed from a shared outer disk.

Their runs start with the holes far apart, so the minidisks grow large. Magnet fields pile up at each horizon till they hit a cap. Near those caps, field snaps drive bursts that should flare in heat and X-ray light. Total inflow steadies as the disks arrest. The state is a new outcome for such paired flows.
arxiv-2509-18354:
Finding flaws in factory images often takes a library of normal examples to learn from. Mehrdad Moradi, Shengzhe Chen, Hao Yan, and Kamran Paynabar ask what can be done with one flawed image alone. Their 2025 paper presents SSDnet, a method that finds odd spots with no training data at all. It leans on a bias built into image networks: they favor natural patterns.

The method feeds patches of the test image itself into the network and asks it to rebuild them. Masking, patch shuffling, and a touch of noise stop the network from just copying the input. A scoring rule based on structure, not just pixels, guides the rebuild. On the MVTec-AD test set the method scored near-perfect detection marks. It also beat prior methods on a fabric data set. No labels or reference images were used at all.
arxiv-2509-18454:
StarCraft II games give researchers a controlled world for testing learning agents. Andrzej Białecki and four co-authors present SC2Tools, a toolset and data interface for that research. Their 2025 paper argues that tooling shapes how fast a field grows. Heavy data work can shut out researchers with less coding support.

The toolset has modules for handling game data and for building larger data sets. Some tools work beyond StarCraft II for general data set building. The team used them to build one of the largest StarCraft II tournament data sets so far. A separate interface for PyTorch and PyTorch Lightning makes the data easy to load. The modular design leaves room for growth. The authors say shared tools and a standard workflow will widen who can join game and esports research.
arxiv-2509-18554:
Big data arrays with many axes, called tensors, are often stored in a compressed Tucker form. Daniel Appelö and Yingda Cheng propose two new algorithms for that form in this 2025 paper. The first is a cross approximation that samples only a few fibers, or lines, of the array per step. Fiber choices follow a known interpolation rule.

The method, called Cross2-DEIM, scales well and uses modest memory while iterating fast. The team builds a fast Poisson equation solver on it, useful alone or as a helper for other solvers. The second method, Tucker-AA, solves nonlinear tensor equations with Anderson acceleration, a way to speed fixed-point steps. Warm starts and rank trimming keep the compressed size in check. Tests on three-dimensional nonlinear equations show the pair performs well. The work targets fast, low-memory computing for multi-axis data.
arxiv-2509-18754:
Video language models get better answers when they can call expert tools, but the tool set keeps changing in real use. Yuyang Liu, Meng Cao, Xinyuan Shi, and Xiaodan Liang present COLT in this 2025 paper. COLT teaches open video models to keep learning new tools from a stream. Older methods assume a fixed tool shelf and forget old tools as new ones arrive.

A learnable tool codebook acts as the memory for tool skills. For each user request, matching tools are picked by similarity between the request and stored tool features. The team also built VideoToolBench, a video-centered instruction set for tool use. On older video benchmarks and on their new set, COLT reached top scores. It acquired tools one after another without the usual forgetting. The authors frame continual tool learning as the realistic setting for deployed video assistants.
arxiv-2509-18954:
Self-driving cars and robots need to know exactly where they are, and laser scanners help them match what they see to a map. Minoo Dolatabadi and four co-authors study the Iterative Closest Point method, the standard tool for that matching. It often errs in bare spaces with few landmarks, or in busy scenes with moving objects. Wrong matches can throw off a pose estimate with no warning.

Their system learns to predict the matching error before the match is run, and it needs no ready-made map to do so. Each laser scan gets a full estimate of its likely error in position and heading. Fed into a Kalman filter, those estimates cut location errors in the standard KITTI test data and make tracking steadier.
arxiv-2509-19354:
When disaster strikes, responders need to reason about roads, coordinates, and where hospitals and shelters remain reachable, and language models are weak at that spatial thinking. Ahmed El Fekih Zguir and two co-authors present GeoResponder, a framework that teaches such reasoning through a layered instruction curriculum. Lessons are stacked by cognitive level, anchoring word meanings to the continuous map of coordinates and enforcing basic spatial axioms inside the model.

Evaluations span four cities with distinct street topologies and a range of response tasks. The tuned model beat both leading foundation models and specialist baselines by a wide margin. The authors argue that language models can begin to internalize geographic structure, not just recite facts about places. Their results point toward assistants that could support time-critical disaster response, where a wrong turn costs lives.
arxiv-2509-19554:
Yi Ren's thesis watches deep learning the way physics watches motion: through forces. One training example pushes on the model's handling of another, and Ren splits that push into two parts. The first part is how alike the two examples are. The second is how strong the update force is at that moment.

That split explains a range of puzzles. Some examples take odd, winding paths to being learned. Certain fine-tuning methods for language models work while close cousins fail. Simple, structured patterns tend to be learned before messy ones. The framework also suggests fresh tactics for training. Ren presents it as a developing lens, not a finished theory. A systematic way to read training dynamics could guide model design the way force diagrams guide engineering.
arxiv-2509-19654:
Health time series, such as heart or activity signals, shift shape as people's habits change. Kevin Garcia and three co-authors build a self-supervised method that learns from unlabeled signals and resists those shifts. Their trick uses a symbol-based summary of each series, which ignores small warps, moves, and noise. A contrastive learner is guided by that summary toward stable features.

The authors target distribution shift caused by differing human behavior across users and days. Their method, they report, beats rivals by a clear margin where shifts are strong. No hand labels are needed for the main training pass. Robust features matter for digital health tools that must work on new patients without retraining. The symbol-guided design offers one route to that robustness.
arxiv-2509-19854:
Two algebraic worlds, mosaics and join-semilattices, turn out to be mirror images, and Alessandro Linzi has now checked that mirror inside a proof assistant. The formalization in Isabelle/HOL covers the object part of the equivalence. It verifies that the two translations undo each other exactly. Large language models assisted throughout as reasoning aides.

The source result grew from work on hypercompositional structures tied to quantum logic. Machine-checked proof removes doubt that human refereeing can miss. It also shows a workflow: AI help inside, formal certainty outside. Formal libraries grow one such project at a time. The paper offers both a verified theorem and a case study in AI-assisted proving. That pairing may matter as much as the algebra itself.
arxiv-2509-20054:
A famed claim links the pattern of entanglement in a bulk system to the modes at its edge. Yuxuan Guo, Sheng Yang, and Xue-Jia Yu widen that link for key fermion systems at a phase change point. At that point, they prove an exact tie between the bulk entanglement spectrum and the edge energy spectrum. The count of edge modes can be read from the bulk pattern alone.

The tie holds in any number of dimensions for free fermions with on-site symmetries. Lattice tests in the computer back the proof. Phase change points sit between phases, where hidden order is hardest to spot. A clear mark of that order fills a real gap. The bulk pattern is also easier to compute than edge states, so the link helps in practice.
arxiv-2509-20354:
EmbeddingGemma, a compact model that turns text into numerical vectors, is introduced in a 2025 arXiv report led by Henrique Schechter Vera and Sahil Dua with a large Google team. Embeddings power search, ranking, and retrieval inside many products. A small open model that rivals big ones would suit phones and other on-device uses. Their model has three hundred million parameters.

The training recipe borrows knowledge from larger models in two ways: a warm start from an encoder-decoder setup and a geometric distillation step. A spread-out regularizer keeps the vectors expressive and robust. Checkpoints from varied data mixtures were merged for generality. On the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark, the model beat earlier leaders, open and proprietary, with under five hundred million parameters. It matched models twice its size and held up under quantization and truncation.
arxiv-2509-20554:
Samuel Blitz closes a gap in conformal geometry in a 2025 arXiv paper. The field studies shapes up to smooth stretching. For a surface set inside a larger space, a small set of basic forms builds all low-order conformal invariants. The low orders were known. What stayed open was whether forms of higher order could exist in the last few cases.

Blitz proves they cannot when the surface inside has even dimension. With that bar in place, the full list of conformal fundamental forms is now complete. Such a bar has real worth: it ends a search, since no one need hunt for forms that provably are not there. The proof is short and dense, meant for experts in the field. Its upshot is a cleaner base for the study of conformal invariants.
arxiv-2509-20654:
The solar wind near the Sun is heated by turbulence, but the exact heating process is not settled. Trevor Bowen and nine co-authors examine that question in a 2025 paper using Parker Solar Probe observations. They focus on the sub-Alfvenic wind, the region still connected to the solar corona.

The team tests whether waves traveling along the magnetic field can explain the observed ion heating. They find that this resonant heating falls short. Random, uneven heating fits the data better, they report. The strongest heating comes from rare, large events, so the patchy nature of the turbulence must be counted. The results link probe data closely to coronal heating physics.
arxiv-2509-20854:
Shrinking a neural network to run on small hardware usually costs accuracy, especially at very low precision. Abdur Rehman and five co-authors propose a fix in a 2025 paper on quantized model distillation. Their method is called Game of Regularizer, or GoR.

Training a small quantized model with a teacher's help mixes two losses: the task loss and the distillation loss. Their different gradient sizes often fight each other. GoR learns just two extra parameters that adjust the balance between the losses as training proceeds. The authors test the approach on image classification and object detection. They report better convergence and stronger small models, a result they frame as punching above the model's precision weight class.
arxiv-2509-21154:
Rewarding only a model's final answer seems coarse, yet a popular training method secretly rewards the steps too. Michael Sullivan and Alexander Koller prove that claim about GRPO in a 2025 paper accepted for ICML 2026. GRPO, group relative policy optimization, normally trains with an outcome reward model.

The authors prove that GRPO with an outcome reward equals a process-reward-aware method with a specific Monte-Carlo process reward, given mild assumptions. That lens exposes a flaw: the objective interacts badly with uneven process steps and rewards, at times hurting exploration and at times exploitation. They propose a simple change to the method to ease the flaw. The paper reframes how builders should think about credit assignment when training reasoning models.
arxiv-2509-21254:
Training a neural network under fairness or safety constraints that involve chance needs dedicated software. Its authors are Andrii Kliachkin and 3 co-authors. Some tasks need fairness or safety limits while a network learns. Those limits may be stochastic, meaning they involve chance. Many toolkits exist, but none is a standard yet. The paper presents a new Python package for this task.

The package is called humancompatible.train and is built on PyTorch. It is made to be easy to extend. The authors implement several algorithms for stochastically constrained problems that had no prior implementation. They compare two of its algorithms on a fairness constrained deep learning task. The package is shared in a public code repository.
arxiv-2509-21554:
Speaker diarization labels who spoke when, and accents plus domain can hurt its accuracy. Chibuzor Okocha and 2 co-authors study diarization on African accented English in a 2025 paper. General and clinical dialogues are compared under a strict error protocol that scores overlap. Multiple production and open systems were evaluated. A consistent penalty appears for clinical speech.

Error analysis ties much of the penalty to false alarms and missed detections. Short turns and frequent overlap in clinical talk explain that pattern. Fine tuning a segmentation module on accent matched data reduced error but did not close the gap. The authors contribute a controlled cross domain benchmark and an error decomposition approach. Overlap aware segmentation is a practical next step.
arxiv-2509-21754:
Xiaotong Li, Karel Adámek, and Wesley Armour write about a rare kind of star in this 2025 astronomy paper, published in Astronomy and Computing. Ultra-long-period pulsars flash on very slow cycles, and only a few have ever been found. Most search tools miss them entirely. Photo-based searches can find them but raise many false alarms.

The authors built FITrig, a fast search method that runs on graphics cards. It works two ways: one branch reads images, and the other mixes images with frequency data. In tests it ran several times faster than a leading rival tool on huge images. It also cut false alarms sharply and could spot pulsars far fainter than the steady sources around them, in both real and simulated telescope data.
arxiv-2509-21854:
Models that answer questions about images can go wrong at the very first step: seeing. Songjun Tu and eight co-authors tackle that failure in this 2025 paper. When a multimodal model misreads a picture, the error flows through every later step of its reasoning. Standard fine-tuning improves reasoning but does little about the faulty seeing underneath.

Their method, called CapPO, trains the model under a caption-based rule. Answers given from the raw image must agree with answers given from a written caption of the same image. That rule anchors reasoning to faithful visual content. A second part scales the training signal, rewarding runs that stay consistent and damping runs built on false clues. Across ten benchmarks on math and general reasoning, CapPO gained clear accuracy over its base model, and error checks showed far fewer mistakes that start with misperception.
arxiv-2509-22254:
Elena Pulvirenti, Frank Redig, and Hidde van Wiechen study a model of self-propelled particles that run and tumble, like bacteria. The particles move on two copies of a discrete ring, called layers, and switch between them. The switching rate depends on the whole population through a mean-field interaction. Their 2025 paper asks two questions: what does the population look like at large scale, and how likely are rare departures from that picture?

The first answer is the hydrodynamic limit: as the system grows, the particle density follows a deterministic equation. The second is a large deviation theory, which prices the probability of unlikely density paths. The authors' main tool is a weakly perturbed version of the system. Its hydrodynamic equations turn out to describe exactly the trajectories that realize the large deviations.
arxiv-2509-22354:
Christoph Unger and Hendrik Buschmeier explore whether relevance theory, a major account of how listeners infer unspoken meaning, can be rebuilt in probabilistic terms. When speakers imply more than they say, listeners recover the implicature by judging what is relevant. Cognitive science has lately taken a probabilistic turn, and a Bayesian framework called Rational Speech Act theory already models simpler cases, from reference games upward. Their 2025 paper asks how far that Bayesian machinery extends toward relevance-theoretic pragmatics.

The test phenomenon is conversational implicature itself, the classic case of implicit meaning. The authors examine how a Bayesian model would have to be shaped to capture relevance-guided inference, given that relevance theory explains comprehension through a balance of cognitive effects and processing effort. The paper is exploratory: it maps the fit and the friction between the two frameworks rather than reporting experiments.
arxiv-2509-22454:
Daniil Shlenskii and Alexander Korotin speed up a class of image generators built on electrostatics. These models, called PFGM++, match diffusion models at one limit and beat them at finite extra dimension. Like diffusion models, they need slow equation solving to make each sample. The pair recast the speed-up task as an inverse problem.

Their method trains a fast generator whose induced electric field matches the teacher model's field. They derive a workable training objective for that match. At the diffusion limit, the method closely recovers a known distillation approach. In tests, the distilled generators matched or beat teacher quality in a few steps. One-step training also converged faster at finite dimension.
arxiv-2509-22554:
Alexey Lichkunov, Konstantin Stankevich, and Alexander Studenikin study how a flickering axion-like field scrambles neutrinos. Neutrinos shift flavor as they travel, and a noisy background field can blur that pattern. That blurring is called decoherence. Axion-like particles are a proposed kind of light particle that could form such a field. The team set up an equation for the neutrino state in Redfield form.

From that equation they worked out the part that drives the blurring. They then gauged how fast the field flickers and how strongly it couples to neutrinos. Those gauges rest on bounds for decoherence drawn from reactor neutrino tests. The work ties a dark matter candidate to a neutrino effect that can be measured.
arxiv-2509-22754:
Merve Atasever and 7 co-authors compare self-driving planners from rival leaderboards on one common track. The field judges planners on separate platforms, each with its own data and scenarios, which blocks fair comparison. The team drew representative methods from the CARLA, nuPlan, and Waymo ecosystems. Eight planners were then run under the CARLA Leaderboard rules as the shared standard.

The planners span learning-based and rule-based designs, from InterFuser to a diffusion planner. The study maps each method's strengths and weaknesses under identical conditions. From that map, the authors draw out prevailing trends and common challenges. They close with directions they see for advancing motion planning research.
arxiv-2509-22954:
Luís M A Bettencourt and 3 co-authors measure how much income detail a city's map holds at each scale. Cities mix broad patterns with strong local quirks, so studies often pick one scale and miss the rest. The team use statistical learning tools to score spatial information scale by scale. They apply the method to income data from over nine hundred US metro areas.

Rich and poor households turned out more spatially sorted than middle-income ones. Each neighborhood also showed its own level of income specificity and inequality. Averages alone hide those contrasts. The authors argue for methods that zoom both in and out. Such tools could serve other complex systems beyond cities.
arxiv-2509-23054:
Masked image modeling trains vision models by hiding patches, but random hiding wastes effort on background. Ruilang Wang and 5 co-authors guide the masking with text prompts instead. Vision-language models locate the regions a prompt names. Their framework, Mask What Matters, then masks key regions more and background less. That yields better semantic alignment during self-supervised training.

Tests spanned brain MRI, chest CT, and lung X-ray data. The method beat prior masked modeling tools on classification accuracy. Detection scores for boxes and masks also rose. It did so with far lower mask rates than usual. The team argue text control makes self-supervision more goal-aware.
arxiv-2509-23254:
Predicting where antibodies grip antigens from sequence alone would speed vaccine and therapy design. Zhang-Yu You and 4 co-authors built ABConformer for that task. The model rests on a Conformer backbone that reads local and global sequence traits. A physics-inspired sliding attention replaces plain cross-attention. It recovers residue-level contacts with no 3D structure input.

Given both sequences, the model predicts paratopes and epitopes. Given the antigen alone, it predicts pan-epitopes. On a recent SARS-CoV-2 data set, scores set a new best. Ablation tests credit sliding attention for much of the precision gain. Code will be released open source on acceptance.
arxiv-2509-23354:
Around twenty neutrons, some nuclei flip their shell order in the island of inversion. Subhrajit Sahoo and Praveen C Srivastava compute that region from first principles. Chiral two- and three-nucleon forces supply the input interactions. An ab initio valence space method handles the many-body problem. The focus is odd-mass neon and magnesium isotopes.

Single-particle levels evolve into the island through particle-hole jumps across the shell gap. Computed states and magnetic moments match experimental data well. Rotational bands in two magnesium isotopes emerge from normal and intruder configurations. Weak, moderate, and strongly prolate shapes appear at low energy. The work maps exotic nuclear shapes from fundamental forces.
arxiv-2509-24154: Elham Matinpour asks what low Morse index forces on minimal surfaces that carry Y-singularities, points where three sheets meet. Her focus is the class with index one, the lowest nontrivial case. She proves a rigidity result that gives partial uniqueness for that class. Within complete, two-sided minimal surfaces in three-space that carry Y-singularities and have Morse index one, the Y-catenoid stands out as the key example.
arxiv-2509-24254:
What a firm says on earnings day can move its stock as much as the numbers do. Yuntao Wu and 4 co-authors test how the text of earnings press releases predicts announcement-day returns. They used well over a hundred thousand releases across nearly two decades, comparing word-count methods with BERT-based embeddings.

Soft information in the text proved as informative as the earnings surprise itself, and a finance-tuned BERT scored best. Combining models added strength and clarity. Prices already reflected release content at the market open, so a leak would hand traders an edge. Topic analysis also exposed a self-serving slant in how managers narrate results.
arxiv-2509-24454:
Haipeng Lu and Mei Yu study positive solutions of problems driven by the fractional Laplacian, an operator that couples distant points. They cover both steady and time-evolving cases. With a mountain pass argument, they prove bounded, classical positive solutions exist where the growth term stays tame.

A moving planes method then shows those solutions are symmetric or monotone in the first variable. Where growth runs too strong, or the exponent turns negative, no such solutions exist at all. The pair also analyze how solutions behave far away, filling out their profiles. The methods extend to wider nonlocal equations with more general operators.
arxiv-2510-00354:
Shicheng Liu and Qilong Zhai wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on checking the accuracy of a numerical method after the fact. Their target is a fourth-order singularly perturbed problem, a class where tiny parameters create sharp layers. The weak Galerkin method solves such problems on a mesh, but users need to know where the mesh fails. A posteriori error estimators answer that need from the computed solution itself.

The authors first lay out the method's discrete spaces and numerical scheme. They then build a residual-type estimator that any user can compute directly. Proofs establish the estimator is reliable, never missing real error by much, and efficient, never inventing phantom error. Numerical experiments in the paper confirm the theory on test problems. Such estimators let software refine meshes automatically where the solution is roughest. That adaptivity is vital for singularly perturbed problems with thin internal layers.
arxiv-2510-00454:
Wang Zhang and five colleagues published this 2025 paper on cleaning noisy images without any clean examples to learn from. Self-supervised methods train on pairs of noisy images, mapping one noisy version to another. The authors first measure a spectral bias in that setup with a new similarity metric. Two flaws follow: fine high-frequency detail gets lost, and the network absorbs high-frequency noise while fitting detail.

Their network, SCNet, attacks both flaws in the frequency domain. A selection strategy picks which frequency bands to train on, speeding convergence. A Lipschitz-based constraint limits how eagerly kernels chase high-frequency noise. A final module separates detail from noise and rebuilds detail from a low-rank representation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world noise confirmed the design's effectiveness. The authors offer the frequency-domain view as a fresh perspective for the denoising field.
arxiv-2510-00554:
Andrew Gan and Zahra Ghodsi published this 2025 security paper on proving that machine learning artifacts are authentic. Models and datasets now flow from strangers' repositories straight into production systems. A poisoned file can slip in because nothing checks its provenance. Cryptography could sign everything, but giant artifacts make naive verification painfully slow. Their system, Sentry, moves the checking onto the graphics processor itself.

Signatures tie each artifact to its developer's identity at creation time. Verification happens on the fly as data streams into GPU memory, even bypassing the CPU entirely. The team accelerated Merkle trees and lattice hashing with memory tricks tuned for graphics hardware. Benchmarks showed speedups of about two hundred seventy fold for model checks. Dataset authentication ran about one hundred eighty times faster than the CPU baseline. The authors call Sentry the first practical route to authenticated machine learning supply chains.
arxiv-2510-00754:
Kikuchi develops a unified theory of treatment effect boundaries in this 2025 arXiv paper on econometrics. Policy effects often fade with distance from a treated place and with time since treatment began. Spatial studies and timing studies usually treat those two decays apart. Kikuchi models both with one reaction-diffusion process, so a single pair of parameters governs reach and persistence.

The framework yields a testable ratio linking the spatial boundary to the temporal one. Simulations show boundary estimates with errors under ten percent in realistic settings. Applied to United States wildfire damage data, the estimated boundary of about 198 kilometres and 2.7 years matched the theory's prediction closely. A European broadband case instead exposed a limit, since network effects there grow rather than decay.
arxiv-2510-01054:
Mourrat surveys the state of spin glass theory and its famous Parisi formula in this 2025 arXiv review. Spin glasses model many simple units interacting through random, conflicting couplings, and the Parisi formula predicts their free energy as the system grows large. That formula is proved for a broad classical family, yet many natural models still sit beyond its reach. Worse, naive generalizations of the formula give predictions that are demonstrably false for those models.

Mourrat explains the failure through a guiding example, a bipartite spin glass with two types of spins. He then presents a different viewpoint in which the limiting free energy should solve a Hamilton-Jacobi equation. A precise conjecture captures that idea, and several partial results support it. The review closes by linking that equation to an alternative, un-inverted form of the Parisi variational formula.
arxiv-2510-01454:
Naharas and co-authors at UCLA choose which training examples a vision-language model actually needs by watching how images and text align during a trial run. Redundancy bloats instruction datasets, yet earlier selection methods could not beat random sampling at any size. A theorem anchors their approach: similar cross-modal attention implies similar learning gradients.

A small proxy model fine-tunes first, and each example's attention trajectory gets recorded. Clustering those trajectories and sampling evenly across clusters strips the duplicates. Half of one major dataset and most of another proved disposable without performance loss. Stable trajectories mark the examples worth keeping from each cluster. Vision-language instruction tuning is the specific workload being slimmed. Random selection is the embarrassing baseline finally beaten. Gradients, not surface similarity, define redundancy in the proof. Less data also means cheaper fine-tuning runs downstream every time.
arxiv-2510-01554:
Herderschee and Wall limit how far a scalar field can wander along the path of a light ray. Such fields fill theories of gravity, and their drifts can bend light or shift black hole horizons. Anthropic arguments about other universes often invoke enormous drifts to reach friendlier vacua.

Starting from a classic focusing equation, the authors derive a clean quantitative bound on the drift. The bound needs only that other fields obey a standard energy condition. Some exotic spacetimes with naked singularities hit the bound exactly. In cosmology, total drift grows at most in step with expansion, whatever the inflation model. A proposed quantum version swaps the energy condition for a stronger focusing rule. Light paths are the natural rulers here, since gravity bends them measurably. Model-independent limits are rare and valuable in early-universe debates. The result disciplines speculation with geometry.
arxiv-2510-01954:
Su and thirteen co-authors let multimodal language models emit visual answers directly in this 2025 paper. Today's multimodal models often describe locations as text coordinates, an indirect route that caps accuracy. Dense tasks like segmentation are nearly impossible through that bottleneck. Their paradigm, Patch-as-Decodable Token, treats image patches as tokens the model can output.

Visual reference tokens come from patch embeddings of the query image and interleave with the model's text output. A lightweight decoder converts those outputs into detection boxes, segmentation masks, and grounding predictions. Each token is processed independently at every pass, and the embedding table grows dynamically. That design sharpens localization and separates look-alike objects. Training randomly samples reference tokens under a robust per-token loss. Across four visual tasks, the system reached state-of-the-art results, even against much larger multimodal models. The code is publicly available for follow-up work.
arxiv-2510-02054:
Cook, Holwerda, and Robertson argue for a richer ultraviolet filter set on a future space observatory in this 2025 proceedings paper. The Habitable Worlds Observatory is still early enough in design to accept instrument suggestions. Ultraviolet imaging remains sparse across the sky, even in heavily studied deep fields. The authors test how filter choices affect galaxy measurements made from spectral energy distributions.

They compare the broad near- and far-ultraviolet filters of the retired GALEX mission against three narrower Swift UVOT filters. GALEX-style bands produced larger errors in the ultraviolet slope of galaxy spectra. They also constrained a galaxy's star formation age only weakly. The narrower filters could trace the important dust attenuation bump near a key wavelength, which the broad bands largely missed. The authors recommend at least one far-ultraviolet filter plus three medium near-ultraviolet bands. That mix pairs GALEX's reach with UVOT's finer sampling.
arxiv-2510-02154:
Giuloni, Di Giuseppe, and Di Paola simulate Italy's wheat system to test sustainability policies in this 2025 paper. Farm policy lands on wildly different farms, varying in size, land, climate, and irrigation. A single representative farm cannot capture that spread. Their agent-based model starts from a real survey of Italian farms and scales up to national size.

Two further components widen the lens beyond the farm gate. A global model of international wheat markets feeds world prices into local decisions. An environmental tool scores the impacts of the production those decisions produce. Local output then pushes back on prices, closing the feedback loop. Policymakers can run candidate policies through the whole system before enacting them. The framework shows where a rule helps one farm type while hurting another. Sustainability evaluation becomes a simulation exercise instead of a guess.
arxiv-2510-02354:
Saha and co-authors show that brain meaning signals ignore the surface form of sentences. Their 2025 neuroscience paper models the human language cortex. The team asked how abstract meaning codes in that region are. They predicted brain responses using model embeddings. Some embeddings came from images generated for each sentence. Others came from paraphrases of the same sentence. Averaging several image embeddings predicted brain activity well. The scores sometimes rivaled large language model predictions. Averaging paraphrase embeddings also beat any single wording.
