Enriched paraphrases did better still. Adding implied details, like syrup on a pancake, raised accuracy further. Those enriched versions even beat the original sentences. The cortex never saw the images during the experiment. Meaning there seems stored in a form beyond words or pictures. Averaging strips away surface noise and keeps shared sense. Brain language research gains a strong clue.
arxiv-2510-02654:
Yu, Liu, and Cui teach image generators to sample smarter noise during reinforcement learning. Their 2025 machine learning paper presents a method called Smart-GRPO. Flow-matching models now produce high quality text to image results. Their deterministic nature fights reinforcement learning, though. Random noise injections add the needed randomness crudely. Such perturbations waste updates and destabilize training. Smart-GRPO searches over the noise itself, iteratively. Candidate perturbations get decoded into images. A reward function scores those images. The noise distribution then shifts toward higher reward regions.

Experiments beat baseline methods on reward and visual quality. Fewer updates went to hopeless directions. Training grew steadier and converged better. Noise stops being a nuisance and becomes a control knob. Aligning generators with human taste needs that control. The approach ports across flow-matching frameworks. Future reward design can build on the same loop.
arxiv-2510-02754:
Jiang and co-authors measure how rough a special family of curves can be. The curves come from recurrent fractal interpolation. Such a curve is built by repeating scaled copies of itself. It passes through given data points, yet it stays jagged at every scale. The authors study the box dimension of the curve's graph. Box dimension is a number that gauges roughness. A smooth line scores one, and a plane-filling curve scores two.

Their method tracks matrices built from the curve's vertical scaling rules. They prove that the key values of these matrices behave in a steady, one-way fashion. The matrix values then give upper and lower bounds on the dimension. In some cases the bounds meet, which yields an exact formula. One worked example lands near one and a half. The tools extend to broad classes of fractal curves.
arxiv-2510-02854:
Ye and co-authors present a framework that lets classical programmers write quantum software. A developer must encode the problem, build circuits, pick hardware, and read raw output. The framework is named C2Q. It hides that stack behind three modules. An encoder sorts the problem and builds a quantum-ready form. A deployment module then picks hardware by fidelity, speed, and cost.

A decoder turns the quantum output back into a plain answer. Tests ran across simulators and real noisy quantum devices. The encoder finished most tasks it was given. The hardware picker chose well for jobs up to fifty-six qubits. The full pipeline handled hundreds of Python snippets and JSON inputs. Success rates were high on both input types. On real hardware, the framework cut coding effort by a large factor. Manual work with low-level kits took far longer.
arxiv-2510-02954:
Skullerud and the FASTSUM team refine computer studies of hot nuclear matter. Lattice QCD simulates quarks and gluons on a grid. Anisotropic lattices make the time steps much finer than the space steps. The team presents first results from a new grid set. Its time spacing is half that of their earlier sets. The anisotropy factor reaches seven, a record for the group.

Early results cover three fronts at once. One is the chiral transition of the plasma. Another is a merging of vector and axial-vector channels. That merging signals restored symmetry at high heat. The third is heavy quarkonium, bound states with bottom quarks. Comparisons with coarser grids show steady progress. One will use fully realistic light quark masses. The work tightens control over grid effects in plasma studies. Transport traits of the quark-gluon plasma are the long-term prize.
arxiv-2510-03054:
Zawadzka and co-authors build a light-emitting diode from stacked atomic sheets. The stack uses a magnetic semiconductor as both electrodes. A boron nitride layer serves as the tunnel barrier. A single layer of tungsten diselenide glows in the middle. Earlier designs tuned brightness by shaping the barrier. This team tunes it through the electrodes instead. Their density of states shifts in and out of alignment.

Brightness did not grow smoothly with voltage. It rose and fell as the bias climbed. The tunneling current, by contrast, grew in a steady way. Resonant alignment opened bright paths at some voltages. Misalignment shunted energy into dark paths at others. The glow pattern mirrored the computed electrode density of states. That match shows emission can probe an electrode's inner structure. The device worked at room temperature throughout. Electrically modulated light from such stacks suits compact photonics.
arxiv-2510-03254:
Benfield and co-authors harden text classifiers against attackers who may only bend their data so far. Adversarial training imagines an enemy rewriting inputs to slip past detection. Pessimistic bilevel models train the defender against that worst case. Unrestricted enemies, though, can warp text into nonsense. Defending against impossible attacks then weakens real-world performance. Their model constrains how far the adversary may move. Cosine similarity measures change without demanding convexity of the problem.

The learner builds a detector at the upper level. The adversary edits data at the lower level to evade it. Movement limits keep the edited data true to its message. Earlier regularized versions could only penalize plain Euclidean distance. The new formulation drops that restriction entirely. Experiments on text-based scenarios compared both approaches head to head. The constrained model won on average across the trials.
arxiv-2510-03454:
Yan, writing for the STAR Collaboration, presents a 2025 arXiv report on particle flow patterns in small nuclear collisions. Smashing deuterons into gold and oxygen into oxygen at energy creates droplets whose behavior puzzles physicists. The question is whether such systems form quark gluon plasma, a fluid that flows as one. STAR measured sideways flow patterns, called elliptic and triangular flow, in both systems at the RHIC collider. The two systems start with very different shapes yet yield similar particle counts.

Measured flow strengths scaled cleanly with the starting shapes of each collision. That match supports a fluid response like the one expected from plasma droplets. The pattern also helps pin down how much tiny lumps inside nucleons shape the start. Detector coverage let the team check flow along the beam line, where fake signals proved large and needed removal. Small systems thus look more fluid like than many expected.
arxiv-2510-03654:
Macsai and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper converting a mass spectrometer at the University of Manitoba into a steerable low energy proton source for testing particle detectors. Silicon detectors for neutron and neutrino experiments need calibration with protons of energy and position. The Manitoba II machine makes protons in a Penning ion source, selects them by energy and momentum, and steers the beam across a detector's face. Its job was characterizing the Nab experiment's silicon detector.

The source isolates thirty kiloelectronvolt protons with an energy resolution of three hundred electronvolts. Most beam spots measured about one square millimeter, small enough to study pixels without charge leaking into neighbors. A scan across one Nab pixel pinned the spot diameter near three square millimeters. The team ran at ten protons per second to keep noise down during detector tests. The spectrometer now serves as a calibration station for low energy physics detectors.
arxiv-2510-03954:
Bary and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on getting reliable medical labels without wasting expert time. Screening programs ask several doctors to judge each case, because single opinions vary. Asking everyone about everything is costly, and experts are scarce. The authors build a system that asks extra experts only when a case looks hard.

Their algorithm labels cases as they arrive, with no prior knowledge of the experts' skill and no pre-labeled training data. It keeps gathering opinions on a case until its confidence passes a set threshold. Easy cases finish after few opinions, while hard ones draw more reviewers. On three multi-annotator medical datasets, the approach cut expert queries by up to half. Accuracy stayed comparable to a baseline that queried evenly. The design fits real screening pipelines, where cases stream in continuously. Smarter allocation could lower costs while keeping diagnostic labels trustworthy.
arxiv-2510-04254:
Strong presents this 2025 arXiv paper constructing a strict version of higher categories through enrichment. An (infinity,1)-category can be modeled as a category enriched in infinity-groupoids, where composition holds only up to coherent higher equivalence. Strictification asks how much of that coherence can be replaced by exact algebraic structure without losing essential information. Strong first strictifies each hom space from an infinity-groupoid to an omega-groupoid under the Gray tensor product.

A second, global step replaces the Gray product by the Cartesian product. Strong conjectures that this strictification functor is conservative, meaning it reflects equivalences rather than collapsing distinct structures. The conjecture is proved for two dual special classes: 2-truncated and 2-connected source categories. The paper also builds an incoherent walking equivalence that simplifies the path-lifting condition for fibrations, reducing the check to cells of dimension at most three.
arxiv-2510-04354:
Badithela and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on evaluating robot policies with statistical confidence while minimizing expensive hardware trials. Modern manipulation policies generalize broadly, but labs typically test them in a handful of real runs with no statistical assurance. Simulation is cheap and plentiful, yet biased by the reality gap. Their framework, SureSim, formalizes the combination as prediction-powered inference.

A small set of paired evaluations, the same conditions run in simulation and on hardware, measures the simulator's bias. Non-asymptotic mean estimation then yields honest confidence intervals for real-world performance. Tests covered a diffusion policy and a multitask fine-tuned pi-zero model across varied objects and initial conditions. SureSim saved roughly a fifth to a quarter of the hardware evaluation effort for equally tight performance bounds. Rigorous evaluation protocols like this become essential as robot foundation models claim broad generalization.
arxiv-2510-04454:
Xiangchi Yuan and six coauthors at Georgia Tech wrote this 2025 paper on training language models to reason. Two training styles dominate: supervised fine tuning on worked examples, and reinforcement learning from the model own attempts. Each style alone has limits, and mixing them often makes the model forget skills from the first round. The team built a plug in framework that blends the two styles as training runs.

The framework picks hard examples and feeds them to supervised training during the reinforcement phase. To fight forgetting, it computes loss only on high uncertainty tokens. It also freezes the weights that matter most for the reinforcement skills. The mix works with many choices of base algorithms, since it sits on top of them. The results set new best scores on reasoning tests. They used only a small slice of the data that earlier top methods needed.
arxiv-2510-04754:
Fuyuki Kitagawa, Ryo Nishimaki, and Nikhil Pappu wrote this 2025 paper on leasing secret keys that borrowers cannot keep. Secure key leasing uses quantum states to lend a key for a task. The borrower returns a deletion certificate proving the key is gone. After that, they should be unable to run the function at all. Use leases many keys, so security must survive collusion among borrowers. That goal was poorly understood, above all beyond decryption.

The authors open new construction routes. They define a multilevel form of traitor tracing, a tool for fingering leaked keys. A compiler then turns tracing for any task into collusion resistant leasing for that task. From it they build a bounded collusion resistant leasing scheme for pseudorandom functions. The security rests on the LWE hardness assumption. Two more compilers upgrade signature leasing and add resilience against verification queries. The results widen leasing toward quantum cryptography.
arxiv-2510-04854:
Cheyu Lin, John Martins, and Katherine Flanigan wrote this 2025 paper on reading social interaction from body movement alone. Smart spaces could respond to how people interact, not where they stand. That vision needs machines that recognize gestures, greetings, and emotional displays between people. Cameras see all of it, but recording faces in spaces raises privacy alarms. Depth sensors offer a way out, since they capture skeletons rather than faces.

The study compares five skeleton based recognition algorithms on a data set. The set holds twelve kinds of interaction. They range from emblem gestures with set meanings to affect displays that show feeling. Recognizing the pair as a unit, rather than solo actors, is the challenge. The results gauge how far depth based methods have come on social signals. Such sensing could let buildings foster encounters instead of moving crowds. Infrastructure that understands interaction can be designed for community, not throughput.
arxiv-2510-05054:
Peter Van Katwyk and Karianne J. Bergen work on making AI predictions honest about doubt in this 2025 arXiv paper. A model can be unsure for two different reasons. The data itself may be noisy, or the model may simply lack knowledge. Keeping those two apart matters in medicine, driving, and science.

Their system, HybridFlow, estimates both kinds of uncertainty inside one model. A normalizing flow handles noise in the data. A flexible probabilistic predictor handles the model's own knowledge gaps. The design plugs into existing architectures without hurting accuracy. Across depth estimation, standard regression benchmarks, and an ice-sheet emulator, its uncertainty scores were better calibrated than rivals. The scores also tracked the model's actual errors more closely.
arxiv-2510-05154:
Shenzhe Zhu and four co-authors test whether AI summaries fairly represent public voices in this 2025 arXiv paper. Large deliberations produce thousands of free-form opinions for policymakers. Language models can summarize them, but may quietly underrepresent minority views. Judging summary quality usually relies on other language models, which agree poorly with humans.

The team built DeliberationBank, holding 3,000 participant opinions across ten questions. Human annotators added 4,500 ratings on representativeness, informativeness, neutrality, and policy approval. From those ratings they trained DeliberationJudge, an evaluator that aligns with humans better than general-purpose judges. Benchmarking 18 summarizer models then exposed a consistent flaw. Every system tended to underrepresent minority viewpoints in its summaries.
arxiv-2510-05254:
Filipp Sporykhin and Holger Homann benchmark a high-order fluid solver on modern supercomputers in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their code uses a nodal discontinuous Galerkin scheme in space. Runge-Kutta methods advance it in time. One source runs on many-core CPUs and on Nvidia and AMD graphics processors through Kokkos and MPI.

Counterintuitively, higher order meant faster simulations in their tests. Eighth-order runs reached a target accuracy with much less computing time than third-order ones. Scaling stayed strong up to 64 AMD graphics cards and hundreds of CPU cores. Graphics processors won big only for large grids, beyond about ten million degrees of freedom. Small grids ran faster and greener on CPUs. Newer GPUs also needed larger grids to pay off, a rebound effect for energy use.
arxiv-2510-05354:
Sagnik Saha and Hector O. Silva test a shortcut for computing black hole ringdown tones in this 2025 arXiv paper. A disturbed Kerr-Newman black hole rings at quasinormal mode frequencies set by its spin and charge. Gravity and electromagnetism perturb together, making exact calculations heavy. The Dudley-Finley approximation freezes one field to decouple the pair.

The authors compared the approximation against full coupled calculations across the spin-charge space. For the main modes, real frequency parts agreed typically within 10 percent. Imaginary parts, which set damping, agreed within about 1 percent. Near the extremal limit they mapped where long-lived zero-damped modes appear alone or beside damped ones. Analytic formulas give the boundaries between those regions, guiding future ringdown studies.
arxiv-2510-05454:
Kwon and Sun study a common trap in measuring whether a policy or treatment works. Many studies assume the effect is the same for everyone in the sample. When effects differ across people, that shortcut can miss the true average effect. Adding flexible terms can fix the bias, but the estimates often turn noisy and unstable.

The authors propose regulaTE, an estimator that shrinks the flexible terms toward the simple model. The shrinkage is tuned to balance worst-case bias against noise under a bound on effect spread. They also build confidence ranges that stay valid when treated and control groups barely overlap. Tests cover settings where treatment is as good as random and cases with staggered start dates. An R software package from the team puts the estimator into practice. The method gives applied researchers a practical way to report honest uncertainty.
arxiv-2510-05654:
James and colleagues measure how wide fast radio bursts really are. A burst's observed width mixes its intrinsic duration with scattering from turbulent plasma. That mix biases population studies and host galaxy work. Their 2025 paper de-biases both distributions using bursts with known redshifts.

The sample holds twenty-nine bursts from the CRAFT survey on ASKAP. The authors model completeness before fitting the underlying distributions. Neither distribution shows a downturn across the probed range up to tens of milliseconds. Width rises like a Gaussian in log space before flattening out. Scattering looks log-uniform above a small threshold rather than lognormal. A lognormal shape is about a hundred times less likely for scattering. Searches should extend to higher time widths, the authors urge. Their updated model yields ten percent more bursts at redshift one in population simulations.
arxiv-2510-05754:
Chiozini and colleagues turn point-hunting in topology into a transfinite game. A Hider secretly picks a point in a T-zero space. A Seeker names open sets and learns whether the hidden point lies inside. Their 2025 paper measures how long the Seeker needs in the worst case.

Two ordinal invariants record the game lengths for points and for subsets. The authors prove sharp inequalities linking them to Scott's pseudoweight and to space size. They compute the numbers for Cantor cubes and double-arrow space powers. Sums and products make the two invariants behave strikingly differently. Stationary subsets of cardinals also get values in the paper. For metric spaces, the point number equals the logarithm of the space's size. The subset number, by contrast, can grow arbitrarily large there. Whether every countable ordinal occurs remains an open question. Whether these games are always determined is left open.
arxiv-2510-05954:
Barbieri and Démoulin model the solar corona as collisionless plasma heated only from below. The corona exceeds a million degrees above a far cooler chromosphere. Whether direct coronal heating is required remains the classic open question. Their 2025 kinetic model deposits all heating at the chromosphere-transition region interface.

Heating events are localized and intermittent across that interface. A coarse-graining procedure turns them into non-thermal boundary conditions. Analytic stationary solutions of the Vlasov equation follow from those conditions. Velocity filtration then creates suprathermal distributions and the temperature inversion. Realistic density and temperature profiles emerge with a transition region and hot corona. No energy is deposited inside the corona itself at any point. The result is independent of the heating increments' statistical distribution. Sparseness of the heating events is the essential ingredient. Intermittency alone, the authors conclude, explains the transition region's formation.
arxiv-2510-06054:
Zhao studies differential equations driven by randomness when the probability model itself is uncertain, in a 2025 mathematics paper. Such equations, called G-SDEs, sit inside G-expectation theory, a framework built for deep uncertainty. Classical proofs usually build a solution under one chosen probability measure at a time.

Zhao instead constructs the solution directly on the space of all possible paths. When an equation has exactly one strong solution under each candidate measure, those solutions agree wherever their path sets overlap. Zhao patches them into a single process that works under every measure at once. The patched process is the unique quasi-sure solution, and it can be measured consistently across all the candidate models. The picture treats each measure as a filter that selects plausible paths, which may guide robust methods in finance and control.
arxiv-2510-06354:
Shrestha and Srinivasan redefine language model bias as deviation from a desired distribution in a 2025 computational linguistics paper. Prior mitigation work aimed at demographic parity by default. Sometimes the goal is matching real-world distributions for factual grounding, so the target should depend on the application.

They fine-tune with a weighted adaptive loss aligning gender–profession outputs with the chosen target. The method preserves language modeling ability while steering outputs. Experiments use three profession sets from 2024 United States labor statistics: male-dominated, female-dominated, and balanced. Three masked language models showed bias under both targets. The adaptive method achieved near-complete mitigation under equality. Under real-world targets it cut bias by thirty to seventy-five percent. Autoregressive models showed no equality bias but clear real-world bias. Llama Instruct models cut that bias by fifty to sixty-two percent after fine-tuning.
arxiv-2510-06554:
Yue Hu, Zanxia Cao, and Yingchao Liu work on protein alignment, a basic task in bioinformatics. Their 2025 paper introduces a framework called UniOTalign. Alignment means lining up two protein sequences to find matching parts. Classic methods use dynamic programming, which follows one best path through the sequences. That path view struggles when similar parts appear in a shuffled order.

UniOTalign instead treats alignment as a global matching problem from optimal transport theory. It represents each protein as a spread of features taken from a pretrained protein language model. A special distance then finds matches that respect both feature similarity and internal shape. The method handles proteins with different lengths with ease. In experiments, it recovered known alignments and beat path-based methods on shuffled cases. Cases like domain shuffling and circular permutation are exactly where the transport view helps most.
arxiv-2510-07354:
Wichert presents a quantum memory scheme that stores many binary patterns in one small quantum state. The 2025 paper encodes a set of binary vectors into a superposition held by as many qubits as each vector has bits. A permutation technique arranges the storage more simply than the classic Ventura and Martinez method. An extra reduce step can shrink the state further through parallel operations. Retrieval is the harder half of the problem, the author stresses.

Standard Grover search fails here because the stored patterns are not uniformly weighted. Wichert's permutation trick repairs that mismatch. The modified search then finds a stored pattern in a number of steps set by the count of patterns, not by the size of the whole space. The rival trick needs steps set by the larger space size.
arxiv-2510-07454:
Tame-Narvaez, Ciprijanovic, Gardiner, and Cerati bring simulation-based inference to a chore every neutrino experiment faces: tuning its interaction simulator. Their 2025 paper is the first application of the technique to this problem. Neutrino interaction theory is incomplete, so collaborations nudge model parameters until simulations match data. Traditional tuning uses simple optimizers that will strain under future campaigns' complexity. Simulation-based inference instead trains a neural network to map data directly to plausible parameter values, complete with uncertainties. The team tested it on a previous tuning study from the MicroBooNE experiment.

Fed mock data built by the MicroBooNE procedure, the algorithm recovered the correct parameter values. The test used established simulation and comparison codes from the field. This proof of principle suggests next-generation experiments can tune richer models with honest error bars. Efficient tuning matters because every oscillation measurement inherits the interaction model's flaws.
arxiv-2510-07554:
Chizat, Marion, and Yesbay map the large-width behavior of dropout, the training trick that randomly switches off network units. Their 2025 paper studies two-layer networks trained by gradient descent at the mean-field initialization scale. Dropout's effect depends on a three-way race among dropout rate, learning rate, and width. The analysis resolves the asymptotics into five distinct nondegenerate phases. Practice has long assumed dropout acts like a penalty term discouraging large weights.

At realistic learning rates the penalty vanishes. Dropout instead becomes a random geometry technique: gradients are thinned at random after the passes that compute them. The limiting dynamics are mean-field jump processes, with each neuron updating on its own Poisson or Bernoulli clock.
arxiv-2510-07654:
Pan and four coauthors wrote this 2025 computer vision paper on video virtual try-on. The task replaces a person's clothing in a video with a target garment. The garment must move naturally with the body across every frame. Modern video generators built on diffusion transformers are powerful but costly to adapt. Earlier designs needed many extra trainable parts and heavy computation. The authors propose a lighter route that they call Once is Enough.

Their method edits the clothing only in the first frame, using an image try-on model. Pose and mask guidance then steer the video model to carry that look through later frames. This one-time injection avoids a separate garment branch in the network. Tests showed top-level quality with far fewer trainable parameters and lower computing cost. The approach could make realistic try-on video cheaper for online clothing retail.
arxiv-2510-07754:
Liao, Belo, Moon, Steimle, and Feit wrote this 2025 human-computer interaction paper on tuning interfaces with fewer user trials. Human-in-the-loop optimization refines a design by watching people use it. Each round of real users is slow and costly. Past speedups reused earlier user data, which is also scarce. The authors propose giving the optimizer a head start from simulated users instead of real ones.

Their framework, HOMI, first trains the optimizer on synthetic users generated from predictive models of behavior. A new Bayesian method, NAF+, learns its search strategy through reinforcement learning on that synthetic crowd. The trained optimizer then adapts quickly with real users. The team evaluates the approach on mid-air keyboard design, a virtual reality typing task. Their results argue that model-informed priors can cut the human cost of interface tuning. Designers could personalize layouts for varied users without huge studies.
arxiv-2510-08054:
Moon and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper presenting RetouchLLM, a photo retouching system that edits images by writing code instead of applying a trained black box. RetouchLLM needs no training data at all. A vision-language critic compares the input photo against a reference and names the differences. A code generator then writes executable operations to close those gaps.

The system refines the image step by step, much as a human retoucher would. A style-guided selection score keeps iterations converging. Experiments showed the approach generalizes across retouching styles and handles high-resolution images. Users can steer the process in natural language, making each adjustment interpretable. Because every edit is visible code, nothing is hidden. The authors plan broader operations and workflow studies. Such tools suit photographers who want automation without surrendering judgment.
arxiv-2510-08154:
Mančinska and Theil wrote this 2025 quantum information paper classifying every quantum channel that respects two natural symmetries. Many tasks feed a channel many copies of one state, so permuting the copies changes nothing. Rotating every copy by the same unitary rotates the output the same way. The authors classify all channels honoring both symmetries through their extremal points.

Each extremal channel factors into three steps. A unitary Schur sampling stage runs first, an irrep-level symmetric channel acts in the middle, and the adjoint sampling closes the sequence. The team turns this into a streaming implementation needing far less memory. Applied to state symmetrization, symmetric cloning, and purity amplification, the method gives polynomial-time algorithms with exponential memory savings. For symmetric cloning they present the first efficient algorithm with explicit memory and gate bounds. Symmetry, fully understood, converts directly into computational savings.
arxiv-2510-08554:
Kevin Rojas improves reinforcement learning for diffusion language models in a 2025 arXiv paper. These models write text in parallel, refining a full draft step by step, unlike word-by-word models. Fine-tuning them with rewards is hard because exact likelihoods cannot be computed. An earlier method guessed token likelihoods by unmasking one step, which proved badly biased.

Sequence-level likelihoods give a cleaner base, with a bound called the ELBO as a stand-in goal. Such methods stayed rare because scoring that bound is costly and noisy. Rojas splits the score's noise into its sources and swaps parts for fast, fixed integral estimates. The new method, Group Diffusion Policy Optimization, uses semi-fixed Monte Carlo schemes with provably lower noise. In tests, GDPO gained steadily over pretrained checkpoints. It also beat diffu-GRPO, a leading baseline for this task.
arxiv-2510-08654:
A. Pathania and co-authors hunt for hidden gamma-ray pulsars among unidentified Fermi telescope sources in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Fermi Large Area Telescope has surveyed the gamma-ray sky since 2008. Its latest catalog, 4FGL-DR4, lists seven thousand one hundred ninety-five sources from fourteen years of data. About a third have no known counterparts at other wavelengths, leaving their nature open.

The team classifies these unassociated sources with two supervised machine learning methods: Random Forest and Extreme Gradient Boosting. Features come from long-term Fermi observations recorded in the catalog itself. Their focus is picking out new gamma-ray pulsar candidates for follow-up study. They also explore how data balancing choices affect classification quality on this skewed source population. Correct classification guides population studies and pointed multi-wavelength observations of the most promising candidates.
arxiv-2510-08754:
David Nguyen, Zulfiqar Zaidi, Kevin Karol, Jessica Hodgins, and Zhaoming Xie teach a four-legged robot to play table tennis in a 2025 arXiv paper. Matching human speed, accuracy, and spin handling is a stern test for legged robots. Their system combines fast perception, path prediction, and agile whole-body control on a Spot quadruped. External cameras localize the ball at high speed during rallies.

Physical models with learned residuals infer ball spin and predict trajectories from the camera feed. A novel model predictive control formulation then plans full-body motions to intercept and return the ball. A continuous range of stroke strategies emerges automatically from different return objectives, rather than being hand-programmed. Real-world evaluation measured each component's accuracy separately. The robot aimed and returned balls with varying spin types, and rallied with human players in demonstrations.
arxiv-2510-08854:
Abhijeet and co-authors design spacecraft controllers that are both optimal and provably stable, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Mission planners want the cheapest flight path over an unlimited horizon, the long-run best plan, but spacecraft motion is nonlinear and hard to optimize directly. Pure optimization can also produce plans that drift unstable. The team splits the problem into two phases joined at a chosen target region around the goal.

In the first phase the craft flies its true nonlinear dynamics, steered by a finite-horizon plan whose final cost nudges it into the target region. Inside that region, gentler linearized dynamics take over under a regulator with an infinite horizon. The authors prove the combined scheme settles at the goal under stated assumptions, and that its extra cost vanishes as the region shrinks. Simulations covered pointing a spacecraft, docking with a target, and landing softly on a planet.
arxiv-2510-09254:
Urbaniak and co-authors teach a robot arm to dodge new obstacles after seeing just one demonstration, and an invented one at that, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Learning-based motion planners usually hunger for large datasets or costly human demonstrations. Their method starts from a single artificial demonstration encoded as a Dynamic Movement Primitive, a compact formula capturing a motion's shape. Reinforcement learning then reshapes that formula again and again, generating a diverse library of near-optimal, collision-free paths for many obstacle arrangements.

A small neural network learns the library's pattern: given obstacle dimensions and location from a point cloud, it outputs the primitive settings for a suitable path. In simulation and on a real robot, the system beat the standard RRT-Connect planner on computation time, execution time, and path length. It also produced distinct routes for different obstacle shapes and gripper sizes.
arxiv-2510-09354:
Yunxiang Zhang and seven co-authors ask whether long reasoning can be coaxed from a big model without any training, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Strong reasoning models write long chains of thought with backtracking and self-checking, but teaching that skill normally takes heavy extra training. The team instead works at decoding time, when the model picks each next word.

Their method, ThinkLogit, uses logit arithmetic, meaning it adds and subtracts the model's raw word scores, to borrow reasoning habits from a much smaller guide model. A variant also trains the small guide to fix the big model's errors. Across six benchmarks in maths, science, and coding, the guided model gained about twenty-two percent over its plain self, and the tuned variant gained about twenty-four percent. The trick even worked across model families, with almost no extra cost.
arxiv-2510-09654:
Zeshan Khan, the sole author, introduces TreeNet in a 2025 arXiv paper, a layered ensemble method for medical image analysis. Neural networks, decision trees, and ensemble methods each detect disease well when data is plentiful. Medical imaging, though, often has limited data and uncertain quality, the exact setting where those methods wobble.

TreeNet layers the three approaches, integrating features drawn from neural networks, from ensemble learning, and from tree-based models into one system. Its decisions stay interpretable, which matters in clinical work. Judged by accuracy, precision, and recall, and by training and evaluation time, the method reached an F1 score of zero point eight five with full training data. With half the training data it scored zero point seven seven, a drop of only zero point zero eight while halving training effort. The author presents TreeNet as suited to medical scenarios where data cannot be taken for granted.
arxiv-2510-09754:
I Flores, M Mezcua, and V Rodríguez Morales hunt hidden black holes in dwarf galaxies in a 2025 arXiv paper. Dwarf galaxies host low-mass black holes that illuminate how the giant black holes in big galaxies grew. Spotting them as active galactic nuclei is hard because they are faint and compact, so the team combines optical and radio views.

They start with four dwarf galaxies whose emission line patterns from the SDSS MaNGA survey hinted at active nuclei. New radio images from the Very Large Array let them compare each galaxy's radio output with what star formation alone would produce. One of the four shows radio emission consistent with an active nucleus, matching the optical diagnosis. Its jet power rivals that of massive radio galaxies, and it hosts an outflow able to escape its own gravity.
arxiv-2510-09854:
Shi and co-authors introduce NG-Router in this 2025 arXiv paper on nutrition question answering. Their system uses several cooperating AI agents, guided by a graph, to give personal dietary advice and help prevent diet-linked chronic disease. Single agents, the team argues, reason too weakly on domain detail for this task.

The authors name two limits they target. Multi-agent systems are hard to design well, and too much background context can swamp the final decision step. NG-Router routes each question through graph-supervised collaboration, so agents share structured knowledge instead of raw text. The design aims to keep the reasoning focused while still drawing on the nutrition knowledge the question needs.
arxiv-2510-09954:
Huang and Nicolas de Saxcé study rational points in flag varieties in this 2025 arXiv paper in number theory. A flag variety is a geometric space built from nested subspaces, and its rational points are those with rational coordinates. The question is how those points gather near a chosen real point.

The authors approximate a real point by rational points and rescale the picture around it. They show that, with the right rescaling, these approximations equidistribute, meaning they spread evenly rather than clumping, when the target point is chosen at random from a natural measure. The result gives a precise statistical law for how rational points fill in the space near a typical point.
arxiv-2510-10054:
Rosas proves a result about zeros of power series in this 2025 arXiv paper in complex analysis. The theorem links two series built from the same coefficients. If the weighted series with factorial factors is entire, meaning defined and smooth on the whole complex plane, and the coefficients do not terminate, then the plain series has infinitely many zeros.

Rosas then applies the result to give alternative proofs about the Le Roy functions, a family of special functions defined by such series. Fresh proofs of known facts often expose which hypotheses really matter. Here the factorial weighting turns out to control the zero pattern of the unweighted series, a link that was not obvious before.
arxiv-2510-10254:
Lai and co-authors test video models as zero-shot learners in medical imaging in this 2025 arXiv paper. Large generative models, scaled up with simple autoregressive training, have shown strong zero-shot generalization, working on new tasks without task-specific training. The authors ask whether that power crosses into medicine.

They apply autoregressive video modeling principles directly to medical imaging tasks, although the model was never trained on medical data. Success would mean foundation models can reason about scans they were never built for. Failure would mark a clear limit of transfer. Either way, the study probes how far the emerging zero-shot behavior of video models extends into a high-stakes domain.
arxiv-2510-10654:
Seyed Mohammad Hassan Erfani and five co-authors teach a climate model to fake its own atmospheric chemistry, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Full interactive chemistry in Earth system models is costly, because many gases and aerosols must be transported at every step. NASA's GISS ModelE often uses precomputed monthly averages instead, but those cannot feed back on the weather in real time. The team's Smart NINT instead predicts concentrations live, from surface emissions and meteorological data.

Their machine learning emulator uses a spatiotemporal design matched to how tracers evolve. It processes the lowest 20 levels of the atmosphere. At the first pressure level it scored an R-squared of 0.92 and a Pearson correlation of 0.96 against the reference fields in their evaluation. Performance stayed high through level 15, then eased as concentrations fell. Crucially, the emulator held up on data from different periods than its training set, a key need for climate projections.
arxiv-2510-11154:
A single photon can carry far more than one bit when information is encoded in the shape of its light beam. Suraj Goel, Bohnishikha Ghosh, and Mehul Malik review quantum information processing with spatially structured light in this 2025 arXiv article. They focus on qudits, quantum units with more than two states, encoded in the transverse-spatial degrees of freedom of photons. Qudits promise larger channel capacity and better robustness to noise than plain qubits.

The review examines top-down circuit designs that use complex mode-mixing transformations in free space and in fibers. Platforms covered include multi-plane light conversion, complex scattering media, and multi-mode and multi-core fibers. These circuits manipulate and measure multi-dimensional and multi-mode quantum states in practice. The authors also discuss how the same platforms have performed multi-party operations and multi-outcome measurements, opening routes toward scalable photonic quantum information processing.
arxiv-2510-11254:
Questionnaires designed to measure sexism, racism, or moral attitudes in people are now routinely handed to language models, and their scores are quoted as if they measured the model. Jana Jung, Marlene Lutz, Indira Sen, and Markus Strohmaier test whether that practice is sound in this 2025 arXiv paper. They evaluate the reliability and validity of psychometric tests applied to large language models across the three constructs.

Reliability came out moderate across variations of test items and prompt wording. Validity was the problem: convergent checks against theory-based correlations between tests, and ecological checks against what models actually do in real downstream tasks, raised alarms. Crucially, test scores did not align with downstream behavior, and in some cases correlated negatively with it, indicating low ecological validity. The authors argue tests cannot simply be transferred from humans to models without adaptation and systematic validation first.
arxiv-2510-11654:
A fake headline can erase billions from markets in minutes, yet most misinformation detectors are opaque classifiers that cannot show their evidence. Daniel Berhane Araya and Duoduo Liao build FinVet, a multi-agent fact-checking framework for financial claims, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The design goal is verdicts a compliance officer could audit: backed by sources, carrying confidence scores, and explicitly flagging uncertainty when the evidence runs out.

FinVet combines two retrieval-augmented generation pipelines with fact-checking agents, merging judgments through confidence-weighted voting. Processing adapts in three tiers according to retrieval confidence, escalating from metadata extraction to full model-based analysis only when needed. On the FinFact dataset the framework reached an F1 score of 0.85, improving ten percent over its best single pipeline and thirty-seven percent over standalone retrieval-augmented approaches. In finance, they argue, attribution and honest uncertainty flags matter as much as accuracy.
arxiv-2510-11854:
Cristóbal Corral, Borja Diez, and Eleftherios Papantonopoulos chart exotic solutions of conformal gravity, a theory that keeps physics unchanged under local rescalings. They study gravitational instantons, which are Euclidean, time-frozen solutions used to compute quantum effects. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks which of these instantons secretly equal Einstein gravity solutions in disguise, and finds a family that does not.

Starting from a one-parameter extension of the Kerr-NUT-AdS metric, they compute conserved charges with the Noether-Wald method. The charges receive corrections from conformal gravity's extra linear modes, which they identify. Continuing the solution to Euclidean form, they locate where it becomes regular and self-dual, then apply the Dunajski-Tod theorem to prove it is not conformally Einstein. Adding nonlinear matter, a conformally coupled scalar field and ModMax electrodynamics, yields further instantons. Their partition functions and charges stay finite, thanks to conformal invariance.
arxiv-2510-11954:
Sam Yu-Te Lee and five colleagues tackle a subtle failure of workplace chatbots. Enterprise assistants retrieve documents before answering, and when the retrieval misses the user's intent, the answer can be perfectly correct yet useless, a response the authors call irrelevantly right. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces VizCopilot, a prototype that shows users the retrieved context instead of hiding it.

VizCopilot pairs topic modeling with document visualization, letting users inspect and modify the context the chatbot will use. The team used it as a design probe within a research-through-design study. Visualization helped users spot and fix misaligned context before answers were generated. It also changed the users themselves: they adapted their prompting strategies to steer retrieval toward relevance from the start. Weaknesses remain in verification support, especially for close reading and for deciding how far to trust AI summaries. The authors chart future work on personalization and proactivity.
arxiv-2510-12154:
Fang and He prove strong positivity results for canonical bases in modified quantum groups, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. A canonical basis is a special basis of an algebra whose multiplication rules have remarkably simple coefficients. Quantum groups are algebraic structures that arise from symmetries in physics, and the modified form allows lowest and highest weight modules, which are basic building blocks of representations.

The main theorem says that structure constants coming from spherical parabolic subalgebras always lie among the natural number polynomials in the quantum parameter and its inverse. For quantum groups of finite type this means multiplication and action coefficients are positive. The proof uses a thickening construction, which embeds an approximation of a tensor product into the negative part of a larger quantum group. Positivity is then inherited from the well understood basis of that larger group.
arxiv-2510-12254:
He and co-authors introduce FedMMKT, a federated learning framework that improves image generation and local task models together, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Text to image models are versatile, but adapting them to specialized tasks needs task specific data that privacy rules often keep locked away. Meanwhile phones and connected devices hold rich multimodal data that cannot simply be pooled.

Federated learning trains models across devices without moving raw data to a central server. FedMMKT uses that setting for a two way knowledge transfer: a text to image model on the server and task specific models on clients enhance each other using decentralized multimodal data. This design avoids the impractical demand that small client devices host and fine tune a huge generative model themselves. The authors present the framework as a way to bring specialized image generation to private, distributed data sources while keeping that data in place.
arxiv-2510-12954:
Rychkovskiy introduces a guidance stack for image diffusion models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Latent diffusion models such as Stable Diffusion sharpen images under classifier-free guidance, but pushing that guidance too far causes oversaturation, tone drift, and texture artifacts. Lowering it costs sharpness and prompt faithfulness. His system, CADE 2.5, adjusts guidance during sampling without any retraining.

Its central module separates the guidance signal into low and high frequency parts and reweights them. It rescales the guided prediction's energy to match the positive branch. It also removes the part that runs parallel to the unconditional direction. A light spectral monitor switches between conservative and detail-seeking modes as image structure firms up. Across Stable Diffusion samplers the method improved sharpness, prompt adherence, and artifact control at moderate guidance scales, and a companion stabilizer added natural micro-texture at high resolutions.
arxiv-2510-13154:
Zahraei and Asgari benchmark cultural alignment of language models for the Middle East and North Africa in this 2025 arXiv paper. Models trained mostly on Western, English data may distort the values of other regions, and the MENA region is rarely covered in evaluation. Their benchmark, MENAValues, is built from large official human surveys across sixteen countries, keeping full population response distributions.

Models were probed under combinations of three perspective framings, neutral, personalized, and third-person observer, and two language modes, English and the localized native languages Arabic, Persian, and Turkish. Three phenomena stood out. Identical questions drew drastically different answers across languages. Asking models to explain their reasoning worsened cultural alignment. And models sometimes refused sensitive questions while their internal probabilities revealed strong hidden preferences. In native languages, models also collapsed diverse nations into simplistic monolithic groups.
arxiv-2510-13254:
Zhang and co-authors rethink graph domain adaptation through frequency in this 2025 arXiv paper. Graph neural networks excel on networks from social graphs to molecules, but moving a model between domains fails when graph structures shift and multi-layer processing smears local details. The authors' insight is spectral: viewed as signals on a graph, low-frequency components carry domain-invariant global patterns while high-frequency components hold domain-specific local detail.

Their network, FracNet, splits the graph into high- and low-frequency parts and adapts each appropriately, while a contrastive learning framework sharpens the blurred decision boundary between domains. The paper backs the design with rigorous theoretical proof of its superiority. Extensive experiments showed significant improvements over leading domain adaptation approaches. The authors argue frequency-aware treatment is the missing discipline in graph transfer learning.
arxiv-2510-13454:
Go and co-authors build VIST3A, a text-to-3D generator made by stitching two large pretrained models together. Their 2025 arXiv paper joins a text-to-video generator with a feedforward 3D reconstruction network. The video model supplies rich latent content from a text prompt. The reconstruction model then decodes that content into consistent scene geometry.

Stitching requires finding the decoder layer that best matches the generator's latent output. That search needs only a small, unlabelled dataset, the authors report. A second step aligns the generator with the stitched decoder using direct reward finetuning. This keeps the produced latents decodable into convincing 3D scenes. Across several generator and decoder pairings, VIST3A clearly beat earlier text-to-3D models that output Gaussian splats. With a suitable base model, it also produced high-quality point maps from text.
arxiv-2510-13654:
Meyer, Kaltenpoth, Zalipski, and Müller warn that benchmarking time series foundation models is full of traps. Their 2025 arXiv paper examines how these zero-shot forecasting models get evaluated today. Like language models, they train on huge scraped collections of series. That scale makes clean test data hard to guarantee for any benchmark.

Their review finds benchmark datasets that poorly represent real forecasting tasks. Many evaluations ignore where and when series were recorded, flattening key structure. Leakage risks abound, since training and test sets overlap in murky ways. Models can also memorize global shocks, like crises or pandemics, and fake local skill. Muddy data splits inflate scores and mislead comparisons between models. The authors call for principled new evaluation designs from the community. Testing on truly future, unseen data is their headline safeguard.
arxiv-2510-13754:
Mañas and Rojas study Uvarov-type perturbations of mixed-type multiple orthogonal polynomials posed on the step line. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in a matrix framework, since several measures act at once. The perturbations multiply the measure matrix by polynomial factors on either side. Some discrete point masses can also be added to the measures.

These moves reshape the moment matrix in a finite-band way. The associated Markov-Stieltjes function transforms rationally under the same operations. The authors derive explicit connection formulas tying perturbed polynomials to the original family. Determinant conditions spell out when the new orthogonality exists at all. Algebraic fallout includes changes to the block-banded recurrence operators driving the polynomials. Spectral data encoded in the Markov-Stieltjes functions shifts in step. A worked example perturbs the Jacobi-Piñeiro family nontrivially. The framework unifies the Christoffel, Geronimus, and Uvarov transformations in one matrix picture.
arxiv-2510-13854:
Keita, Homan, and Diarra bake linguistic rules into a neural tagger's loss so it learns Zarma part-of-speech tagging from unlabelled text alone. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves low-resource languages, where annotated corpora barely exist. Transfer learning demands parallel data and heavy pipelines many communities lack. Pure rule systems, meanwhile, shatter on ambiguity.

Their framework, R2T, turns a multi-tiered rule system into extra terms in the training objective. An adaptive term teaches principled uncertainty on words never seen in training. The rule-trained BiLSTM reached 98.2 percent accuracy on Zarma tagging in their tests without a single labelled sentence, beating a fine-tuned AfriBERTa baseline, the authors report. For named entity recognition, R2T works best as pretraining before light fine-tuning. Fifty labelled sentences then sufficed to beat a baseline trained on three hundred.
arxiv-2510-13954:
Richard Dyer and Christopher J. Moore examine the ringdown of merged black holes, the fading gravitational-wave signal emitted as the new black hole settles down, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The ringdown is a sum of quasinormal modes, tones with specific frequencies and decay rates set by the black hole's mass and spin. Picking out which tones are really present in a signal is statistically tricky.

The authors built a fully Bayesian, data-driven framework and applied it to high-accuracy simulated waveforms from a public catalog. They identified overtones, backward-spinning retrograde modes, and nonlinear modes up to third order. Several high-order overtones appeared near the merger, confirming they matter for modeling the early ringdown. The team tabulated mode content across many start times. They found no late-time power-law tails, as expected for these waveforms.
arxiv-2510-14354:
Siddharth Tourani and co-authors align three-dimensional scans from depth cameras without labeled training data, using keypoints that agree with themselves around a cycle, in this 2025 arXiv paper. RGB-D registration, lining up color-plus-depth views of a scene, underpins robotics and augmented reality, and mountains of unlabeled scans exist to learn from.

Their approach uses cycle-consistent keypoints as salient anchors. A point matched from one view to another and back again should return to itself. Enforcing that coherence during matching improves correspondence accuracy beyond what geometric and feature similarity achieve. A pose block couples a gated recurrent unit, which remembers past estimates, with transformation synchronization. Together they blend multi-view information to refine the alignment. The method surpasses self-supervised registration methods on the ScanNet and 3DMatch benchmarks, even beating some older supervised methods, and its components improve pipelines when integrated into them.
arxiv-2510-14654:
Klahn and co-authors study, in a 2025 arXiv paper, when pockets of fluid trapped in porous rock or soil suddenly break loose and flow. Such clusters sit inside the pores during two-phase flow, held by surface tension against the pressure pushing them. Predicting the tipping point matters for groundwater, oil recovery, and carbon storage.

The authors build a simple quasistatic model from geometry, mass conservation, and a mechanical balance condition. It yields coupled differential equations, one per opening of a cluster, and it pinpoints the critical Bond number, the ratio of driving pressure to surface tension, at which a cluster mobilizes. The model runs far faster than direct simulation and sweeps parameter space easily. It also exposes a flaw in current mean-field theories: their predicted scaling of the largest stable cluster can only hold if the exponent varies with the system's parameters.
arxiv-2510-15154:
Barbara Lopez-Doriga, Anya R. M. Jones, and Kunihiko Taira study what happens when a swirling gust slams into a wing at extreme strength. Their 2025 arXiv paper varies the wing's thickness and camber, its built-in curve, alongside gust size, strength, starting position, and angle of attack. Past work on gust encounters had mostly used very thin wings, leaving the role of real wing shape unclear.

Simulations showed flow patterns and lift forces departing strongly from calm-flight values as gusts grew larger or stronger. Where the vortex started changed the steep velocity shifts near the wing's front edge, either softening or sharpening the lift spike. Lift swings grew with angle of attack until leveling near ten degrees, in a pattern reminiscent of stall. Thicker wings, notably, suffered smaller lift swings, which the authors trace to weaker vorticity shed from the leading edge.
arxiv-2510-15354:
Saqib Qamar builds a tool that outlines skin lesions in microscope-style photos to support early skin cancer checks, in this solo 2025 arXiv paper. Outlining lesions by hand is slow, and labeled examples for training are scarce. His framework, MIRA-U, learns from a mix of labeled and unlabeled images instead of demanding full annotation.

A teacher network, pre-trained by hiding parts of images and reconstructing them, labels the unlabeled photos and rates its own confidence in each label. A student network then learns from those weighted labels. The student blends convolutional layers, which read local texture, with transformer blocks, which read wider context, joined by cross-attention links. On two public datasets the system reached a Dice score of about 0.92 while using only half of the data as labeled examples. That beat both reconstruction-based rivals and plain convolutional baselines, with the clearest gains when labels were fewest.
arxiv-2510-15454:
Rodrigo Guedes Lang and five colleagues unify the analysis of a gamma-ray observatory that uses two very different kinds of telescope. Their 2025 arXiv paper concerns H.E.S.S., an array that catches flashes from gamma rays hitting the atmosphere. One huge telescope reaches the lowest energies alone, while four smaller ones work together at higher energies.

Combining both modes in one analysis had proved difficult, so results used one mode at a time. The new analysis sorts each event into one of three types based on its measured shape parameters, with each type dominating a different energy band. It also improves the separation of gamma rays from background particles and sharpens energy and direction estimates. Sensitivity improved by roughly a quarter to nearly a half across most energies. Tests on real data from the Crab Nebula confirmed the wider coverage and smaller uncertainties.
arxiv-2510-15654:
Some disk stars look too young for their chemistry, challenging how the Milky Way formed. Yuxi Lu leads a twelve-author team following up such candidates in this 2025 arXiv paper. The candidates are dwarf stars rich in alpha elements yet apparently fast-rotating and young. Earlier work picked them out by rotation, since lithium can expose merger products among dwarfs. The team took high-resolution spectra with the PEPSI instrument at the Large Binocular Telescope.

The spectra confirm three additional stars that are most likely genuinely young. Three of the four known stars share similar iron levels around minus zero point five. They are about five billion years old, hinting at a common formation pathway.
arxiv-2510-15854:
Xiaofeng Cai, Linghui Kong, Dmitri Kuzmin, and Li Shan design a numerical scheme for plasma kinetics that stays reliable as a plasma turns quasi-neutral. The Vlasov-Poisson system tracks a distribution of particles under their own electric field. In the quasi-neutral limit the Debye length shrinks, and naive schemes fail unless the grid resolves that tiny scale.

Their method pairs a conservative semi-Lagrangian discontinuous Galerkin discretisation with a reformulated Poisson equation drawn from moments of the Vlasov equation. The semi-Lagrangian part keeps mass conserved locally and sidesteps the usual time-step restriction, while the Galerkin part gives high-order accuracy for fine phase-space structure. Cai and his three co-authors prove asymptotic stability, consistency, and the preserving property. Tests confirm accuracy and efficiency across both quasi-neutral and ordinary regimes.
arxiv-2510-15954:
Hongzheng Shi, Yuhang Wang, and Xiao Liu test a diffusion-based filter for tracking wildfire spread in real time. Fire managers need accurate, live forecasts, and data assimilation improves them by merging remote-sensing observations with numerical fire models. The filter they study, the Ensemble Score Filter, was built for high-dimensional nonlinear filtering.

The filter leans on a score-based generative diffusion model to represent the forecast distribution. The three authors give the technical details for the wildfire setting and run numerical investigations of the coupled system. Their results show the filter beating alternatives on accuracy and stability while staying computationally efficient. They judge it robust and practical for live fire work and share their code publicly, which lets fire modelling groups test the method on their own cases.
arxiv-2510-16054:
Zheng Hui and four co-authors teach an agent to decide, chunk by chunk, what may safely leave a user's machine for a strong remote model. Prompts often carry sensitive data, forcing a hard trade: remote power with exposure, or local privacy with weaker answers. Static rewriting pipelines break language flow and strip task-critical facts along with private ones.

Their framework, Privacy-R1, treats that privacy-conscious delegation as sequential decision-making and trains the router with reinforcement learning. The agent learns to shield replaceable personal identifiers locally while sending task-critical ones onward when the gain justifies it. A new medical data set with dense personal information tests the hard cases. The team reports a new best point on the privacy and utility frontier, arguing that learned adaptive policies are necessary for sensitive deployments.
arxiv-2510-16354:
Naotaka Ukai, the sole author, studies image cleaning maths in a 2025 paper. The work links two equations that clean grain from grey images while eyeing edge direction. A nonconvex energy, a cost with more than one low point, drives the pair. The snag is how to set the starting direction field, a choice past work left vague.

Ukai drops the time slope of the direction field from the scheme. The start field then gets fixed by the step scheme itself. He proves the scheme has one stable path that shifts gently with inputs. An energy bound holds along the way as well. The result gives image tools a firm base for this model.
arxiv-2510-16454:
Gregory Kucherov and Yakov Nekrich tackle a string puzzle in their 2025 paper. For any text, one gauge counts how many distinct chunks it has at each chunk length. The peak of that count, scaled by length, gives a score tied to text compression. They ask how to keep that score fresh as text streams in, one letter at a time.

They give two methods that update the score as each new letter lands. One takes a small mean cost per letter, and one caps the worst cost per letter. Both costs grow only with slow log steps in text length. The team says these are the first fast live methods for the task.
arxiv-2510-16554:
Juan Schmidt leads four co-authors in a 2025 report on a new crystal they grew and found. The crystal blends europium, platinum, and aluminium in a near-fixed ratio. X-ray tests, both on powder and on single crystals, map its form. It takes a six-sided cell type with no known twin in past records.

Magnet tests across heat and field show how its europium moments line up. Below 2.8 kelvin, the moments lock in an anti-aligned pattern. Kelvin is a heat scale that starts at absolute zero. Resistance tests across heat back the picture of its traits. New compounds like this give labs fresh ground for magnet studies.
arxiv-2510-17054:
V. Hnizdo revisits a well-known electromagnetism paper in a 2025 note. The paper is Jackson's influential 2002 article on gauge transformation. Gauge choices are bookkeeping options for describing electric and magnetic fields. Jackson moved between two gauges using two auxiliary functions.

Hnizdo outlines how Jackson likely derived the equations governing those functions. One function produces the target gauge's vector potential directly through its curl. The other must be subtracted from the starting potential instead. Confusing those two roles has tripped up many readers. The note separates them cleanly and shows each step's purpose. Teachers and students of classical electromagnetism gain a clearer path. The clarification preserves a standard reference's usefulness for future classes.
arxiv-2510-17854:
Jitendra Sharma, Arthur Carvalho, and Suman Bhunia ask how to tell whether an image was made by a person or by an AI system. Their approach turns images into numeric codes and compares how close the codes sit to each other. The hunch is that AI images cluster near other AI images, and human work clusters apart.

The team tests the idea with five coding models on a mixed set of images, paired with a blockchain record of origin. Readers get a working plan for checking image sources at a time when fake pictures are easy to make and hard to spot.
arxiv-2510-18154:
Antonio-Gabriel Chacón Menke, Phan Xuan Tan, and Eiji Kamioka label the reasoning traces of language models sentence by sentence for safety work. Watching a model's chain of thought can catch harmful plans, but whole-trace labels hide exactly when a worrying behavior starts. Their data set marks behaviors like raising a safety concern or guessing at user intent.

Those marks support probes that read the model's inner activations rather than its words alone. Steering vectors drawn from the labels can detect, and even influence, the behaviors mid-reasoning. Safety researchers get finer tools for models that might hide unsafe thinking behind clean text.
arxiv-2510-18254:
Sion Weatherhead, with Flora Salim and Aaron Belbasis, tests whether language models truly reflect, in a 2025 study. Reflection here means catching and fixing your own mistake while working. Models often write text that sounds reflective, but sounding reflective is not the same as checking constraints.

The team asked eight leading models to write valid science test items, then revise them. First attempts were poor, often with no valid items out of four required. Revisions helped only slightly and often repeated the same rule violation. Reasoning-branded models did no better, suggesting outside checks, not model self-talk, ensure reliable work.
arxiv-2510-18454:
Atharvan Dogra and his four co-authors ask a pointed question. Does training models to be funnier make them more harmful? They use humor as the test case. They score jokes for funniness, bias, and toxicity. Six models took part in the tests. A clear pattern showed up fast. Harmful jokes earned higher humor scores. Role-based prompts made the gap grow. That hints at a feedback loop. Generators and judges push each other toward edgier jokes.

New measures based on information added more detail. Harmful cues made word choices less certain. Yet for some models they made harmful punchlines feel more expected. Bias may sit deep in the learned sense of humor. A satire task checked these trends with human judges. It confirmed them. Biased and toxic jokes gained about ten to twenty-one percent in humor score. They also showed up more often among jokes rated funny.
arxiv-2510-18554:
Federico Barbero and his eight co-authors show that the training data used to align an open model can be pulled back out of the finished model. Alignment training teaches models skills such as following instructions, staying safe, and reasoning over long texts. Measuring what leaks by exact text matching, however, badly undercounts the leak, because small surface changes hide copies that are nearly identical in meaning.

Using embedding models, which compare texts by meaning, the team found far more recoverable data, by their cautious estimate about ten times what string matching suggests. Models readily gave up data from their later training phases, and that recovered data could train a fresh base model back to a meaningful share of the original performance. The authors flag an overlooked risk, and note that distillation may quietly pass a teacher's original data to its students.
arxiv-2510-18654:
Daniel Csillag and Diego Mesquita make a modern statistical tool safe to use with private data. E-values are a flexible way to test hypotheses and control risk, allowing valid conclusions at any stopping time under weak assumptions. But when the underlying data are sensitive, such as medical records, publishing an e-value can leak private information.

The authors give a general method that converts an ordinary e-value into a differentially private one, meaning its release provably reveals little about any single person's data. The conversion adds a specially designed biased multiplicative noise while keeping the result statistically valid. Their analysis shows the private versions keep strong detection power and match the originals in the long run. Experiments on online risk monitoring, private health care, and prediction tasks show the approach working in practice.
arxiv-2510-19354:
Eylon Zohar, Israel Nelken, and Boaz Rafaely build a small neural network that mimics the human auditory periphery, the first stage of hearing, for speech signals. Classic models of that stage are faithful but random in detail and slow to compute. This limits large experiments and any use that needs answers in real time.

Their compact convolutional encoder reproduces the average firing-rate pattern, called a neurogram, across frequencies from the respected reference model, while skipping random spiking on purpose so identical inputs give identical outputs. Matching the reference closely at far lower cost opens hearing simulations to larger studies and interactive tools.
arxiv-2510-19454:
Elian Vanderborght and Henk A Dijkstra build a reduced model of ocean circulation. The global overturning circulation carries heat, carbon, and salt. Older simplified models missed three observed features. Overturning below the surface follows geostrophic balance. Mixing is much stronger near boundaries. Southern Ocean upwelling is partly driven by wind-linked motion.

Their model tracks temperature in a semi-enclosed basin. The eastern and western boundaries carry the flow. A periodic southern channel joins the basin. All three features enter in a consistent way. Climate researchers can test flow ideas fast, before full ocean simulations.
arxiv-2510-19854:
Elizabeth Cucuzzella and three co-authors develop an interpretable way to read the internal structure of tropical cyclones from satellite images, aimed at forecasting intensity changes a day ahead. Most storms evolve far from land-based instruments, so satellites are the main source of information, yet their complex structures are hard for forecasters to interpret in real time. The authors apply a multi-resolution analysis based on the discrete wavelet transform.

The method compresses a storm's fine structure into a small set of descriptive quantities. Those features correlate strongly with rapid intensity change, the dangerous strengthening forecasters most need to catch. The Atlantic basin is the focus, and the authors note deep learning systems can build directly on these wavelet features for short-term intensity guidance.
arxiv-2510-19954:
Joe Meyer and six co-authors present RELATE, a feature encoder that lets graph neural networks ingest multi-table relational data without bespoke plumbing for every schema. Relational databases naturally form heterogeneous graphs, but existing networks need a separate encoder module for each node type and column, blocking reuse. RELATE instead shares one encoder per data type: categorical, numerical, textual, and temporal.

A Perceiver-style cross-attention block then compresses each node's mixed features into a fixed-size, order-invariant representation, so any general-purpose graph network can consume it. On the RelBench benchmark, paired with two different graph models, RELATE came within three percent of schema-specific encoders while using up to five times fewer parameters. The design supports pretraining across datasets, aiming at foundation models for relational data.
arxiv-2510-20154:
Anthony Dubreuil and three co-authors test whether stereotypes sway large language models when they label stance in text with no training examples. Stance detection marks a statement as against, in favor of, or neutral toward a target, and it often touches political views. Bias in this task has been largely overlooked compared with hate speech or sentiment work.

The team automatically tagged posts in existing stance datasets with two attributes: the dialect of a social group and the complexity of the text. Model decisions shifted with those attributes in stereotyped ways, for example linking pro-marijuana views with low text complexity and African American dialect with opposition to Donald Trump. The findings show a measurable fairness risk.
arxiv-2510-20754:
Nima Torbati, Anastasia Meshcheryakova, Ramona Woitek, Diana Mechtcheriakova, and Amirreza Mahbod present ACS-SegNet, a network that outlines tissue regions in microscope slides to aid disease diagnosis. Clean outlines matter because treatment calls often rest on which tissue type fills which area of a slide.

The design joins two encoders, a classic convolutional net and a transformer based segmenter, and fuses their features with attention so fine edges and wide context both count. On two public slide data sets the model tops prior methods and baselines on overlap scores. Code is shared in a public repository, so clinics and labs can test the method on their own slide collections.
arxiv-2510-21154:
Furkan Ok, Amir Bahrami, and Christophe Caloz study a quantum effect called Klein tunneling, where particles pass through barriers that should block them. Their work asks whether changing electric and magnetic potentials over both space and time can trigger the effect at much lower energies than a fixed setup allows.

Using derived rules for how particles move in such a setup, they find slanted transitions linking states of opposite energy without those states needing to overlap. A gap appears whose size depends on speed, with no transmission inside a certain speed range and transmission returning beyond it. Threshold energies drop by up to ten thousand times, pointing toward tests with flying-focus fronts and fast electron beams.
arxiv-2510-21254:
Victoria J. Hodge, Colin Paterson, and Ibrahim Habli review methods for spotting out-of-distribution data in AI-driven autonomous systems. Such data differ from anything the system trained on, and failing to notice them can undermine safety in high-stakes settings where people rely on the machine.

The review first defines key terms, then looks at what pushes data out of distribution and why proving safety for these systems is hard. It sorts detection methods by where they can serve across the machine learning life cycle, from data preparation through to operation. The authors also flag cautions for engineers who add such detectors to a system, and close with open problems that must be solved before autonomous systems can be trusted broadly.
arxiv-2510-21954:
Mykola Haltiuk and Aleksander Smywinski-Pohl tackle a bottleneck in adapting language models to new tongues. The bottleneck is the tokenizer, which chops text into the pieces a model reads. A fixed tokenizer built for other languages handles low-resource tongues badly. Differently scripted languages suffer too.

Swapping tokenizers usually means guessing new embeddings from word meaning alone. That ignores how the model actually uses the pieces. Their method, MATT, watches attention patterns inside a source model instead. It records how pieces talk to each other. That behavior is distilled into the new model as a warm-up. Ordinary training follows. Across varied language settings, the transfer recovered much of the original skill. It did so within a few hours of computing. Meaning-only baselines were beaten. Model behavior, the authors argue, should guide the handoff.
arxiv-2510-22054:
Yuli Slavutsky, Sebastian Salazar, and David M. Blei improve on a classic way to combine predictive models. The classic way averages models with fixed weights. That wastes a simple fact. In mixed populations, different models win on different inputs. The best blend should change from case to case.

Their method lets the weights depend on the input. It is called input adaptive Bayesian model averaging. An adaptive prior carries the input dependence. Fast approximate inference then works out which model to trust for each new case. The authors prove guarantees for the method. The guarantees compare it with an oracle that picks the best single model per input. Tests ranged from personalized cancer treatment to credit card fraud detection. The adaptive blend gave predictions that were more accurate. They were also better calibrated than fixed blends and earlier adaptive rivals.
arxiv-2510-22254:
