Eric W. Bridgeford leads a seven-author team writing rules for scientists who code with AI assistants. The tools plainly speed up software work. In research, though, a fast program that is subtly wrong is worse than a slow one. The paper aims at speed without surrendering quality or validity.

Ten practical rules sit under four themes. The first theme is preparing and understanding the problem before generating anything. The second is managing context and the back-and-forth with the tool. The third is testing and validation strong enough to catch plausible nonsense. The fourth is code quality through iterative improvement. One insistence runs through all of them: human agency. The researcher keeps the decisions, the domain judgment, and the responsibility. The rules are working habits for labs adopting these tools now.
arxiv-2510-22454:
Linhan Wang and six co-authors aim to speed up particle picking in cryo electron tomography, where finding proteins inside cells is slow because hand labels are scarce. Many collected tomograms sit unused for lack of labels. Their framework, SemiETPicker, learns from a few labelled examples plus a large pool of unlabelled volumes.

One part detects particles through heat maps, while a teacher student setup trains both roles together under sparse labels. Extra tricks include pseudo labels from several views and a tomogram specific dropout method. On a large public data set, scores rose clearly above supervised baselines, showing the value of unlabelled data.
arxiv-2510-22554:
Random walks that can jump far, on a grid that wraps around like a cycle, are the subject of a 2025 mathematics paper by Robert Griffiths and Shuhei Mano. Each step adds a random vector whose entries are updated by circulant matrices, which wrap rows around in a regular pattern.

Griffiths and Mano seek the structure of these walks and expansions for their transition rules. They extend the model to a torus, a space made of circles, by shrinking steps and letting the grid refine. Special polynomials become the key building blocks in a grouped view, and examples cover cutoff and mixing times, plus a central limit result.
arxiv-2510-22654:
Choosing among learning algorithms costs money, because letting an expert train also uses a budget. Ilgam Latypov, Alexandra Suvorikova, Alexey Kroshnin, Alexander Gasnikov, and Yuriy Dorn study that management problem in 2025, where only a limited number of self-learning experts may train each round.

Their algorithm, M-LCB, picks one expert to act and at most a set number to learn in each round. Confidence bounds built from observed training losses guide those choices under mild prior knowledge. The authors prove regret bounds that scale with each expert's own regret. Tests use both parametric models and bandit algorithms as the managed experts.
arxiv-2510-22854:
Popular fit tests can miss real departures from a model. Christian T Covington and Jeffrey W Miller introduce a stronger test in 2025. It is called PITOS. It builds on the probability integral transform. That transform turns data values into uniform scores under the null.

PITOS applies the transform to pairs of order statistics. Order statistics are sorted sample values. Each pair yields a uniform value under the null. Values convert to p-values by a simple map. A Cauchy method combines many pair results. Type I error stays near valid levels. Runtime is fast, near n log n. Local departures show much higher power.
arxiv-2510-22954:
Liwei Jiang leads a team of ten researchers who examine how language models give alike answers to open questions. Models often struggle to produce varied, human-like creative replies. Repeated exposure to similar outputs could narrow human thought over time, yet diversity has been hard to measure at scale.

The group built Infinity-Chat, a set of twenty six thousand real open-ended queries with many valid answers. They also offer a taxonomy for sorting kinds of sameness in outputs. Their study, called Artificial Hivemind, gives researchers a fuller way to judge whether models echo each other too much.
arxiv-2510-23054:
Nephtalí Eliceo Martínez-Pérez and Cupatitzio Ramírez study the quantum cosmology of supersymmetric, higher derivative models. The models they use are uniform and smooth in all directions, yet built with higher derivative terms.Quantum cosmology applies quantum rules to the universe as a whole and asks how it began. Their 2025 work revisits actions written with superfields in earlier studies.

They give versions of those actions that match in the classical limit. Boson fields get second order equations, and fermions get first order ones. Once quantized, the fermion rules yield a state with several parts, removed by the energy and supersymmetry rules. The team finds wavy solutions whose large scale limit looks like fast early growth. Exact solutions with a smooth exponential shape then give likely values for the first curvature, matching the model without supersymmetry.
arxiv-2510-23254:
Tianyi Ma, Tengyao Wang, and Richard J Samworth study how well a pretrained Transformer adapts in context when test tasks differ from training tasks. Pretraining draws tasks from a mixture over difficulty levels. At test time the tasks come from one fixed level, possibly shifted, with the shift bounded by a chi-squared divergence.

The authors analyze optimal in-context adaptivity and distributional robustness in that setting. Their theory clarifies when a model trained on mixed difficulty can still perform on a shifted target. Such results guide expectations for deploying language models on tasks unlike their training mix.
arxiv-2510-23754:
Piyali Chakraborty and a co-author prove Plancherel-type identities tied to Fuglede's conjecture, a famous question linking tiling and Fourier analysis. The setting involves unbounded sets on the real line that tile the line by shifts from a finite set, paired with sets that serve as their spectral duals. The identities relate integrals over such dual pairs, extending a formula beyond its usual bounded setting.

Their main result gives a clean two-way statement. An open set tiles the real line by the shifts zero through p minus one exactly when it admits a spectrum of a specific form. That form is Lebesgue measure on a short interval, repeated at every integer. Along the way, the authors show the Fourier transform between certain unbounded tiling sets in duality is surjective, meaning every target can be hit. The result sharpens the tiling-spectrum dictionary that Fuglede's conjecture predicts.
arxiv-2510-24254:
Madhurima Panja and eight co-authors build a probabilistic machine learning framework to forecast Arctic precipitation and its severity. Rain and snow in Arctic maritime places like Bear Island and Ny-Ålesund matter for climate risk and early warnings in exposed marine regions. The team first studies how precipitation links to drivers such as temperature, humidity, cloud cover, and air pressure across time scales.

They use wavelet coherence to map those links across time and frequency, then a decomposition method to weigh joint causal effects among drivers. The forecasting model builds on that causal analysis, aiming to predict both the dynamics and the severity of precipitation events in these vulnerable Arctic settings.
arxiv-2510-24454:
Ekaterina Amerik, Andrey Soldatenkov, and Misha Verbitsky, three authors, prove a conjecture. The setting is hyperkähler manifolds, special shapes with rich symmetry. A bimeromorphic map reshapes such a shape while keeping most structure. Wierzba and Wisniewski showed such maps split into simple flops in dimension four. Hu and Yau guessed the same split works in each dimension.

A Mukai flop blows up a ruled part, then shrinks it another way. Hu and Yau allowed first cutting out thin parts of the shape. The trio prove the guess for shapes with maximal holonomy. Holonomy tracks how directions twist when moved around loops. Their proof splits any such map into wall-crossing flops. The result settles the shape-changing rules for this whole class.
arxiv-2510-24654:
Pengcheng Qiu leads a team with thirteen co-authors who train language models to act as doctors in a fake clinic. Their agent must pick tests step by step, track how the case shifts, and then settle on a final call. Static training sets do not teach such step by step plans well.

They built DiagGym, a world model trained on health files, as a safe place to learn by trial. Their agent, DiagAgent, learns from rewards over many turns of talk and tests. A bench set of about twenty two hundred checked cases from four sources then grades how the agents do.
arxiv-2510-24954:
Aaron Bernstein leads a team with nine co-authors who take a fresh run at a past guess on graph short cuts. The guess asked if short cut edges could be added to a graph so all reach paths get short, at near no size cost. A past work broke the guess as first stated, and bounds since grew tight.

The team notes the old break leaves one door open: new mid points, not just new edges. With mid points let in, their attacks break all known low bounds on short cuts. In the other way, they rule out the ideal trade of size and span when a key cap holds. The work sorts what the true guess should have said.
arxiv-2510-25354:
Adrien Weihs, Andrea L Bertozzi, and Matthew Thorpe study hypergraph learning. Their 2025 math paper studies semi-supervised learning problems. Hypergraphs model multiway effects between many items. Semi-supervised learning uses few labels and much unlabeled data. They pose variational problems on random geometric hypergraphs. The goal is understanding actions with large data.

They establish asymptotic consistency in the large-data limit. Scaling regimes ensure well-posed, nontrivial label propagation. Without such regimes, labels could collapse to constants. Discrete minimizers converge to continuum formula answers. Those answers involve a density-weighted p-Laplacian formula. They also propose Higher-Order Hypergraph Learning, called HOHL. It uses multiscale regularization from Laplacian powers. Subgraphs induced by the hypergraph supply those Laplacians. For point clouds, an quick surrogate is studied. Numeric tests on benchmarks support useful utility.
arxiv-2510-25654: Steffen Schultze and Helmut Grubmuller present a Bayesian approach to MINFLUX localization microscopy, in a 2025 paper. MINFLUX locates fluorophores with nanometer precision by targeted scanning with an illumination profile that has a minimum. Current scanning patterns rest on heuristics and may be suboptimal. Their rigorous Bayesian method aims for maximal resolution from either minimal detected photons or minimal exposures. From simulated localization runs, they estimate the approach should cut the photons needed for one-nanometer resolution by about a factor of four.
arxiv-2510-25854:
Mingyuan Wang, Guus Avis, and Stefan Krastanov speed up the design of circuits that clean up noisy quantum states shared among many parties. The states are GHZ states, a standard form of multi party entanglement, which means the parties share linked quantum outcomes. Simulating such circuits in the usual way grows very costly as qubits are added.

Wang and the team give a listing and simulation method whose cost for these special gates stays constant, rather than growing with system size. Fast simulation lets them search for distillation circuits, which purify noisy states, that beat prior designs by a wide margin. The method also extends to related graph states and can be tuned to a chosen noise model.
arxiv-2510-26054:
Hyowon Park and Ivar Martin show, in theory, how a layered magnetic material could display a large topological magnetoelectric effect. Their structure places a triangular lattice of cobalt ions between layers of niobium disulfide. When cobalt spins form a non coplanar pattern with uniform handedness, the material shows a large anomalous Hall effect, a voltage sideways to a current caused by magnetism.

If the handedness instead alternates between layers, the Hall signal cancels and a magnetoelectric effect appears, where an electric field creates magnetization. Park and Martin verify with first principles calculations that a sideways electric field does induce orbital magnetization, with a coupling as large as the value they report. Strain can tune the coupling between layers and switch between states.
arxiv-2510-26254:
Merilin Sousa Silva and Sina Ahmadi test whether language models can tell loanwords from native words. A loanword is borrowed from another language and gradually absorbed into the borrowing language lexicon. Human speakers, especially in bilingual communities where a dominant language presses on a minority one, can often spot such words.

Silva and Ahmadi evaluate multiple pretrained models, including large language models, across ten languages, with explicit instructions and context provided. Models perform poorly at the task in their tests. The results support earlier evidence that modern language systems show a bias toward loanwords over native equivalents. The authors discuss implications for tools that serve minority languages and for language preservation under lexical pressure.
arxiv-2510-26354:
Stephen Wan, Wei Liu, and Michael Strube investigate how much surrounding context helps when classifying discourse relations in scientific papers. A discourse relation links two text spans, for example as cause, contrast, or elaboration, and inferring that structure is a first step toward finding evidence for AI generated scientific claims. Scientific writing is an understudied genre for this task.

Wan and the team run a preliminary comparison of pretrained language model and large language model approaches to discourse relation classification. Their experiments show that context, defined through discourse structure, is generally helpful for the classification. They also analyze which scientific discourse relation types benefit most from added context, giving guidance for later evidence finding systems.
arxiv-2510-26554:
Samantha Creech, with eleven co-authors, counts hidden black holes in a deep X-ray field. Some active galactic nuclei are Compton thick, wrapped in so much gas that even hard X-rays struggle to escape. Such objects may make up a large share of all nuclei nearby, yet they are hard to spot.

Creech and the team study the North Ecliptic Pole Time Domain Field, home to the deepest NuSTAR survey yet. They combine NuSTAR data from four cycles with XMM-Newton observations to analyse sixty hard X-ray sources spectroscopically, a first for that catalogue. The observed share of Compton thick sources was about thirteen percent down to a stated flux limit. After correcting for the bias that hides such sources, the underlying share rose to about thirty-two percent, in line with population models and earlier surveys.
arxiv-2510-26754:
Benjamin Freiman, with seven co-authors, designs a faster hunt for wave-like dark matter. Their protocol uses an array of superconducting cavities, hollow resonators of very high quality, prepared together in an entangled state with a set number of photons. Dark matter passing through would leave a faint signal in such cavities.

Freiman and the team spread the quantum state across the array and then gather it back, using an entanglement-distribution operation. The scan rate grows with the square of the cavity count times the photon factor, well beyond classical single-cavity methods under matched conditions, while thermal excitation stays the dominant background. They test robustness against decoherence and beamsplitter flaws in theory and simulation. The needed parts, they note, already exist on current platforms.
arxiv-2510-26854:
Yu Li, with twenty-two co-authors, builds a scientific encyclopedia out of verified reasoning chains. Most scientific writing compresses reasoning, showing conclusions without the steps that justify them, which blocks verification and hides links across domains. Their framework decompresses it, building a knowledge base of long chains of thought whose endpoints can be checked.

Li and the team use a Socratic agent, guided by a curriculum of about two hundred courses, to generate about three million first-principles questions. Independent solver models answer them, and only chains with consensus, verifiable endpoints survive filtering. A search engine retrieves derivations that end at a target concept, and a synthesizer narrates them into articles. The first SciencePedia holds about two hundred thousand entries across six fields, with higher knowledge density and lower error than a baseline without retrieval.
arxiv-2510-26954:
Adam Winchell argues that the Turing Test no longer separates human thought from machine thought in a useful way. Strong artificial intelligence systems already pass the old imitation game, where a judge chats without seeing who answers. Winchell notes that these systems also raise ethical worries and use large amounts of energy.

His update keeps the game but adds the energy spent answering as part of the score. Judging thought through efficiency ties the abstract question to finite real resources. The change also gives the test a clear, measurable finish line that the original lacks. Readers get a prompt to weigh time saved by these systems against their full resource cost.
arxiv-2510-27254:
Rajan Agarwal and Aarush Gupta present LLINK, a method that treats a low-resource language as an added modality for a language model. Instruction-tuned models underperform on non-Latin, low-resource scripts because tokenizers fragment their words and cross-lingual links stay weak. LLINK conditions a frozen decoder without changing its tokenizer or retraining it.

First, sentence embeddings from a frozen multilingual encoder are aligned into the decoder latent space at a reserved position through a lightweight contrastive projector. That vector then expands into soft slots consumed through minimal adapters. Bilingual retrieval improves substantially, and judged question answering strongly prefers LLINK over both the base model and direct fine-tuning. Gains trace to reduced tokenization inflation and stronger alignment, though numeric fidelity remains a residual weakness.
arxiv-2510-27454:
Vitalii Vertogradov and Maksim Grigorev trace how an exotic black hole fades away in this 2025 paper. The Kiselev black hole is ringed by an anisotropic fluid, one whose push differs by direction. It has two horizons, two points of no return. Unlike the simplest black holes, its heat need not soar as it shrinks.

They track Hawking temperature, the heat tied to slow evaporation, as mass and fluid strength vary. In most runs the hole cools to zero as it evaporates. Some runs first spike in heat and pass a phase change marked by a jump in heat capacity. The key is the null energy condition, a basic rule about energy flow. Where the rule breaks everywhere, horizons merge and heat is choked. Where it holds, evaporation looks standard.
arxiv-2510-27554:
David Shi and Kevin Joo rank paid online services by trust, not volume, in this 2025 paper. A protocol called x402 lets programs pay for application interfaces, data feeds, and AI inference over plain web requests, using cryptocurrency. As software agents shop among such services, they need discovery: which provider deserves trust. Fake reviews and spam farms poison naive rankings.

Their algorithm, TraceRank, treats payments as endorsements. Reputation seeds at known addresses, then flows along payment links, weighted by amount and freshness. Services favored by high-reputation payers outrank busy services fed by many low-reputation ones. That weighting resists Sybil attacks, where one actor fakes many identities. Paired with semantic search over plain-language queries, the system answers agent queries with quality picks.
arxiv-2511-00054:
Gio Huh, Dhruv Sheth, and Rayhan Zirvi introduce SpatialTraceGen, a framework that creates high-quality reasoning traces to teach smaller vision-language models spatial reasoning. Large models handle complex spatial problems by decomposing them and using tools strategically, but step-by-step training data for that skill is scarce. Their system distills a large teacher's reasoning into multi-hop, multi-tool traces.

An automated verifier checks the generated traces, a key innovation for keeping distilled data trustworthy. AI readers get a data pipeline for deployable spatial reasoners. Fine-tuning small models is cheap only if the traces they learn from are right, so verification is the bottleneck this framework attacks.
arxiv-2511-00354:
Amierul Aqil Khairi and Uri Shumlak report experiments on the ZaP-HD device, a test bed for a fusion concept called a sheared-flow-stabilized Z-pinch. Inside, a graphite electrode faces plasma that is both very hot and very dense while carrying large pinch currents. The question is how fast the electrode wears away, and by which process.

Measurements taken during shots show carbon loss above what physical sputtering alone predicts, but close to what sublimation, direct evaporation, predicts. Sublimated carbon ionizes inside the sheath near the surface and can redeposit, a recycling loop that heals the electrode. Sputtered carbon causes most net loss. Surface checks after exposure show smoothing and cracks from repeated heating, supporting the recycling picture and easing confidence in the design.
arxiv-2511-00554:
Phil Blandfort and Robert Graham red-team activation probes, cheap internal monitors that watch a model's activations for risky behavior. Probes are attractive for their low cost and latency, but their robustness under real adversarial pressure was largely untested. The authors ask what failure modes appear when an attacker works black-box, with no access to weights or gradients.

Their lightweight procedure wraps an off-the-shelf language model with iterative feedback and in-context learning, needing no fine-tuning. A case study on probes for high-stakes interactions surfaced interpretable weaknesses: legalistic wording triggered false positives, while bland procedural tone slipped through as false negatives. Constraint-based attacks kept some vulnerabilities alive even after fixes. Simple prompted red-teaming, they argue, can anticipate failure patterns before deployment and guide hardening.
arxiv-2511-01054:
Sama Salarian and colleagues examine fairness in synthetic medical data. Made up patient records promise wider research access without exposing real patients, but if the synthetic data skew the mix of demographic groups, studies built on them can mislead clinical decisions.

Using the MIMIC-III hospital data set, they measure how faithfully several GAN based tools cover protected subgroups, using a logarithmic disparity metric. Many subgroups came out badly over or under represented compared with the real data. Their remedy, MedEqualizer, is a model agnostic augmentation step that enriches underrepresented groups before generation begins. With it, the new data sets came out far more balanced across groups.
arxiv-2511-01154: Sinho Chewi, Aram-Alexandre Pooladian, and Matthew Zhang study the stability of the Kim-Milman flow map in a short note. The flow map is also known as the probability flow ordinary differential equation. The authors state the scope of the note. Stability is measured against changes in the target measure. The measuring stick is relative Fisher information.
arxiv-2511-01454:
Sergio Torres Aguilar translates Latin with a drafting pipeline, under a title quoting the proverb about not teaching Minerva, the goddess of wisdom. Latin is morphology rich and low resource, a hard case for language models. His method never fine tunes the big model at all.

First, a fine tuned multilingual translation model of modest size produces a structurally faithful draft. A zero shot large language model then polishes the draft, optionally with retrieved example passages added to its context. The system is tested on a standard in domain benchmark and on a new, harder out of domain set of twelfth century Latin letters from Chartres, which is released with the pipeline. Performance ends up statistically comparable to a top tier proprietary baseline.
arxiv-2511-01554:
Aditya Kapoor, Yash Bhisikar, Benjamin Freed, Jan Peters, and Mingfei Sun study how teams of learning agents should talk to each other. In multi-agent reinforcement learning, communication helps coordination but bandwidth is scarce, and earlier methods mostly decided only whether to send a message, not how many bits it deserved.

The authors extend Differentiable Discrete Communication Learning so it handles unbounded signals, turning it into a plug-in layer for any architecture. Agents demonstrably learn to raise precision when a task moment matters and lower it when it does not. Plugged into four leading algorithms, the layer cut bandwidth by more than tenfold while matching or beating prior performance. A plain Transformer policy using it also matched specialized designs, supporting a simple-is-enough lesson.
arxiv-2511-01654:
Congcong Chen, Xinyu Liu, Kaifeng Huang, Lifei Wei, and Yang Shi protect graph neural networks running in the cloud. These models power traffic prediction, recommendation, and question answering. But moving them to cloud services exposes training and inference data to theft. Earlier privacy techniques are so heavy that the cloud bill itself blocks adoption.

Their framework, Panther, runs the computation under four-party secure computation. It executes a secure array access protocol asynchronously. It also randomly pads each node's neighbor list, to hide the graph's structure. The authors prove privacy for both training and inference. In evaluation, Panther cut training time by about 75 percent. It cut inference time by about 83 percent. Both figures are averages against prior privacy-preserving approaches. The trade is far less money for the same protection.
arxiv-2511-01754:
Arnold Beckmann and Anton Setzer propose a new formal logic for reasoning about who may access what in a computer program. Hoare logic, the classic tool for proving programs correct, inspired the design. But the authors argue access security needs its own fundamentally different system. They call it access Hoare logic.

They define the formalism and give examples showing its usefulness and its difference from ordinary Hoare logic. They prove the system both sound and complete. So everything it proves is true, and everything true can be proved. A formal link back to standard Hoare logic is established as well. The authors also demonstrate a fundamental difference from other approaches to program analysis, in particular incorrectness logic, positioning access reasoning as a discipline of its own.
arxiv-2511-01854:
Elias Lumer and four colleagues fix a routing problem in multi-agent language model systems. In these systems a top-level agent delegates to sub-agents, each commanding hundreds or thousands of tools or MCP servers. Retrievers that match a query against a short agent description first often pick the wrong agent, because the description hides the fine-grained tool that actually fits.

Their Tool-to-Agent Retrieval embeds tools and their parent agents in one shared vector space. Metadata links them. A query can land on the exact tool, then climb to its agent. Or it can start at agent level. Either way, it avoids the dilution that comes from chunking many tools into one text. Across eight embedding models, the method improved Recall@5 by about 19 percent and nDCG@5 by about 18 percent over the previous best agent retrievers on the LiveMCPBench benchmark.
arxiv-2511-01954:
Jennifer Burt, Xavier Dumusque, and Samuel Halverson review the craft of precise radial velocity measurement, the wobble method that has delivered most known exoplanet masses. Watching a star's spectrum shift as an unseen planet tugs it lets astronomers weigh the planet and pin its orbit, feeding studies of exoplanet interiors and atmospheres.

The review traces how the methodology evolved over two decades. It surveys modern spectrograph designs. These instruments work on optical and near-infrared light. They can be calibrated to a stability better than 50 centimeters per second, over years. It covers data reduction and post-processing techniques. These suppress instrument systematics and, hardest of all, the star's own variability. The review then turns to methods for detecting planets in the data. It shows how to disentangle true planetary signals from stellar noise.
arxiv-2511-02054:
Natalia Puczek, Tobias Géron, Rebecca Smethurst, and Chris Lintott ask whether a galaxy's surroundings change how its central bar rotates. Bars are elongated structures of stars, dust, and gas found in a large share of nearby spiral galaxies, and theory suggests tides from neighbours might slow them down. The team used a standard method applied to spectroscopy from the MaNGA and CALIFA surveys, then matched the results with neighbourhood density for 286 galaxies.

Bars in crowded environments did rotate more slowly, with a median rate measure of about 1.65 compared with about 1.39 in sparse regions, a difference unlikely to be chance. The authors describe the result as the first observational test of the idea that fast bars form in isolation while slow bars are triggered by interactions.
arxiv-2511-02254:
Tan Tran and Canh Pham design fast algorithms for a broad optimisation problem: choosing a set of limited size that maximises a function with diminishing returns. The function need not be monotone. Such DR-submodular objectives appear in applications like revenue maximisation, and good approximation algorithms with few function evaluations are valuable. The authors propose two algorithms, FastDrSub and a better version, FastDrSub-plus-plus.

The first guarantees an approximation ratio of 0.044 relative to the optimum while asking only on the order of n log k questions, where n is the number of candidate elements and k the set size limit. The second raises the guarantee to nearly one quarter of optimal at similar cost. The authors describe these as the first constant-ratio algorithms for the problem at that low complexity. Experiments on revenue maximisation showed them beating current methods in both query count and solution quality.
arxiv-2511-02354:
Qingyun Sun and six co-authors tackle a weakness of graph neural networks: they generalise poorly when the world changes underneath them. Graphs that evolve over time, from traffic to social networks, are generated inside environments that themselves drift, so test data rarely match training data. Existing dynamic graph models largely ignore that environmental drift when the goal is prediction on out-of-distribution data.

Their framework, EvoOOD, first fits a sequential variational auto-encoder that models how the environment evolves and infers its distribution over time. An invariant-pattern recognition step then uses those inferred environments to find spatio-temporal patterns that stay stable despite diversification. Finally, fine-grained causal interventions on individual nodes, using mixtures of sampled environments, separate the stable patterns from the shifting ones. The authors report the method beating alternatives on real and synthetic dynamic datasets under distribution shift.
arxiv-2511-02754:
Zebin Wang and six colleagues built DANIEL, a method for learning shared patterns from health records held at many hospitals. Privacy rules block pooling the raw data, and classic graphical models strain under high dimensions and mixed sources. Their 2025 framework revisits the Ising model, a Markov random field workhorse, and makes it distributed and scalable.

The method optimizes a non-convex surrogate loss with a two-factor gradient method, cutting both compute and communication costs against convex rivals. Tests used records from over fifty-eight thousand patients at two large medical centers. DANIEL beat alternatives at global representation learning and at downstream tasks like finding relationships, sorting patients into phenotypes, and clustering them. The authors see wide promise for federated statistics.
arxiv-2511-02854:
Yixiang Chen and four colleagues study how code-generating models can improve their own answers when no test cases are at hand. Real coding settings often lack an interpreter to check drafts, so models must balance refining a draft against scrapping it for a fresh one. Their 2025 framework, SELF-REDRAFT, builds on Self-Refine and pushes the model to redraft solutions that look deeply flawed.

Given the same budget of rounds, SELF-REDRAFT beat Self-Refine once both settled. Yet the team found much room to grow. The models gave weak feedback on their own drafts, and their judgment of which drafts were flawed proved fragile. Balancing styles also differed sharply between models. The study sets a baseline for this balancing act and names feedback and judgment as the weak points to fix.
arxiv-2511-02954:
Ivor van der Hoog, Eva Rotenberg, and Daniel Rutschmann revisit a textbook problem: does a list contain a repeated value? A classic result says sorting is essentially forced in the worst case. But that bound assumes few repeats. Their 2025 paper asks for bounds that depend on the input's duplicates. They draw those duplicates as a graph linking equal items.

For any fixed duplicate pattern, no deterministic method can beat the best rival by much. An adversary argument caps the possible gain. They also give a matching method that runs within a small factor of optimal for every pattern. Set intersection, a close cousin, turns out strictly harder by the same measure. The pair of results draws a clean line between the two problems.
arxiv-2511-03354:
Wasimul Karim and co-authors review how generative artificial intelligence is reshaping bioinformatics work. Their survey follows a formal review method and poses six guiding questions about designs, results, focus, limits, and data use. Fields covered run from gene sequences and proteins to cell readouts, structures, and drug hunting.

Specialized models, trained with biology in mind, generally beat general-purpose ones on these tasks. Strengths cluster in reading molecules and in merging unlike data kinds into one picture. Weak spots include uneven data and narrow testing, which the authors flag for later work. The review gives life science teams a clear ledger of where generative tools already help and where care is still due.
arxiv-2511-03454:
Angel David Rios Ortiz and Javier Sendra-Arranz describe the space of point clusters on curves with fold-like singular points. A Hilbert scheme of points collects all ways to place a set number of points on a curve, counting collisions with care. Fold singularities look locally like coordinate axes meeting, a mild but rich kind of pinch.

The authors count and describe the scheme's separate components and dissect the singularities of each. Combinatorial patterns govern much of that geometry, linking counts to arrangements. Such schemes underpin enumerative geometry, where counting point setups solves wider counting problems. Fold curves offer a tractable family where the full component structure can be named rather than guessed.
arxiv-2511-04254:
Maria Bergemann and Richard Hoppe review 3D radiation transfer without local thermal equilibrium, the modelling layer between telescope spectra and nearly all that astronomers infer about stars, planets, and explosions. Spectra encode structure, surface flows, mass loss, and composition only as surely as the transfer models used to read them.

Standard models show systematic shortcomings in uneven, time-dependent settings, the review explains, while full multi-frequency 3D solutions remain brutally hard to compute and full of shortcuts. Standard solutions and recent method advances are surveyed. Uses span cool and hot stars, multi-epoch kilonova spectra, and rocky exoplanet atmospheres, showing where 3D non-equilibrium treatment changes the answers in a real way.
arxiv-2511-04354:
Yaru Liu and Yucheng Wang propose a general plan for producing Mpemba effects in open quantum systems, where a state farther from equilibrium can relax faster than a nearer one. In quantum settings the effect usually appears only for specially chosen starting states, which limits its reach and use for control.

A temporary bond-dissipation quench weakens or strengthens slow relaxation modes, reshaping each pathway regardless of system or starting state. Both the effect and its anti version become available on demand. Tests cover dephasing and boundary dissipation systems, with cold-atom setups sketched. Controlled dissipation emerges as a handy tool for faster relaxation and nonequilibrium protocols.
arxiv-2511-04454:
Hao Zhu leads four authors on fitting reinforcement learning models to behavior under bandits. Such models describe how humans and animals choose among options with unknown payoffs. Fitting them well is key before any claim about decision making can stand.

The team writes the fitting task as one broad optimization problem covering many common models. They then analyze when that problem is convex and when it is not. A new solution method follows, built on convex relaxation and optimization. Tests in simulated and real bandit settings compare it with standard benchmarks, giving researchers a firmer way to recover learning parameters.
arxiv-2511-04854:
Alvaro Prat leads five authors with SigmaDock, a fragment-based diffusion model for molecular docking. Docking predicts how a drug-like molecule sits inside a protein pocket. Generative methods sample poses fast, but often produce chemically implausible shapes.

Their scheme first splits each ligand into rigid-body fragments using structural chemistry rules. The model then learns to reassemble those stiff pieces inside the pocket. Diffusion runs on the rotation-and-translation group, so each fragment moves as a solid body. Working at fragment level should improve plausibility, generalization, and cost over atom-by-atom generation for drug discovery.
arxiv-2511-05054:
M. Z. Mo and co-authors watch copper melt in less than a blink, using bursts of electrons to take snapshots of its atoms. Slow melting is set by heat and pressure, but fast melting shows how bonds break and how energy flows into the lattice.

At loads two to four times the melt threshold, melt starts at the surface just below the usual melt point, then runs through the bulk. Computer models of atoms match the data and point to weak energy flow from electrons to lattice. Both lines land on one shared time for the bulk change.
arxiv-2511-05154:
F. Lesjak and co-authors set upper bounds on the air content of two puffy hot Jupiters, KELT-11b and WASP-69b. Both planets should show strong air features in starlight that filters through their skies during transit, if clouds do not block the view.

The team took high-resolution spectra over several transits with the CARMENES tool and used cross-matching to hunt for molecule signs. They bound the shares of key species and the pressure where cloud decks sit. Even a non-detection is of use here, since it caps what these swollen worlds can hold in their skies.
arxiv-2511-05254:
Leandro Souza and co-authors propose a gate-based quantum genetic algorithm for finding the best real-valued solution to a hard task. In their design, each candidate is a quantum circuit whose measured bits decode into a vector of real numbers.

Evolution acts on the circuits themselves, with mutation and crossover that swap gate blocks. Two forms allow fixed depth or depth that adapts as search goes on. Fitness comes from quantum sampling, using the mean decoded result. The plan aims to let circuit shape itself evolve toward strong solutions for users.
arxiv-2511-05354:
I. Simonenko and co-authors grow centimeter-scale single crystals of cesium lead bromide, an all-inorganic perovskite, with a theory-guided plan. Large, clean crystals of this material are hard to make by easy methods, yet they are prized for light-based devices.

Their plan tunes each step of antisolvent vapor growth with theory. A nine-to-one mix of two solvents was picked to balance how much solid dissolves and how fast it forms. Ethanol was then chosen as antisolvent from the same kind of analysis. The paired route gives a recipe others can copy.
arxiv-2511-05454:
Jake Kettinger studies finite groupoids built from configurations of lines in complex three-dimensional projective space. Given a point and two skew lines, one line through the point meets both, a classic fact he turns into a machine.

That line lets him define a projection from one line to another, with a skew line as aide. The projections become the morphisms of a groupoid whose objects are the lines in a configuration. For select complex configurations, the automorphism groups stay finite. The work links a simple incidence trick to rich algebraic structure.
arxiv-2511-05754:
Giovanna Cottin and Francisca Garay report on Niñas Atómicas, a workshop that brings Chilean schoolgirls into real particle physics. The program aims to build critical thinking and the transferable skills scientists use daily. Girls from across Chile apply, and each year female scientists guide them for two weeks.

The girls learn particle physics, electronics, programming, and scientific method by building a working muon counter of their own. With those detectors they measured the muon flux and the muon's lifetime themselves. The authors describe the teaching plan, give the detector build in detail, and share how the 2024 and 2025 cohorts experienced the workshop. They offer the account to physics outreach and education communities.
arxiv-2511-05854:
Zepeng Bao and co-authors teach small models to catch hallucinations in large language models, the fluent but false statements such models produce. Checking must be cheap and fast, so small models are the practical tool. But training a small model to copy a fixed checking routine fails, because false claims come in many patterns.

Their framework, LEAP, first lets a strong teacher model explore checking strategies through a failure-driven loop. That planning skill is distilled into a small student. A proactive correction step lets the student review and improve its own plan before running it. On three benchmarks LEAP beat leading methods, and the authors offer it as a scalable safety check.
arxiv-2511-06054:
Alessio Arcudi and co-authors generalize the Isolation Forest, a popular method for spotting anomalies in data. The classic method isolates odd points by random splits, but its splits are rigid and biased. Their version, FuBIF, lets real-valued functions, not just single features, decide each branch of the isolation trees.

That freedom makes tree building far more flexible. A companion algorithm scores which features matter across the possible models, restoring interpretability that isolation methods often lack. The paper lays out how the framework works, tests it against established methods, and discusses its theory. An open-source implementation is provided. The authors aim at anomaly detection that is both more adaptable and easier to explain.
arxiv-2511-06254:
Teng Shi and colleagues rebuild generative recommendation around parallel generation instead of one-token-at-a-time decoding. In generative recommendation, each item is a short sequence of discrete tokens called a semantic ID. Standard models generate those tokens left to right, which blocks attention to later tokens and lets early mistakes poison the rest.

Their system, LLaDA-Rec, uses discrete diffusion to produce the tokens in parallel with bidirectional attention and a flexible generation order. A parallel tokenization scheme, two masking designs, and an adapted beam search make the approach workable. On three real-world datasets it beat both classic ID-based recommenders and leading generative ones.
arxiv-2511-06654:
Fangu Chen proves a number theory result about supersingular primes, special prime numbers at which certain geometric objects behave in an simple way. Elkies had shown that elliptic curves over real number fields have infinitely many such primes. Chen extends that infinitude result to some abelian fourfolds from classes constructed by Mumford.

The result also covers certain classes of Kuga-Satake abelian varieties, which are higher-dimensional relatives of elliptic curves. The proof studies deformation spaces at closed points of an integral model of a Shimura variety, building on work by Madapusi. It also analyzes real points on a Shimura curve, following Shimura, linking the arithmetic of these varieties to the distribution of their supersingular primes.
arxiv-2511-06754:
SlotVLA is a system for robot control built by Taisei Hanyu and twelve co-authors. Instead of feeding a robot model one dense picture embedding, it breaks a scene into separate objects and the relations between them, much the way people reason about a tabletop task. The team also built LIBERO+, a benchmark dataset for testing this object-and-relation style of reasoning.

LIBERO+ adds box and mask labels plus tracking of each object over time to robot demonstration data. SlotVLA itself uses a slot-based visual tokenizer to keep object identities steady, a decoder focused on relations, and a language model module that turns the result into actions. Tests show the approach needs far fewer visual tokens while generalizing about as well as denser models.
arxiv-2511-07254:
Maksym Luz and Mykhailo Moklyachuk solve an interpolation problem for complex seasonal random series. The sequences have periodically stationary general increments of fractional order, a structure that blends cyclostationary, integrated, and fractionally integrated patterns. Interpolation here means finding linear functionals built from values that were never seen, using the rest of the record, which is itself seen through a periodically stationary noise series.

When the spectral density tables are known, the authors give formulas for the mean-square errors and the spectral characteristics of the optimal fit. When the densities are uncertain and only admissible sets are given, they derive the least favorable spectral densities and the minimax, robust spectral characteristics of the optimal linear fit. The results extend robust estimation theory to data with long memory and repeating seasons.
arxiv-2511-07454:
Seokcheon Lee offers a geometric reading of a puzzling trend in supernova data. Fits to Type Ia supernovae suggest the inferred Hubble parameter drifts slightly with redshift. That drift is often written as a power-law departure from standard cosmic time dilation.

Lee shows the pattern can arise from a small, gauge-dependent rescaling of cosmic time inside the Robertson-Walker metric. Background distances tied to the Hubble radius stay unchanged under that rescaling. Apparent changes in supernova brightness distances and light-curve durations then share one cause. The argument reframes an apparent anomaly as a coordinate effect rather than new physics.
arxiv-2511-07754:
Hiroshi Yokota models how orientation changes phase splitting in mixtures, a process cells use to organize their interiors. The minimal model mixes isotropic molecules, direction-sensitive molecules, and a solvent. Flory-Huggins mixing theory joins Maier-Saupe orientation theory to capture both effects.

For some interaction strengths, two phase lines appear and merge through their critical points, fusing two critical points into one. Droplets then form unusually fast because the transition turns weakly first-order. Such acceleration could matter inside cells where timely compartment formation is vital. The theory gives experimenters knobs to look for in synthetic mixtures.
arxiv-2511-07954:
Nimish Kumar Mahapatra studies a new family of cyclic septic number fields built from the Hashimoto Hoshi construction. Septic fields have degree seven, and their Polya group measures an obstruction linked to unique factorization of ideals. The family is indexed by integers and seems to produce unusually large Polya groups.

Mahapatra computes each field discriminant explicitly and describes when the Polya property holds under a stated condition. The family contains infinitely many non-Polya fields with unbounded group size. Assuming a standard conjecture, it also contains infinitely many Polya fields, and many fields prove non-monogenic with index one.
arxiv-2511-08054:
Yunqi Shi and colleagues introduce a macro placement method for chip design that works by repeated prototyping and packing. Macros are large circuit blocks whose positions strongly affect timing, power, and wire length. Their method first groups macros across levels and clusters cells with performance, power, and area awareness.

A placement prototype from DREAMPlace gives reference positions, then an angle based step spreads macros near the chip edge. A packing tree search adjusts groups and members under design constraints, repeating with subsets each round. Across seven cases, timing slack improves markedly over a leading academic placer and over the earlier conference version.
arxiv-2511-08154:
Fayez Abu-Ajamieh, Shinsuke Kawai, and Nobuchika Okada revisit the fermion mass problem of the SU(5) grand unified theory with machine learning. The original Georgi Glashow model cannot reproduce the observed pattern of fermion masses. Two known fixes add either a forty five dimensional field interaction or a twenty four dimensional one, and the authors ask which fix stays more beautiful, meaning closer to the original model.

Under that closeness measure, the twenty four dimensional option wins in both supersymmetric and non supersymmetric versions. Generalizing with a continuous parameter and optimizing numerically points to a value near zero point eight as closest to the original theory.
arxiv-2511-08854:
Casper Christensen and Logan Riggs Smith take apart small transformer models in parameter space, hunting for the internal pieces that carry recognizable concepts. Mechanistic interpretability has decomposed toy models this way before, but the step to real, trained language models had not been taken.

The method, Stochastic Parameter Decomposition, is updated with a causal importance function suited to sequential data and a new loss. On a toy induction-head model it recovers the expected two-step circuit exactly. Applied to GPT-2 small, a genuine pretrained model, it surfaces subcomponents matching interpretable concepts such as golf and basketball. The authors present the work as a first bridge between clean toy decompositions and the messy parameter spaces of modern models, with handles that could later support direct intervention.
arxiv-2511-09154:
Souji Shizuma studies the prisoners and hats puzzle, a family of games where each prisoner wears a colored hat and must guess its color. Versions differ in how many prisoners and colors are involved, and in what the players may learn. The key divide is whether everyone declares a guess at once, or one after another.

Shizuma proves a general theorem about when a winning strategy exists for the non-simultaneous version, where later players hear earlier guesses. He then examines how building such strategies connects with the Axiom of Choice, a foundational assumption in set theory. The paper also compares the sequential case with the simultaneous one, where no player hears anyone else.
arxiv-2511-09354:
Martin Vejvar and Yasutaka Fujimoto make it easier to ask the same question of different kinds of graph databases. Their dataset, Spider4SSC, pairs natural-language questions with equivalent queries in SQL, SPARQL, and Cypher. Producing it required translating thousands of SPARQL queries into Cypher reliably.

Their parser, S2CLite, is a lightweight, rule-based translator inspired by programming-language compilers, needing no underlying RDF graph or external tools. On a standard test set it reached about 78 percent parsing accuracy. The previous state of the art managed near 44 percent in their comparison. Queries both systems parsed executed correctly about 97 percent of the time with S2CLite. The dataset holds 4,525 unique questions with matched query triples.
arxiv-2511-09554:
Isaac Robinson and four co-authors search automatically for object detectors that are both fast and accurate on a user's own dataset. Big open-vocabulary detectors often stumble on domains unlike their pretraining data. Their RF-DETR approach skips fine-tuning a heavy vision-language model. It fine-tunes one base network, then explores thousands of architectures sharing its weights.

Weight-sharing neural architecture search traces the accuracy-latency trade-off curve without retraining each candidate. The nano version reaches about 48 average precision on COCO in their tests. It beats its nearest real-time rival by more than five points at similar speed. The largest version tops 60 average precision on COCO, a first for real-time detectors, they report. It also beats a grounding model on Roboflow100-VL while running twenty times faster.
arxiv-2511-09754:
Sarthak Khanna, Armin Berger, Muskaan Chopra, David Berghaus, and Rafet Sifa tackle financial forecasting when the economy changes character. Models trained in one market regime often collapse in another, and simply mixing price numbers with news sentiment does not adapt. Their framework, called macro-contextual retrieval, anchors each forecast in past periods whose economic conditions look similar to the present.

The system embeds indicators such as inflation, unemployment, yield spread, and growth together with news sentiment, then retrieves matching past regimes at prediction time without retraining. Trained on seventeen years of S and P 500 data, it was tested on Apple and Exxon Mobil in 2024. It was the only approach with positive out-of-sample trading results, and its retrieved cases form readable evidence chains.
arxiv-2511-09954:
O. K. Khattab and seven co-authors publish two new radio continuum catalogues of the Small Magellanic Cloud from the ASKAP POSSUM survey. One image, at 944 megahertz, lists 36,571 sources, and a second at 1367 megahertz lists 15,227, each with arcsecond-scale resolution. The Aegean software generated the point source lists, giving astronomers fresh coverage of this nearby galaxy at two frequencies.

Cross-matching with an earlier MeerKAT catalogue found more than twenty-one thousand common sources at the lower frequency and over twelve thousand at the higher one. Combining the matched sets let the team estimate spectral indices for the full collection. The catalogues sharpen the picture of radio source populations in the Cloud and showcase what current telescopes can survey.
arxiv-2511-10254:
Jiulong Wu and six co-authors present Facial-R1, a model that analyzes facial emotions with explanations, not just labels. The task joins three subtasks: naming the emotion, recognizing the facial action units that compose it, and reasoning from those units to the emotion. Vision-language models attempt this but hallucinate explanations and often reason toward a label their own observations do not support.

Facial-R1 aligns reasoning with recognition in three stages: instruction tuning for basic emotional reasoning, reinforcement training with emotion and action unit labels as rewards. A data synthesis loop that expands training data from earlier stages. The team also built FEA-20K, a benchmark with over nineteen thousand annotated samples. Across eight benchmarks the model reached state-of-the-art results with strong interpretability.
arxiv-2511-10354:
Andrea Schimmenti, Valentina Pasqual, Fabio Vitali, and Marieke van Erp turn heritage texts into knowledge graphs that a computer can search, with help from large language models. Heritage writing holds rich claims in loose prose, hard to query in a planned way. Their method, ATR4CH, runs in five steps, from basic study and schema design through pipeline build, tuning, and full scoring, pairing ontology work with model-based pulling at each stage.

A case study on debates over the authenticity of disputed items in Wikipedia used three language models in a row. Scores were very high for metadata and proof pulling, mid-range for entity and claim pulling, and smaller models held up well, which cuts cost. The team warns that human checks in post-processing are still a must.
arxiv-2511-10654:
Javier Marín tests an assumption that agentic software quietly relies on: that a large language model can reliably tell whether a deadline window is still open or has already closed. He characterizes this temporal constraint processing across eight production-scale models using deadline detection tasks.

The results expose deployment risks. Performance is bimodal, with models scoring either about 95 percent or about 50 percent accuracy, and mere formatting changes swing scores by 30 to 60 percentage points. Failing models show extreme action bias, with false positive rates of 100 percent, and model size does not predict success. Fine-tuning on 200 synthetic examples helped models with partial ability, but Marín argues the skill needs dedicated architecture, not just more training.
arxiv-2511-10754:
Maximilian Gaschler, Andreas Schäfer, and Sebastian Waeber use holography to study a predicted anomaly effect in Weyl semimetals, materials whose electrons behave like relativistic particles. Their model is a hairy magnetic black brane in an Einstein-Maxwell-Chern-Simons-dilaton theory, with the scalar and gauge fields fully back-reacting on the geometry.

Driving the system with time-dependent sources, they follow the response after an electric pulse ends. The dual theory's anomaly produces current oscillations that live long at low temperature. Non-linear effects do speed the decay, by a temperature-dependent amount, yet the lifetime of the time-translation symmetry breaking states can still be made arbitrarily large by cooling enough after the quench. The authors note the effect might be realizable experimentally in Weyl semimetals.
arxiv-2511-10854:
Vade Shah and Jason R. Marden compare two ways of charging electricity users for peak demand, the maximum load that strains grids and risks blackouts. Under anytime peak pricing, each consumer pays for their own individual maximum consumption; under coincident peak pricing, they pay for what they use during the system-wide peak.

Modeling the market as a strategic game, the authors characterize equilibrium peak demand under both schemes. With perfect information, coincident pricing never produces a higher equilibrium peak than anytime pricing. With imperfect information, though, the coordination coincident pricing encourages can backfire and create larger peaks. Preliminary results suggest progressive demand charges, rather than flat per-unit fees, might keep the coordination benefits while softening the miscoordination risk.
arxiv-2511-11054:
Xiang Li, Jun Liu, and their colleagues build a tuning-free method for estimating a target value and its noise spread together when data have heavy tails. Heavy tails mean rare extreme values can wreck standard estimates, and most robust tools need the spread in advance or a tuning choice. Their Catoni-type frame solves two linked equations at once, with no tuning step.

The frame is worked out for mean estimation and for two forms of regression. The authors prove error bounds that match what an oracle that knew the spread could do, under only a mild moment assumption. A new proof toolkit based on a mirror theorem handles the non-convex equations.
arxiv-2511-11154:
Colin-Marius Koch and Michael Wilczek compare models of active particles, tiny self-driven units such as swimming algae, to see which model choices change group behavior. Two things govern such behavior: the single-particle model and the setting it runs in. Most studies vary the setting, so this study varies the model itself, guided by algae that move in a self-made oxygen gradient.

They vary contact rules, particle shape, drive style, and where mass sits inside the particle. In dilute settings, unlike models gave alike stats, but in dense settings group behavior split apart. The lesson is that models must match the real agent's fine traits to transfer.
arxiv-2511-11554:
Ziyang Zheng, Malte Schneider, and Luca Amendola study tests of the cosmological Euler equation. This equation governs how matter moves under gravity. The tests must work even if dark matter is slightly viscous. They must also allow failure of the equivalence principle, or gravity beyond general relativity. Untangling those three effects is the hard part.

A measure of principle violation is extended to a new form. The overlap between viscosity effects and principle violation is spelled out. In the small-viscosity limit, the principle can still be tested. A model-free measure of present-day dark matter viscosity is also defined. It can be read from galaxy counts by matching two galaxy groups. Forecasts for three coming surveys complete the study.
arxiv-2511-11654:
Sayambhu Sen and Shalabh Bhatnagar supply the missing theory for a popular traffic trick: letting each signal in a city act as an independent reinforcement learning agent. Cities such as Bangalore suffer severe congestion, and multi-agent Q-learning has cut delays in practice, but nobody had proved the method settles down.

Independent learners make convergence delicate, because every agent's environment keeps changing as the others learn. Stochastic approximation tools are used to study stability and convergence for the cooperative signal control task. A rigorous footing matters before cities trust learning systems with real intersections, and the analysis clarifies when cooperation among signals can be expected to stabilize.
arxiv-2511-11854:
Vahid Hemmati and six co-authors schedule fleets of urban air mobility vehicles so their flight plans cannot conflict, balancing demand against limited airspace capacity. Flying taxis will share constrained corridors, and separation must be guaranteed before takeoff rather than negotiated in the air.

Pairwise conflict avoidance starts from delayed departures computed with simple kinematics to hold safe distances, then scales to many agents through an optimization that sets departure times as traffic density grows. Average delay measures the price of safety. Simulations in varied multi-agent settings and real-world style use cases show large delay reductions while keeping operations collision-free, a planning layer future air taxi services will need.
arxiv-2511-12154:
Gustavo Polleti, Marlesson Santana and Eduardo Fontes introduce a foundational model for open banking data that learns from very few transactions. The model joins structured fields and free-text descriptions of each transaction into one representation. It adapts masked language modeling, a self-supervised method, to sequences of transactions.

In their study, the approach beats classical feature engineering and older sequence methods, and it works especially well when data are scarce. They describe it as the first large-scale study of its kind across thousands of financial firms in North America. Such representations could support fraud checks, credit risk work and customer insight across banks and regions.
arxiv-2511-12354: Tatsunari Watanabe and Ma Luo prove, over any field of characteristic zero, that the homotopy exact sequence of algebraic fundamental groups for the universal curve with unordered marked points does not split. The same nonsplitting holds for the universal hyperelliptic curve. Their approach extends a result of Chen to the profinite setting. It uses relative completions to detect that no such section exists. In short, the split is ruled out in full.
arxiv-2511-12454:
Moreom Akter and four co-authors investigate how feedback from active galactic nuclei, the bright centers of galaxies, affects star formation in red spiral galaxies. Red spirals are unusual because spiral galaxies are usually blue and actively forming stars. The team compares hundreds of red and blue face-on spirals drawn from low-redshift galaxy clusters, using optical and X-ray data.

Line-ratio diagrams that classify nuclear activity show most red spirals carry signs of an active nucleus or a related low-ionization region, consistent with feedback that quenches star formation. Blue spirals, by contrast, often show high X-ray brightness tied to activity that may be boosting star birth. The results support feedback acting in both directions.
arxiv-2511-12654:
Offer Kopelevitch studies the eigenvalues of the complex Ginibre ensemble, a standard model of random matrices whose entries are random complex numbers. He looks at an unusual event: a fixed share of the eigenvalues lands outside a disk that is slightly smaller than the disk where they normally gather. Conditioned on that rare overcrowding event, the eigenvalue pattern is no longer described by the usual determinantal formulas, except in one limiting case.

Kopelevitch still manages to estimate how likely the event is, for large matrices, and to describe how the eigenvalues arrange themselves in three regions. Inside and far outside the disk, the pattern looks like an ordinary Ginibre ensemble. Near the disk's edge, after rescaling, it matches a known point process that appears near a hard wall. The paper adds rare-event detail to a classic random matrix model.
arxiv-2511-12754:
Benjamin Li and nine co-authors build an agent that can team up with partners it has never met. In human-agent teams, people bring their own habits, and those habits can change mid-task, so a fixed partner model fails. The authors' framework first learns a latent space of strategies from agent trajectories using a variational autoencoder, then clusters that space into recognizable strategy types. A cooperator agent trains against partners of each type.

When a new partner arrives, a fixed-share regret algorithm updates the agent's guess of the partner's type during play. Tests used a modified Overcooked game, a two-player cooking task with time pressure and many possible strategies, plus an online study with human players. The agent beat existing baselines when paired with novel human and agent teammates. The work targets real teamwork settings where reading a partner quickly is the whole job.
arxiv-2511-12854:
Alexander Lindermayr, Kirk Pruhs, Andréa W. Richa, and Tegan Wilson study coflow scheduling, the problem of routing many machine-to-machine transfers through a reconfigurable network. The standard theory assumes every transfer is large, so demand is modeled as whole units moved in a sequence of matchings. Real workloads include small transfers that bulk-tuned algorithms handle badly. The authors ask what fractional matchings and indirect routing can do in that small-demand regime.

They design algorithms that perform much better for small demands than the literature's bulk-oriented methods, and they compare the two relaxations to see which buys more. Splitting transfers, or routing them indirectly, changes what schedules are possible. The paper is theoretical, aimed at data center networking, where coflows from distributed jobs compete for the same fabric and small flows should not wait behind bulk assumptions.
arxiv-2511-13054:
Bo Fang and five co-authors make video models actually look at the video. Reasoning models adapted to video often reason from text habits and sparse frames, shortcutting around the visual content and hallucinating. Their Pretext-GRPO algorithm rewards the model, inside the standard R1 reinforcement pipeline, for solving pretext tasks about transformed visual inputs, so it cannot succeed without genuinely processing what it sees. ViSS-R1 integrates that self-supervised signal directly into post-training: the model must answer both pretext questions about the transformation and the user's real question, identifying the transformation and mentally reconstructing the original video.

Across six widely used video reasoning and understanding benchmarks, both the algorithm and the full framework outperformed prior approaches. No new human labels are needed: the supervision is manufactured from the videos themselves.
arxiv-2511-13154:
Gianluca Inguglia and three co-authors hunt gravitational waves by teaching a network what normal noise looks like. Their target is short bursts, under about two seconds, such as mergers that form intermediate-mass black holes, which are hard to separate from detector noise but brief enough for cheap machine learning. A deep convolutional autoencoder learns to reconstruct ordinary time-frequency spectrograms; anything it reconstructs badly is flagged as an anomaly. Tested on Einstein Telescope mock data, the initial system caught twenty-three percent of injected intermediate-mass merger signals in a single detector.

Adding weak supervision transformed the results: the model recovered every injected merger of that class. Regardless of mass or signal strength, at about four and a half false alarms per year for one interferometer. The pipeline flags anomalies without yet classifying them, a deliberate first stage.
arxiv-2511-13254:
Shalini Maiti and 10 co-authors show how careful averaging of model weights can lift large language model scores without new training. Averaging, called souping, is cheap, but plain averages can harm skills that need fine precision. Their method, SoCE, chooses and weights models in a more guided way.

SoCE groups benchmark questions into clusters whose scores barely move together, then finds an expert model for each cluster. It combines those experts with tuned weights rather than equal shares. The approach raised scores and stability across several domains and reached top results on the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard, a public test of tool use by language models.
arxiv-2511-13354:
Tsviatko V. Rangelov, George D. Manolis, and Petia S. Dineva derive a half-plane Green's function for elastic waves in a one-dimensional hexagonal quasicrystal sheet. Their setting uses anti-plane strain, where motion points out of the sheet plane. Green's functions give the response to a point source and anchor many later calculations.

The authors obtain a frequency-dependent fundamental solution together with the half-plane Green's function in analytic form. They also give closed-form free fields for shear waves traveling through the sheet. The results lay groundwork for grasping how quasicrystals behave under dynamic load and for building sharper computational methods for them.
arxiv-2511-13554:
Eduardo Abi Jaber, Elie Attal, and Dimitri Sotnikov give a fast way to simulate Hawkes processes, which model events that trigger more events. Classic exact simulators draw jump times first, so their cost is random and can explode with busy activity or sharp kernels. The new scheme works on a fixed time grid with set cost.

Using the affine Volterra structure, they first simulate the integrated intensity and event counts from inverse Gaussian and Poisson laws, then recover jump times easily. The method covers any non-negative, locally integrable kernel, even singular ones. They prove weak convergence in a standard topology, and numerical tests showed large speed gains with high accuracy.
arxiv-2511-13854:
August Berklas and Jonathan Pober test how much a popular analysis tool for early-universe radio data depends on its own built-in model. The 21 cm signal from neutral hydrogen is a leading probe of the Epoch of Reionization, when the first stars lit up the cosmos. The sampler 21CMMC pairs with the simulation code 21cmFAST to draw limits from telescope data.

The pair made two fake data sets that differ only in how the code marks ionized bubbles, then checked whether the sampler recovered the right answers. It did so only when the sampling model matched the model behind the fake data. Their finding pushes the field toward analysis methods that lean less on one assumed model.
arxiv-2511-13954:
Nilay Kumar, Priyansh Bhandari, and G. Maragatham read emotions from brain waves while modeling how brain regions talk to each other. EEG signals offer a direct window on emotional activity, but many recognition systems ignore the shifting interplay between cortical areas. Their model, RBTransformer, turns the signals into band entropy tokens tagged with electrode identity.

Attention blocks then build an electrode-by-electrode map of learned dependencies, letting the network capture inter-cortical dynamics in latent space. A classification head reads the result and names the emotion. The design aims at higher accuracy by treating emotion as a moving pattern across the whole cortex rather than a set of isolated channel readings.
arxiv-2511-14054:
Zhongwei Shen studies how the ground state of a magnetic Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator fades across a domain. The operator comes from a Schrödinger problem with a magnetic potential in a bounded Lipschitz domain, and a parameter controls the field strength. The magnetic field is assumed to vanish only in controlled, finite-type ways at the boundary.

Shen proves that once the field strength passes a threshold, the ground state decays exponentially away from the boundary region where the field vanishes to the highest order. In other words, the state concentrates near special boundary points picked out by the field's vanishing pattern. The result adds to the spectral theory of magnetic Steklov problems.
arxiv-2511-14254:
B. Ananthamoorthy, Debbijoy Bhattacharya, P. Sreekumar, and one co-author find more faint ultraviolet sources by respecting how background light actually behaves. Catalogs from the UltraViolet Imaging Telescope aboard AstroSat were built with simpler background assumptions. Because photon counts follow a Poisson distribution, modeling that distribution properly lets real faint sources stand out from noise.

Tested on sparse fields, the Small Magellanic Cloud, and a field in M31, the method recovered many more sources than earlier UVIT studies, with gains ranging widely by field. Most new sources sit at the faint end of the brightness range. Counterparts at other wavelengths were identified for most of them, opening new classes of ultraviolet objects to study.
arxiv-2511-14554:
Mohammad Romani presents ForensicFlow, a deepfake detector that fuses three kinds of forensic evidence. Modern fakes hide flaws that a single network branch can miss. One branch checks global visual inconsistencies with a compact convolutional model. A second branch hunts fine texture anomalies with a transformer. A third branch reads spectral noise patterns.

Attention based pooling weights frames with the strongest evidence most heavily. Adaptive fusion then weights each branch by forgery type. Trained on a celebrity deepfake data set, the model reports high accuracy and area under the curve. Ablation tests confirm each branch helps. Heat maps show focus on true manipulation zones like face edges.
arxiv-2511-14754:
Leon Kleebank, Frank Vewinger, and five co-authors report the first observed critical scaling for the ideal Bose gas class of phase changes. Near a phase transition, key quantities blow up in patterns set by the system's universality class. Interacting quantum gases share the XY model class, but theory predicts a noninteracting Bose gas forms a class of its own.

The team studies a two-dimensional gas of photons that barely interact, held in a microcavity and cooled through contact with a dye reservoir. By measuring how correlations stretch near the condensation point, they extract the key exponent. The value tests a long-standing prediction that had never met an experiment before.
arxiv-2511-14854:
Emma Albertini, Michael L. Graesser, and Gabriel Herczeg show that two famous recipes for copying gravity solutions into electromagnetism are secretly the same. The double copy idea turns hard Einstein equation solutions into easier Maxwell and wave solutions. One recipe uses the Kerr-Schild form of a spacetime, while the other uses twistor geometry and a tool called the Penrose transform.

For a broad family of self-dual vacuum solutions, the authors prove the two recipes agree. The proof stays elementary, leaning on null changes of coordinates and on functions over twistor space. A worked example with a rotating charged-like spacetime shows the match in detail, with a longer companion paper promised for full proofs.
arxiv-2511-14954:
Sam Chow and Qing-Long Zhou study how well points on a torus can be approximated when the target itself keeps moving. A sequence of integer matrices repeatedly transforms a fixed vector, and the question is which other vectors are hit, again and again, by shrinking boxes around the transformed points. This twisted setting blends number theory with the geometry of tori.

Under mild conditions, the authors prove a sharp either-or law for the size of the good set, valid for almost every starting vector under broad fractal measures. Dropping all limits on the box sizes, they prove the same law for almost every vector in the ordinary sense. The work settles a variant of an open problem in the area.
arxiv-2511-15354:
Hanyue Wang and forty-six co-authors measure higher order galaxy grouping using galaxy multiplets from a major spectroscopic survey. Multiplets are small groups of nearby galaxies treated as single objects. Their grouping relative to the general galaxy field is measured with an efficient estimator. Luminous red galaxies from the second data release supply the sample.

Multiplets cluster more strongly than single galaxies, tracing more massive dark matter halos. Mock catalogs from large simulations underpredict that multiplet grouping, even while matching normal pair grouping. Standard halo occupation models thus miss multiplet properties. The mismatch shows multiplets carry extra constraining power. Future galaxy models must reproduce this higher order signal to be considered complete.
arxiv-2511-15754:
Yuhan Liang, Huiping Han, and twelve co-authors show electric control and readout of antiferromagnetism in a layered device at room temperature. Antiferromagnets order magnetically but show no net magnetization. That promises fast, dense, low-energy storage, yet the same trait makes their order hard to probe or control. Their stack places a heavy metal on an antiferromagnetic insulator grown on a ferroelectric substrate.

The magnetic order is detected through an anomalous Hall signal, an extra voltage tied to magnetism. Ferroelectric and piezoelectric effects from the substrate change that signal by a third in a lasting way. Synchrotron X-ray checks confirm the effect. Polarization seems to be the main control lever, a step toward efficient spintronic devices.
arxiv-2511-15854:
Steven Adams, Elize Alwash, and Luca Laurenti present a Python package that approximates Gaussian mixture models by discrete ones, with error guarantees. A Gaussian mixture models data as a blend of bell-shaped parts. Quantization replaces it by finitely many points, needed for control and checking of physical systems. Their tool measures the error in Wasserstein distance, which compares two spread patterns by transport cost.

The package builds on leading quantization methods and extends them for scale. It also adds sigma-point methods, a classic sampling approach, behind a modular interface that supports custom schemes. Benchmarks cover high-dimensional, large, and degenerate mixtures. Results show accurate approximations at low cost, ready for use in cyber-physical pipelines.
arxiv-2511-16054:
