Gwen Yidou-Weng, Ian Li, and five co-authors present Learning to Look Ahead, a hybrid method for controlling language model generation with exact future reasoning. Controlled generation must enforce sequence-level rules about syntax, style, or safety that depend on tokens not yet produced, making exact conditioning of an autoregressive model intractable. Hidden Markov model surrogates can answer future questions exactly but usually ignore context weakly.

Their design conditions a shared tractable surrogate on base model embeddings through a small neural head that sets only a latent prior per prefix. All next-token candidates are scored in one batched forward update, avoiding costly rescoring. Experiments improve continuation likelihood over standard surrogates and extend lookahead control to vision-language models.
arxiv-2511-16654:
Elias Lumer and seven co-authors compare two ways of letting a language model search multimodal knowledge bases in retrieval-augmented generation, using financial documents full of charts and tables. The common pipeline summarizes each image into text before indexing, which throws away visual detail the answer may need.

On a new benchmark of forty question-answer pairs from earnings calls, direct multimodal embedding retrieval beat the summary-based approach clearly. It stores images natively in the vector space, and it gained thirteen points in mean average precision and eleven in discounted cumulative gain at rank five. Judged answers were also more accurate and factually consistent. The study shows summarization is a lossy bottleneck and native image embeddings preserve context worth keeping.
arxiv-2511-16754:
Douglas P. Finkbeiner, Joshua S. Speagle, and Tanveer Karim present GSPICE, a data-driven method for cleaning stellar spectra without leaning on precomputed stellar templates. Spectral pipelines must mask cosmic rays, fix wavelength solutions, and estimate noise while staying neutral about what objects might appear, a tension for template-based tools.

GSPICE models an ensemble of spectra as a multivariate Gaussian and predicts each pixel's expected value and variance from the other pixels. Comparing observations against those predictions exposes outliers, which can then be masked or replaced by the estimates. Applied to 3.9 million LAMOST spectra, variants of the method caught both single-pixel cosmic ray hits and extended systematics such as bad wavelength calibrations, and characterized the true per-pixel uncertainties. An application to diffuse interstellar bands shows the value of data partitioning.
arxiv-2511-16854:
Mohammad Khateri and eleven co-authors survey deep learning methods for MRI super-resolution, the software recovery of high-resolution scans from cheaper low-resolution ones. High-resolution magnetic resonance imaging is clinically valuable but costly and constrained by hardware trade-offs, so a reliable software upgrade path matters.

The survey examines the field from four angles at once: computer vision, computational imaging, inverse problems, and MR physics. It organizes methods into a taxonomy and studies architectures, learning strategies, benchmark datasets, and metrics, with attention to the quirks of clinical and research settings. Open challenges and future directions are spelled out, and the authors maintain a public collection of resources, tools, and tutorials. The result is a map for newcomers and a checklist for specialists.
arxiv-2511-17154:
Ignacy Mermer, Jakub Muszyński, Jakub Możaryn, and Krystian Rosłon propose an AI assistant for operators of the FIT detector in the ALICE experiment at CERN. Operators run a control system where faults must be judged fast, often with partial clues. The proposed assistant is meant to help spot the fault and suggest a fix while the run is still live.

The design pairs a large language model with a guarded search over checked FIT documents and past faults. Answers are to be drawn from that verified material, so advice stays tied to real procedures rather than free invention. The paper is a proposal, setting out the build and its aims; a working tool would still need trials with the operator team before it could guide real shifts.
arxiv-2511-17554:
Sumon Kanti Dey and six co-authors show how a respected health benchmark can misjudge a chatbot built for a different culture. The team evaluated a sexual and reproductive health chatbot serving an underserved community in India against HealthBench, OpenAI's rubric-graded benchmark for medical conversation. The automated grader scored the chatbot's answers consistently low. Human annotators and public health experts, reading the same answers, often found them culturally appropriate and medically sound.

The mismatches clustered around Western assumptions: how the law frames certain topics, norms about breastfeeding in public, which foods count as safe in pregnancy, and insurance-based cost expectations. The authors argue the failure lies in the rubric, not the chatbot. They call for culturally adaptive evaluation frameworks that hold quality standards while recognizing the norms and constraints of the populations a system actually serves.
arxiv-2511-17654:
Deepak Bolleddu presents Dialogue Diplomats, a multi-agent reinforcement learning system built to resolve conflicts and build consensus through dialogue. Negotiation matters where autonomous agents with competing goals must cooperate. Fixed rules adapt poorly when settings change. The system joins deep reinforcement learning with structured dialogue protocols. Agents negotiate over many rounds and adjust their play as the exchange unfolds.

Three parts carry the design. A Hierarchical Consensus Network mixes attention with graph neural networks. It models how agents depend on one another and where conflicts live. A Progressive Negotiation Protocol structures the multi-round dialogue, with adaptive concessions. A Context-Aware Reward Shaping step balances each agent's own goals against the shared goal. Bolleddu offers the system as an end-to-end design for joint choices in complex, changing settings.
arxiv-2511-17854:
Allen Roush and six co-authors introduce DeepDebater, an autonomous system built to take part in full competitive policy debate. Strong persuasion that is evidence-based and adapts its strategy is a hard test for AI, and earlier debate systems worked in shortened formats for lay audiences. DeepDebater instead aims at the complete, unmodified two-team format used in schools and colleges, with speeches, cross-examination, and rebuttals.

Teams of language model agents divide the work, critiquing each other through rounds of retrieval, synthesis, and self-correction drawn from a large public evidence corpus for policy debate. A live presentation pipeline lets the system perform end to end. The authors present it as a step toward machines that can argue a case at full length under real contest rules.
arxiv-2511-17954:
Freek Holvoet, Christopher Blier-Wong, and Katrien Antonio build spatial embeddings, compact numeric summaries of place, to improve insurance risk modeling. Climate, weather, and demographic data are rich but messy and high dimensional, so they are hard to feed into standard predictive models.

Their contrastive framework aligns satellite images and map features from across Europe with coordinate based codes, producing embeddings that any data set with coordinates can use. A French housing price case and a Belgian flood claims case both show better prediction and clearer risk classification than raw coordinates alone. The effects also generalize to regions without training data.
arxiv-2511-18254:
Siyi Li and six co-authors, Eric Eaton among them, estimate how each point in a laser scan moves between two scans. Self driving cars use such scans to track motion. Top methods train on one sensor type and are tested on the same type, so skill on new gear stays unclear.

The team find a surprise: for motion, training on many data sets helps, with no change to the model. Skill tracks the speed of the things seen in training more than the sensor used. Guided by that clue, they build UniFlow, a feed forward model that works on new sensors with no new training. A shared motion sense, learned from mixed data, beats narrow per sensor training.
arxiv-2511-18354:
Yixi Chen, Muhammad Bilal, Tie Ma, Zafar Ayyub Qazi, Marco Canini, and Suhaib Fahmy argue that the web needs rebuilding for its new main readers: AI agents. Pages are still structured for human browsing, and publishers have no native way to expose the meaningful units inside their content. A few large AI providers therefore crawl, chunk, and index the web on their own terms, leaving publishers little say over representation or credit.

Their proposal, AISTRAL, adds a publisher-controlled layer to the web. Publishers expose units such as passages, claims, and tables through governed interfaces they control, and a semantic resolver, like the domain name system but for meaning, helps agents find the right units. The authors frame the gap as structural, not something better crawling can fix.
arxiv-2511-18654:
Nayu Dong, Townim Chowdhury, Hieu Phan, Mark Jenkinson, Johan Verjans, and Zhibin Liao fabricate brain tumors in MRI scans to train tumor finders. Marked tumor scans are scarce, which starves auto segmentation tools. Hand built fakes take expert time, while deep generators need many marked pairs to start, the very thing that is missing.

Their Tumor Fabrication frame works in two stages from healthy scans alone, plus a small marked set. A coarse stage plants a rough tumor; a generative stage then refines it to look real. The flow is fully auto and yields large sets of paired scans and marks. More true looking training data should lift tumor segment skill in low data clinics. The trick is to fake well, not just much.
arxiv-2511-18854:
Yujing Wang and Weize Hong add language models to Git bisect, the tool that hunts the commit that broke a build. Classic bisect assumes a crisp pass fail test at each step. Real projects break that: flaky tests flicker, regressions skip around, and code drifts in sense from upstream.

Their frame walks the commit line with structured chain of thought checks at each step, built to cope with noise. Open and closed models are graded for the role, and one code model is fine tuned on a curated set of sense labeled diffs. Weak supervision, human fixes, and self consistency filters cut label cost. Across open projects the hunt gains a clear margin in points. Fault hunts get a semantic eye.
arxiv-2511-19054:
Yue Sun and three co-authors report evidence for a fundamental current limit in a superconductor, using narrow bridges carved step by step from a single crystal of iron selenide. Reaching the depairing limit, where current itself breaks paired electrons, matters for both physics and for quiet devices free of vortex motion noise.

As the bridge narrows, the critical current density grows by more than tenfold, signaling the depairing limit. In the narrowest bridge, thinner than the magnetic penetration depth, the critical current stays robust in a magnetic field, strong evidence for a vortex free state created by geometric constraint.
arxiv-2511-19654:
Stephen C Gravereaux and Sheikh Rabiul Islam compare two ways to tune language models for malware detection, asking whether a cheap adaptor can match full fine-tuning. Trustworthy malware verdicts need explanations a human can read, not just a label. Full fine-tuning updates every weight and scores best, but it is expensive. Low-rank adaptation, which trains only a small added component, is far lighter, and the team tests five of its configurations against a fully tuned baseline.

Explanation quality is scored with standard text metrics and a semantic similarity measure. Full tuning wins overall, by up to about a tenth on the main scores. Mid-range adaptors, though, beat it on two metrics while cutting model size and training time by roughly four fifths. The study maps the trade-off for security teams weighing cost against clarity.
arxiv-2511-20354:
Han, Luo, Qi, Rocha, and Wan locate forged regions inside 3D Gaussian splatting scenes. Their 2025 paper presents GS-Checker for tampering localization. Editing tools now reshape 3DGS scenes with ease. Malicious edits can fake content or steal ownership. Finding exactly which Gaussians changed is the defense.

Each Gaussian gains a tampering attribute flag. The flag learns to mark edited primitives directly. A contrastive mechanism compares key attributes between neighbors. Inconsistent Gaussians stand out against their surroundings. That comparison happens at the true 3D level. A cyclic optimization loop refines the flags repeatedly. No expensive hand-labeled 3D supervision is required. Experiments show accurate localization across edit types. Robustness held under various distortions of the scenes. Owners can audit released models for silent changes. The method guards both rights and public trust. 3D content forensics gains its first dedicated tool here. Code accompanies the paper.
arxiv-2511-20554:
Shah and Menezes test whether smarter marketing diversifies who shows up to code. Their 2025 paper studies recruitment for CodeDay, a student hackathon program. Open computing events often promote through affluent channels. Their pools then miss low-income and marginalized students. The program serves middle and high schoolers in the Pacific Northwest.

Marketing changed in three planned ways for the test. Promotion to affluent families was cut back on purpose. Targeted school-based messages replaced broad ads. Cost supports were stressed from the first promotion onward. Attendance and self-reported backgrounds were compared before and after. The share of low-income and marginalized students rose clearly. Overall attendance did not fall despite narrower promotion. Research rarely isolates marketing's own effect from program design. This study gives practical guidance for fair recruitment. Teacher and community partner channels carried the outreach.
arxiv-2511-20854:
Sree Bhattacharyya and colleagues harvest in 2025 a free source of memory data: tip-of-the-tongue posts, where people describe a half-remembered video and ask the internet to name it. Lab studies of what makes images memorable are slow and costly; one earlier dataset of 2,205 samples took two years to build. The team's ToT2MeM collection instead holds over 470,000 content-recall pairs. Its video subset alone pairs 82,500 clips with the words people used trying to recall them.

Two models show the data's value. Fine-tuned on ToT2MeM, vision-language models beat GPT-4o at writing open-ended recall descriptions of visual content. A second model, trained contrastively, performs multimodal tip-of-the-tongue retrieval, matching a vague description to the right clip. Both are firsts for memorability research, and the dataset is public.
arxiv-2511-21254:
Mridhula Venkatanarayanan and five coauthors set ground rules for simulating a lead-free solar material in 2025. The material, alpha-FASnI3, swaps toxic lead for tin in a perovskite crystal, but it degrades as the tin oxidizes, and published computer models disagree on its structure. The culprit is the tin atom's lone pair, two idle electrons that push the atom off-center through a pseudo-Jahn-Teller instability.

Systematic tests by Venkatanarayanan and her coauthors find the smallest sound model. A 4 by 4 by 4 supercell with randomly oriented FA molecules removes fake electric fields and keeps the cubic shape. Getting the band gap right also demands a hybrid PBE0 functional with spin-orbit coupling and a nonlocal dispersion correction acting together. Their warm simulations show the tin off-centering stays local and robust at room temperature, while matching the measured 300 K gap needs an even larger 6 by 6 by 6 cell.
arxiv-2511-21454:
Rahul Arora and Liton Majumdar test whether telescope data can tell a flat model of an alien atmosphere from a fully three-dimensional one, in 2025. One-dimensional models average a planet into a single column, while 3D circulation models track winds and day-night contrasts. Using the hot Jupiter HD 189733b, the authors ran 1D models and 3D models with both simple and full radiative transfer, under equilibrium and disequilibrium chemistry.

Arora and Majumdar find significant spectral differences, with 3D models generally showing weaker features. Their circulation runs also show sluggish heat redistribution deep down but fast winds aloft, shifting the hottest point eastward by about 16 degrees, matching earlier telescope hints. Feeding the spectra through a JWST noise simulator gives detection strengths from about 2 to 8 in transmission. In emission they range from about 6 to 37. Those numbers guide how many transits observers must stack.
arxiv-2511-21554:
Tom Markvart reimagines a solar cell as a steam engine made of light, in a 2025 theoretical essay. His model treats the cell as a mechanical open-cycle thermodynamic engine. Absorbed photons first thermalize, their electron-hole pairs settling at fixed volume, and that step produces chemical potential, the usable energy currency. The light beam's expansion under one-sun illumination and the drawing of current then appear as isothermal lost work, energy spent as the engine runs.

Markvart pushes the analogy to a pointed conclusion: the voltage a cell delivers corresponds to availability, the maximum useful work extractable, in the thermodynamic bookkeeping. That identification feeds back into the Shockley-Queisser detailed balance limit, the standard ceiling on solar efficiency, and produces a correction to it. The paper is a conceptual reframing rather than a device study, using photon number, beam spread, and entropy per photon to rebuild photovoltaics from first principles.
arxiv-2511-21754:
Jana Vráblíková and Bert Jüttler approximate the envelope, the outer boundary swept out, of planar domains that deform over time, in 2025. Envelopes matter wherever shapes move, but computing them for evolving domains is hard. The authors approximate the envelope with circular arc splines, curves prized for flexibility plus computational simplicity.

Their route runs through the medial axis transform, a skeleton-like graph describing a domain, lifted into Minkowski space, which mixes space with a time-like coordinate. Circular arcs there correspond exactly to arc spline domains. As a domain evolves, each branch traces a surface, and the envelope becomes a cyclographic image, a swept tube, of finitely many curves. The paper proposes and compares two pairs of approximation methods. A sweep-line algorithm with optimal complexity trims redundant envelope branches. Free-form domains are unions of simple worm shapes, each from one curve segment.
arxiv-2511-21854:
Bandyopadhyay and colleagues model how strong magnetic fields reshape iron-carbon alloy microstructure during heat treatment. Their phase-field model, a computer method that tracks growing regions of different crystal phases, couples chemistry taken from a standard thermodynamic database with magnetic demagnetization effects and elastic strain. They simulate the transformation from ferrite to austenite, two crystal phases of the alloy, at 1,023 kelvin under applied fields up to 20 tesla.

The model reproduced the elongated particle shapes experiments see at 8 tesla: chemistry alone grows round particles, magnetism stretches them along the field. Elasticity adds flat faces, together producing brick-like elongated particles under combined coupling in the simulations. Growth sped up with more carbon and slowed with stronger fields and larger misfit strain. In multi-particle runs, field-aligned neighbours merged while side-by-side ones ripened, guiding magnetically assisted heat treatment design.
arxiv-2511-21954:
Gruza and Łełyk work in mathematical logic on whether our axioms pin down the structures they describe. A scheme, a template generating infinitely many axioms at once, is called definite when it forces a unique structure, so every statement gets a fixed truth value. The best-known case is internal categoricity, where a theory described from inside determines its structure up to isomorphism.

The authors introduce a refined notion, Phi-definiteness, meant to unify and extend the scattered categoricity-like notions in the literature, including internal categoricity, strong internal categoricity, and intolerance. They argue the definition is robust, not an artefact of wording, and give concrete example schemes that separate these notions from one another, showing the concepts genuinely differ in strength. They close by asking how definite the induction and replacement schemes are, bearing on whether mathematical statements have determinate truth values.
arxiv-2511-22854:
Vamosi and Forkert make two AI models argue about cause and effect, and both improve. Causal inference is less a single calculation than a weighing of competing what-if scenarios. Their framework, CRAwDAD, stages it as a debate: one reasoning model produces a structured causal inference, the other hunts for logical flaws. On disagreement they challenge each other and revise until converging.

On CLadder, a benchmark tying questions to formal causal graphs across all three rungs of Pearl's ladder, debate paid off handsomely. DeepSeek-R1's accuracy rose from 78.03 percent to 87.45 percent, counterfactual questions jumping from 67.94 percent to 80.04 percent in the reported runs; Qwen3 improved from 84.16 percent to 89.41 percent. Strong models gained even from debating weaker partners, and both open models beat GPT-4's 70.40 percent baseline before debating. Diverse perspectives, not just bigger models, are a resource for causal problem-solving, they argue.
arxiv-2511-23254:
Amies-King and Lucamarini report the longest unrepeated White Rabbit time synchronization link yet demonstrated, stretching the commercial timing technology far beyond its usual range of tens of kilometres. White Rabbit normally delivers sub-nanosecond accuracy with picosecond precision over optical fibre. Long-haul stretches, including underwater cables, offer no place for intermediate amplifiers, which is why such distances had barely been attempted.

By carefully selecting and optimizing the endpoint hardware on standard telecom fibre, the pair synchronized clocks over a single 300-kilometre span with 51.34 dB of loss, reaching 99.86 percent uptime while keeping picosecond-level precision and sub-nanosecond accuracy, even in highly asymmetric link configurations. The result points to a scalable, standardized timing backbone for future quantum networks, where key distribution and entanglement swapping across cities all depend on clocks that agree almost perfectly.
arxiv-2512-00054:
G. K. Skinner and J. F. Krizmanic comment on claims for a large, thin lens proposed for color astrophotography. The lens is a polymer flat, diffractive design, optimized at several wavelengths over a set bandwidth. Its advocates promote it as a cheap route to large-aperture astronomy.

The comment argues that an earlier paper from the same group overstated the lens efficiency. Correcting the record matters because telescope makers may invest based on published numbers. The exchange is a normal, healthy part of optics research. Optimized at a number of wavelengths over a prescribed bandwidth is the design claim the comment examines and qualifies.
arxiv-2512-00754:
Asim Ghosh and Bikas Chakrabarti compare three ways to measure inequality in a 2025 paper. The Gini index dates to 1912, the Pietra index to 1915, and the Kolkata index to 2014. All three grow out of the Lorenz curve from 1905, which plots how income or wealth is shared across a population.

Each index sums up the curve's message in a different single number. Ghosh and Chakrabarti work out the exact relations among the three. They then test those relations on real data. Knowing how the measures connect helps economists translate between studies that picked different indexes.
arxiv-2512-00854:
Nguyen Thi Nguyet Nga, Nguyen Huy Thao, and Phung Van Dong propose a particle that does double duty in a 2025 physics paper. Their candidate is a neutral, vectorlike fermion, a particle much like known matter particles but with mirrored partners. Unified theories suggest such fermions might exist.

A slight break in a lepton-like symmetry can make these fermions nearly paired, forming quasi-Dirac states at the tera-electron-volt scale. The authors show such states can generate neutrino masses through a radiative process, where mass arises from loop effects. The same setup can keep dark matter stable. One particle type explaining two mysteries is an attractive economy.
arxiv-2512-01354:
Zhongjie Jiang argues that flaw-free fake data can harm AI models. Fake data is often made smooth and clean. Human text is not. It holds odd tails, quirks, and bounds from how minds work. Training on smooth data alone strips those traits out.

Over time that loss can speed model collapse. The model starts to copy its own bland output. Jiang shows that mimicking human bounds can reverse that slide. Keeping some imperfection in training data may help models stay sharp, varied, and closer to real human text. The claim reframes fake data quality: fluency and smoothness alone are poor guides if the end goal is a model that keeps learning.
arxiv-2512-01654:
Aaron Beyen, Faezeh Khodabandehlou, and Christian Maes study slow changes to steady nonequilibrium processes. A steady process still flows, with heat or current at play. Slow cyclic changes add excess to key traits. Those traits include activity and entropy flux.

The excess takes a geometric form, a Berry phase. Its potential and curvature encode the response. The team evaluates those terms for slow drives. Geometric response laws help design small engines and sensors that work far from equilibrium. Berry terms are geometric, so they depend on the path of the drive, not its speed, which gives them a robustness experiments can exploit.
arxiv-2512-02054:
The vacuum of space may act like a material when fields grow strong. Some theories let it break CP symmetry, the mirror rule that links matter and antimatter. Three authors, Ospedal, Turcati, and Duarte, study this kind of electrodynamics in 2025, one where the field equations are not linear.

First they work out the field equations and how waves move through a magnetic background. They find the CP-breaking term makes the vacuum respond in unlike ways along unlike axes. Then they compute small shifts to the heat laws of blackbody radiation. The work tests how strange vacuum behavior would show up in light and heat.
arxiv-2512-02254:
How can you tell whether a real network plausibly came from a given random model? Narayan Sabhahit and a large team address in 2025 the construction of typical networks from a model, deterministically, so that a dataset can be compared against what the model usually produces.

Network scientists constantly judge whether a model explains an observed network, from friendships to protein interactions. A deterministic way to build the typical case gives that judgment a concrete reference point. The work strengthens the basic statistics of networks, where randomness is both the model and the obstacle to testing it.
arxiv-2512-02354:
Aadityan Ganesh, Clayton Thomas, and S. Matthew Weinberg study the rules that set fees on blockchains. When users pay to get a transaction included, the fee rule shapes what miners and users do. A good rule should be simple to follow on chain, with no gain from gaming the system.

Their 2025 study adds a stricter test: a miner should gain nothing from a side auction held off chain. The authors characterize fee rules that pass this off chain influence proof test. The results help designers build fee markets that stay fair even when side deals are possible. Fee rules shape trust, and trust is what lets a chain gain and keep its users.
arxiv-2512-02554:
Changxiao Ma and eight co-authors generate fake pedestrian images to train person recognition systems. Person re-identification matches the same person across cameras, but large labeled datasets are hard to build. Privacy limits and labeling costs keep real data scarce.

Synthetic people could fill the gap, yet past generators often lose the person's identity or give users little control. OmniPerson is a unified generator built to preserve identity while staying controllable. Better synthetic data could improve recognition training without filming more real people, a gain for both accuracy and privacy. Fake crowds can be made in bulk, while real crowds take time, cost, and care to film on the street.
arxiv-2512-02654:
Víctor Mayoral-Vilches and six co-authors report a banner year for their security AI in hacking contests. Capture the Flag events test teams on real style security puzzles under time pressure. The authors ask whether such competitions are becoming obsolete as AI agents improve.

Their system, Cybersecurity AI, is described as topping multiple major events in 2025. The authors report it outranked thousands of human teams again and again. Whether or not contests fade, results like these force a rethink of training, defense, and how security skill is measured. Scores like these will push schools and firms to train staff in new ways for a new kind of foe.
arxiv-2512-02954:
Jared Siegel and eight co-authors measure how strongly exploding stars and black holes push gas around inside cosmic structures. Baryon feedback redistributes gas away from the dark matter layout and suppresses the matter power spectrum on small scales. The size and scale pattern of that suppression are uncertain.

The team reads feedback strength from X-ray gas mass fractions, kSZ effect profiles, and galaxy galaxy lensing together. Three probes agreeing point to strong feedback, per the title. Pinning feedback down is essential before weak lensing surveys can turn galaxy shapes into tight cosmology. Three eyes that agree beat one eye that shouts, and that is the strength of the case this team puts in print here.
arxiv-2512-03054:
Ciro Benito Raggio and eight co-authors make federated medical learning cheaper so poorer hospitals can join. Federated learning lets institutions train shared deep learning models without pooling their data. Heavy resource demands, though, exclude centers with limited computing, widening healthcare disparities.

Their green AI approach freezes parts of the encoder adaptively during training. The test task converts MRI scans to CT like images across sites. Lower cost training invites more diverse hospitals in, which improves the shared model and spreads its benefits more fairly. Low cost is not a side gain here; it is the point. A tool priced out of poor wards helps just the wards that need it the least in all the world.
arxiv-2512-03154:
Some early galaxies seem too bright for their age. Jacqueline Antwi-Danso and a large team study one such galaxy in this 2025 work. The Webb telescope found many bright galaxies in the first few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

Such galaxies may be seen during bursts, when star formation spikes for a short time. The team presents a galaxy they describe as a descendant of those first systems. Its traits can test ideas about quenching, when star birth shuts down. The work helps trace how the first galaxies grew and then settled. Its life story links the bright youth of galaxies to their quieter later years.
arxiv-2512-03254:
A treatment may help some patients and not others. Philippe Boileau and co-authors study how to detect such differences in this 2025 work. The usual test assumes all patients gain the same benefit, which is often false.

To find real differences, the traits that modify the effect must be measured well at the start. The authors offer a differential variance method that leans on few assumptions. Sound detection of varied effects helps doctors target treatments. It also stops trials from missing benefits in subgroups. Variance-based tests ask whether effects spread out, a clue that subgroups truly differ.
arxiv-2512-03354:
Judging a new ad policy offline could save firms real money. Hongseon Yeom and co-authors study off-policy evaluation for ad auctions in this 2025 work. Online A/B tests, the gold standard, use much engineering time and risk revenue from weak variants.

Off-policy methods reuse logged data instead, but ad auctions are harder than recommender systems. Policies there are often deterministic, always picking the same action. The authors add stochastic modeling to make evaluation reliable. Better offline tests let ad platforms improve without costly live trials. Stochastic policies match how ad auctions really randomize, which sharpens offline estimates.
arxiv-2512-03654:
Sheoran and Dev show how to coax spin currents out of magnets whose symmetry seems to forbid them. Spin currents promise low-power chips, but plain antiferromagnets and higher-order altermagnets ban them outright. Their 2025 analysis uses spin point group theory to find the loopholes.

Electric fields, strain, and mixes of the two can tip these solids into states where spin flow is allowed. Magnetoelectric and piezomagnetic couplings break that symmetry. Quantum and transport math on five test materials backed workable cases. Charge-to-spin turning came close to one hundred percent through one route and reached about forty percent through another, in real settings.
arxiv-2512-04554:
Marco Pintore, Maura Pintor, and Dimosthenis Karatzas show how a forged document can trick systems that answer questions about pages. Document question answering reads a page image and replies from its content, with no separate text step. That design is handy but opens a new attack path. Their 2025 arXiv paper crafts edits that the eye cannot see yet the model reads as real content.

The attack algorithms reshape a document in faint ways tuned to a goal. One goal plants a chosen false answer. Another aims to break answers across the board. The team tested the forgeries on two leading end-to-end models, including Pix2Struct. Both systems fell for the fakes at troubling rates. Such results warn builders of document tools in law, finance, and health care. Defenses must check not just what a page says to people, but what a model sees in it.
arxiv-2512-04954:
Rajneil Baruah presents a technique for estimating what parameters plausibly produced some data, without ever training on sample answers. The task, amortized posterior inference, suits high-dimensional inverse problems where each new dataset would otherwise need a fresh, costly analysis. His 2025 arXiv paper trains normalizing flows with likelihood-weighted importance sampling, so the flow learns straight from the model and the observed data.

Benchmark tasks in two and three dimensions, with posteriors split into several islands, expose a subtle flaw. Flows that start from a single-humped base distribution paint false bridges of probability between the islands. Starting instead from a Gaussian mixture with the right number of humps sharply improves the fit. The lesson is plain: match the base's topology to the target's shape. Cosmologists and engineers who invert complex models gain both speed and honesty from such flows.
arxiv-2512-05054:
Radu Precup and Andrei Stan adapt a classic variational tool, the Nehari manifold method, into the language of fixed point theory. The Nehari method sorts candidate solutions of an equation by their energy and has long belonged to calculus of variations. The authors rebuild it for systems of operator equations. The goal there is to find inputs that an operator returns unchanged — fixed points. They lean on Schauder's and Schaefer's fixed point theorems rather than on energy minimization.

The framework is deliberately open-ended, leaving room to combine the Nehari-style sorting with other fixed point principles later. To show the machinery works outside abstraction, the authors apply it to a system of nonlinear integral equations, where the method delivers solutions. The result widens the reach of a well-tested idea, giving analysts a new route to existence proofs for coupled systems that resist variational treatment.
arxiv-2512-05354:
Yang Zheng and six co-authors introduce SplatPainter, a model for editing three-dimensional Gaussian scenes by painting in two dimensions. Gaussian splatting has made photorealistic three-dimensional assets easy to create but hard to refine: diffusion-based or optimization-based editors are slow, damage the asset's identity, or lack fine control. SplatPainter instead predicts updates to a compact, feature-rich Gaussian representation directly from the user's edits in one or more views.

Test-time training makes the workflow state-aware and iterative — the model adapts as the editing session proceeds, rather than treating each stroke as a fresh problem. One architecture handles local detail refinement, local paint-over, and consistent global recoloring, all at interactive speeds. By keeping edits feedforward instead of optimizing from scratch, the system preserves what the artist already liked. The authors present it as a step toward fluid, intuitive authoring of three-dimensional content.
arxiv-2512-05454:
Dan Cristofaro-Gardiner surveys a family of Weyl-type laws recently proved in low-dimensional symplectic geometry. Weyl laws, in their classical form, link the counting of vibrations or eigenvalues to the volume of the underlying space. Their symplectic cousins do something similar for capacities and periodic orbits in the geometry of phase spaces. Several such laws have been established lately, and they have already found striking applications.

The survey introduces the laws and what they are good for, then sketches a number of the proofs so readers can feel how the formulas are obtained and applied. As a survey by a contributor, the article doubles as an invitation: it organizes a fast-moving corner of symplectic geometry around its most usable results. Readers get the statements and the shape of the arguments — enough to see why these counting laws have become tools for problems far from their origins.
arxiv-2512-05554:
Hadrien Oliveri, Christophe Godin, and Ibrahim Cheddadi sketch a physics of how plants take shape. A plant is an open, out-of-equilibrium system: cells drink water osmotically, walls yield and stiffen, tissues push against each other, and form emerges from the fluxes. The authors argue this is active matter: matter that consumes energy to move and grow. Plant morphogenesis, they argue, deserves a theory in those terms, one that integrates water transport, tissue mechanics, and their biological regulation.

Drawing on the history of growth geometry and mechanics and on recent experiments, they lay out the modelling challenges. Chief among them: coupling imbibition at the cell scale to deformation at the tissue scale, under molecular control. Their outline is programmatic: steps toward a unified theory where regulation, force, and flow shape form. For a field split between genetics and mechanics, the paper is a bid to reunite the explanation.
arxiv-2512-05854:
Alexis Quintana and eight co-authors redraw the map of young star groups near the Sun using the Gaia satellite's precise star positions and motions. OB associations are loose families of massive stars, born together and drifting apart. They trace recent star formation. Old lists, some eighty years old, are overtaken by Gaia's astrometry. The team starts from a complete census of about twenty five thousand O and B stars within a kiloparsec of the Sun.

A clustering algorithm sorts those stars into fifty six OB associations, doubling the number known in this volume. Cross checks confirm the list is sound. The authors measure each family's mass, star count, spread of velocities, and expansion age. Most, thirty eight of the fifty six, are expanding in at least one direction, and a dozen expand across the sky in both. The new map sharpens the story of local star birth.
arxiv-2512-06254:
X Li, K Adamek, and their co authors build a faster pipeline for spotting brief radio flashes in the sky and pinning down where they came from. Next generation radio telescopes will pour out data far faster than old tools can scan. A flash may last a blink, so the search must keep pace without losing faint events.

Their pipeline pairs a new imaging tool that is tuned for passing events with a detector that flags them. The imager cleans up faint signals far better than standard tools and places them more precisely on the sky. In a test on a huge data set from the MeerKAT telescope, the full run took only a few minutes on one graphics chip, using modest memory. Trials on pulsar fields, both steady and flickering, showed robust results. Fast, exact spotting like this helps astronomers chase the sources of fleeting radio bursts.
arxiv-2512-06554:
The MMGPDs Collaboration, with Anoushiravan Moradi, Muhammad Goharipour, and co authors, measures the proton's electric and magnetic shape from a photon scattering process. Form factors describe how charge and magnetism spread inside the proton, and their slopes at small momentum transfer give the proton's charge and magnetic sizes, a topic of long debate. The team uses exclusive photon production data in the range where a simpler process, Bethe Heitler scattering, dominates the signal.

That dominance is a gift: the simpler process depends directly on the very form factors they want. Fitting the data with several standard shapes for the factors, they find the data pin down the electric factor well in their range, but say little about the magnetic one. Their charge radius comes out on the small side, in line with a recent high precision result. The method offers a second route to the proton's size.
arxiv-2512-06754:
Shrreya Rajneesh, Rakesh Kumar Sahoo, and Manoranjan Sinha control a soft robot arm for space use without any model of its body. A continuum arm bends along its whole length, which gives it dexterity in tight, obstacle rich places. That same endless flexibility, plus hidden friction and shifting stiffness, makes model based control unreliable: predicted motions drift, and the math can hit false singularities.

Their controller skips the model. It starts from a rough measured Jacobian, the map from tendon pulls to tip motion, and refines that map online as the arm moves. A real time optimizer picks each tendon step while keeping tendons from going slack and respecting shape limits. A new tension term in that optimizer curbs axial squeeze. Across circle, pentagon, and square paths, the arm converged smoothly with sub millimeter steady accuracy, and no calibration at all.
arxiv-2512-07454:
Amir Mohammad Akhlaghi, Amirhossein Shabani, Mostafa Abdolmaleki, and Saeed Reza Kheradpisheh wrote this 2025 language technology paper. Training a large language model for a low-resource language is costly. Their question is whether a small English-only model can be taught a new language cheaply.

Their model, Persian-Phi, starts from Microsoft's compact Phi-3 Mini. A staged learning plan first warms the model up with short bilingual stories. That step aligns the word embeddings before any heavy training begins. Light fine-tuning methods then adapt the model with modest hardware. Continual pretraining and instruction tuning follow in the same careful order. On an open Persian leaderboard, the small model performs on par with far larger rivals. The recipe, they argue, can carry strong models into other under-served languages. The finished model is shared in public for anyone to use.
arxiv-2512-07554:
Jianping Jiang and Frederik Ravn Klausen wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on a famous model of magnetism. The planar Ising model places tiny magnets on a square grid. At its critical temperature, far-apart magnets usually stay faintly linked.

The authors work just off that critical point, with a small outside field applied. They prove the linked influence between distant points fades exponentially fast. Their proof is deliberately simple and elementary in style. It weaves together three classic tools from the model's theory. A high temperature expansion handles one side of the argument. Random-cluster and random current pictures handle the other sides. One new ingredient does the heavy lifting in the middle. In the near-critical current picture, many loops of modest size appear. Two external edges tie each such loop's path to a ghost field. That loop abundance is what forces the decay in the end.
arxiv-2512-07954:
Alix Merolle and Quentin Glorieux wrote this 2025 optics paper on measuring a stubborn quantity. Group velocity dispersion describes how a medium spreads light pulses by color. In hot atomic vapors near resonance, standard methods for it fail.

Absorption, pulse distortion, and nonlinear effects corrupt the probe signal. Broadening tricks and interferometers both drown in that noise. Their method uses a steady laser with weak phase modulation instead. A slow photodetector watches the light after it crosses the vapor. The red and blue sidebands pick up different phase shifts on the way. The transmitted modulation contrast then oscillates as the frequency is scanned. At set frequencies the contrast vanishes completely, cleanly marking the dispersion. The idea borrows from spectroscopy tricks used in fluids of light. Applied to hot rubidium vapor, the scan maps dispersion across wide detuning. Different vapor temperatures extend the map further still.
arxiv-2512-08054:
Abdurro’uf, Dan Coe, Tom Resseguier, and a large international team of astronomers posted an observational study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is the brightest known galaxy beyond redshift six, a strongly lensed system nicknamed the Cosmic Spear. Gravitational lensing magnifies it, letting the James Webb Space Telescope resolve its young star clusters and star forming clumps in unusual detail.

New Webb imaging and spectroscopy reveal bright clumps plus a tail of three extremely compact star clusters, seen multiple times through the lens. Corrected for lensing, the clusters are only a few parsecs across yet hold millions of solar masses, making them far denser than local star clusters. Their ages are just millions of years, but their dynamical ages suggest they are gravitationally bound. The brightest clump hides a compact, intense star forming core. The study shows what the first generations of star clusters looked like.
arxiv-2512-08254:
Yun Liu, Tao Li, Guanghui Yue, and colleagues, computer vision researchers in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their method restores real world photos degraded by scattering, the haze like effect found in fog, sandstorms, underwater scenes, and remote sensing. Earlier methods lean on a single prior, or train on synthetic images and then struggle with real ones.

Their approach, called SFP, draws priors from both the spatial and the frequency sides of an image. In space, inverting a degraded image reveals a pattern tied to how much light the medium lets through, which guides recovery of the true scene. In frequency, two new observations steer a targeted boost for the bands that scattering weakens. A weighted fusion merges both results into the final picture. Across many real scattering scenarios, SFP beat leading methods and generalized well.
arxiv-2512-08354:
Yi Jian Du and Chongsi Xie, theoretical physicists in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is scattering amplitudes in Einstein Yang Mills theory, which mixes gravity with a gauge force. They seek a formula that rewrites the theory one loop integrand using only simpler Yang Mills integrands. The integrand is the core object in a loop calculation.

Their route starts from an algebraic construction of special numerators shared by related theories. Using a forward limit trick, they first write the integrand through tree level amplitudes. A two step expansion breaks those into scalar amplitudes, then rebuilds the result from Yang Mills integrands. They prove the expansion works when the coefficients in both steps meet one loop consistency conditions. Strikingly, those coefficients match the Yang Mills scalar formula exactly. They call that shared structure the right base for building the special numerators in both theories.
arxiv-2512-08454:
Joseph Lehec, a mathematician in France, posted a short note on arXiv in December 2025 about a famous inequality in convex geometry, the Blaschke Santalo inequality. A 2024 paper by Courtade, Fathi, and Mikulincer proved a related result, the symmetrized Talagrand inequality, using stochastic calculus, following the spirit of Borell classic proof of the Prekopa Leindler inequality. That symmetrized result can be read as a dual form of the functional Santalo inequality.

Lehec modest purpose, as he puts it, is to simplify their argument. He first recalls Borell original stochastic proof in brief. He then shows one simple twist in that proof which recovers the functional Santalo inequality directly, rather than through its dual form. Short notes like this matter in mathematics: a cleaner proof is easier to teach, to check, and to adapt to new problems. Readers who found the 2024 argument heavy are given a lighter route to the same destination.
arxiv-2512-08554:
Alexandre Dupont Bouillard, a mathematician in France, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. His subject is polyhedra built from induced trees and induced paths inside chordal graphs, a well structured family of networks. Extended formulations rewrite such a polyhedron in a higher dimensional space where optimization becomes easier. He constructs them for both objects.

The key step is proving that certain extended incidence vectors form a Hilbert basis for chordal graphs. That single fact yields the formulations, and also shows both polytopes have the integer decomposition property in this graph class. The tree formulation is compact. The path formulation needs exponentially many inequalities. He identifies which ones shape the faces, and gives a larger face defining set listable in polynomial time. As payoffs, finding the heaviest induced tree or path in a chordal graph becomes polynomial time solvable.
arxiv-2512-08754:
Jason Hughes and a large team report a multi robot system built for remote triage after mass casualty incidents. The system pairs aerial drones with ground vehicles that work as a team. The aim is to find victims, assess injuries, and set priorities for care without putting first responders at risk in the early phase.

Drones locate casualties and provide overhead views, while ground vehicles use special sensors to measure vital signs and to detect and locate physical injuries. Unlike past work focused on search alone, this system covers the full triage chain. That chain includes victim location, vital sign checks, injury severity grading, mental status assessment, and merging data for responders. Built for a defense research challenge, the system shows how robot teams can extend human capacity in disaster response and help save more lives.
arxiv-2512-09054:
Alon Arad and Saharon Rosset propose new ways to calibrate probability predictions in multi class learning. Well calibrated probabilities guide sound decisions, so their accuracy matters beyond raw accuracy scores. Isotonic regression works well for binary calibration, but its one versus rest extension to many classes has lagged behind in practice.

Their methods are built to respect probability normalization, a natural demand that earlier isotonic methods ignored. One method builds normalization directly into the fitting step. The other recasts the problem as a total order isotonic regression in both directions. Tests span text and image classification data sets and several model designs. The new method always improves log likelihood and expected calibration error over prior options. The authors ground the methods in assumptions that users already expect to hold. That mix of principle and results aims to make isotonic calibration practical again for multi class problems.
arxiv-2512-09154:
Rahul Kumar Padhy, Aaditya Chandrasekhar, and Amir Mirzendehdel present PILL CoDe, a method for the inverse design of polypills, single tablets. Polypills enable fixed dose combination therapy and tailored release schedules, and additive manufacturing can now print multi part tablets with custom release profiles. In practice, designs are still tuned by ad hoc parameter sweeps.

Their method optimizes tablet geometry and filler layout together to match a prescribed release curve. Shape is described by a supershape family, while filler spread is represented by a coordinate based neural network. Dissolution follows coupled equations for phase change and diffusion. The full process is built to be end to end tracked, so gradients guide optimization. Case studies with single phase and multi filler tablets match both steady and non steady target profiles well, showing a systematic route to custom release design.
arxiv-2512-09454:
Ronny Jean-Marie-Desiree and colleagues characterize a nanosecond electrical discharge struck in pure ammonia gas, using a plane-to-plane impulse dielectric barrier discharge. Such discharges matter for plasma applications, but how the discharge establishes itself, moment by moment, is not fully understood. The team set out to track its dynamics directly.

They combined fast imaging with electrical measurements, varying the applied voltage, gas pressure, and the size of the gas gap. Comparing current traces with the images exposed a strong correlation: the speed of the fast excitation and ionization wave matches the speed at which the current rises. That link appears only in the diffuse discharge mode, where a clear luminous front can be defined, and it holds with a single systematic proportionality across all the conditions studied. The authors propose further work to test how far that proportionality extends across other parameters.
arxiv-2512-09654:
Jakub Proboszcz leads a team asking whether an artist's work can be shown to have trained a generative audio model. That is a pressing copyright question as diffusion and autoregressive audio models grow in quality and are trained on corpora of recordings. Their tools are inference attacks, statistical tests run against the trained model.

Membership inference attacks, which test whether a sample was in the training set, prove weak at scale: for models trained on large datasets the per-sample signal is too faint. The team focuses on dataset inference, which pools the faint evidence across many samples, matching how artists hold collections of works rather than single files. Adapted from earlier text and vision research, dataset inference succeeds in the audio domain. The authors present it as a practical mechanism for copyright holders to check whether their catalogues fed a model, and for improving dataset accountability.
arxiv-2512-09854:
Muneeb Ur Raheem Khan studies how to reduce social bias in language model outputs without retraining the models. The work covers English and Urdu, a lower resource language where biased output is a known problem. His approach works at inference time, on the text a model produces. A preference ranking model scores candidate answers for bias and usefulness. Three methods are compared: plain generation, picking the best of several samples by score, and step by step refinement guided by the scorer's critiques.

The test set holds two hundred English prompts and their Urdu counterparts, spanning gender, ethnicity, religion, nationality, disability, profession, age, and class. One commercial model generated candidates while another scored them. Both guided methods improved clearly over the baseline in both languages. Urdu fairness scores stayed lower under every method, pointing to structural gaps in multilingual training. The two guided methods improved along different paths.
arxiv-2512-09954:
Pravin G presents CIDP, a design for anonymous communication on tactical military networks. The author states a trilemma: strong anonymity, low latency, and low overhead supposedly cannot coexist. CIDP claims to break the deadlock by adding entropy at the physical layer. Rapid modulation of antenna sidelobes injects randomness that masks transmissions, spreading signals toward the antenna's null space. Three parts work together: a network controller, a safety filter, and sidelobe tuning.

The controller uses Lyapunov drift methods to keep queues stable while maximizing entropy injection. A control barrier filter provably holds jitter within strict bounds for real time flows. The author extends the classic anonymity bound with a physical layer term, arguing that overhead and latency can shrink toward zero as injected entropy grows. Simulations and an FPGA prototype are reported, with larger anonymity sets and tight jitter compliance at small throughput cost.
arxiv-2512-10054:
Logan Robbins proposes an architecture for language models that write several document sections in parallel, inside the model itself. Ordinary autoregressive models have a single token frontier: each next word depends on everything before it. Existing parallel systems bolt external branches around an unchanged model. Robbins instead trains one architecture owning several causal frontiers at once. A planner at prompt time writes three outlines. Each outline routes to its own decoder stack, which shares a frozen lower trunk of knowledge with the others, and the decoders exchange delayed latent messages through a notes bus.

The paper is explicit about its status: it presents theory, design, and a preregistered evaluation protocol, not a positive result. Training and held out evaluation are still in progress. The proposed tests are causal and demanding: swapping or removing plans, ablating the message bus, a parameter matched control, and blinded human fact audits.
arxiv-2512-10254:
Juan Sosa, Erika Martínez, and Danna L. Cruz-Reyes turn Bayesian network statistics on the complete studio discographies of thrash metal's Big Four: Metallica, Slayer, Megadeth, and Anthrax. Starting from raw audio, they build song similarity networks in four layers, one each for loudness, brightness, tonality, and rhythm, enriched with outside information about each song. Each layer becomes a nearest neighbor graph of songs that sound alike in that feature. A family of hierarchical probit models is then fitted, with global and layer baselines, song sociability effects, pairwise covariates, and competing latent structures.

For every band, the richest specification, with stochastic block communities, predicted and fit best. Underneath, the networks are sparse but structured. Album membership and temporal proximity shape which songs connect. Latent communities and hub songs cut across albums and eras, grouping tracks by sound rather than chronology.
arxiv-2512-10454:
Ian Mochida and co-authors extend a well-used theory for computing the infrared spectra of water. The mixed quantum and classical approach developed by Skinner and others predicts the shapes of water's spectral lines well. But it was rarely used to predict their actual strength, which blocked direct comparison with measured spectra. Strength matters when spectra are used to judge samples.

The extended method computes the full complex refractive index of water directly, replacing the normalised scale of older studies. For the OH stretching region, the results matched experiments in both shape and intensity. The calculations also showed that a local field effect, the way nearby molecules reshape the light field, is essential to getting the intensity right. The approach now opens fresh analysis of bulk water, thin films, and small water clusters.
arxiv-2512-10654:
Sabrina Bonandin, Konstantin Riedl, and Sara Veneruso prove that a popular swarm optimisation method really finds the global answer. Consensus-based optimisation sends a cloud of particles wandering a rough energy landscape, pulled toward a shared consensus point weighted by the Laplace principle, so the swarm explores and exploits at once. It works on nonconvex, nonsmooth problems, but the practical, time-stepped version lacked a full guarantee.

The authors prove strong mean-square convergence of the discrete algorithm to the global minimiser for a rich class of objectives, covering both isotropic and anisotropic diffusion. Their result states clear conditions on the tuning settings and gives convergence rates in both the step size and the particle count. The proof views the discrete scheme through stochastic differential equations, borrows classical finite-time theory, and handles the awkward non-Lipschitz coefficients by discarding a small-probability event controlled by fine moment estimates.
arxiv-2512-10954:
Sicheng Mo and colleagues ask whether images in a diffusion model run could be made together instead of each one alone. In standard use, every sample is generated in isolation, so no information passes between them. Their method, Group Diffusion, shares the attention mechanism across a whole group of images during generation.

Shared attention lets images denoise jointly and learn links both inside each image and between different images. Larger groups showed stronger cross-sample attention and better quality, and the team devised a measure that tracks image quality scores closely. Built on standard diffusion transformers, the method improved results notably on a common benchmark. The work opens cross-sample work at inference time as a new lever for generation.
arxiv-2512-11554:
A T Eberlein and C N Pope tackle a classic puzzle in black hole physics. The math for a charged black hole, called the Reissner-Nordström solution, looks broken at its horizons, yet that break is only a flaw of the map, not of space itself. Earlier work placed the plain Schwarzschild hole inside a flat six dimensional space, but charged holes were only mapped in part.

Eberlein and Pope give the first full map for the whole charged hole, using a flat space with nine dimensions. They write the map with plain local formulas and as level sets of simple functions. The second horizon forces extra terms that the older map did not need.
arxiv-2512-11754:
Abhirup Bhattacharya and Onkar Parrikar compute how excited states bend entanglement in holographic theories. In holography, the entanglement of a ball shaped region maps to a surface in a curved bulk space. Turning on a double trace source in the boundary theory warps both the bulk shape and that surface.

The team computes the entropy shift to second order in the source strength from the boundary side. The terms become flowed correlation functions, which they then draw as Witten diagrams in the bulk. One graviton exchange diagram neatly reproduces the canonical energy term of the quantum Ryu-Takayanagi formula. The match confirms how bulk back reaction reshapes the entanglement wedge.
arxiv-2512-11954:
Alexander J Dittmann, Geoffrey Ryan, and Luciano Combi run the first systematic study of eccentric binaries drinking from thin accretion disks. Circumbinary disks steer the orbits of paired stars and paired black holes. Most past simulations used thick disks, fit for stellar pairs, leaving thin disk behavior open.

Thin disks drive pairs to spiral in fast and pump their orbit eccentricity hard. Thick disks settle pairs near eccentricity 0.425, while thin ones push past 0.6. The range of low eccentricities that decay to zero also shrinks for thin, low viscosity disks. The team traces these shifts to pressure effects in the inner flow. Black hole pairs in thin disks should stay eccentric into detector bands.
arxiv-2512-12154:
Hua Ma and six co-authors address a safety risk for energy forecasting in a 2025 paper. Large language models built for time series now forecast power use with no new training. Attackers can tweak inputs in small ways that fool these models, and such fakes are hard to spot.

Their plug in detector makes shorter copies of an input and compares the forecasts they produce. Real inputs give stable forecasts, while attacked inputs give forecasts that disagree. Tests used three models, TimeGPT, TimesFM, and TimeLLM, and three energy data sets. The method held up well under both black box and white box attacks.
arxiv-2512-12354:
Brian Hopkins and Aram Tangboonduangjit study restricted integer compositions in a 2025 math paper. A composition splits a number into an ordered sum of parts. Carlitz required neighboring parts to differ. Arndt later placed conditions on chosen pairs of parts rather than on single parts, opening a new family of counting problems.

The authors combine and generalize both notions. They prove counting results with direct combinatorial arguments and with generating functions, tools that pack counts into a single formula. Their work connects to gap-free compositions by Hitczenko and Knopfmacher. It also links to Rogers-Ramanujan partitions, a classic topic in number theory.
arxiv-2512-12454:
The HADES Collaboration reports the first observation of light hypernuclei in silver silver collisions in a 2025 paper. Hypernuclei are atomic nuclei that contain a lambda hyperon, a heavier cousin of the proton. At a collision energy of 2.55 GeV, the team saw two kinds, with three and four total particles, emitted near mid-rapidity.

They rebuilt the hypernuclei from their two body weak decays, using a neural network to sort signal from background. Yield patterns suggest feed-down from excited states boosts the four particle kind. Lifetime measures came out at 239 picoseconds for the three particle hypernucleus and 209 for the four particle one. The second sits 4.5 sigma below the free lambda lifetime.
arxiv-2512-12654:
Hassan Mujtaba, Hamza Naveed, and Hanzlah Munir model authorial style in Urdu novels through character interaction graphs in a 2025 paper. Authorship studies usually rely on word and style cues in the text itself. Narrative structure is less explored, above all for low resource languages like Urdu, where tools and data are scarce.

Each novel becomes a graph: characters are nodes, and edges mark characters appearing near each other in the story. The team compares hand built structural features, node level semantic summaries, unsupervised graph embeddings, and supervised graph neural networks. On 52 Urdu novels by seven authors, learned graph representations beat the baselines by a wide margin, reaching up to 0.857 accuracy under a strict author aware protocol.
arxiv-2512-12954:
Felipe Atenas, Farhana Ahmed Simi, and Matthew Tam study relocated fixed-point iterations, algorithms that repeatedly apply a rule until the result stops changing. Such methods sit behind many tools for splitting hard problems into simpler parts. Speed guarantees for them were incomplete.

The authors prove the method converges at a linear rate when the rule meets a linear error bound. The proof also covers the case where the rule is a contraction, steadily pulling points closer. As key uses, they derive the same fast rate for the relocated Douglas-Rachford method and for resolvent splitting methods with changing step sizes.
arxiv-2512-13254:
Pamela Klaassen and co-authors report a non-detection: the ALMA telescope found no sign of J1407b in 2024 follow-up observations. A source seen in 2017 had been a candidate for the object that caused a famous 2007 eclipse of the star J1407. Proper motion said it should appear at a new spot in 2024.

The Band 7 observations reached a noise limit of 17.5 microjansky at one sigma. Nothing appeared at the 2017 spot or at the expected 2024 position. The team rules out a dusty object as the cause of the 2007 eclipse. Null results like this one clean up a long-running exoplanet puzzle.
arxiv-2512-13654:
John E. Ortega, Dhruv D. Joshi, and Matt P. Borkowski study how large language models classify United States Supreme Court cases. Such cases are a hard test: long sentences, complex legal terms, and non-standard structure. The authors focus on memorization, meaning how models use stored patterns when they classify.

They test the latest fine-tuning and retrieval methods on two topic tasks, one with 15 labels and one with 279 labels. Methods include parameter-efficient fine-tuning and auto-modeling. Prompt-based models with memory, such as DeepSeek, proved more robust than past BERT-based models. They scored about 2 points better than prior non-prompt models on both tasks. The work helps explain when memorization helps legal classification.
arxiv-2512-13754:
Sakshi Ahuja and Subhankar Mishra present OpenProposal, a proof-of-concept platform for open review of research funding proposals. Funding choices shape science, yet agency review stays closed, unlike the open peer review that changed paper publishing. Closed systems limit accountability and block systematic improvement.

Built with Next.js, React, and Prisma, OpenProposal shows public reviews, author rebuttals, and transparent decisions in a working web system. It tries to protect sensitive details such as budgets while opening the rest. The design adds community engagement and reviewer accountability, plus data-driven views of the review process. The authors stress that empirical validation is still needed, and frame the work as a technical base for future funding review studies.
arxiv-2512-13954:
Masamune Oguri and co-authors release catalogs of galaxy clusters and luminous red galaxies from the final Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program data. The survey covers about 1200 square degrees. Such catalogs support cosmology by mapping large-scale structure across much of cosmic time.

The cluster catalog holds more than 10000 clusters with richness above 15, out to redshift one point three eight, with over 600,000 probable red member galaxies. Cluster photometric redshifts show scatter better than about zero point zero one. Stacked weak lensing signals out to redshift 1 update the mass-richness relation. The luminous red galaxy catalog holds about 6 million objects out to redshift one point two five. Their redshift scatter is better than about zero point zero two between redshifts zero point four and one.
arxiv-2512-14054:
Humaira Tasnim and co-authors present a dual-detector framework for autonomous aerial vehicle landing on helipads. Reliable helipad detection is essential without GPS or in poor visual conditions. Single detectors such as YOLOv8 struggle across the extreme scale change of descent, from tiny helipads at altitude to large ones near touchdown.

Two YOLOv8 experts are trained on scale-tuned versions of the HelipadCat data set, one for far range and one for close range. Both run in parallel, and a geometric gate picks the prediction matching the vehicle's viewpoint. Tests in a closed-loop setting that pairs CARLA rendering with NASA's GUAM flight engine showed better alignment stability and landing accuracy than single-detector baselines.
arxiv-2512-14154:
Yimin Wu and Tomoo Kikuchi study how new ideas reshape finance in a 2025 paper using data from 75 countries between 1982 and 2021. They ask whether innovation grows stock markets more than banks, and how the quality of a country institutions affects that link.

Their baseline result is that innovation raises stock market activity, efficiency, and size relative to banking. Good institutions strengthen the effect on activity and efficiency but weaken it for size, which suggests banks play a larger role where institutions are strong. For efficiency the moderating effect can be nonlinear. The findings point to more than one funding channel for new firms and technology.
arxiv-2512-14754:
Jianshuo Dong and coauthors ask whether top language models follow instructions reliably, or only when a request is phrased the standard way. Models score near the ceiling on the IFEval benchmark, yet real users change wording, framing, and task setup all the time. Their 2025 paper calls the missing skill nuance oriented reliability.

The team built IFEval++, a test made of cousin prompts that carry the same intent with small differences, plus a new score called reliable@k. They ran 20 commercial and 26 open source models through it. Scores fell by as much as 61.8% after small wording changes. The paper also maps the weakness and tries three fixes, arguing that steady behavior under rewording is the next test models must pass.
arxiv-2512-14854:
Pouria Mazloumi and Xiaofeng Xu study the hidden algebra behind signals from the early universe. Their subject is cosmological correlators, measures of how fields in the infant cosmos varied together from place to place. The math of these measures has symbol letters, which mark where the formulas can blow up or branch.

For a scalar field tied to the shape of space in a simple way, the authors sort those letters. In tree level ladder cases with n sites, the letters are governed by cluster algebras of type A with index 2(n-1). A one loop bubble case splits into a union of two A3 cluster algebras. Knowing these structures gives theorists a tool to bootstrap, or build up, exact formulas for such signals.
arxiv-2512-14954:
Buu Phan and two coauthors solve a mismatch that blocks a common way of shrinking language models. Distillation trains a small student model to copy a big teacher, using ratios of next token likelihoods. That math needs both models to share one vocabulary, yet students often use smaller tokenizers to save memory on edge devices.

The authors find a hidden recursive structure inside byte pair encoding, the tokenizer method both models use, and build a scoring framework on it. When the student vocabulary is a subset of the teacher's, their method gives exact likelihoods with one model pass per token. Distilling Qwen2.5-1.5B this way cut memory by up to 12 percent and raised task scores by up to 4 percent. For arbitrary vocabularies, a lossless procedure plus a fast approximation lifts math reasoning accuracy on GSM8K by over 2 percent.
arxiv-2512-15154:
Ting Wang and six coauthors design update rules for the Channel Knowledge Map, a tool planned for sixth generation wireless networks. The map links a user's position to channel state information, using knowledge of the surroundings to cut signaling overhead. A map built once goes stale as the environment changes, yet retraining it often wastes heavy data and computing.

The authors define a Map Efficacy Function that captures slow aging and sudden environmental shifts. Update scheduling becomes a fractional programming problem, which they solve two ways: one algorithm guarantees the global optimum, and a second is near optimal at near linear cost. For unpredictable settings they derive a threshold rule: update at once when decay outruns resource cost growth, else delay. Predictable settings reward longer term plans that bend those rules for global gain.
arxiv-2512-15354:
Andreas Buchinger and three coauthors build a general theory for approximating evolutionary equations, the framework R. Picard introduced in 2009 for time dependent problems. Such equations cover many models in physics where a state evolves under a rule that mixes space and time derivatives.

The theory can serve as a foundation for numerical analysis of these equations, telling users when a discrete scheme can be trusted to shadow the true solution. To show the machinery at work, the authors apply it to a spatial discretization of the heat equation using spectral methods. The study is a groundwork paper: it aims to give one approximation theory for a whole class of evolution problems, rather than case by case proofs.
arxiv-2512-15454:
Xiang-Xiang Sun and co authors study the short range behavior of pairs of nucleons in a 2025 nuclear physics paper. Common calculation methods soften the forces between nucleons, which washes out detail about how they act at very close range. The team builds a way around that loss.

They construct wave functions that do not depend on that softening step, using results from No-Core Shell Model calculations with chiral forces. Two patterns prove strikingly stable across force choices. One concerns the two body density ratio in a key channel compared with the deuteron. The other compares total densities with the alpha particle, which is nearly free of cutoff effects.
arxiv-2512-15554:
Researchers present WuppieFuzz, an open source fuzzer for REST APIs, in a 2025 paper. Many business processes depend on web services whose endpoints can hide security flaws. With vast numbers of endpoints, manual testing cannot keep up, so automated fuzzing is attractive.

Built on LibAFL, WuppieFuzz supports white box, grey box, and black box testing. From an OpenAPI specification it builds request sequences, then mutates them with REST specific and standard mutators. Coverage feedback guides which sequences to send next, helping reach deep states in the software. It automates harness creation and offers several report types. Tests on the Petstore API assess the white box approach and different power schedules.
arxiv-2512-15654:
Gayatri Ghosh studies hybrid leptogenesis in a minimal SO(10) grand unified model in a 2025 paper. Leptogenesis explains the cosmic excess of matter over antimatter through processes involving heavy neutrinos. Here both Type I and Type II seesaw sectors act at once, with heavy Majorana neutrinos and scalar triplets each nearly degenerate.

That near degeneracy resonantly boosts each sector, and loop interference between the two adds a new source of CP violation that vanishes if either sector is absent. A flavour covariant density matrix treatment tracks coherence, spectator effects, and washout. The observed baryon asymmetry can be matched at heavy mass scales of ten to the tenth to ten to the twelfth giga electron volts.
arxiv-2512-15754:
Ziyu Chen and co authors survey reconfigurable intelligent surfaces in real systems from security and privacy angles in a 2025 paper, dated December 12. These surfaces reshape wireless environments by steering radio waves. Most research stresses their communication benefits, while real uses in homes, vehicles, and factories raise little studied risks.

The survey maps scenarios by whether the user and the attacker each have such a surface. It shows how surfaces enable listening in, jamming, and spoofing, and reviews defenses such as added security algorithms, attacker disruption, and early spotting of rogue surfaces. A companion collection gathers open tools, data sets, and demos for future work on secure surface use.
arxiv-2512-16154:
Manjari Bagchi and a large team make the case for hunting pulsars in dense star clusters in a 2025 paper posted to arXiv. Globular clusters pack stars so tightly that, per unit of mass, they hold about 1,000 times more X-ray binaries and radio pulsars than normal regions. So far, 345 radio pulsars are known in such clusters.

These pulsars probe cluster structure, gas, magnetic fields, and history, and some test exotic physics. One might even be the first known pulsar orbiting a black hole. The authors argue deep searches with the SKA need only a few beams and can start during early commissioning. Conservative forecasts more than double the known population, while an optimistic one reaches about 1,700 detectable pulsars in the full array. Early SKA science could therefore start here.
arxiv-2512-16554:
Kobi Shiran and Noam Soker model an exploding star in their arXiv paper, posted in 2025. Supernova 2024ggi, a core-collapse event, showed a photosphere, the visible surface of the expanding debris, whose growth changed character over time.
