A single shell of ejecta can only produce one kind of curve, so something structural must differ.

Their toy model stacks two shells: a light spherical outer shell and a heavy elongated inner one. In the first week the outer shell forms the photosphere, then thins until the elongated shell takes over, flipping the radius curve from concave to convex as observed. The authors connect the shapes to the jittering jets explosion mechanism, which they argue fits this supernova and its polarization better than the standard neutrino-driven picture. They present the work as growing evidence for jets.
arxiv-2512-17054:
Rajiv Thummala and Gregory Falco ask where a spacecraft workload should run: on board, in an orbital data center, at a ground edge node, or in Earth cloud. Each tier trades latency, reliability, power, link limits, cost, and legal fit in unlike ways.

Their frame turns placement into a scored optimization. Measurable metrics are normalized, feasibility limits applied, and a single utility score ranks tiers, even when data are incomplete. Two sample workloads show how the scoring picks a home tier and why. The method gives mission designers a structured, extensible way to reason about compute placement as space architectures grow more mixed.
arxiv-2512-17154:
Zhedong Zhang and coauthors present InstructDubber, a movie dubbing method that aligns speech to a silent performance without heavy face-processing pipelines. Dubbing must match lip motion and the emotion and rhythm of the on-screen acting, in seen and unseen visual styles alike.

A multimodal language model first reads the video, script, and prompts and writes plain dubbing instructions about speaking rate and emotion. A duration module mines those rate notes to predict phoneme lengths that fit the lips. An emotion module, tuned on true dubbing emotion, predicts prosody. Speech is then rendered from script, duration, and prosody. On three benchmarks it beat prior tools in both in-domain and zero-shot tests.
arxiv-2512-17654:
Felix Lehner and four co-authors teach a small neural network to map invisible radiation scatter around a patient during live X-ray work. In interventional radiology, doctors guide tools inside the body under X-rays, and stray scatter bathes the whole room. Knowing where that scatter pools, minute by minute, protects staff who stand there all day.

Exact scatter math is far too slow for live use, so the team trained networks on simulated rooms built with a Monte Carlo tool. A standard human phantom torso served as the scatter source. Three data sets of rising complexity taught the models, and all data and code are public. The best variants matched true fields well in the zones that matter most, giving safety officers a fast planning aid.
arxiv-2512-17754:
Yun-Hua Chen fits several decays of the Bs meson into one coherent story, hunting clues about a mystery particle. When a Bs meson dies, it can leave behind the X(3872), an exotic state whose inner makeup, part molecule, part charmonium, has puzzled physicists for two decades. Chen compares its decay pattern with that of the ordinary psi(2S) charmonium.

One framework, respecting unitarity and analyticity for the leftover pion and kaon pairs, fits all the measured spectra at once. The ordinary state's couplings match its sibling decay, as expected. The X(3872) couplings come out about half as strong, evidence it is no pure charmonium. A bit player, the f0(1500), turns out to matter in both decays. Predictions for unmeasured ratios follow.
arxiv-2512-18054:
Ahmad Sheykhi asks whether the expansion of space can be read as a heat story. One view treats gravity as a surface effect of heat rules at the cosmic horizon. Another, from Padmanabhan, says new space itself appears as the universe ages, driven by a gap between surface and bulk counts.

Sheykhi feeds a power law link between mass and horizon size into both views. Each path yields the same altered equations for how the universe expands, a match he reads as a sign the link runs deep. He also checks that the broad heat rule, that total disorder never falls, still holds for the cosmos inside its horizon.
arxiv-2512-18154:
Xiao Hu Mo and coauthors work out how to describe charmonium decays into pairs of mesons. Charmonium states are bound pairs of a charm quark and its antiquark. Their decays follow patterns that test how the strong force acts between quarks, and the paper uses symmetry analysis plus a description of magnetic transitions.

The paper sets out parametrization forms for these quasi two body decays and draws from them the meson mixing angle, the form factor, and the size of symmetry breaking effects. As groundwork, the team computes the electromagnetic cross sections for scalar and pseudoscalar final states, eight in all, with the current algebra method. They also spell out the math for four kinds of final states in full. The result is a shared language for comparing decay data across experiments.
arxiv-2512-18254:
Mingcheng Ye, Jiaming Liu, and Yiren Song present Loom, a model that weaves text and images into one flowing sequence. Such mixed output suits step by step guides, style swaps, and builds that need words and frames in turn. Past open models often lost the thread over long runs.

Loom first turns an order into a stepwise plan, then makes each frame while glancing at a few past frames and the whole text plan. That lean memory keeps long sequences on track and cheap to run. On mixed tasks it beat the open baseline Anole by an average of 2.6 points on a 5 point scale. A fresh set of 50,000 tutorial sequences supports the training.
arxiv-2512-18454:
David Graber and three co-authors tackle a trust problem in drug discovery software: models that predict how molecules bind often fail quietly on inputs unlike their training data. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, builds a detector for such out-of-distribution cases in protein-ligand complexes, whose 3D graphs mix geometry with atom types.

Their framework trains a diffusion model on the training distribution alone, with no labels. A unified diffusion over coordinates and atom identities yields per-sample likelihoods through a probability-flow equation, giving a principled typicality score. Tested by holding out whole protein families, the scores flag the unseen families and track the errors of a separate binding-affinity model. Extra statistics from the diffusion paths sharpen the detector further, beating likelihood-only baselines.
arxiv-2512-18554:
Aofei Chang, Ting Wang, and Fenglong Ma tackle hallucination in medical AI, where a model that reads scans and writes reports can invent findings. They blame two flaws: weak visual representation learning and attention that drifts away from the regions that matter. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and accepted at AAAI 2026, proposes MEDALIGN, a light alignment distillation framework.

MEDALIGN transfers visual alignment skill from a medical CLIP model into a large vision-language model. One loss aligns the similarity structure among visual tokens; a second steers attention toward diagnostically relevant areas. Across report generation and medical question answering benchmarks, the method improves both accuracy and interpretability, producing outputs better grounded in the image. For clinical tools, that grounding is the difference between a helpful draft and a dangerous one.
arxiv-2512-18654:
Rahim Rahmati-asghar introduces a new way to layer vector bundles in this 2025 algebraic geometry paper. A hierarchical filtration stacks a bundle through subsheaves of equal rank, where each step's quotient lives on a divisor. The longest possible stack defines a number the author calls hierarchical depth. He bounds this depth using the determinant class and gives exact formulas for smooth curves and for varieties of Picard rank one.

For surfaces, depth changes in an additive way along the steps of the minimal model program, with an explicit formula linking a surface to its minimal model. As a payoff, depth connects to degeneracies in algebraic-geometric codes, and simplifying a surface through the program improves code parameters. The invariant thus links bundle theory, birational geometry, and coding theory.
arxiv-2512-18954:
Zaidao Han, Risa Higashita, and Jiang Liu teach self-driving systems to imagine what the camera cannot see. Semantic scene completion asks for a full 3D map, geometry plus labels, from one image. Seen and unseen regions pose different problems, and mixing their training signals dilutes both. Their network, VOIC, posted to arXiv in December 2025, splits the job with two decoders.

An offline strategy first extracts clean labels for visible voxels from dense ground truth. The visible decoder then builds high-fidelity priors for what is seen, while the occlusion decoder reasons globally about what is hidden, guided by those priors and cross-modal interaction. On SemanticKITTI and SSCBench-KITTI360, VOIC beats existing single-camera methods on both completion and segmentation, reaching state-of-the-art results. Separating confidence levels, the authors show, beats forcing one network to be equally sure about everything.
arxiv-2512-19154:
Geraud Nangue Tasse, Matthew Riemer, Benjamin Rosman, and Tim Klinger teach agents to remember only what matters in worlds where the distant past can matter again. The common fix, stacking recent frames, grows costly as the needed history lengthens. Yet most old observations, they note, have no effect on what happens next.

Their meta-algorithms keep a small, adaptive stack of chosen memories instead of a fixed window. The stack can still express deep dependencies on a few key moments. That design cuts the memory and compute burden for both acting and learning. The work targets sequence-model agents being pushed toward messy, real-world tasks.
arxiv-2512-19254:
Zhen-Zhen Zhang, Hua-Lei Wang, Kui Xiao, and Min-Liang Liu explain why a superheavy nucleus, rutherfordium-252, lives a little longer than expected. The nucleus was recently found to fission in under a microsecond. A high-spin isomer state seems oddly stable against that split, possibly resting on a shape isomer.

Improved potential-energy calculations, with shapes constrained along the fission path, reveal the balance at work. Triaxial bends, pear-like asymmetry, and higher-order shape terms each shift the ground and isomeric valleys. The authors also point out a new multipath decay route that can shorten the isomer's life. Together, these effects explain the swapped stability of the two states.
arxiv-2512-19354:
Zhenyang Huang, Xiao Yu, Yi Zhang, and Decheng Wang build ReasonCD, a model that finds changes in satellite image pairs based on what the user actually means. Change detection flags where two images differ inside regions of interest. People often describe that interest vaguely, and systems fed such implicit wording fail almost completely.

ReasonCD uses a large language model's reasoning to mine the hidden intent behind a request, then runs detection guided by that intent. On the public BCDD dataset it posted an F1 score above ninety-two percent. The authors also test its reasoning skill directly, claiming a clear step beyond explicit-text guidance.
arxiv-2512-19454:
David Fajman, Maciej Maliborski, Maximilian Ofner, and Todd Oliynyk find a sharp threshold in how cosmic fluids behave on an expanding background. The Euler-Poisson system couples a self-gravitating fluid to gravity, while cosmic expansion drains energy from the flow. They set the expansion as a power of time and start near a uniform state.

Above an expansion exponent of two thirds, matching the matter-dominated era, small disturbances stay small for all time. At or below it, numerics show shocks form from arbitrarily small data. The pair of results draws a critical line for stability in this cosmological model, a boundary modelers can now test other fluids against.
arxiv-2512-19554:
Yongxin Wang, Zhicheng Yang, Meng Cao, and Mingfei Han train multimodal reasoners by studying their failures instead of discarding them. In verifiable-reward learning, a batch where every attempt fails gives no gradient, and a lone success teaches nothing about its near-miss siblings. Their CARE framework turns those errors into the lesson itself.

An anchored-contrastive objective gathers a tight group around the best attempt plus hard near-miss negatives, with a rescue rule for all-wrong batches. Reflection-guided resampling then rewrites one representative failure and re-scores it with the same checker, minting fresh positives. Accuracy and training smoothness both improve, with failures supplying more of the signal.
arxiv-2512-19654:
Six researchers led by Diptarka Chakraborty open a new front in clustering theory: keeping cluster labels stable over time. Classic metric clustering worries about stable centers, but applications care that points keep their assigned names when data shifts slightly. A clustering whose labels churn between runs is hard to use, even if its centers barely move.

The team defines label consistency formally, measuring the label distance between two consecutive solutions, and then designs algorithms that respect it. For the classical k-center and k-median problems they give consistent approximation algorithms, trading a controlled amount of accuracy for stability. The work starts a research direction rather than closing one, setting definitions and first guarantees that later algorithms can improve on.
arxiv-2512-19754: Five mathematicians, James Anderson, Ara Basmajian, Ruben Hidalgo, Perry Susskind, and Edward Taylor, wrote this memorial tribute to their colleague Bernard Maskit. A shorter version appeared in the August 2025 issue of the Notices of the American Mathematical Society, the profession's flagship magazine. The version preserved here is the expanded text of that tribute, giving the authors more room than the Notices printing allowed.
arxiv-2512-20054:
Xiao-Tian Xu and four co-authors trace a detailed route by which two massive stars become a merging pair of black holes. Most massive pairs never manage it. Past work on the stable mass transfer channel leaned on heavy shortcuts, and its claims stayed vague. Their models follow pairs from the zero-age main sequence to black hole birth. Spin inside the stars is tracked. So are mass and angular momentum passed between the stars.

The gainer star's inner build turns out to matter a lot. It shapes a later phase of reverse mass transfer. Black hole spins and mass ratios then land in the range that wave detectors report. That range covers primaries of ten to twenty-five solar masses. Many progenitor pairs of this kind are known. The team concludes the channel likely adds to the seen merger pool. The study appeared in Nature Astronomy.
arxiv-2512-20554:
Miguel Palma and co-authors pack more work onto trapped-ion quantum computers. Quantum cloud queues grow because machines run one circuit at a time, wasting capacity. Multi-programming runs several circuits in parallel, but existing packers were designed for superconducting hardware with its limited connectivity and crosstalk.

CircPack instead targets modular trapped-ion devices built on the quantum charge-coupled device architecture. It treats static scheduling as a two-dimensional packing problem with hardware-specific shuttling constraints. Against superconducting-based approaches, fidelity improves by up to about seventy percent, utilization by over sixty percent, and layer counts drop by a third. Scheduling also balances across clusters of independent modules. The approach makes a case for trapped ions as cloud workhorses.
arxiv-2512-20754:
Daine L. Danielson and Gautam Satishchandran examine a strange effect near black holes: quantum superpositions fall apart there. Recent work showed that soft radiation, very low-energy particles crossing the horizon, carries away the information that keeps superpositions alive. States outside the hole create telltale states of long-range fields inside it.

The authors extend a classic mathematical theory so it can handle these soft radiation states from memory effects. They then compute how distinguishable such states are, using tools from state discrimination and error correction. Their conclusion is striking: any horizon scrambles its surroundings as effectively as if its interior were packed with perfect observers.
arxiv-2512-20854:
Shelly Schwartz, Oleg Vasilyev, and Randy Sawaya question a classic search metric: recall, the share of all relevant documents a system finds. In live knowledge bases that keep growing, nobody knows the total number of relevant items, so recall cannot actually be computed. Teams still report substitutes of doubtful value.

The authors tested established workarounds by comparing each metric against language-model judgments of answer quality built from retrieved documents. Their datasets each carried only a handful of relevant documents per query. They also propose a simple new quality measure that performed well in these tests. It too needs no count of all relevant documents, matching real deployment conditions.
arxiv-2512-20954:
Xiang Zhang, Siqi Sun, and nine co-authors bring chain-of-thought reasoning to a domain whose alphabet is too small for it. Protein language models speak in amino-acid tokens. The team formalizes why that limited expressiveness blocks the intermediate reasoning steps. Those steps are what help ordinary language models check and correct themselves. Their answer is reflection pretraining, which adds auxiliary thinking tokens beyond the answer tokens during training.

Theory shows the enlarged token set raises the expressiveness of the biological language. Experiments then show models that learn to self-correct at the token level. They gain substantially over standard pretraining. For protein and RNA modeling, a single residue error can ruin a prediction. A model that can pause, reconsider, and repair its own output is a new capability rather than a convenience.
arxiv-2512-21154:
Nikita Kalinin and Mikhail Shkolnikov build geometric invariants by averaging over tropical structures. Their approach fixes the covolume and averages over all tropical structures of that size. It applies the result to the tropical distance series. That produces functions attached to convex domains. The functions do not change under equi-affine transformations and are expected to enjoy several striking traits. The level sets of these functions are the equi-distant loci of the title.

For bounded domains the limiting shape of the loci remains a conjecture. For unbounded domains opening toward two non-parallel asymptotes, the authors prove the analogue: the loci approach a hyperbola, and its affine curvature is universal, free of the domain's details. An explicit formula for the mean value at the center of the unit disk rounds out the note, anchoring the theory in a computable case.
arxiv-2512-21654:
Zikun Guo, Adeyinka P. Adedigba, Rammohan Mallipeddi, and Heoncheol Lee improve ant colony optimization for planning the paths of a team of robots. Multi-robot path planning must minimize total travel while dividing work fairly among robots. Classic swarm methods handle small cases but converge too early and scale poorly to large, complex environments.

Their framework injects structural knowledge into the search from the start. The distribution of tasks creates a structural prior that constrains where the ants search at initialization. The pheromone update rule favors structurally meaningful connections and includes a load-aware objective balancing total distance against each robot's workload. An overlap suppression step keeps tasks distinct and evenly spread across the team. On benchmarks with varying sizes and team configurations, the method improved route compactness, stability, and workload balance over metaheuristic baselines. The authors point to logistics, surveillance, and search-and-rescue as natural uses.
arxiv-2512-22154:
David Lindner and six co-authors examine control monitoring, the practice of using automated overseers to watch powerful AI agents that operators do not fully trust. Earlier research tested monitoring in simplified setups. Real deployments add complications: many agent copies running at once, oversight that lags behind the agent, attacks spread incrementally across copies, and scheming that hides inside single mildly harmful actions.

The authors compare three monitoring styles, synchronous, semi-synchronous, and asynchronous, which trade latency against safety differently. They introduce a high-level safety case sketch as a tool for comparing these protocols. Their analysis centers on three challenges, oversight, latency, and recovery, explored through four case studies of possible future deployments.
arxiv-2512-22454:
Namish Bansal and four co-authors teach computers to inventory electrical substations from photographs, so grid vulnerability can be mapped without sending crews to every site. Substation gear like transformers faces hurricanes, flooding, earthquakes, and geomagnetic currents, and failures carry heavy economic and safety costs. The team trained and compared sixteen object detection models on a hand-labeled dataset of United States substation images.

The lineup held twelve YOLO models, two RF-DETR models, and two Cascade R-CNN models. RF-DETR-large performed best overall, while alternate energy systems proved easiest to detect and transformers and reactors hardest, being smaller and more variable. Applied nationwide, the best model logged roughly 22,591 component detections across 11,083 substations, with Florida and the Midcontinent region leading their breakdowns.
arxiv-2512-23354:
P. Singh and a nine-author team model the light shows of neutron star mergers that produced both gamma-ray bursts and kilonovae. When two neutron stars, or a neutron star and a black hole, collide, the burst's afterglow and the radioactive glow of ejected heavy elements should both appear. The authors fit afterglow and kilonova together, inside a Bayesian framework built for nuclear physics and multimessenger astrophysics, instead of modeling each separately as earlier work did.

Every burst in the sample shows a kilonova, except one case where its presence could neither be confirmed nor excluded. Binary neutron star progenitors are favored for four events, including the famous GW170817 counterpart, while two others slightly prefer a neutron star-black hole system. The ejected wind mass exceeds the dynamical ejecta mass, and wind mass correlates with jet energy. The study presents joint modeling as a working probe of merger progenitors.
arxiv-2512-23654:
Zvi Bern and six co-authors compute how two non-spinning bodies, such as black holes, scatter off each other under gravity, to unprecedented precision. Their result gives the conservative radial action and scattering angle through the fifth order in Newton's constant, including second-order self-force effects. Such calculations feed the waveform models used to interpret gravitational-wave signals.

The method imports tools from particle physics: scattering amplitudes, the double copy, effective field theory, and multi-loop integration. A major bottleneck, integration-by-parts reduction, was eased by improved algorithms the team developed. For the first self-force sector they obtain a closed-form answer; in the second sector they find striking cancellations among integrals tied to Calabi-Yau geometry, echoing patterns first seen in supergravity calculations.
arxiv-2512-23754:
Eran Agmon and Ryan Spangler present Process Bigraphs, a framework for building biological simulations out of parts made by different groups. Real models span molecules, cells, and tissues, and each part may use its own math. Gluing them together takes care: each part must say which values it reads and writes, units must be matched, and updates must stay in step. Most tools leave those choices buried and unspoken.

Process Bigraphs makes the glue explicit. It grows out of the earlier Vivarium software and sets a shared spec for part interfaces, for nested data, and for the patterns used to compose and run coupled models. An open-source build, Vivarium 2.0, ships with the paper. A demo library of microbe ecosystem models mixes rate equations, dynamic flux balance models, and spatial processes, and in the demos populations sort themselves out in space just from the coupling.
arxiv-2512-24154:
Amir Khosravanizadeh, François Nédélec, and Serge Dmitrieff model actin filaments. Actin helps cells hold shape and move. Its filaments twist into helices. That handedness shapes how they bend. It also shapes how motors walk along them. Atom-level detail is too costly for cell-scale questions. The team built a leaner model instead.

Their coarse-grained filament keeps the twist and handedness. It runs inside Cytosim, an open simulator for the cytoskeleton. Shape and stiffness can be tuned to measured values. Simulations then show handedness at work. Motors drive sideways, chiral motion in two setups. In bundles, motor torques make filaments rotate and coil. Helical buckling appears as well. The patterns recall filopodia in real cells. The framework also fits other helical filaments.
arxiv-2512-24254:
Tadej Novak and Borut Paul Kerševan speed up detector simulation with a language-model trick. Simulating particle physics detectors eats huge computing budgets. Generative machine learning has already accelerated calorimeter simulation. Silicon tracking detectors had not been tried. This work presents the first studies there.

The authors test architectures and pick a GPT-like transformer. It runs in fully generative mode. Correlations between individual hits are preserved that way. Hits become a flat sequence of feature values. The parallel with text generation is deliberate. Words become detector hits in sequence. Performance is judged on the Open Data Detector. The generated tracking quality matches the full simulation closely. The result opens cheap, fast simulation for the part of the detector that tracks charged particles.
arxiv-2512-24454:
E K Berinyuy and five colleagues study quantum synchrony in an optomechanical system. Four modes interact: two optical cavities and two mechanical resonators. The resonators also feel a Coulomb force between them. Three kinds of synchrony are distinguished. Complete, phase-shifted, and phase-only regimes each get examined.

The Coulomb coupling turns out to matter in a selective way. It strongly enhances quantum phase synchrony. Energy exchange and phase coherence between the resonators improve. Complete and phase-shifted synchrony barely change, though. Amplitude and frequency locking are set mainly by the optical drive. Phase alignment depends on the coupling between resonators. The two cavities, linked only through the mechanics, also align over time. That is classical synchrony of the light fields. The effect offers control of group quantum dynamics for sensing and networks.
arxiv-2512-24854:
Duvan Cardona, William Obeng-Denteh, and Frederick Opoku prove boundedness estimates for Fourier integral maps with complex phase functions on Fourier Lebesgue spaces. Such maps generalize Fourier multipliers and appear in wave propagation. Real-phase results by Rodino, Nicola, and Cordero are the model; the complex case is their analogue.

Under a spatial factorization condition of a given rank, the map is bounded when its order is low enough relative to that rank and the integrability exponent. Harmonic analysis readers get sharp conditions for a difficult map class. Complex phases arise in damped and parabolic problems, so the extension has direct use.
arxiv-2601-00054:
Renpeng Zheng, writing alone, studies K-stability for a class of geometric spaces called Q-Fano spherical varieties. His 2026 paper in algebraic geometry uses compatible divisors, special sub-objects of the space, to test stability. The setting assumes a reductive group action in which a Borel subgroup, a standard smaller group inside it, has an orbit that covers a dense open part of the variety.

Zheng shows there is a unique anticanonical Q-divisor that computes the equivariant stability threshold for such a variety. That divisor stays unchanged under the Borel subgroup action, so symmetry picks it out canonically. More importantly, the divisor characterizes K-stability itself: checking this one object settles the stability question. For geometers who work with group actions, the result turns an abstract test into a concrete computation tied to a single canonically defined divisor.
arxiv-2601-00254:
Md Hasan Saju, Maher Muhtadi, and Akramul Azim compare three ways to aim language models at buggy, unsafe code. Finding software flaws early is vital for security. The team tests retrieval augmented generation first. It pulls facts from the web and a weakness database. Supervised fine tuning with small adapters comes second. A dual agent design comes third.

In that design, a second agent audits the first one. A plain baseline model sets the floor. Test data mix a public flaw set with real GitHub code. Five grave weakness classes anchor the labels. Retrieval wins on accuracy and F1 score overall. Fine tuning also performs strongly in the tests. The dual agent adds clearer reasoning and fewer errors. It does so with lower resource overhead. Domain knowledge, in some form, proves decisive.
arxiv-2601-00354:
Ioannis Diamantis, writing alone, treats rivers in the sky as braids that twist around each other over time. Atmospheric rivers are narrow moisture streams in the air. They drive a large share of extreme rainfall. Several filaments often share one weather regime. Standard tools still study each river alone. That habit misses how bundles interact and reorganize.

His framework uses framed braids and braidoids from topology. Each filament becomes one strand in the braid. Crossings in time order form a braid word. A moisture based frame tracks growth or decay inside each strand. Track data from reanalysis feed the construction. Sliding time windows yield braid snapshots across an episode. One strong North Pacific case anchors the test. Braid markers flag structural shifts that centroid paths hide. Moisture surges also stand out more clearly. Weather analysts gain a structural second opinion.
arxiv-2601-00454:
Hyunjun Kim addresses the cost of safety checks for chatbots that hold long conversations. Guardrail models scan dialogues for attacks, but reading every turn of a long history is expensive. Kim proposes Defensive M2S, which trains guardrails on compressed versions of multi-turn conversations, squeezed into a single-turn format with simple templates.

A formal analysis shows training cost drops from quadratic to linear in the number of turns. In experiments, the compressed training data used ninety-three times fewer tokens than full histories. Three guardrail model families were tested on a multi-turn jailbreak benchmark. The best setup caught most attacks while using about ninety-five percent fewer tokens at inference, showing compression can keep safety checks cheap without giving up detection.
arxiv-2601-00654:
Ankit Bhojak and two co-authors prove bounds in a 2026 math paper on averages over whole-number points. The averages at stake sum values over special curved sets of points. One family is named for Birch and Magyar, and one is of Hardy-Littlewood type. The authors track how much these averages can swing as the scale of the set grows. That swing is summed by a gauge called a variational seminorm.

Their bounds say the swing stays in check for a wide range of gauges. The range ties the strength of the norm to the swing gauge in a sharp way. The authors also draw a use in ergodic theory. That field studies long-run runs of systems that keep some total fixed. Bounds like these help show when time averages match space averages. The paper adds firm ground to a hard branch of analysis.
arxiv-2601-00754:
Maria Teresa Parreira, Isabel Neto, Filipa Rocha, and Wendy Ju study how children react when a robot keeps failing to understand them. Adult responses to repeated robot errors are documented, but children's are not. Fifty-nine children aged eight to ten interacted with a robot that misunderstood their prompts three times in a row, in a design adapted from an earlier adult study.

Video analysis showed children behaved much like adults in some ways: they rephrased prompts, changed their tone of voice, and showed growing emotion in non-verbal reactions as failures piled up. Differences from the adult pattern also appeared. The study informs how robots for children should recover gracefully from communication breakdowns rather than repeating the same failure.
arxiv-2601-00854:
Igor Lodin and three co-authors present, in 2026, a vision system that tracks a scene on small, low-power gear. Such gear cannot run heavy image parsing on every frame. Their system keeps two living maps, which they call canvases. One canvas holds the still parts of the scene and changes slowly. The other holds moving parts and updates fast.

Both canvases sit in a fixed frame, steadied against camera shake. A heavy parser runs only when motion hints that something new has shown up. That gate cut parser calls by more than thirty times in their tests. Mean handling time per frame fell by more than twenty times. The tests ran on recorded clips at modest resolution. The still and moving overlays stayed coherent across the clips. The design suits cameras that must watch for hours on a small battery.
arxiv-2601-01054:
Thummala and 4 co-authors address a gap in checking computer chips for hidden tampering. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at microcontrollers in the supply chain, where X-ray checks and tearing parts apart work well but cost too much and take too long for wide use.

Instead, the team measures tiny changes in power use while a chip runs. A neural network learns what normal power traces look like from clean chips only, then flags traces that differ. Tests cover several kinds of tampering. The authors argue the method could sit between simple function checks and costly lab work, giving makers a faster middle screening step.
arxiv-2601-01154:
Balaganchi Bhargava and five co-authors speed up a quantum trick for preparing states gently and quickly. Adiabatic methods change a system slowly so it stays in its ground state, but slow is costly. Counterdiabatic terms cancel the jumps that fast change causes, yet those terms are nonlocal and hard to build with standard circuits.

The team's digital-analog framework mixes built-in multi-qubit interactions with single-qubit rotations to realize those terms directly. For any fixed level of accuracy, the method needs only a constant number of analog blocks, no matter how large the system grows. They show the method on two-dimensional spin models and study its errors. Constant depth is a sharp change from methods whose cost grows with system size. The work could help quantum simulation, optimization, and state preparation on today's noisy hardware.
arxiv-2601-01354:
Hiroki Wadati, Kohei Yamamoto, and Kohei Yamagami review how ultrafast X-ray methods watch transition-metal compounds change in trillionths of a second. X-ray absorption and related magnetic techniques can single out one element at a time, a power that plain light methods lack. New X-ray free-electron lasers and tabletop high-harmonic sources now push those tools into the femtosecond range.

The review covers pump-probe studies where a laser pulse strikes a material and X-rays snapshot what follows. Highlights include laser-driven loss of magnetism, spin-state switches, and shifts in charge and structure. The authors also track progress in tabletop X-ray spectroscopy and its pairing with large facilities. Together, these methods let researchers watch charge, spin, orbital, and lattice motion unfold together. That view is key to learning how to control quantum materials with light.
arxiv-2601-01554:
MOSI AI and 25 co-authors present a single model that writes down speech, marks who spoke, and stamps when each part was said. Meeting records need all three jobs done well together. Older systems split the jobs, lose track of speakers over long talks, and often fail to give exact times.

Their model, MOSS Transcribe Diarize, handles talks up to ninety minutes with a very long context window. It was trained on large amounts of real, messy recordings. Across public and in-house tests, the authors report it beat leading paid systems. The work points toward meeting notes that need less hand fixing after the call ends.
arxiv-2601-01654:
Bai, Lee, and Pomerleano study number-theoretic structures hidden in the quantum geometry of special six-dimensional shapes. Calabi-Yau threefolds sit at the heart of string theory, and each carries a quantum connection that deforms its classical geometry. Working over p-adic numbers for a prime above three, the team examines that connection on even-degree quantum cohomology.

They show it yields a Fontaine-Laffaile module, a p-adic object whose Frobenius map opens with a term set by a p-adic Gamma class. Reduced modulo the prime, a divided Frobenius plays the role of a classic Cartier map. They prove a quantum analogue of a result by Katz and end with conjectures for wider settings.
arxiv-2601-02054:
Helium-rich hot subdwarfs are stripped, glowing stellar cores that trace several possible evolutionary paths. Asish Philip Monai and C. Simon Jeffery report a survey with the Southern African Large Telescope. It covers nearly seven hundred such stars. They build a classification system driven by the data itself. Human templates are not used.

Principal component analysis plus spectral clustering yields six major clusters. They match the classical subdwarf classes. Connected sequences run between them. Finer sub-clusters sit inside the helium-rich groups. For the hottest stars, the data-led approach even revised the standard classification. Motion measurements from the Gaia mission then show disk stars dominate most classes, while helium-rich and very hot subdwarfs include a notably larger share of halo stars, hinting at different origins.
arxiv-2601-02254:
Jay Kuri tackles identity checks in places where networks have failed, such as disaster zones, or where networks cannot be trusted. Normal systems need to reach an online authority, a directory, or a revocation service to confirm who someone is. When that link is gone, trust cannot be checked at all.

Kuri introduces a model called the Zero Infrastructure Capability Graph. Identity, permission given to another person, and cancellation of that permission are each written as signed statements that can be judged locally by fixed rules. The working system, Vouchsafe, builds those statements from widely used tools such as Ed25519 signatures and JSON Web Tokens. No new cryptography and no online service are needed at check time.
arxiv-2601-02354:
Shadi Ali Ahmad, Ahmed Almheiri, and Simon Lin look for traces of the inside of a black hole in quantities defined far outside it. Boundary correlation functions carry analytic structure that can be continued mathematically, and some continuations follow paths, called geodesics. That pass through the interior of rotating and charged black holes and come out in a future universe.

Working in the WKB approximation, a semi classical method, they carry out those continuations for momentum space correlators in several black hole settings. Position space versions need different continued pieces, which appear as corrections beyond the basic WKB picture. The rotating BTZ black hole gives an explicit check, and the AdS Schwarzschild case yields the bouncing path. The method may also probe whether inner horizons are unstable.
arxiv-2601-02554:
Morgan R. Frank and four co authors test a widely told story, that ChatGPT's release in late 2022 damaged job prospects in occupations exposed to artificial intelligence. Using monthly United States unemployment insurance records, they measure unemployment risk by occupation and place. Risk in AI exposed occupations began rising in early 2022, months before ChatGPT existed, which breaks the simple story.

Millions of LinkedIn profiles tell the same tale from the hiring side, with graduating classes from 2021 onward entering AI exposed jobs at lower rates than earlier classes, again before the launch. A third data source, millions of course syllabi, cuts the other way for education. Graduates whose courses were more exposed to language models searched for jobs for less time after ChatGPT and earned higher first job pay in exposed occupations. The authors conclude the launch is a poor natural experiment for judging AI's labor effects.
arxiv-2601-02654:
Richard Huang, David R. Nelson, and Suraj Shankar revisit Euler buckling, the sudden bending of a rod under compression, for polymers at finite temperature. Biological and physical systems are full of such rods, from microtubules to carbon nanotubes. A polymer shorter than its persistence length acts semiflexible and rod like, but real polymers can also stretch. And that extensibility couples to cheap bending modes in nonlinear ways once a load is applied.

Heat driven undulations change the instability dramatically in a fixed strain setting. The authors identify a Ginzburg like length scale beyond which thermal wiggles soften the effective Young's modulus, even while the polymer stays semiflexible. Perturbative calculations and Monte Carlo simulations agree on the picture. The result matters wherever warm, stretchy filaments carry compressive loads.
arxiv-2601-03254:
Bastien Vanderplaetse, Xavier Siebert, and Stéphane Dupont help researchers interpret the private languages that AI agents invent. In emergent communication studies, agents develop their own signaling systems with no explicit programming. But few tools exist for working out what the messages mean. Their algorithm, ASRD, automatically detects semantic rules inside those message streams.

ASRD pulls out recurring patterns from messages exchanged by agents trained on two datasets for the Lewis signaling game, a standard testbed in the field. It then links the patterns to specific traits of the input data the agents were describing. By tying message fragments to concrete traits, the method makes later analysis much simpler. It gives researchers a systematic way to read an emergent language, instead of guessing at it.
arxiv-2601-03354:
Samrat Sen and five co-authors make mock telescope images of the tiny plasma jets that may help heat the Sun's corona. The jets, called nanojets, are small, fast, and short-lived. They are tied to magnetic reconnection at very small scales, and they are hard to observe directly. Without mock images, models and telescope data could not be compared fairly. The team models two magnetic flux ropes merging, which produces nanojet-like signatures.

The model was run with the MPI-AMRVAC code. From it, the team built mock extreme-ultraviolet views that match what the SDO/AIA instrument and the upcoming MUSE mission can see. Those views are then compared with a real observation of the jets. Matching the look of the event, in the same lines telescopes see, is a step toward deciding whether merging flux ropes explain the corona's nanojets.
arxiv-2601-03454:
Leonid Berezansky, Elena Braverman, and Alexander Domoshnitsky review what is known about stability in delay differential equations, where today's change depends on past values. They focus on exponential stability, meaning solutions shrink toward zero at a steady fast rate. The review covers old criteria and adds new uniform tests for a scalar equation with several delayed terms.

Both smooth and rough, merely measurable, coefficients are covered. The authors then use a global linearization approach, applying linear results to nonlinear versions of the equation. Their proofs rest on bounds for solutions and on a classic theorem about splitting solution behavior. Numerical examples show the tests at work. Delay equations model epidemics, control systems, and population change, so sharp stability tests have broad use.
arxiv-2601-03654:
Bahadur Yadav and Sanjay Kumar Mohanty combine quantum computing with a signal tool called the ridgelet transform to forecast financial series and pick portfolios. Their Quantum Ridgelet Neural Network breaks price data into multi-resolution pieces, so both local wiggles and global trends become visible. Ridgelet features also reduce the number of qubits needed, a practical concern on today's small quantum machines.

Forecasts then feed a mean-variance portfolio problem, rewritten in a standard binary form and solved with the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm. The study begins from a theoretical single-qubit formulation of the model. Hybrid designs like this test whether quantum steps can earn their place inside real finance pipelines, rather than serving as decoration on classical workflows.
arxiv-2601-03854:
Ziyi Yang, George Pîrlea, and Ilya Sergey present a framework for building first-order logic formulas from examples, aimed at inferring invariants of transition systems. Invariants are the safety facts a spread-out system must never break, and finding them on its own is a long-standing bottleneck in checking. The authors first study and sort current methods for encoding formula building inside answer set programming.

From that survey they propose orthogonal slices, a technique that splits the search space into handy chunks and enables two forms of step-wise pruning of candidates. Built into their FORCE framework, the mix greatly speeds up a state-of-the-art algorithm for spread-out system invariant inference. The framework also makes it easier to compose varied inference approaches, opening new tweaks for checking the protocols behind cloud infrastructure.
arxiv-2601-03954:
Loïc Dubois, writing alone, gives an algorithm for computing the intrinsic Delaunay triangulation of a closed polyhedral surface. Surfaces can be shown as portalgons, flat polygon sets with edges glued in the abstract. That is simpler than 3D meshes but has a flaw called unbounded happiness: a shortest path may revisit one polygon endlessly. Delaunay triangulations were lately shown to avoid that flaw, making them the right frame for surface algorithms.

Given the surface as a triangular portalgon, the method computes the triangulation whose vertices are the surface's singularities, the points whose angle around them differs from a full turn. Its running time is polynomial in the triangle count and in the log of the aspect ratio. Fast intrinsic triangulations support geometry work on surfaces exactly as given, without embedding tricks.
arxiv-2601-04054:
Yayati Jadhav and Amir Barati Farimani tackle the inverse design of mechanical linkages that trace a wanted path. Linkage design is hard because joint positions, link layout, and motion limits interact in a strongly non-linear way. Small shifts in a joint can change the whole traced path, and the design space grows fast.

The pair build LinkD, which grows a linkage as a graph one joint at a time. A causal transformer predicts the discrete layout step by step, while a diffusion model refines each joint position and its links to earlier joints. Bad joints that lock or collide can be rebuilt on their own. The method handles systems with up to twenty nodes and is presented as scalable to larger mechanisms.
arxiv-2601-04254:
Brady Steele and Micah Katz run a controlled comparison of rule-based matching and multi-agent language models on multi-hop reasoning. Multi-hop tasks need facts combined across documents, not just found in one place. Their synthetic framework holds the task fixed while methods and models vary, which isolates what each approach truly adds.

Across one hundred twenty trials with four mid-scale models, a clear split appears. Rules score perfectly on structured retrieval yet almost fail on cross-document reasoning, while multi-agent systems show the reverse pattern and lead on reasoning. Extra agents help only models that already reason well enough, which suggests amplification rather than rescue. Active parameter count, not total count, predicts mixture-of-experts performance, and a smaller newer model beats a larger older one, pointing to training quality.
arxiv-2601-04554:
Wenlin Zhang and eleven co-authors replace the riskiest step in recommender research — experimenting on real users — with simulated ones, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Online A/B testing is how platforms compare recommendation models, but it costs money, time, and user goodwill. Language-model agents promise a cheaper substitute, yet existing agents cannot see pages or behave like shoppers in a real interface.

Their A/B Agent framework builds a recommendation sandbox where a multimodal agent browses multiple pages as a user would, perceiving text and images, carrying fine-grained preferences, consulting its action memory. even tiring like a person. The team validates the stand-in from three angles — model, data, and features — and finds the simulation data it generates can itself train better recommenders. The work makes the case that a well-built simulated user can shoulder much of the A/B burden.
arxiv-2601-04654:
Ryutaro Oshima, Yuya Hosoda, and Youji Iiguni build a speech recognizer that censors as it transcribes, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The design welds a speech model's encoder to a language model's decoder, so one system produces the transcript and simultaneously masks hate-related words, limiting exposure to harmful content. The obstacle is data: teaching the masking behaviour needs annotated hate speech audio, which barely exists.

Their workaround manufactures the data. A language model drafts text samples with chain-of-thought prompting guided by cultural context and examples; speech synthesis voices them. And a filtering step keeps only samples that text classifiers agree are genuinely hateful, with the agreement threshold setting the dataset's hate level for a gradual curriculum. The trained system masked hate words with accuracy near fifty-nine percent, beating previous baselines, and the curriculum improved both transcription and censorship.
arxiv-2601-05054:
Kousuke Kuto and Kazuhiro Oeda build a math world where prey can hide in a safe zone in a 2026 paper. In their world, prey can slip into a refuge where the hunters may not go. The hunters, for their part, move in a set way toward spots rich in prey. That style of move is far-sighted: the hunters react to prey at a range, not just at their feet, unlike the near-sighted moves most past work used.

The pair first show the time-based form of the world is sound, with clean rules despite the sharp edge of the refuge. They then study the still states of the world. They ask how the refuge and the set move style shape those states. The work can guide the design of wild refuges, where the size and spot of a safe zone can make or break a prey stock.
arxiv-2601-05154: Sumit Kumar's 2026 paper asks how far apart two algebras sit, and if that gap holds when algebras are joined. Two such gaps have names: the Kadison-Kastler gap and the Christensen gap. Kumar proves both gaps stay put under set joins of the kinds he names. He also works out a string of such gaps by hand, for algebras inside crossed-product algebras. Such results tell math folks which calls of near or far can be trusted when systems are joined.
arxiv-2601-05354:
Estepan Ashkarian and 3 co-authors work out the top rule of best control for systems driven by rough noise in a 2026 paper. Rough paths rule such systems in fields from the money world to works of steel, where the noise is far more wild than the stock smooth kind. The top rule, the Pontryagin maximum principle, states what a best path must meet. The team draw it out for soft forms of control, side by side with Q-functions, scores that grade each choice of act.

Their new tool takes the slope of the score as the best path is poked by a spike, a brief, sharp change of act. From the small-scale Q-function they draw a plan to lift a policy step by step, for tasks with a curb on cost. Best control for rough worlds takes sound choice tools to ground where stock rules fail.
arxiv-2601-05854:
Frieder Lindel and 3 co-authors determine in 2026 the optimal light state for driving multi-photon transitions in atoms. The rate of such transitions depends on the light field's higher-order coherence, so shaping coherence can raise the rate. They consider a weak, fixed-intensity, narrow-band field with a capped photon number hitting a short-lived multilevel atom.

Their result is restrictive in a useful way: no quantum properties of the light need to be exploited. Classical mixtures of coherent states are already optimal for this perturbative single-mode regime. That conclusion simplifies the experimental search for better multi-photon driving, since exotic quantum light sources would add difficulty without improving the transition rate under the conditions studied.
arxiv-2601-06054:
Marketing copy must pass compliance checks before it ships. Alberto Purpura and 2 co-authors present a 2026 workflow that uses reasoning language models for that review. The system checks text against a list of requirements and flags problems, without relying on an external knowledge store.

The paper compares ways of training models for the job. Supervised fine-tuning and a group-based reinforcement method are both tested. The authors also check whether small models do better when they generate reasoning steps before answering. Finally, they test how different reward functions, alone and combined, affect performance when training with the reinforcement method. The goal is a review process that catches issues reliably and explains its thinking.
arxiv-2601-06554:
A passkey can roam from phone to phone through a firm's cloud. That means trust in the firm, like it or not. Kemal Bicakci and 3 co-authors sketch a new base for passkeys in a 2026 paper. Their base locks a soft key tool with a hard token of the type used for state-grade e-sign marks.

In the base plan, the cloud holds just the locked form of each key. The sole way to unlock sits in the user's hard token. A tough twin plan adds a blind math step tied to a local check, like a PIN. That step stops the sync key from use in any other rite. The tough plan is drawn and weighed, not built. Both plans look like plain passkeys to web sites. The paper gives the model, the threat list, a build of the base plan, and test scores.
arxiv-2601-06754:
Dixi Yang and six co-authors find how swimming germs stick fast to a wall in a 2026 paper. Swarms of germs stick in a flash from thin, weak broths of them. Flows push germs to hug walls but can not hold them there in a stable way.

Charge forces at walls push germs off more than they pull them in. Yet the germs stick fast, which those forces can not explain on their own. The team joins lab tests with large runs on a fast machine. Two germs are used in the tests: Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. Both sit in a two-part mix of water-based gels for the lab work. They find that wet-linked phase split acts as a trap based on energy. The split of the mix at the wall traps the germs there, they report.
arxiv-2601-06854:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Luigi Romano and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers semilinear single-track vehicle models with distributed tyre friction dynamics. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. The work introduces a new family of single-track vehicle models that incorporate a distributed representation of transient tyre dynamics. Whilst simultaneously accounting for nonlinear effects induced by friction.

The core of the proposed framework is represented by the distributed Friction with Bristle Dynamics (FrBD) model. Which unifies and extends classical formulations such as Dahl and LuGre by describing. The rolling contact process as a spatially distributed system governed by semilinear partial differential equations (PDEs). Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-06954:
Research by Holger Boche and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with arithmetic complexity of solutions of the dirichlet problem. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The classical Dirichlet problem on the unit disk can be solved by different numerical approaches. The two most common and popular approaches are the integration of the associated Poisson integral and, by applying Dirichlet’s principle.

Solving a particular minimization problem. For practical use, these procedures need to be implemented on concrete computing platforms. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07454:
Yuxuan Hu and colleagues introduce WaveMan, a sensing system for humanoid robots, in this 2026 preprint. Their goal is room-scale human interaction perception inside homes. Two demands shape the work: robots must cope with users standing anywhere, and they must respect user privacy. Cameras can fail the second demand, so the team turns to radio sensing instead.

WaveMan uses millimeter-wave signals, which can sense people without recording images. Earlier mmWave systems, the authors note, generalize poorly to new distances or viewpoints. A system trained in one spot may misread a person in another. WaveMan is built to handle that spatial variation across a whole room. The paper matters for home robotics, where privacy and reliability must come together.
arxiv-2601-07854:
Jing Wang and coauthors look for immune patterns that point to recovery from Long COVID. The after effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection can last for months. What drives full relief of symptoms is still not well defined. The team studied 97,564 checks over time from 13,511 people in the study. Vaccine records were linked to those checks. Their 2026 preprint splits mere passage of time from change tied to vaccines.

Recovery trajectories vary widely between patients. A density measure of immune traits may show why some get well faster. Large longitudinal data let the authors watch trajectories rather than single snapshots. To split plain gains with time from vaccine linked gains matters when staff advise patients. The study speaks to clinicians and scholars managing Long COVID care. It searches for measurable signs that recovery is on track. The scale is large, and that scale is what lets faint trends show up at all.
arxiv-2601-07954:
Haoan Jin and colleagues align language models with Chinese medical ethics using human-centered methods. Language models now serve many healthcare tasks. Aligning them with medical ethics, especially in complex real cases, remains underexplored. Their 2026 preprint presents MedES, a dynamic, scenario-centric benchmark. It is built from 260 authoritative Chinese medical, ethical, and legal sources. The scenarios reflect challenges in clinical decision-making.

Ethics in medicine involves consent, confidentiality, and duties that vary by situation. A benchmark drawn from real authoritative sources tests those nuances better than generic questions. Chinese sources matter because norms and law differ across countries. Human-centric construction keeps clinicians and ethicists in the loop. The paper serves medical AI scholars and health policy readers. It argues alignment must be tested where care actually happens.
arxiv-2601-08154: M. Anzorena and a large team report a Forbush decrease seen on May 10, 2024. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses the ALPAQUITA air-shower array to record the event. A Forbush decrease is a sharp drop in cosmic rays after solar activity disturbs Earth's space environment. The array covers a wide rigidity range, from 70 to 1000 gigavolts. Observations across that range show how the drop varies with particle energy. Such records help space weather researchers link solar events to effects measured on the ground.
arxiv-2601-08654: Yihan Hong and co-authors present Rulers, a framework for robust language model evaluation with locked rubrics. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation promises scalable rubric-based grading. Aligning frozen, black-box judges with human standards stays hard due to generation randomness. The authors reframe judge alignment as a criteria transfer problem. They isolate three failure modes: rubric instability from prompt sensitivity, unverifiable reasoning, and scale misalignment with human grading. Evidence-anchored scoring aims to fix all three for more trustworthy automatic grades.
arxiv-2601-09554:
Rayan Chouity, Charbel Hannoun, Jihad Fahs, and Ibrahim Abou-Faycal ask when the best estimate of a stable random variable is a simple linear one. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies jointly stable random variables under two dependence models. Stable laws are the heavy-tailed distributions that arise from generalized limit theorems.

One model takes a linear mix of two independent stable variables; the other is a sub-Gaussian symmetric stable vector. In both cases, the authors show the conditional mean estimator is linear. They also find the linear estimators that minimize dispersion. Simple optimal rules matter in signal processing, where stable noise models fit real interference.
arxiv-2601-09854:
Ben Lang explores puzzles that arise when a multi-level atom talks to light in a waveguide. His 2026 arXiv paper studies the optical dipole interaction between a multi-level quantum system and a single-mode waveguide of any local polarization. Several of the findings look paradoxical at first sight.

One case gives two non-orthogonal quantum states. Each sends photon flux in the opposite direction from the other. The paper works through such cases and resolves them. Waveguides are the wiring of photonic quantum devices, so exact results matter. Resolved paradoxes sharpen the theory that device designers rely on.
arxiv-2601-09954:
Nahid Alam and a large team name a blind spot in vision and language models. These models pair a photo with text. They have grown fast in skill. But they still fail at where things sit in a scene. Left, right, near, and far trip them up.

The team blames how the models are built. Most use an image coder trained to match text to a whole photo. The photo is cut into tiles and laid flat in a line. That flat line drops the two way shape of the scene. The paper tests this flaw and maps where it bites most.
arxiv-2601-10054:
Nick Truong, Pritam Karmokar, and William Beksi built a test set for motion seen from under water. Under water shots are hard to read. Light fades by hue, dust clouds the view, and light is dim in patches. True motion is near out of reach to mark by hand.

Event based cams offer a way past these ills. They mark change with fine time steps and a wide light range. The set is named UEOF. It gives marked motion data for such cams under water. Labs can use it to test and train their tools on the same base.
arxiv-2601-10254:
Irina Abdullaeva and co authors test if AI has a raw feel for shape. Most shape tests let a model work it out by steps. That tests algebra more than sight. A model may pass yet lack a true sense of space. The team made a new test set named NoReGeo.

The set asks for direct shape calls. Can a model tell if lines cross, if a point sits in a shape, or if forms match? No step work should be needed. The set thus tests if shape sense is built in. It gives a clean check that past sets did not.
arxiv-2601-10654:
A short note in operator algebra takes up the Connes embedding problem, a long-running question about von Neumann algebras. The note shows that a certain completely bounded map exists. The map runs from a C*-algebra with the lifting property into a QWEP von Neumann algebra. The key point is what the map cannot be.

The map is not strongly similar to a *-homomorphism, the nicest kind of map between such algebras. That gap between bounded maps and star-shaped maps carries the result. Notes of this kind sort out which algebra maps can be cleaned up and which cannot.
arxiv-2601-10954:
Nikko John Leo S. Lobos solves the Dunkl-Schrödinger equation exactly for the Deng-Fan potential. The Deng-Fan potential models how atoms bind in a molecule. The Dunkl version of the equation adds reflection terms that appear in some quantum models. Exact solutions are rare and prized, since they anchor numeric methods.

Lobos uses the Pekeris approximation to handle the centrifugal singularity, the blow-up at the center. He then applies the parametric Nikiforov-Uvarov method. The result is closed-form expressions for the energy spectrum and the radial wavefunctions, written with Jacobi polynomials. Spectroscopists and theorists gain formulas they can evaluate directly for this molecular model.
arxiv-2601-11054:
Zhejian Zhang and co-authors search for galaxy cluster-scale strong lenses in the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. Strong lensing by a whole cluster bends light from distant galaxies into arcs. Such systems are rare. They are prized tools for probing dark matter and dark energy, and they magnify the distant universe beyond normal reach.

Large imaging surveys now offer the raw material to expand the lens sample. The authors mine the DESI Legacy data for cluster-scale candidates. Each new lens is a natural telescope and a weighing scale for dark matter at once. A bigger sample sharpens both uses. The work feeds follow-up campaigns that turn candidates into confirmed, modeled systems.
arxiv-2601-11354:
Weiyi Wang, Xinchi Chen, Jingjing Gong, Xuanjing Huang, and Xipeng Qiu build a space benchmark. Their 2026 preprint is named AstroReason-Bench, on agentic planning. Space missions pose planning tasks of many unlike kinds. Past tools solved each kind with its own algorithm.

The bench tests one unified agent across that spread. A central agent picks tools from a kit to plan each task. That shift, from split tools to one agent, is the core move. Fudan University and the OpenMOSS team back the work. The bench can show where a general agent still fails. It can also show where one agent now beats narrow tools.
arxiv-2601-11454:
Yashpal Singh, Juan Peralta, and Koblar Jackson trace errors in reaction barriers. Their 2026 preprint extends work on self-interaction corrections. Density functional theory is the workhorse of computational chemistry. Its barrier heights for reactions can err in known ways.

Adding Perdew-Zunger self-interaction corrections improves those heights much. The team gives a detailed orbital-by-orbital account of the fix. They test three semi-local functional approximations in the study. Those sit on the three lowest rungs of Jacob's Ladder. That ladder ranks functionals by the data they use. The title notes stretched bond errors that rise and fall. Orbital views show which states drive the correction's gains.
arxiv-2601-11554:
Triloki Nath, Manohar Choudhary, and Ram Pandey solve a generalized waist problem. Their 2026 preprint gives an optimality condition and an algorithm. The root puzzle came from John Tyrell at King's College London. He challenged his PhD students with it years ago.

The puzzle posits three given lines in space. They are pairwise disjoint and not all parallel. A triangle must place exactly one vertex on one line. Each vertex sits on a distinct one of the lines. The claim is that a unique least-perimeter triangle exists. The generalized waist form widens that classic setup. Conditions tell when a candidate triangle is optimal. An algorithm then computes the winner in practice.
arxiv-2601-11654:
Kaustubh Shejole and Gaurav Mishra speed up interactive image segmentation. Their 2026 preprint gives an index named PSSI-MaxST. Graph-based methods split an image into foreground and background. User inputs guide where that split should fall.

Existing methods often carry high computational costs in use. They can also react too sharply to user inputs. When foreground and background share like colors, quality drops. The team's index scores pixel-segment similarity for the task. Intensity and smoothness features feed that similarity score. A maximum spanning tree then drives the segmentation. A faster index could make interactive editing feel instant.
arxiv-2601-11754:
Andrew Mummery studies gas disks that swirl into black holes while also blowing gas out. He works with the thin disk rules in Newtonian gravity. The maths track how the disk mass spreads and drains with time.

He finds Green's function forms for the case with outflows. In set limits, the forms are plain and exact. They look much like the classic forms with no outflows, due to Lynden-Bell and Pringle. Yet the fine points and what a scope would see are quite unlike. The forms help link disk maths to real light from such systems.
arxiv-2601-11854:
Yifei Zhang, Hooshang Nayyeri, Rinat Khaziev, and their co-authors build a test bed for chat agents that do tasks. New agents use large models plus many tools and APIs. They can hold long talks, juggle mixed goals, and act ahead of time on their own.

Old test sets do not check these new skills in a set way. Their frame, called ATOD in the work, fills that gap. It tests how agents plan, track context, and use tools over a long task. Such tests help buyers pick agents with proof, not claims.
arxiv-2601-12254:
Kazuki Yamauchi, Masato Murata, and Shogo Seki filter speech data cleaned by generative tools, using confidence scores. Generative speech enhancement can make clean speech from noisy clips. That could turn noisy text-to-speech sets into high-grade ones.

But such tools can hallucinate, dropping sounds or changing the speaker. Old quality gauges often miss those flaws. Their confidence-based filter aims to catch them. Clean sets with fewer hidden flaws train better speech tools.  The filter aims to keep clean clips pure at scale.  Such reviews help new teams skip paths that failed in the past.
arxiv-2601-12554:
Iman Peivaste and a large team review how artificial intelligence is reshaping materials science and engineering. AI tools now help researchers handle complexity, speed up discovery, and design better materials. Faster algorithms and growing stores of data drive this shift. The team say AI skill is fast becoming essential for materials researchers.

Their review maps the current landscape of the field first. It then names the key challenges that still block wider use. Data quality, trust in models, and links with physics all loom large in such reviews. Last, they chart future paths for the field. A survey of this breadth serves newcomers and veterans alike. It shows where AI already pays off and where care is still needed.
arxiv-2601-13154:
Krystof Chrappova, Jeremiah P. Tidey, Christopher Bell, and Simon R. Hall solve the crystal plan of a wet rubidium ruthenium oxide. They also probe its magnetism. The oxide holds water in its plan, which makes it a rich case for study.

They read the plan from three dim electron diffraction, taken from lone grains of a powder made in the lab. The plan sits in a named symmetry class, with cell edges they report. Such care with tiny grains shows how far electron tools can go when X-ray routes fail. For chemists, the plan is the base for all talk of how this oxide acts.
arxiv-2601-13454:
Qingyang Zhang grows distance correlation to data in named groups, for use in big feature hunts. Distance correlation is a score for how two sets of marks lean on each other, in any form. In its stock form it needs number marks. Group marks, such as kind tags, need a code first.

Zhang lets the code be broad. One hot codes fit plain kinds. A semicircle code fits ranked kinds. The code keeps the span facts among kinds, which past tools threw out. That keep lifts the score's skill. In high dim hunts, the score can screen which traits matter for an out come. Such a screen cuts junk traits early.
arxiv-2601-13554:
Kazuki Yokomizo, Aashish A. Clerk, and Yuto Ashida set the base caps of continuous Gaussian quantum metrology. Metrology is the science of fine marks. In continuous form, a sensor reads a stream of light that a system sheds to its world. That stream can carry facts bit by bit as it leaves.

For bosonic systems, those with light like bits, no full account of the best mark grade was known. The team gives that account. Their caps state how fine a mark can be at best, what eva the tool. Such caps tell sensor teams when to stop tune and when a new form is need to gain more.
arxiv-2601-13654:
Shashank Kumar Ojha, Jyotirmay Maity, and Srimanta Middey study how electrons meet domain walls in strontium titanate in 2026. That crystal is a famed test bed for solid-state physics, studied for over seventy-five years. Its traits link structure, charge flow, and response to electric fields in rich ways. Domain walls are thin borders where the crystal's inner pattern shifts.

The team asks what happens when electrons cross or gather at these walls. Walls can act as paths or traps for charge in oxide devices. That makes them of worth for new kinds of electronics. The work adds to the long study of a crystal that keeps teaching new lessons.
arxiv-2601-13854:
Leyang Xue and co-authors explain how abrupt phase transitions can start and grow in 2026. A phase transition is a sudden shift of a system to a new state. Abrupt ones jump, rather than glide, between states. The micro steps that drive such jumps are not fully understood.

The team sets out a theory based on internal node dependencies in a lattice. Branching-driven nucleation is their name for the growth process. Small seeds branch outward through dependent nodes, tipping the whole system. The frame could apply to magnets, networks, and social cascades alike.
arxiv-2601-13954:
Adrien Meyer, Didier Mutter, and Nicolas Padoy cut the labeling cost for finding landmarks in medical images in 2026. Object detection models need costly bounding box annotations to learn. That cost limits how far such models can scale in medicine. Weakly semi-supervised detection uses a single point per instance instead of a box.

Point annotations take far less time yet keep a localization signal. Their system, DExTeR, uses class and instance experts for this weak setup. Detecting anatomical landmarks aids diagnosis and guides interventions. Cheaper training could bring these tools to more hospitals.
arxiv-2601-14254:
James G. Rogers, James E. Owen, Ethan Schreyer, and James Kirk study small planets in this 2026 paper. Their targets are sub-Neptunes, worlds between Earth and Neptune in size. What these planets are made of inside is still an open question in exoplanet science. The team looks at gas leaking away from them.

Their method uses sightings of hydrogen or helium escaping from a planet's outer layers. From those rates, they set bounds on the mean molecular weight of the planet's envelope. The logic is a simple timescale argument. A planet needs a big enough store of light gas to keep losing it at the rate seen today.
arxiv-2601-14354:
Yongchao Huang reworks a learning design in this 2026 paper. The design is the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, or JEPA. It learns by predicting latent representations, inner codes of data, rather than rebuilding raw inputs. That makes it a scalable path for self-supervised learning. It also sidesteps high-entropy observations, inputs packed with hard-to-predict detail.

Past JEPA versions use deterministic regression objectives, fixed targets with no room for chance. Huang argues that this hides probabilistic meaning and limits use in stochastic control, where outcomes vary. His version, VJEPA, is variational. The title calls such models probabilistic world models, built to carry uncertainty about what comes next.
arxiv-2601-14554:
Zhiyuan Guo, C. W. Walter, Eli S. Rykoff, and the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration present a galaxy selection method in this 2026 paper. Luminous Red Galaxies are prized tracers for cosmology surveys. The team introduces IRMaGiC, an algorithm built on RedMaGiC. It is designed to enhance the selection of such galaxies across the redshift range one to two.

That range pushes past where optical selection alone works well. IRMaGiC extends selection into the infrared by joining data from two surveys. They are LSST and the Roman High Latitude Imaging Survey. Readers get a method to pick a clean, uniform galaxy sample at distances where the old tool thinned out.
arxiv-2601-14754:
Guolin Nan, Zhijian Li, Feng Mei, and Zhihao Xu study localization in a non-Hermitian quasicrystal in this 2026 paper. The system is a one-dimensional generalized Aubry-André-Harper chain. It has asymmetric nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor hoppings. Those hoppings are generated by a Bernoulli imaginary gauge field. A quasiperiodic onsite potential completes the setup.

The team studies anomalous localization in this chain. Localization means states stay trapped in small regions instead of spreading. Mobility edges are the energy borders between trapped and spreading states. Non-Hermitian systems can break the usual rules for both. Readers get a study of where those borders sit when the gauge field itself is disordered.
arxiv-2601-15354:
Peng Chen and Jun Jing find how precise a quantum measurement can be when a helper qubit joins in. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with quantum metrology, the science of measuring with quantum probes. Their probe is a spin ensemble, a crowd of spins acting as one sensor.

The ensemble is coupled to a single ancillary qubit, a two-level helper. The coupling follows a Heisenberg XXZ interaction, a standard form for spin systems. The protocol is measurement-based: the qubit is read to learn about the ensemble. The authors derive the precision limit of that weak-coupling setup.
arxiv-2601-15554:
T. Hanaguri probes two intertwined orders in a layered superconductor in a 2026 arXiv paper. The material is 2H-NbSe2, a well-studied layered compound. Inside it, a charge density wave coexists with superconductivity. How the two affect each other is the paper's question. Hanaguri studies the cleaved surface of the material. The tool is scanning tunneling microscopy at ultralow temperature.

Spectroscopic imaging maps the superconducting gap across that surface. The gap spectrum shows intricate structures, he reports. Those structures reflect anisotropic gaps that open on multiple Fermi surfaces. Surface charge order can reshape the gap in subtle ways. Mapping that interplay helps physicists model layered superconductors. Such materials are testbeds for how competing orders share one crystal.
arxiv-2601-15654:
Arman and Prasanta K. Panigrahi study states of light with very fine structure in a 2026 arXiv paper. Phase space is the map where a light state's traits are drawn. Some states hold structures smaller than the Planck scale. Those tiny features can boost sensitivity in measurement. The authors use non-Gaussian operations to enlarge such states. Bigger fine structure, in the right form, can mean a stronger metrological edge.

Part of the work tests photon-added cat and kitten states. Adding photons broadens these states in phase space. The authors observe a sensitivity gain from that broadening, at higher energy cost. They also build states with weak squeezing and displacement. These are resources labs can actually reach. The balance of gain against cost is the practical thread.
arxiv-2601-16154:
Sam Slezak and coauthors bound how fast open quantum systems reach rest. Their 2026 preprint deals with Lindblad maths for a system tied to a bath.
