Weak ties to a bath stand for heat flow and rest in many cases. They also stand for Gibbs draws used in quantum code. The speed to rest sets run times for both acts.

The team shows that speed can stay in a set time bound. That bound is of the poly type, not a fast growth type. Firm time bounds help teams trust Gibbs draw code. They also set true heat time scales for open systems. The work links heat maths to code run times.
arxiv-2601-16454:
Wonjun Lee, Hyukjoon Kwon and Gil Young Cho use join links to glue chance in quantum states. Their 2026 preprint deals with how to make full chance states fast. Such states serve many tasks in quantum work and tests. Local chance steps alone make full chance at high cost. Join links, called entanglement, may be the key stock for the task.

The team shows links let local steps build world chance. They bound the cost with the second Rényi entropy, a link size. Tight bounds tell how much link stock a build must spend. That spend sets the true price of chance states. The work names links as the core stock for chance.
arxiv-2601-16554:
Čekanavičius and Jokubauskienė sum near forms for sums of same spread steps. Their 2026 preprint deals with sums of free steps on a grid. Each step has the same law and a flip fair form. The sum law is near a compound Poisson law in such cases. That near law is the mate law that tracks the sum.

The team adds a next term signed law of Hipp type. Next terms cut the flaw of the first near law much. Bergström type growth gives the flaw size in firm terms. Sharp near laws serve chance sums in risk and queue work. The work is a pure chance maths study.
arxiv-2601-16854:
Irfan Mahmood, Adeena Iqbal, and Sohail Mumtaz study a lone wave in a noisy, damped world. The wave obeys a fifth-order KdV rule. Loss drains the wave as it runs. Chance kicks shake it as well. Their 2026 preprint works out how the wave's push spreads in chance terms.

They find a clear form for that spread, tied to a chance clock. The form then trims down to a famed Painlevé rule. Such trims link big wave rules to small, known ones. That link can aid work on fluids, light, and plasma waves. It shows deep ties among rules once seen as far apart.
arxiv-2601-16954:
Ba-Thinh Lam and a team of eight co-authors sort scans where labels are scarce and sources mix. Scan tools must tag each point in a health image. Tags take costly work by scarce pros. Scans also come from many sites and gear types. Those mixes shift how scans look in hard ways. Their 2026 preprint trains tools that shrug off those shifts.

Their tool learns from part-tagged scans across mixed sources. A cluster-based align step joins the sources' traits. No source tags are known in the mix. Sound tags from mixed sources aid small clinics most. Such tools could spread pro-grade reads more wide.
arxiv-2601-17154:
Shivanshu Tripathi, Hossein Mohsenzadeh Yazdi, Maziar Raissi, and Hamed Mohsenian-Rad model fast grid waves with physics-coded nets. New grid gear, like solar and wind links, acts fast in faults. Old gauges are too slow and coarse to catch those acts. Wave gauges now give fine, synced raw wave marks. Their 2026 preprint learns from those marks with less data.

Physics rules built in the net cut its data needs. The net tracks wave forms through fault spans. True tracks help guards act in time. They also help plan grids with more green gear. Data-lean tools suit grids where marks are dear.
arxiv-2601-17454:
Muhammad Ahmed Atif and three co-authors test a common belief in multi-agent learning. The belief says central value learning improves teamwork and stability. The team tests it in a fully tabular predator-prey gridworld. They compare independent and centralized Q-learning head to head. Embodiment limits shape the test. Agent speed and stamina are set as hard constraints.

Such tight control shows when central learning truly helps. It also shows regimes where bodies, not brains, drive outcomes. They call those regimes embodiment-induced coordination regimes. The lesson is broad for robot teams. Design the body and the learner together. A gridworld proof can steer real multi-robot work.
arxiv-2601-17554:
The CMS Collaboration presents a machine learning upgrade to particle-flow reconstruction. Particle flow builds a full list of particles from each collision at the CMS detector. It is central to how CMS reads events at the CERN LHC. The current code rests on physics-based heuristics. Learned models can replace some of those hand rules. The paper gives a full event interpretation with the new method.

Learned flow could sharpen measures of jets and missing energy. It could also speed event reads at huge data rates. CMS handles some of the largest data flows in science. Gains there ripple to all its physics results. The work tests learning inside a flagship detector.
arxiv-2601-17654:
Ruofan Wu, Jae-Won Chung, and Mosharaf Chowdhury present Kareus for energy use in large model training. AI compute demand grows at an unprecedented rate. Energy supply does not keep pace. Energy is now an expensive, contended resource. Recent work cut training time and cost in many ways. Kareus targets dynamic and static energy jointly.

Joint cuts matter because idle draw is a large share of bills. A scheduler that trims both can save at data center scale. Lower energy per model eases grid strain too. The work comes from the University of Michigan team. It treats energy as a first-class design goal. That stance fits an era of power caps.
arxiv-2601-17854: Yuto Nakajima and Hiroki Takahasi prove a result about Hurwitz continued fractions, a way of expanding complex numbers in steps. Their 2026 preprint looks at numbers whose partial quotients contain scaled copies of any finite grid pattern. The quotients are read as points on an integer grid, and the copies appear again and again. They show that the set of such irrational numbers has Hausdorff dimension one.
arxiv-2601-18454:
Gabriel Barrenechea, Cristian Cárcamo, and Abner Poza build a math tool to grade a kind of heart and blood scan. The scan tracks flow in time as well as in space, so staff can watch blood move through the heart. A good grade needs a check: how far is the flow in the scan from a flow that obeys the laws of fluids?

The team split the flow in the scan into the part they take as truth and a gap part. They then solve for the gap with a firm form of the flow laws, built to stay calm in hard cases. Tests of the tool show how the grade shifts with scan flaws. A firm grade could help staff trust a scan or ask for a new one. It could also guide firms that build the scan kit.
arxiv-2601-18554:
Alberto Purpura and four colleagues built a new test for how well language models obey asks. A model may do a task well yet miss a set rule in the ask. Past tests blur those two things: a fail could mean weak skill or weak rule care. The team want a test that grades rule care on its own.

Their test, named MOSAIC, builds fresh tasks on the fly with up to a score of set rules in each ask. Rules can cover length, form, tone, and what must or must not show up. Each rule is graded on its own, so staff can see which kinds of rule a model drops. A fine test like this could help firms pick models for work where rules are law. It could also show where models need more training.
arxiv-2601-18654:
Juan Wu, Zhe Zhang, and Amit Mehra study when a maker should tag their work as made by AI. Smart tools have cut the cost of text, shots, and clips, so feeds fill with work of mixed worth. Sites now ask makers to tag AI work. Tags are backed by checks that can miss, and by fines for those who skip the tag. Makers must weigh the gain of a hid tag next to the risk of a fine.

The team model that choice and ask what rules make self-tags work. If the fine is too light, few will tag. If the check is too weak, tags lose their worth. Their work maps the mix of check and fine that makes tags a fair sign. Sites could use that map to set rules that keep trust in feeds.
arxiv-2601-18754:
Mohamed Amine Ferrag, Abderrahmane Lakas, and Merouane Debbah build a test suite for drone agents run by language models on next-gen nets. Such drones fly in tasks where a fault can do real harm. They must act well while foes try to fool or break them. Past test suites grade how well drones think, fly, and use the net. They say far less on how the drones stand up to attack.

The new suite grades three traits at once: how safe the agent is, how well it holds up when hit, and how far it can be trusted. It sets those grades in the world of fast new nets, where links are swift but threats are swift too. A full suite could help teams ship drone agents with proof of their strength. It fills a clear gap in the field.
arxiv-2601-18854:
Chandana Pati and S. M. Mallikarjunaiah teach a smart net to learn the stretch laws of stuff that can't stretch past a cap. Such stuff is found in rubbers, in flesh, and in soft man-made solids. As the pull grows, the stretch nears its cap and the stuff grows stiff in slope. Old maths laws state that cap in a plain way. But their sharp bend makes them hard to fit from test data.

The pair build the cap into a net whose form staff can read. The net learns the law from data while the cap holds by build. A law that can be read, and that can't break its cap, is fit for design work. It could guide parts made of flesh-like stuff, from seals to soft robots. The work joins strict maths with learn tools in a clean way.
arxiv-2601-18954:
J. Sebastian Monzon, Frank C. van den Bosch, and Martin P. Rey predict the faint star halos around galaxies like our own. In the standard picture, these halos grow as small galaxies fall in and get torn apart. The team adds new semi-analytic tools to a framework called SatGen to track those stolen stars.

They run the tools across large sets of merger trees, the family trees of growing galaxies. That spread lets them study how much luck shapes each halo's final form. Two twin galaxies can end with quite unlike halos, and their stats show how wide that spread should be.
arxiv-2601-19154:
Shun Takagi and Seng Pei Liew sharpen the math of shuffled privacy. In distributed data analysis, each user's data is first scrambled locally, then shuffled among users to hide who sent what. Shuffling boosts privacy a lot, a fact past work proved using only the local privacy level as the knob.

Those old bounds can be loose and can miss how the guarantee behaves as settings change. The pair analyze the shuffle past the pure local case. Tighter bounds mean data curators can promise stronger privacy, or collect finer data under the same promise.
arxiv-2601-19254:
J. C. F. Balzan and three co-authors read the fine grain inside fast radio bursts. These bursts are millisecond flashes from deep space whose inner structure may reveal what makes them. Their framework, FIRES, models the burst's dynamic spectrum as a pile of tiny Gaussian shots with polarized light.

They apply it to two bursts caught by the CRAFT survey. The model reproduces key patterns: scattering smooths the angle swings on the trailing edge, while the leading edge keeps more of its inborn structure. Reading the grain this way turns each burst into a probe of its source and its path.
arxiv-2601-19454:
Chayan Majumdar, Utkarsh Patel, Supriya Senapati, and Sudhanwa Patra work on two open puzzles in particle physics. Neutrinos have tiny masses that the Standard Model does not explain. Dark matter, the unseen mass in galaxies, also sits outside that model. The authors study one extension that tries to address both at once.

Their model adds a new symmetry, based on the difference between baryon and lepton number. In this setup, neutrino masses are not put in by hand. They arise through a loop process, where new particles run in a circle and generate the mass indirectly. Such masses are called radiative. The same added particles can also offer a dark matter candidate. The paper maps out how this shared framework could work.
arxiv-2601-19554:
Jérôme Touguet and six colleagues work on shaping intense laser beams. A quasi-Bessel beam keeps its narrow core over a long distance, unlike a normal focused beam. Such beams are made with a device called an axiparabola. They are prized in high-intensity laser work, where a long, even focal line is useful.

In practice the brightness along that line wobbles up and down. Those unwanted oscillations limit what the beams can do. The team traces the physical cause of the distortions. They then build a general strategy to control the brightness along the axis of the beam. A smoother focal line should make these lasers better tools for research and industry. The work joins optical design with hard experimental needs.
arxiv-2601-19654:
Paolo Matteo Simonetti and six colleagues speed up the computer models used to study how planets form. Planet formation is tracked with n-body codes, which follow many objects pulling on each other by gravity. Fully interacting simulations are the next frontier, but they are brutally expensive to run. The team presents Mercury-Opal, a version of a known code rebuilt for graphics processors.

Graphics processors run many simple calculations at once, which suits gravity between many bodies. Moving the code to them should let researchers follow larger systems for longer times. Mercury-Arches, the parent code, is a standard tool in the field. A faster version opens studies that were out of reach. The paper describes the port and what it enables.
arxiv-2601-19754:
Élie Casbi works in representation theory on categorifying cluster algebras of finite type. Cluster algebras are algebraic structures built from patterns of exchange. Categorification lifts them into richer worlds of categories, where numbers become objects. Earlier categorifications used abelian categories; this paper proposes a triangulated monoidal version.

Given a Dynkin quiver, Casbi builds a bounded homotopy category from a symmetric monoidal category defined through Auslander-Reiten theory. That classical theory describes how representations of a quiver fit together. The framework aims to capture finite-type behaviour in this new setting. This new frame could unify several known constructions. The work is a foundational proposal for others to develop. The plan is bold but clear. It builds step by step from a known base. Each step can be checked by hand. That care is the point of the work. The frame is meant for wide use.
arxiv-2601-19954:
Alistair Shilton generalises a classical identity for Hermite polynomials. These polynomials appear across physics and probability, from quantum oscillators to Gaussian analysis. For one variable, the multiplication theorem describes how the polynomial behaves when its argument is scaled. Shilton extends the result to Hermite polynomials in several variables.

A general multiplication theorem for the multivariate case was missing. Such identities let practitioners rescale arguments instead of recomputing from scratch. They also reveal structure shared across dimensions. Multivariate Hermite polynomials underlie modern methods in statistics and signal processing. Completing the basic identity toolkit supports those applications. The paper is a compact contribution to a classical theory. The new rule works in two or more dims. The old one worked in just one. That jump is the whole point here. The old one-var rule is a school room staple. The jump to more vars is not a small step.
arxiv-2601-20254:
Hengrui Luo develops wavelet tree ensembles for regression when data live on a triangulable manifold, a curved surface that can be cut into triangles. The learners are unbalanced Haar wavelet trees. Their atoms sit on geodesic triangles, the shortest-path triangles on the surface, and they form an orthonormal system under the empirical measure of the sample.

Stacking these trees into additive ensembles gives a flexible regression method that respects the geometry of the data. Many real datasets, from brain surfaces to climate fields, live on curved spaces rather than flat ones. Methods built for the surface itself can capture patterns that flat methods distort.
arxiv-2601-20554:
Yaacov Pariente and Vadim Indelman study risk-averse planning for robots that must act under partial observability. Such planning is modeled with POMDPs, where the agent cannot see the full state. The authors use the iterated conditional value-at-risk, a dynamic risk measure that guards against bad outcomes rather than optimizing the average.

They develop a policy evaluation algorithm for this risk measure with finite-time performance guarantees. Those guarantees do not depend on how many actions the agent has. Risk-sensitive planning matters wherever an average-good plan can still end in disaster, from driving to medical dosing.
arxiv-2601-20654:
Qian Gao and Ruikang Zhong use reinforcement learning to optimize beamforming for three-dimensional pinching antenna systems that both sense and communicate. They propose a three-dimensional deployment scheme for the pinching antenna array, aiming to improve integrated sensing and communication performance. Realizing that potential takes joint design.

Antenna positions, time allocation, and transmit power must be optimized together, to maximize the total communication rate under target sensing rates and an energy budget. Pinching antennas, which can be placed along a waveguide where needed, offer a flexible new hardware base for such joint designs.
arxiv-2601-20854:
Aníbal Silva and three co-authors test where transformers belong inside a classic generative model. Their 2026 paper concerns tabular data generation. Tables are a hard domain for generative models. The standard variational autoencoder, or VAE, is built from multilayer perceptrons. It struggles to model links between features. Mixed data types, such as numbers beside categories, make the task worse.

Transformers offer a contrast. Their attention mechanism is well suited to complex feature interactions. The authors explore transformer placement within the VAE design. Placement matters: the encoder, the decoder, or both could host attention. The study weighs which spot gives the best tables. Its results guide builders of synthetic data tools for business and science.
arxiv-2601-21054:
Rami Atar, Leonid Mytnik, and Gershon Wolansky study a swarm of particles that branch, wander, and thin out. Their 2026 paper concerns trimmed branching random walks. Particles perform random walks on a fine grid. When one particle branches, another is removed from the most populated site. This density-dependent selection keeps the swarm in check. The rule couples every particle's fate to the crowd.

The authors connect this process to a free obstacle problem. Free boundary problems ask where a region ends when the edge itself is unknown. That link lets tools from partial differential equations describe the swarm's spread. The result is a cleaner picture of the swarm's long-run shape. Such models echo population growth with local competition. The paper is probability theory with a geometric payoff.
arxiv-2601-21254:
Daniel Eyles, Emmanuel Lassalle, Adam Stokes, Ramón Paniagua-Domínguez, and Ahsan Nazir study superradiance, where many quantum emitters act together. When emitters share coherence, they release light that is stronger and more directed than usual. A key tool for describing the emitted light tracks how photon counts relate across two times.

For large groups of emitters, exact tracking of that relation is too costly to compute. The authors present sampling methods that make the job practical. Their approach lets researchers describe big ensembles without tracking every emitter in full detail. That opens studies of light sources and sensors built on collective emission.
arxiv-2601-21354:
T. Fujii and co-authors probe a superconductor that is also a Weyl semimetal, using nuclear resonance and magnetic tests under pressure. The material, a layered molybdenum telluride, hosts unusual electronic states. Pressure squeezes the lattice and shifts how it behaves.

The team tracks the superconducting transition and the field needed to kill it as pressure rises. Resonance data add a microscopic view of the electrons at work. Together the measures show how pressure tunes the superconducting state. Such maps help physicists link the material's odd topology to its ability to carry current with no resistance.
arxiv-2601-21554:
V. Carruba, R. Sfair, and O. C. Winter report a newly found asteroid that shares Venus's orbit and may one day threaten Earth. About twenty such Venus co-orbital asteroids are known. Several could drift into hazardous paths over thousands of years.

The team identifies the new object, named 2025 TV10, and charts its motion for the first time. They then assess whether its path could bring it close to Earth. Early tracking of such objects is vital, since small nudges grow over millennia. The work adds one more body to the watch list for planetary defense.
arxiv-2601-21654:
Hao Shen, Hang Yang, and Zhouhong Gu build a stable benchmark for deep research systems that search academic literature. Such systems plan queries, call tools, and synthesize answers over many steps. Testing them against live search services is a reproducibility trap.

Live backends drift over time, hit rate limits, and return different results per run. That variance makes fair comparison between systems almost impossible. ScholarGym fixes the environment so runs can be repeated and compared honestly. A stable gym lets the field measure real progress in automated literature research instead of noise from the tools.
arxiv-2601-21754:
Haoyu Wang and nine co-authors argue that language-based trial and error falls behind learning from experience. Language models excel at tasks framed in words. On unseen tasks that are symbolic or spatial rather than verbal, they lag badly.

Earlier work blamed the mismatch between training text and the test setting. The authors press further, contrasting verbal feedback loops with learning from lived experience in the environment. Their claim favors agents that improve by acting and observing, not by reading critiques alone. The distinction shapes how the next generation of agents should be built and trained.
arxiv-2601-22054:
Baorui Ma, Jiahui Yang, Donglin Di, and Xuancheng Zhang scale up training for metric depth estimation, teaching machines to judge real distances from images. Scaling has powered vision foundation models, but depth is harder. Training data come from mixed sensors with different noise, camera-dependent biases, and ambiguous scales.

Their 2026 preprint introduces a pretraining approach designed to learn from exactly such noisy, heterogeneous sources rather than waiting for clean data. More usable depth data means models that measure the world more accurately. Metric depth feeds robot navigation, augmented reality, and driver assistance, where knowing something is near is not enough and the actual distance decides the action.
arxiv-2601-22254:
I. Lamperti and a large team report fast gas flows from a nearby galaxy with two bright cores. Their 2026 preprint uses new data from a tool on the Very Large Telescope in Chile. The galaxy, MCG-03-34-64, may host two active black holes close to each other.

The team map gas that streams out at high speed yet holds very little dust. They trace the flows in the glow of hot gas near the cores. Such outflows can shape how a galaxy grows and forms stars. Close pairs like this one are rare test beds. They show two cores at work at once.
arxiv-2601-22354:
Jinyong Hahn, Zhipeng Liao, Konrad Menzel, and Quang Vuong extend a classic model-choice test to panel data. Panel data track the same units over time, a staple of economics. Their 2026 preprint generalizes the Vuong test, which picks between rival models by fit, using modified profile likelihoods.

Fixed group effects break the plain likelihood's nice traits, so a fix is needed. The team ground the test in an information yardstick. Sound choice tests keep policy math honest. The work is technical econometrics with wide use. It repairs a tool many rely on.
arxiv-2601-22454:
Yijun Ma, Zehong Wang, Weixiang Sun, and Yanfang Ye built a learner that reads the deep patterns of graphs that change over time. Temporal graphs track ties that form, fade, and shift. Their 2026 preprint notes that most tools are built for one task and lean on narrow claims, like short memory or fixed neighborhoods.

Their Temporal Graph Pattern Machine aims to learn the change patterns themselves. A pattern-first tool could serve fraud hunts, network watch, and spread forecasts at once. It could also move across fields with less rework. The work seeks a general engine for change.
arxiv-2601-22654:
Michael Urs Lars Kastor, Jan Rottmayer, Anna Hundertmark, and Nicolas Ralph Gauger built a U-Net surrogate that predicts cancer-cell dynamics under set parameters. Their 2026 preprint pairs a careful solver, written in C++, with a data-driven model. The target system mixes diffusion, flow, and reaction on a flat domain of cell types.

The solver gives trusted runs; the surrogate gives fast ones, tuned by the parameters. Fast, faithful forecasts let teams scan many drug or growth cases. The model keeps its logic open to inspection. The work serves the math side of cancer research.
arxiv-2601-22754:
Guillermo Gil de Avalle, Laura Maruster, and Christos Emmanouilidis pull machine-readable steps from factory troubleshooting guides with vision-language models. These guides pack diagnosis into flowchart-like diagrams, where layout and technical words jointly carry the sense. Their 2026 preprint seeks to extract that know-how in structured form.

Structured steps can feed operator support tools on the shop floor. Workers could then get the right fix path at the right moment. The hard part is reading diagrams as a human would. The work tests how far current models get. It serves a very practical need.
arxiv-2601-22954:
Yuezhou Hu and nine co-authors improve diffusion language models, which write text by refining many tokens at once. Unlike standard models, they can decode tokens in parallel. But common block-wise versions keep only the most confident tokens and throw the rest away, wasting compute.

Their residual context approach keeps more of that work instead of discarding it each round. Reusing context should make parallel writing faster and less wasteful. Efficient diffusion models could rival standard models for chat and drafting at lower cost. Residual context is the core idea: information the old remasking step discarded is carried forward instead of recomputed.
arxiv-2601-23254:
Baoyi Wang and eight co-authors study grep-like retrieval for repository-level code completion. Completing code across a whole project needs cross-file context, but context windows are limited. Retrieval frameworks fetch the right snippets, using semantic indexing or graph analysis of the code structure.

Their empirical study tests simple grep-style retrieval, based on literal text search, against fancier methods. They also optimize the simple approach for this task. A strong showing by plain search would simplify tooling for coding assistants everywhere. Limited context windows force the retrieval question: cross-file dependencies cannot all be pasted into the prompt.
arxiv-2602-02454:
Ansh Kumar Sharma and 5 co-authors train robot policies inside a learned world model instead of the physical world, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Real robot interaction is expensive, expert demonstrations are limited, and software simulators differ enough from reality to hurt manipulation. World models learned from real video and action data offer a fourth option.

Their system, World-Gymnast, fine-tunes a vision-language-action policy with reinforcement learning inside an action-conditioned video world model. A vision-language model rewards the imagined rollouts. On the Bridge robot setup, the approach beat supervised fine-tuning by up to eighteen times and software simulation by up to two times. It also trained on new instructions and scenes generated by the world model itself. Test-time training in a novel scene and joint improvement of model and policy both worked.
arxiv-2602-02554:
Jingwen Xu and 11 co-authors train code models on code alone by making documentation and code reconstruct each other, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Code tasks usually need curated code-documentation pairs, which are costly and scarce for less-used languages. Their system, BatCoder, removes the pair requirement with back-translation.

Documentation is first generated from code. The generated documentation must then reconstruct the original code. How close the rebuilt code is to the original becomes an implicit reward for reinforcement learning. Both directions improve jointly. Training can therefore use raw code corpora, greatly widening the pool. On the HumanEval and MBPP benchmarks, a seven-billion-parameter model beat strong open-source rivals in single-attempt pass rates. Results also scaled steadily with more training data and larger models.
arxiv-2602-02654:
Shamim Haque's 2026 study, with 2 co-authors, asks which of two twin stars nature actually prefers. A strong phase transition inside dense matter can create a second stable branch of compact stars: hybrid stars with quark-matter cores sharing the same mass as fully hadronic stars. Both branches resist small perturbations, so stability alone cannot pick a winner.

Large general-relativistic simulations perturbed stars on each branch with varying strength. Every star showed a critical perturbation threshold. Below it, the star oscillates on its original branch. Above it, the star migrates to the neighboring branch while conserving rest mass. The thresholds differ between twins, so the favoured configuration is the one whose branch segment tolerates the largest kick. That corrects the common assumption that twin-branch stars win by default. Binding energies alone can predict the winner without simulations.
arxiv-2602-02754:
Alejandro Cuevas and 1 co-author measure what happened after United States law criminalized synthetic non-consensual explicit imagery and its most notorious hosting site shut down, in a 2026 paper. Generative tools made such imagery easy to create, and it causes significant harm to victims. The federal TAKE IT DOWN Act and the MrDeepfakes closure formed a compound intervention to study.

Three forums with dedicated subforums for this content were tracked against their other explicit genres using a synthetic control design. Across websites, sharing and requests for the imagery increased after the intervention, and some forums gained new contributors. Effects varied in timing and size across platforms. The authors conclude the intervention redistributed activity rather than suppressing it. Deplatforming and regulatory signals alone, the evidence suggests, may move where and when such material is produced and shared instead of reducing its prevalence.
arxiv-2602-03054:
Healthcare robots should be designed with the people who will live with them, argue Yuanchen Bai and 4 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Co-design grounds embodied artificial intelligence in real contexts, which matters in high-stakes healthcare. Earlier efforts often targeted one setting and stopped at low-fidelity prototypes, limiting what could be learned about deployment trade-offs in practice.

The authors ran a fourteen-week workshop with twenty-two participants from many disciplines. The team explored reducing non-value-added task burdens in emergency departments, long-term rehabilitation facilities, and sleep disorder clinics. Moving from abstract brainstorming to high-fidelity prototypes, with educational scaffolds, helped participants grasp real trade-offs. Eight guidelines emerge for considerate embodied systems that are attuned to context and grounded in deployment.
arxiv-2602-03354:
Network boxes that can still track encrypted QUIC flows are designed by Hari Hara Sudhan Selvam, working with 1 co-author, in a system called QASM. Stateful middleboxes provide security and value-added services in company networks by identifying flows exactly. QUIC, the transport behind HTTP/3, encrypts traffic and supports connection migration. That obscures flow meaning and disrupts devices such as address translators, rate limiters, and load balancers. Kubernetes deployments are affected too.

Their general system lets middleboxes track QUIC connections reliably even when endpoints change address or port. A prototype preserves middlebox functionality with HTTP/3. Overhead stays negligible, under five percent on throughput and latency. It worked well even at high connection migration rates, addressing a practical blocker for QUIC adoption in firms.
arxiv-2602-03454:
A vision-language model may know your face in a photo yet know nothing about your life with the people in it. Yeongtak Oh and 5 co-authors name that gap contextualized visual personalization in a 2026 paper. The task asks a model to recognize a person's own visual experiences and retrieve the matching context when a new image arrives.

Their framework, CoViP, treats personalized image captioning as the core training task. Reinforcement-learning post-training and caption-augmented generation strengthen the skill. Special diagnostic tests rule out shortcuts that rely on text alone, forcing the model to actually use visual context. Existing models, open and proprietary alike, score poorly, while CoViP improves captioning and downstream personalization tasks together.
arxiv-2602-03754:
Plasma wakefield accelerators promise gigavolt-per-meter fields in a tabletop device, but only if the plasma recovers fast enough between shots. G. Parise and 7 co-authors model that recovery at sub-nanosecond scales in a 2026 paper, following the parameters of a hydrogen plasma experiment at SPARC_LAB. The experiment found recovery time depends on initial density in a non-monotonic way.

Ion motion was the suspected cause, and the models test that suspicion head-on. The team runs both particle-in-cell and fluid models of the early plasma evolution in space. Comparing the two approaches also judges how trustworthy cheaper fluid models are for this class of dynamics. The work informs the push toward high-repetition-rate plasma acceleration for research and commercial use.
arxiv-2602-04154:
The best segmentation network depends on the microscope. Mingjian Lu and 6 co-authors prove that with a cross-modal scoring framework for materials images in a 2026 paper. Architectures are usually tested on one imaging type, hiding how rankings shuffle across scanning electron, atomic force, X-ray tomography, and optical microscopy.

Six encoder-decoder combinations across seven datasets showed clear context dependence. One architecture led on high-contrast 2D images; another handled the hardest cases. It adds out-of-distribution warnings and what-if explanations of which fine features drive predictions. Materials labs gain a picking guide plus a trust signal for new samples.
arxiv-2602-04254:
Guessing test cases at random rarely separates good programs from lucky ones. Zeyao Ma and colleagues train an Agentic Verifier for competitive coding in a 2026 paper. Execution-based re-ranking can rescue a model's near misses, if the test inputs separate them well enough.

Their verifier works with execution setups over multiple turns, hunting inputs that expose gaps in how candidate programs act. Targeted counterexamples replace blind sampling. Training combined large-scale synthetic data, rejection fine-tuning, and agentic reinforcement learning. Across five competitive programming benchmarks, the approach strengthens test-time scaling for code writing, where one wrong answer looks just like another without the right test.
arxiv-2602-04354:
Meteorites carry isotopic fingerprints of stars that died before the Sun was born. Marco Pignatari and colleagues present SIMPLE, a public Python tool for reading those fingerprints, in a 2026 paper. Bulk meteorites and their inclusions show isotopic shifts stamped by stellar nucleosynthesis events.

The toolkit compares meteoritic data against ejecta from core-collapse supernova models. Its current release bundles eighteen models from six published sets, spanning three starting masses at solar metallicity. Users can pull predicted abundances for any element and reshape them for direct comparison. Easier matching sharpens debates about the Sun's birth setting and the young Solar System's ingredients.
arxiv-2602-04454:
Tianming Liang and 5 co-authors present a 2026 paper on segmentation, the task of outlining objects in images or video when a user describes them in words. Earlier systems relied only on knowledge frozen inside a large multimodal model, which limits them on new or specialized topics.

Their system, Seg-ReSearch, mixes step-by-step reasoning with external search during the task. A layered reward design trains that behavior, balancing early guidance against later incentives. The team also built OK-VOS, a video benchmark that requires outside knowledge to solve. On that test and two existing ones, Seg-ReSearch beat earlier methods by a wide margin.
arxiv-2602-04654:
Kiseok Yeon counts rational lines lying on diagonal cubic hypersurfaces in a 2026 number theory paper. These are high-dimensional surfaces defined by a sum of cubed terms with integer coefficients, set equal to zero.

Yeon finds asymptotic estimates, meaning formulas that grow exact as counts grow large. The result needs only a set number of variables, improving the past threshold by two. The proof develops a multidimensional shifting variables argument plus a pruning step. It also uses recent progress on the Parsell-Vinogradov system, a linked set of equations. Rational lines are basic building blocks for such surfaces. Sharper thresholds widen the range where their counts are understood.
arxiv-2602-05054:
Engineers who shape a frame for strength must also face doubt in loads and materials. Oğuz Han Altıntaş and Hamdullah Yücel present an adaptive optimization scheme for that task in this 2026 applied mathematics paper. The setup is linear elasticity, and the aim is a shape that works well time after time rather than one tuned to a single guessed case.

Adaptivity runs through the whole method. Error estimates decide how many random samples to draw, how fine the mesh should be, and how long each optimization step can safely be. The step size is tied to an estimate of the shape derivative's Lipschitz constant. The estimates cover both the elasticity solve and the helper deformation task used to find descent paths. Tests on leg-like parts minimized touchdown compliance under unsure contact forces, showing the scheme works end to end.
arxiv-2602-05154:
Turning a quantum algorithm into the pulses that run on hardware is a compiler's job, and speed matters when the machine waits. Aaron Hoyt and 10 co-authors present QASMTrans in this 2026 quantum computing paper. It is a C++ compiler that goes from OpenQASM code to device control pulses for near-term quantum processors.

The compiler targets just-in-time use on testbeds where classical control sits close to the quantum device. It reports compilation more than a hundred times faster than Qiskit on some circuits at similar quality, finishing large, deep circuits in seconds. It links directly with the QICK control system, tailors gate sets at the pulse level along the circuit's critical path. It uses calibration data to place work on the healthiest qubits, and can share one device between concurrent circuits. Pulse-level simulation showed latency cuts and fidelity gains of up to 12 percent on tested circuits.
arxiv-2602-05254: A capset is a set of points in a finite geometry with no three on a line. Cassie Grace and José Felipe Voloch study capsets in this 2026 combinatorics paper, working in vector spaces over the field with three elements. A capset is complete when no further point can be added without creating a line. The authors give constructions of capsets defined by algebraic equations over extension fields of the three-element field. Their constructions include the smallest complete capsets whose size is proportional to the best known lower bound.
arxiv-2602-05354:
Web agents sent to moderate content or enforce policy often face a trap. The visible page suggests one action, while the decisive evidence is buried a few clicks away. Syed Nazmus Sakib and 4 co-authors built a benchmark for that investigative skill in this 2026 preprint, running 39 pages. The hosted title calls the suite PATHWAYS; inside, the benchmark is named MIRAGE and holds 750 multi-step decision tasks.

Tasks span Wikipedia forensics, shopping administration, and Reddit moderation, each with a misleading surface layer and a hidden layer reachable only by active digging. Scoring splits investigation, reasoning, and final decision accuracy, plus a rate of fabricated citations. Eight agents across two model generations showed three stubborn patterns. They reach the right pages but miss the decisive evidence. Hints help them search without reliably fixing decisions, and about one trajectory in eight cites facts that were invented.
arxiv-2602-05454:
Vision transformers that learn task after task tend to forget old skills, a problem known as catastrophic forgetting. Yue Lu, Xiangyu Zhou, and 4 co-authors trace much of that loss to attention drift: as new tasks arrive, the model stops looking at the image regions it used for older tasks. Their fix takes a cue from human vision, where selective attention guards what has already been learned.

The method first records attention maps from the old task and turns them into masks that mark the regions that mattered. While the model learns a new task, those masks block gradient updates in the marked regions, so past visual concepts stay intact. A scaling step keeps update sizes in line so modern optimizers still work well. Tests and visualizations show less forgetting and state-of-the-art results across varied continual learning setups.
arxiv-2602-05554:
Locating a wireless device outdoors from its signal pattern is a first step toward guiding it along the best route. Mohammad Shamsesalehi, Mahmoud Ahmadian Attari, and 2 co-authors build a two-stage system for millimeter-wave MIMO networks, the multi-antenna setups planned for dense urban service. Stage one uses a transformer network that reads sequences of beamformed fingerprint signals, which record how signal strength varies across beams and positions.

The transformer predicts each device's trajectory from those sequences. Stage two runs an informed version of the RRT* path-planning algorithm to find the shortest route to a target, using the predicted paths. Tests use a large ray-tracing data set that models outdoor propagation at a common millimeter-wave band. The authors report that their transformer estimator beat rival designs on trajectory accuracy.
arxiv-2602-05654:
When can a term in lambda calculus, the formal system behind functional programming, be run in reverse? Antonio Bucciarelli, Arturo De Faveri, Giulio Manzonetto, and Antonino Salibra study invertible lambda terms under different lambda theories. A special class called finite hereditary permutations plays the central role, along with its infinite extension.

The authors use inverse semigroups, algebraic structures that generalize groups, to organize the problem. They show that the special terms form an inverse semigroup under any lambda theory. The natural order on that structure matches eta expansion, a known way of growing a term. With those links in place, they prove that the finite hereditary permutations are exactly the invertible terms in every theory between two named extremes. The results recast older findings in a broader frame. The work is aimed at researchers in logic and the theory of programming languages.
arxiv-2602-05754:
Training a model too large for one device splits it across a pipeline, and idle gaps called bubbles waste much of the hardware time. Seonghye Cho, Jaemin Han, and 3 co-authors propose TimelyFreeze, which freezes some parameters adaptively to skip backward computation and speed training. Earlier freezing methods often froze too much and cost accuracy.

TimelyFreeze models the pipeline schedule as a directed acyclic graph and solves a linear program for freeze ratios. The ratios minimize batch execution time while respecting accuracy constraints. On a large language model test, training throughput rose substantially, up to forty percent in the best case, with comparable accuracy. The authors report that convergence held up and that the method generalizes across pipeline parallel settings. The work targets teams that train frontier scale models on clusters. It shows scheduling mathematics, not just hardware, can reclaim idle pipeline time.
arxiv-2602-06354:
Some maps cannot be run backward, yet their long-term behavior can still be coded symbolically. Jing Xun and 2 co-authors study symbolic dynamics for a class of smooth non-invertible maps with singularities and zero Lyapunov exponents. Zero exponents mean nearby paths separate neither fast nor slow in the usual exponential way, which makes the coding delicate.

Blending techniques from recent work by several research groups, they build a countable Markov partition for the well-behaved points of the system's inverse limit space. From that partition, they show a finite-to-one symbolic extension exists for the map on the matching subset of the original space. The result extends symbolic methods to a broader class of maps.
arxiv-2602-06454:
Long reasoning traces from big models are accurate but expensive, and not every step is equally hard. Jiwon Song and 2 co-authors present RelayGen, a runtime scheme that hands easier stretches of a single answer to a smaller model. Earlier efficiency tricks either ignored this variation inside one generation or needed costly token-level routing.

Studying token probability margins offline, they found that coarse segments suffice to catch difficulty shifts. RelayGen learns switch cues for each model pair: when a segment turns easy, the small model continues it, while hard parts stay with the large one. No training is required. Across benchmarks, latency fell substantially with small accuracy cost, and pairing with speculative decoding doubled the speedup.
arxiv-2602-06554:
Training language model agents by reinforcement learning lacks convergence guarantees, especially across multiple turns of interaction. Tianyi Hu and 4 co-authors analyze how update rules and advantage estimators combine, and propose SeeUPO, a method with guarantees for multi-turn settings. They find one combination, REINFORCE with group relative advantage estimation, can reach global optima undiscounted.

Pairing the same estimator with the popular PPO algorithm, however, breaks PPO's monotonic improvement property. No mainstream backbone algorithm, they show, manages to be both critic-free and convergence-guaranteed across turns. SeeUPO fills that gap by treating multi-turn interaction as a sequence of bandit problems, updating turn by turn in reverse order to guarantee steady improvement.
arxiv-2602-06654:
Boyu Chen and six co-authors improve the search system behind food delivery on Meituan, where photos, text, and other signals all help match a craving to a dish. Most such systems train two matching towers together, but the team found that one kind of signal then tends to dominate while others are neglected, and uneven learning speeds cause further trouble.

Their fix trains the model in stages, so each stage focuses on a set task and every signal gets proper attention. They also add tasks that teach the model how compressed semantic codes link queries to items. On large real-world data the method beat strong baselines on standard ranking scores, and a live test on the platform raised both revenue and clicks.
arxiv-2602-06754:
Thibaud Gloaguen, Robin Staab, Nikola Jovanović, and Martin Vechev bring order to the crowded field of language model watermarking. A hidden signal is planted in generated text so its origin can later be traced. Many schemes exist, each designed in its own way, and no shared formulation has tied them together. The paper shows most of them fall out of one constrained optimization problem.

Writing the schemes in that common form exposes the hidden trade-off among text quality, diversity, and detection power that each one strikes. The framework also works in reverse: state a requirement, such as a quality proxy, and derive a scheme that is optimal for it. Experiments confirm that schemes derived from a given constraint do maximize detection power under that constraint.
arxiv-2602-06854:
Mingqian Feng and six co-authors build a stronger stress test for chatbot safety. Multi-turn jailbreaks, where an attacker slowly steers a conversation toward a harmful answer, are the realistic threat, but existing attackers struggle with exploration complexity and drifting away from the original goal. Their framework, SEMA, trains an attacker from scratch, without existing strategies or external data.

A first stage fine-tunes the attacker on self-generated, well-structured multi-turn prompts, stabilizing later learning. A second stage uses reinforcement learning with a reward that penalizes intent drift, combining intent alignment, compliance risk, and level of detail. Without relying on victim feedback, SEMA reached an average attack success rate of about 80 percent across victim models on a standard benchmark, well above prior methods, and transfers across targets.
arxiv-2602-07454:
Most stochastic process models beyond Gaussian processes have intractable posteriors, forcing high-dimensional latent variable inference. Teemu Härkönen and one co-author propose two methods that combine iterated posterior linearization with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, aimed at log-Gaussian gamma processes.

Tests on two synthetic data sets and a multiscale biocomposite stiffness model, plus an experimental Raman spectrum of argentopyrite as a real case, show the methods working where direct methods fail. Stats experts and materials teams get useful samplers for a flexible process family whose uncertainty quantification was out of reach before. The Raman case shows the samplers handling real lab spectra, not only test benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-07654:
Anderson localization halts wave transport in disordered media, and in three dimensions theory predicts a transition at a mobility edge between trapped and spread-out states. Xudong Yu and nine co-authors report the first direct observation of that shift for matter waves, using ultracold atoms in a laser-speckle disordered potential.

Earlier atomic attempts suffered wild energy spread that forced indirect, model-based guesses. A new energy-resolved scheme prepares matter waves with a narrow energy spread and tracks their expansion over long times, revealing the shift. Quantum experts get a landmark prediction confirmed for matter waves, with implications for metal-insulator shifts in electronic systems.
arxiv-2602-07754:
As AI grading spreads in classrooms, students' own views of fairness and trust deserve a hearing. Bahare Riahi and two co-authors study 27 undergraduates in a computer science course whose block-based final projects received both AI and human feedback.

Students worried that AI grading missed context and felt impersonal, even when scores looked consistent. The authors recommend treating AI as a supplement under human oversight, with systems that reflect human judgment, flexibility, and empathy. Framed by an ethics framework for AI, the study gives educators design principles for assessment that students experience as fair and transparent rather than opaque.
arxiv-2602-08354:
Long chains of thought help reasoning models, but longer is not always better, and extra steps can even hurt accuracy. Zixuan Huang and thirteen co-authors find that these models already sense, in some implicit way, when they should stop thinking. Their arXiv paper shows that current sampling methods hide that sense rather than using it.

They introduce SAGE, a sampling approach that lets the model's own stopping sense guide generation. Folded into group-based reinforcement learning as SAGE-RL, it carries the efficient patterns into ordinary single-pass inference. Across hard math benchmarks, accuracy and efficiency both improve markedly. Readers get a route to leaner reasoning that trusts a signal the model already carries.
arxiv-2602-08554:
Designing AI agents for citizens cannot be done by experts alone, yet public participation is hard to sustain and harder to turn into working systems. Eike Schneiders and seven co-authors draw on three participatory workshops from 2025 with members of the public and cross-sector stakeholders. Their arXiv workshop paper uses storytelling and low-fidelity prototyping to surface societal values and expectations.

Three challenges emerge: keeping engagement meaningful over time, building a common vocabulary linking specialists with ordinary participants, and turning speculative input into designs that can actually be built. The authors argue for reflexive, long-term participation as the path to responsible citizen-centric AI. Readers get grounded lessons for anyone inviting the public into agent design.
arxiv-2602-08654:
Efficient photon-pair sources are key for quantum photonics, but most designs are bulky or tied to specific poling tricks. Alessia Stefano and two co-authors report a chip-based setup using linearly uncoupled resonators with angular phase matching. Their arXiv paper confines phase control to a short device section, boosting field strength and interaction length while shrinking the footprint.

An aluminum gallium arsenide on insulator device generates pairs at 3.16 gigahertz per milliwatt under continuous pumping and 5.89 megahertz pulsed. The biphoton Schmidt number of 1.02 signals nearly uncorrelated pairs. Readers get a compact, reconfigurable source that works across many second-order non-linear platforms.
arxiv-2602-08754:
People increasingly use chatbots as thought partners, and that reliance may reshape how beliefs form and persist. Rose E. Guingrich and two co-authors define belief offloading: the process of forming and upholding beliefs is handed to an AI system, with downstream effects on behavior and belief systems. Their arXiv paper draws on philosophy, psychology, and computer science.

The authors clarify the conditions under which belief offloading happens and offer a descriptive taxonomy plus normative implications. They close with directions for measuring its potential and consequences in human-AI interaction. Readers get a precise concept for a familiar worry: outsourcing thinking may quietly outsource believing as well.
arxiv-2602-09154:
News videos flash names on screen, but pulling them out safely, with an audit trail, is harder than it looks. Andrea Filiberto Lucas and one co-author present a hybrid fixed-rule setup for named-entity pulling from broadcast and social-media news video. A curated, even corpus of tagged frames captures the range of modern news graphics, feeding a readable, modular pipeline built for fixed-rule, checkable work.

The finder reaches 95.8 percent mean average precision at IoU 0.5 for graphic spotting. Against AI-made multi-mode rivals, the fixed-rule pipeline trades a little raw accuracy, F-one 77.08 versus 84.18 percent, for openness: even hit rate and recall, no made-up names, and full tracking per stage. A user study finds 59 percent of viewers struggle to read on-screen names in fast broadcasts, confirming the need.
arxiv-2602-09254:
Bystander privacy in smart homes has been studied mostly in the West, and Shijing He and five co-authors turn to China. They analyze 49 smart-home apps through policy review, interface evaluation, and App Store privacy-label checks. Most apps nominally comply with national regulations, yet the study finds wide gaps between written policies and actual implementation.

Traceability analysis exposes inconsistent data controls and opaque data sharing, while bystander privacy for visitors and non-users is largely absent from both policies and interface design. Discrepancies between privacy labels and real data practices further threaten trust and informed consent. The authors offer design recommendations to protect bystanders, clarify privacy interfaces, and make labels credible in non-Western smart-home ecosystems.
arxiv-2602-09354:
Measuring Higgs boson decays is a central goal for future colliders. A 2026 study led by Jianfeng Jiang, with three co-authors, tests a holistic method at the proposed Circular Electron-Positron Collider running as a Higgs factory. Instead of selecting a few signature particles, the holistic approach uses information from every reconstructed particle to pick out signal events. The team estimates statistical precision for the main hadronic decay modes, including decays to bottom and charm quark pairs, gluons, and four-quark final states.

Compared with earlier Snowmass projections for the collider, the holistic approach sharpens precision by roughly two to four times across the modes and channels examined. The paper also tracks how accuracy improves as the training dataset grows, and finds the leading modes nearing their statistical limit. That scaling behavior, the authors note, can also monitor the method's robustness and quantify its uncertainties.
arxiv-2602-09954:
The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1097 carries a ring of furious star birth around its nucleus, a natural lab for star formation under extreme conditions. A 2026 paper led by Sandra Zamora, with two co-authors, uses MUSE integral field spectroscopy to measure the ring's star-forming regions. The team identifies and analyzes twenty-four separate ionized regions within the ring.

Despite the busy nucleus, every region proves purely photoionized, lit by young stars rather than shocks. The gas is metal-rich beyond the Sun's mix, with the highest abundance above five times solar, the richest yet reported. The authors also find a break in a key ionization relation at high metallicity. Local gas supply, the evidence suggests, steers the ring's star formation, and the team also reports likely signs of one of the galaxy's jets.
arxiv-2602-10454:
Baorong Huang and Ali Asiri present a tool for building high-quality translation datasets in a 2026 paper. Parallel corpora now demand layered annotation, not just sentence alignment, and that shift hits structurally divergent pairs like Arabic and English mainly hard. Standard automatic aligners miss deep linguistic shifts and subtle meaning changes.

Their tool, LATA, pairs large language models with expert judgment in a human-in-the-loop workflow. A template-based prompt manager drives the model to segment and align sentences under strict output constraints, while teams review and correct the results. The design aims to combine scalable automation with the sharpness translation research requires, closing the gap between fast alignment and trustworthy annotation.
arxiv-2602-10654:
Derek Christ and five co-authors give DRAM protocols a formal, executable description in a 2026 paper. JEDEC standards grow more complex with each making, and their timing diagrams and command tables resist comprehension. The simplified state machine in each standard misses the parallel work of memory banks.

Their modeling approach uses timed Petri nets implemented in Python, capturing concurrency that state machines flatten. The model is directly executable, enabling testing of results metrics and checks of controller hardware descriptions, DRAM logic, and memory simulators. The paper presents the formal description as both a comprehension aid and a checks tool for engineers building memory systems.
arxiv-2602-11054:
Signals from brains, bodies, and machines often switch regimes without clean breaks. Łukasz Furman and two co-authors build a dynamical microscope that turns multichannel oscillatory signals into circular phase-amplitude traits, then learns a latent path with an autoencoder. Regime shifts are read from path shape and flow, not from hard state labels.

Checks on a coupled oscillator network with switching topology shows the tool recovers law changes even when regimes overlap in state space. Speed and explored variance separate regimes strongly, while other metrics capture shape apart from topology. The frame suits neural, physiological, and physical time series where regime structure hides in motion, not in static clusters.
arxiv-2602-11454:
Private principal component analysis must protect single rows while finding the top direction. Ta Duy Nguyen and two co-authors study differentially private recipes for the top singular vector, following the row-neighbour privacy model. Their novel recipe gives beyond-worst-case guarantees for matrices with low coherence, a structural property common in real data.

A new filtering technique adapts to that coherence setting, departing from prior work that achieved similar guarantees only under a stricter entry-level privacy model. The part joins a long literature on private power iteration, showing that structure in the data, not just worst-case bounds, can buy scores under privacy. The work is theory, with guarantees rather than benchmark claims at its centre.
arxiv-2603-01554:
Akila Siriweera, Janani Rangila, Keitaro Naruse, and colleagues want smart home research open to far more people. Their 2026 work sits in the Society 5.0 vision of a human-centered, tech-rich society. Most home simulators demand deep coding skill, adapt poorly, and cannot grow on their own.

Their agent system runs home simulation through plain language, with no coding needed from the user. Specialized agents share the work and can swap the language model behind them. A search pipeline mixes meaning-based, keyword, and hybrid lookup to pull in home knowledge as needed. Tests find near-best search accuracy, device behavior that matches real home data, and steady scaling across home sizes. That mix could widen who can study safety, energy, and health at home.
arxiv-2603-01754:
Artem Roenko asks how acceleration changes the phase of gluon matter in this 2026 study. Gluons carry the strong force, and their matter shifts between confined and free phases as heat rises. An accelerated observer, like one near a black hole, may feel that shift at a different place or heat.

Roenko runs first-principles lattice simulations in Rindler spacetime, the frame of a steadily accelerating observer. Within set ranges of heat and acceleration, confined and free zones sit side by side in space. The border between zones moves with heat in line with a known prediction, with a small measured drift. At weak acceleration, the critical heat matches the value for matter at rest. The result helps link gravity-like effects to strong-force matter in extreme settings.
arxiv-2603-02354:
Alexandru Radu studies when fluid equations have only one solution in this 2026 mathematics paper. The setting is the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations for incompressible flow on a torus. Solutions are tracked in Lorentz spaces, which sort functions by size in a finer way than usual. Uniqueness was known in the smallest such borderline space.

Larger borderline spaces resist the same proof, due to endpoint obstructions. Radu proves uniqueness in those larger spaces under one added assumption. The assumption is a short-time smoothing effect that restarts at every moment. It is natural in classic well-posedness theories for these equations. The proof restarts the solution formula at each interval and gains a strict contraction. Parabolic smoothing thus replaces the missing endpoint structure.
arxiv-2603-02654:
Seongmin Kim, Giseung Park, Woojun Kim, and colleagues tackle credit assignment in teams of learning agents. Their 2026 paper, written for a multi-agent systems conference, asks how much each agent helped or hurt the shared outcome. Answering that well should speed learning and improve teamwork.

Their estimator, GPAE, computes a separate advantage score for each agent through a value-iteration step based on action chances. That avoids direct action-value estimates and keeps off-policy learning stable. A double-capped sampling ratio further balances sensitivity to one agent's changes against noise from teammates' changes. In benchmark tests the method beat prior approaches, with the clearest gains in coordination and learning speed on complex tasks.
arxiv-2603-02854:
Haokun Liu, Zhaoqi Ma, Yicheng Chen, and colleagues steer a robot by predicting a flow of motion rather than a list of commands. Their 2026 system, CoFL, takes a bird's-eye view plus a language instruction and outputs a continuous velocity field. Paths then emerge by following that field step by step, giving smooth motion that reacts as conditions change.

Training used over half a million bird's-eye image and instruction pairs, built automatically from indoor scan datasets with matching flow fields. On scenes the system had never seen, CoFL beat both modular language-model planners and generative policy rivals. It then ran zero-shot on real robots under overhead cameras across several room layouts. Reliable closed-loop control held up outside simulation.
arxiv-2603-03054:
Sudip Bhujel builds a medical chatbot training pipeline with formal privacy guarantees at every stage. Doctor-patient conversations make rich training material, but standard fine-tuning can memorize and leak rare personal details. His 2026 framework, PrivMedChat, applies differential privacy throughout the alignment process.

Private training covers the supervised stage, the reward model learned from preference pairs, and the final policy tuning. To avoid expensive clinician labeling, preferences are built by pairing physician replies with filtered non-expert drafts. The system is judged on usefulness, safety, and privacy under one consistent accounting scheme. Code is open source. The work offers a practical route to helpful medical assistants that provably limit what any single conversation can reveal.
arxiv-2603-03454:
Peter Adema and three others replicate FairDICE, a method for fair multi-objective learning from demonstrations. Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from recorded behavior only. When several goals compete, FairDICE promises to learn the balancing weights automatically and fairly. Their 2026 replication study checks whether the published claims survive contact with the code.

Much of the theory holds, the replicators find. But a code error quietly reduced FairDICE to plain behavior cloning in continuous environments, and many key hyperparameters were never specified in the paper. With the error fixed, new tests extending the original work show the method can scale to complex environments and high-dimensional rewards. It leans heavily on live hyperparameter tuning, though. Their verdict: an interesting method whose experimental justification needs significant revision.
arxiv-2603-03754:
Priya Pal, Abhijeet Guha, and Aditi Sengupta simulate how a turbine blade's airflow changes character as the flow gets faster. Low-pressure turbine blades, vital to efficient engines, suffer laminar separation bubbles that trigger transition to turbulence, especially off-design. Their 2026 study runs high-fidelity simulations of a standard blade at fixed conditions while the inlet Mach number climbs through the low subsonic range. It uses a numerical scheme built to preserve delicate instability waves.

Faster inflow shrinks both leading and trailing separation bubbles and triggers earlier transition and reattachment. Yet losses grow: suction-side momentum thickness at the trailing edge rises several-fold. The transition pathway itself morphs, from orderly two-dimensional rolls and turbulent spots at low speed to streak-dominated, bypass-like breakdown at higher speed. Budgets of compressible enstrophy show viscous-compressible coupling and baroclinic effects running the vorticity dynamics.
arxiv-2603-03854:
Xi Wu and others study fractional topological invariants in an open quantum system: a periodic Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain subject to gain and loss, described by Lindblad master equations. They first set out the symmetry settings under which integer topological invariants exist, then study how those invariants turn fractional in steady states. The change can come from tuning parameters in the jump operators or arise as a dynamic shift during time evolution.

The authors show that the fractional invariants lose the usual quantized topology, but stretching the Brillouin zone over many cycles restores integer quantization of the total winding. They also show how the effects could be observed in long-range hopping photonic lattices with fractional fillings, using Bloch state tomography. That opens a path to studying fractional topology in open systems.
arxiv-2605-00154:
James T. Sikora and 7 co-authors report new observations of MASCARA-5 b, an ultra-hot giant planet circling a bright star. Earlier observations with another instrument had found iron gas glowing on the planet's dayside, a sign that its upper air is hotter than the layers below. The team watched the planet again just before eclipse.

Using the EXPRES spectrograph, they confirm the iron signal across two nights at solid statistical strength. Searches for two other elements, ionized iron and chromium, found nothing clear. The iron signal also shows a small blueshift, which may come from winds blowing through the planet's upper air. The result firms up the case that this planet's atmosphere heats up with height.
arxiv-2605-00254:
Junsun Choi and 7 co-authors ask whether the costly networks inside AI data centers are really needed for serving mixture-of-experts language models. In these models, much of the running time goes to machines talking to each other, and the industry has answered with expensive high-bandwidth scale-up networks. The authors compare four hardware layouts on cost and performance together.

Cheaper switchless layouts beat the scale-up design on cost-effectiveness in every scenario they explored, in some cases by more than half. A three-dimensional full-mesh layout gave the best balance of speed and cost. They also find today's scale-up links carry more bandwidth than needed, since trimming that bandwidth raised throughput per unit of cost. The advantage of switchless designs looks set to persist in coming hardware generations.
arxiv-2605-00354:
Farshad Noravesh and 3 co-authors generate molecules with a diffusion model that respects chemical symbols instead of washing them out. Many generators encode atom and bond types as simple one-hot labels, discarding symbolic structure. Fingerprint-based rivals suffer hash collisions or map to no valid molecule at all. The team's alternative treats atom and bond codes as learned latent tokens.

Their model, VQ-SAD, first trains a vector-quantized autoencoder whose codebooks then serve as tokenizers for the diffusion process. The large discrete code space balances atom and bond types more evenly, which improves the denoising at the heart of generation. The design is neuro-symbolic, joining symbolic codes with neural learning and a learnable forward process. On two standard molecule benchmarks, the underlying autoencoder slightly beat leading rivals for diffusion-based generation.
arxiv-2605-00454:
Heikki Mäntysaari and 4 co-authors predict what upcoming collider measurements will reveal about the small-scale build of light nuclei. They study exclusive vector meson production in ultraperipheral collisions, near misses of nuclei where one acts as a source of hard photons. The oxygen and neon runs at the LHC make such studies timely, and saturation, the crowding of gluons at small shares of the motion, is the key effect.

Their work uses a color glass condensate framework that varies with the impact point, evolved with standard equations and tuned by a recent global fit to photon-proton and photon-lead data. They give forecasts for coherent and incoherent J/psi production in oxygen-oxygen and neon-neon runs, with error bands drawn from the tuning. Some measures prove touchy to the nuclear model chosen. The damping from saturation grows steadily with nuclear size and energy.
arxiv-2605-00554:
Leandro Liborio and 6 co-authors present version 1.3.0 of MuDirac, an open software tool for the community that studies atoms with a muon in place of an electron. When a negative muon orbits a nucleus, its x-ray transitions carry precise information about the nucleus, above all its charge radius. Extracting that radius means modeling the transition energies accurately, which is where specialized software earns its keep.

MuDirac computes those transition energies efficiently, assuming the nuclear charge follows a standard two-parameter Fermi distribution. From measured energies plus the modeling, users can estimate ground-state nuclear properties such as the charge radius. The authors stress sustainability and openness: the tool is publicly available and built to be maintained, so the relatively small muonic-atom community can share one reliable calculator instead of private, aging codes. It is a software paper, documenting a release rather than reporting a measurement.
arxiv-2605-00754:
Indraneil Paul, Goran Glavaš, and Iryna Gurevych study reward models that score generated code, a tool used to align language models after training. Most code work relies on execution results alone, which only rewards code that runs correctly. The authors instead train and test models that judge code across several criteria and in several programming languages.

They compile a benchmark covering five preference dimensions and eight languages, and profile more than fifty existing models on it. Finding current models weak beyond correctness, they build a large open preference collection and train Themis models in several sizes. Experiments show positive scaling, strong transfer across languages, and clear gains from multi-criteria training.
arxiv-2605-00854:
Naohiro Yoshida models the repeated rise and collapse of financial bubbles with a deliberately simple discrete-time simulation. Earlier work described explosive bubble statistics well, but capturing herd buying and panic selling in one framework has proved harder. Yoshida lets a cubic function of market momentum decide the balance of trading directions, so trend-following dominates as momentum grows.

Once momentum passes a critical level, the same mechanism flips the market into sudden crashes. Trading frequency also rises as that push builds, echoing the self-exciting nature of a Hawkes process. Even this minimal setup recreates surges in both cash flow and price, then sharp collapses, giving a compact account of cycles of overheating and panic.
arxiv-2605-01154:
Caleb Talley and five co-authors describe their approach to ARC-AGI-2, a benchmark of human-intuitive visual puzzles that tests generalization from few examples, symbolic interpretation, and flexible rule use across contexts. Such puzzles are easy for people but hard for machines, making the benchmark a demanding measure of abstract reasoning rather than memorized pattern matching.

Their system is based on a model called TinyLM, with additional fine-tuning applied at test time. Two test-time techniques are used: Test-Time Training and Products of Experts. The reported results show very high accuracy on the training set and much lower accuracy on the evaluation set, a gap that illustrates how difficult unseen ARC-AGI-2 puzzles remain for this approach.
arxiv-2605-01354:
Parin Chaipunya and Fumiaki Kohsaka prove that a classic optimization routine and two of its variants behave well in curved spaces with no bumps, known as Hadamard spaces. The proximal point method inches toward a solution by balancing step size against a penalty, and here the targets are monotone vector fields rather than plain functions.

Before the main results, the pair build the needed groundwork: how tangent spaces work in these settings, what resolvents look like, and which basic facts monotone fields obey. With that base in place, they show the sequences the method generates exist and settle where they should. The work extends a workhorse of convex analysis from flat spaces to a curved world used in statistics, imaging, and geometric data analysis.
arxiv-2605-01754:
Shrestha Dutta and Rudra Banerjee explain why punching holes in a titanium disulfide sheet so often fails to make it a half-metal, the prized state where current flows in one spin only. Experiments kept getting paramagnetic insulators instead, even though each vacancy should carry a magnetic moment.

The missing step is connection. A crystal-field split first steadies one titanium orbital and locks in a strong local moment at each vacancy. But spin-polarized transport needs those moments joined into one spanning cluster, and that happens only past a geometric percolation threshold near an eighth of sites vacant. There the majority-spin band widens from flat to broad with full polarization, while the minority spin keeps a gap. Cell-size effects confirm the story, and too many vacancies jam the network apart, leaving a narrow working window for defect-built 2D spintronics.
arxiv-2605-01954:
Polydoros Giannouris and colleagues present MOIRA, a system for pair trading that learns at two levels at once. Pair trading needs a high-level choice of which assets to pair and a low-level plan for when to trade them. Feedback is slow and unclear, so a loss may come from a bad pairing, bad timing, or both.

MOIRA states both levels as language model policies and updates them only by changing prompts, using written feedback from whole episodes. Keeping the pairing choice apart from execution helps assign credit for gains and losses. The framework is built for settings that change over time, where an agent must revise beliefs as well as remember past policy.
arxiv-2605-02154:
Pengyun Wang studies treatment effects for a target population when the main long-run outcome is mostly missing in the source study. The source study records treatment and short-term surrogates for everyone, but the primary outcome only for a validation subset. The target population gives only baseline covariates. Wang targets the full counterfactual distribution for each treatment, its quantiles, and the quantile treatment effect.

The surrogate is not treated as a stand-in endpoint, and no classic surrogacy condition is imposed. It only improves efficiency under a missing-at-random assumption for the primary outcome. Wang derives the efficient influence function, with three orthogonal parts for target sampling, the surrogate process, and missing outcomes. That yields a cross-fitted one-step estimator with stated properties.
arxiv-2605-02454:
Roberto Pietrantuono and four co-authors set out a vision called Causal Software Engineering. Software teams now make high-stakes choices using code data, field data, and team signals. Tools that spot patterns can say what tends to occur together, but many real questions ask what would happen if the team acted, or what would have happened under a different plan.

The proposed shift is to build causal models into work across the full life of a system, from writing code to running it. The paper lays out a causal-first workflow, a staged path for tools and teams to adopt it, and a plan for benchmarks to track progress. Effect estimates would carry stated assumptions and clear doubt ranges.
arxiv-2605-02954:
