Muhammad Muneeb and David B. Ascher present EFGPP, a framework for predicting complex human traits from mixed genetic and clinical data. A trait's signal is often split across sources: gene variants, summary components, clinical measures, metabolites, and risk scores from genome-wide studies. No single source holds the whole pattern, so the practical problem is how to generate, rank, and combine them well.

The test case is migraine, using a national biobank sample of several hundred people. Scores were built from migraine and depression studies with standard toolkits. The best single data type scored modestly; combining types did clearly better on migraine-focused inputs, and cross-trait depression inputs also helped. Gene features alone did not beat a covariates-only baseline, but derived genetic features beat plain risk scores. The framework is offered as proof of concept.
arxiv-2605-03454:
Tim Scarr, Anandaroop Ray, and Ross C. Brodie set out how to estimate noise in airborne EM survey data. Noise estimates are a required input for imaging ground conductivity. Repeat flight lines over the same ground reveal data variability. But splitting that noise into parts, and correcting for height changes, was scarcely documented.

They detail an algorithm for multiplicative noise with nonlinear height correction. They also give a way to make the noise Gaussian for a valid likelihood. Cross terms in the covariance, usually ignored, are included. For their rotary-wing system, a diagonal covariance proved enough for regularized imaging.
arxiv-2605-03754:
Somnath Mondal studies how to estimate a positive power of the scale parameter of a shifted exponential distribution. Prior information orders those scale values. Such problems matter in reliability analysis and survival studies, where prior knowledge is often at hand and usually improves estimates. The question is which estimators provably beat the rest.

Mondal derives conditions under which equivariant estimators dominate others. The loss functions used are scale-invariant and strictly convex. He builds several such estimators. They improve on the best affine equivariant estimator. One is a smooth generalized Bayes estimator under a non-informative prior. Another rests on the Pitman closeness criterion. A large simulation study and real examples show the gains.
arxiv-2605-03954:
Yasir Mahmood, Jonni Virtema, Timon Barlag, and Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo connect two ways of resolving conflict: subset-maximal repairs of inconsistent databases, and acceptable sets of arguments in abstract argumentation frameworks. Recent work linked repairs under various integrity constraints to such extensions. The authors extend the connection to constraints combining denial constraints with local-as-view tuple-generating dependencies.

Set-based argumentation frameworks, which allow joint attacks by groups of arguments, turn out to be necessary. Repairs under denial constraints alone match the naive extensions, which coincide with preferred and stable ones in the resulting framework. For the tuple-generating fragment, the authors show repairs correspond to preferred extensions, and preprocessing can yield a unique extension that is both stable and naive. Mixing both constraint types breaks the pattern.
arxiv-2605-04054:
Sheng Ran argues that self-generated regime switching, a hallmark of autonomous systems, can arise on its own from a class of learning dynamics most current systems do not use. Machine learning frameworks usually impose regime transitions from outside. Ran classifies dynamics into two kinds. Scalar-reducible ones are expressible as gradient flows driven by a single scalar objective. Scalar-irreducible ones cannot be reduced to that form.

Most existing systems operate in the scalar-reducible class. Using a minimal dynamical model, the paper shows that scalar-irreducible dynamics enable endogenous regime switching. Feedback between fast dynamical variables and slow structural change produces sustained transitions. No external scheduling is needed. The result is offered as a new dynamical model for regime search and a possible route toward self-organized adaptive learning systems.
arxiv-2605-04154:
Sergi Sirera and three co-authors work on modified gravity theories in which an extra field can hide itself near heavy objects, so tests in the solar system still pass. The hard part is telling, from a general theory, which hiding method is at work.

Starting from the full equations for a growing universe, they apply careful limits and derive one master equation for still, round objects. That equation sorts the known hiding methods, recovers the classic cases, and points to a new possible regime whose reach grows in direct proportion to the source mass.
arxiv-2605-04454:
Varad Vishwarupe and three co-authors argue that judging a language model on fixed test inputs cannot by itself establish that a deployed system will behave in line with human values. Benchmark scores are often used to support claims about real-world alignment, which they say is a category error.

They propose indexing every alignment claim to the level where its evidence was gathered, from model outputs up to live deployment. An audit of major benchmarks, coded against an eight-part rubric, finds support for user verification missing everywhere and steerability nearly so. The few interaction-level benchmarks they identify remain fragmented in what they cover.
arxiv-2605-04554:
Zheng and four colleagues make multi-person mesh recovery reason explicitly about interaction. Recovering 3D human meshes from images matters for animation, driving, and virtual reality, but existing end-to-end methods model how people relate only implicitly, through self-attention across person queries. They never reason directly about how people touch objects or each other. InterMesh adds that reasoning: a human-object interaction detector enriches query representations with structured interaction semantics, improving pose and shape estimates.

Two lightweight modules carry the idea into existing architectures with little overhead: a Contextual Interaction Encoder and an Interaction-Guided Refiner. Tests on five datasets, including 3DPW, MuPoTS, and CMU Panoptic, show clear gains over state-of-the-art methods. Joint-position error fell by nearly ten percent on CMU Panoptic and eight percent on Hi4D, with the largest wins in scenes full of complex human-object and inter-human contact.
arxiv-2605-04754:
Omkar B Shende, Marcello Traiola, and Gayathri Ananthanarayanan present a first study of two efficiency techniques meeting. One is approximate multipliers, which save energy by computing products inexactly. The other is mixture-of-experts architectures, which route each input through specialised sub-networks.

They test three expert variants against dense baselines across several image networks and data sets, using a library of eight-bit multipliers that includes an exact reference. Without any retraining, the dense baseline proved the most resilient topology across the convolutional architectures. The expert variants reacted in different ways. The results guide designers who want expert architectures on low-power edge hardware. They can use them while keeping accuracy intact.
arxiv-2605-05054:
Hongxu Chen and eight co-authors rethink flow matching methods that adapt vision-language models from only a few examples. Such methods model the alignment between image and text features as a continuous flow. The authors argue existing versions are limited by clashing geometric assumptions about those pre-trained features, which they expose by splitting features into radial and angular parts.

That split reveals three problems: uneven angular speed from coupling, lost confidence information when radial parts are normalised away, and dataset context dropped during feature extraction. Their warped product framework separates radial and angular dynamics on a suitable manifold. The resulting method aims at cleaner few-shot adaptation of vision-language models.
arxiv-2605-05154:
Mikael Brudfors presents CTseg, free software that segments brain CT scans, aligns them to a standard space, and measures brain volumes. CT is the routine hospital scan, but analysis tools were built mainly for MRI. CTseg adapts a multi-brain generative framework into a CT-specific pipeline whose outputs match the format of the established SPM software.

The tool needs no preprocessing or resampling in deployment and has already been used in studies of stroke, dementia, and brain shape. Validation on paired MR and CT head scans compared segmentation against an MRI-derived reference, plus alignment consistency and volume agreement. CTseg significantly outperformed applying the MRI-based baseline directly to CT images.
arxiv-2605-05354:
Omanshu Thapliyal offers a way to spot data centre contract breaches before they happen by matching transformer attention heads with the contract rules. Such agreements set precise thresholds for power, temperature, and humidity, with tiered fines paid as service credits. Watching alone notices breaches only after the fact, leaving little room to act.

Thapliyal encodes the agreement rules as data objects to build training examples without hand labels, then trains a per-client multi-head model where each head focuses on one rule. The heads learn patterns that precede breaches by about thirty minutes. Alerts are reshaped for finance, operations, and compliance readers, with signed sensor logs bundled for audit.
arxiv-2605-05454:
Marco Galoppo, Thomas Buchert, and Pierre Mourier compute average cosmic quantities directly for our local universe. Using the Cosmicflows-4++ reconstruction of nearby galaxies, they averaged density, expansion, spatial curvature, and backreaction over regions reaching three hundred megaparsecs out. Averaging matters because the local cosmos is lumpy, not smooth.

The energy budget changed with scale, reflecting a nested structure and a large void shell around the local web. Spatial curvature contributed at about the ten percent level on every scale probed. Backreaction, by contrast, stayed near one percent at most, and the averages never settled to the standard background within range.
arxiv-2605-05554:
Judging machine-made audio needs a distance measure that hears what humans hear. Wonwoo Jeong proposes OTAD, a replacement for the widely used Fréchet Audio Distance. The older measure rests on a fixed embedding cost that can hide severe artifacts, and on a Gaussian coupling that dilutes localized contamination.

OTAD fixes each weakness with its own mechanism: a learned Riemannian ground metric for the cost, and entropic optimal transport for the coupling. Across eight encoders, its sensitivity to single bad samples ran two to over three times higher. It also tracked human quality ratings more closely than baseline metrics.
arxiv-2605-05754:
Majorana islands are small superconducting devices whose internal state might be fully knowable while their currents stay puzzling. Yang Tian proves a version of that gap for floating Majorana islands held back by Coulomb repulsion. Even complete knowledge of the island's non-Markovian dynamics does not fix the transport statistics seen in the leads.

In the cotunneling regime, the island state fixes the memory kernels and every island readout. It cannot fix which lead or detector channel supplied an electron or absorbed the energy. The heat bookkeeping, Tian shows, is truly incomplete from island data alone.
arxiv-2605-05854:
Air quality models are usually graded on cleaned local datasets that hide how messy real monitoring is. Xing Xu and five co-authors build AirQualityBench to grade them as they are. The benchmark holds hourly readings from 3,720 monitoring stations worldwide over 2021 to 2025, covering six major pollutants. The data come as the networks recorded them, gaps and all.

Missing data stays missing: the stations' own observation masks are kept rather than filled in. Coverage is uneven, scales differ by pollutant, and running cost counts. Forecasters must cope with the network as it is, making the benchmark a real-world rehearsal rather than a lab exercise.
arxiv-2605-06154:
Kossi Amouzouvi and three co-authors give knowledge graph foundation models a structural vocabulary built from graphlets. Language and vision models rest on discrete units over a fixed grid, but knowledge graphs are irregular and relational, with no shared geometry. Transfer across unseen graphs therefore needs structural patterns that recur from graph to graph, the authors argue.

Graphlets, small connected graphs, serve as those structural tokens in their framework. The method mines a graph between relations by pattern matching, using closed and open paths and star shapes of small size. The framework is model agnostic and needs no retraining of the base approach it extends. Evaluated on 51 knowledge graphs across many domains, adding simple graphlets to the vocabulary beat prior foundation models on link prediction tasks.
arxiv-2605-06254:
Timothé Lemistre studies geodesic simplices inside pseudo-hyperbolic space, the geometry of signature (p, q). A geodesic simplex is the simplest volume bearing shape in such a space, spanned by straight geodesic edges. Whether a given simplex holds finite volume is a basic question with no obvious answer in this indefinite setting, where intuition from ordinary hyperbolic geometry can mislead.

Lemistre gives a cohomological reading of these simplices, recasting their geometry in algebraic terms. From that reading he states a condition that is both needed and enough for a simplex to have finite volume. As a corollary, every ideal geodesic polytope in the pseudo-hyperbolic space of signature (2, 2) has finite volume. The result settles the volume question completely for that signature.
arxiv-2605-06354:
Cătălin Cârstea proves that exact uniqueness in finite dimensional analytic inverse problems on its own yields Hölder stability. Inverse problems ask whether boundary measurements settle an unknown quantity, and uniqueness alone says nothing about how errors in data translate into errors in recovery. Cârstea closes that gap when the measurement operator is real analytic and the parameters live in a finite dimensional open set, with stability holding on every compact subset.

The proof reduces the operator equation and applies a classic distance bound for analytic sets. Fixing countable dense families of inputs and tests, finitely many scalar data entries give the same Hölder recovery, though the proof yields no explicit list, exponent, or constant. The result covers local boundary data for piecewise constant anisotropic conductivities and for piecewise uniform anisotropic elasticity, two model problems in imaging.
arxiv-2605-06454:
Maresa Schröder, Pascal Janetzky, Michael Klar, and Stefan Feuerriegel tackle a hidden failure mode in Bayesian optimization, a method for tuning models when each test is expensive. Even with a correct surrogate model, Monte Carlo noise in estimating the acquisition score can flip which candidate looks best, leading to poor choices.

Their remedy is an orthogonal acquisition estimator that subtracts a carefully weighted control term, cutting estimation variance while preserving the target. The full OrthoBO framework adds ensemble surrogates and a log transformation. Theory and experiments show lower variance, steadier rankings, and strong results on tuning neural networks, including fine-tuning tasks.
arxiv-2605-06554:
Bowen Peng, Subho Ghosh, and Jeffrey Quesnelle introduce Lighthouse Attention, a training method that lets transformers handle very long sequences. Standard attention grows quadratically in time and memory with sequence length, bottlenecking long-context training. Lighthouse wraps ordinary attention with a hierarchical selection step that compresses and later decompresses the sequence adaptively.

The compression pools queries, keys, and values symmetrically while preserving left-to-right order, and it needs no gradient, keeping the backward pass simple. Training runs mostly with Lighthouse, then recovers a full attention model in a short final phase. Small-scale pretraining tests show faster total training and lower final loss than matched full attention.
arxiv-2605-06654:
Yuxing Liu, Jianyu Wang, and Tong Zhang report that fine-tuning a language model with the same optimizer used in its pretraining forgets less old knowledge. Optimizers differ between training stages, and the choice turns out to shape the trade-off between learning a new task and retaining the old one. Matching optimizers beat alternatives and even the parameter-efficient LoRA method on this balance.

Experiments and theory explain why. Each optimizer regularizes activations in its own way, carving a different landscape around the pretrained model. Updates from the same optimizer follow structures that respect that landscape. A comparison of Muon and AdamW also finds Muon memorizes more by rote, hurting small-data reasoning fine-tuning.
arxiv-2605-06754:
Advait Pavuluri and eight co-authors introduce ScarfBench, a benchmark for moving enterprise Java applications between frameworks without changing their behavior. Such migration spans build files, dependency injection, persistence, request handling, and deployment, yet existing benchmarks cover bug fixing and version upgrades, not cross-framework refactoring. The benchmark is built from expert-written versions of thirty-four applications across Spring, Jakarta EE, and Quarkus.

Its 204 tasks hand an agent a working application and a target framework, judged by compiling, deploying, and passing behavioral tests. Five leading coding agents struggle: the strongest passes only about fifteen percent of focused tests, and just one task ends fully equivalent. A failure taxonomy drawn from traces guides future work.
arxiv-2605-06854:
Shucheng Kang and Heng Yang study the geometry of the pseudo-moment cone, a structure underlying polynomial optimization, and how moment matrices break into atomic pieces. A moment matrix built from many weighted point evaluations should decompose into its rank-one atoms, but identifying the right face of the cone is the obstacle. The authors fix the degree and vary the dimension and number of atoms.

For generically chosen atoms in a stated regime, they prove the minimal face is simplicial and generated exactly by the planted atoms. That geometry yields a Carathéodory-type decomposition algorithm for spectrahedral cones, specialized into an efficient atomic decomposition for moment matrices. A stabilized numerical version recovers atoms strongly and may sample high-rank extreme rays beyond the proven regime.
arxiv-2605-06954:
Qinyang He and Yonatan Mintz address pricing for usage-based car insurance, where driving data from telematics shapes premiums. Such programs aim to reward safe driving, but claim costs vary wildly, driver behavior changes, and discount budgets are limited. Earlier work mostly profiled drivers rather than setting prices over time.

The pair build a control framework that learns claim patterns, models how drivers respond to discounts, and spreads discounts across a whole portfolio. They prove the method approaches the best possible result as the portfolio grows. In a large simulation, it beats fixed pricing and lowers both expected losses and claim rates.
arxiv-2605-07154:
Yuchen He and Jing Zhang segment objects in video using sight, sound, and a written referring expression together. The hard part is that which sense matters changes with each expression and scene, while most methods fuse all cues the same way. Their model, PRIMED, borrows an idea from brain science called biased competition.

A prior decoder first judges whether the expression leans on audio, vision, or both, then guides attention accordingly, suppressing less relevant channels. Compact visual tokens supply shared context across fusion stages, and an added alignment loss sharpens object against background. On the standard benchmark for this task, PRIMED reaches leading overall performance.
arxiv-2605-07654:
Iwase and three colleagues offer a cheaper way to tell when a language model reasoning chain can be trusted. Models often improve by sampling several chain of thought traces and taking a majority vote, a method called self consistency. The team noticed that correct traces tend to reproduce their own answer when cut short and regenerated, while wrong traces wander.

They turn that gap into a reliability signal called prefix consistency, which weights each candidate answer by its reappearance rate when the remainder is regenerated. It works without token probabilities or model self ratings. Across five reasoning models and four maths and science benchmarks, prefix consistency predicts correctness better than rivals in most settings. Reweighting votes by it reaches standard majority vote plateau accuracy with far fewer tokens. The saving reaches up to twenty one times fewer tokens, with a median saving of four point six times.
arxiv-2605-07954:
Elia Belli and Daniele De Sensi port a classic scientific kernel, stencil computation, to the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine, an AI chip with massive on-chip memory and parallelism. Stencils drive fluid dynamics and climate codes but are memory-bound on GPUs, starved by the trip to off-chip memory. The wafer-scale engine's distributed on-chip memory promises to remove that wall.

Their CStencil framework implements two-dimensional stencils on the WSE-3, benchmarked fairly against a state-of-the-art GPU solver ported to the same precision on an A100. The wafer engine's mesh and on-chip storage largely eliminated the memory bottleneck, delivering speedups up to several hundredfold. A roofline analysis confirmed the implementation saturates the machine's resources.
arxiv-2605-08254:
Valentino Maiorca, Eleonora Gualdoni, Xavier Suau, Marco Cuturi, and coauthors make activation steering cheap for text-to-image models. Steering beats prompting for stable control. But each new concept needs its own optimization run on the target model. That takes minutes per concept. It fails when concept sets are large or change all the time.

HyperTransport trains a hypernetwork to do the mapping at once. It maps an embedding from a pretrained encoder to the intervention parameters for that concept. CLIP is the encoder in their setup. The one-time training removes the per-concept cost. New concepts can be steered as fast as they can be embedded. Control stays predictable across requests.
arxiv-2605-08354:
Juanxi Tian, Fengyuan Liu, Jiaming Han, Yilei Jiang, and coauthors replace a single reward number with a written rubric when aligning image and video generators with human taste. Human judgment is multi-dimensional, and squeezing it into scalar scores invites reward hacking and hides what the model got wrong.

Their Auto-Rubric as Reward framework first asks a vision-language model to spell out prompt-specific criteria, turning its internalized preferences into independently checkable quality dimensions before any outputs are compared. Training then optimizes against those explicit rubrics rather than an opaque learned proxy. The authors present the approach as more reliable, scalable, and data-efficient than earlier rubric-based rewards.
arxiv-2605-08454:
Yuxiang Luo and Andrew Perrault recover continuous physical dynamics from sparse snapshots. Local supervision fades as the gap between observations grows. The authors replace it with a global rule. A true flow must compose with itself consistently under time shifts. That is the semi-group property of autonomous dynamics.

They train a time-conditioned secant velocity field. They measure its violation of that rule, a quantity they call symmetry rupture. In training, it acts as a regularizer that confines the model to self-consistent flows. At inference, it becomes an oracle. It picks the largest solver step that preserves consistency, with no local error estimates needed. On diffusion-reaction and Navier-Stokes tests, the method posted the lowest rollout error.
arxiv-2605-08854:
Insoo Kim and Jinwoo Shin clean blurred photos with flow models, with no loss of truth to the source. Flow models hold strong priors from vast image sets. But their training aim clashes with repair work. Straight use drops the truth score fast. DeblurFlow bends the flow path to start at the blurred shot, not at noise. The learned field is then the gap twixt blur and clean shot. Plain training turns into gap training.

A dual sampler starts from a high truth guess. It then adds crisp feel at a tiny truth cost. Plain flow on top would wreck the score. A gap tuned latent space cuts code cost up to nine fold. On four blur tests, truth and feel hold up well at fair cost.
arxiv-2605-09054:
Leilei Du and six co-authors protect privacy in endless data streams, where events arrive slot by slot and statistics must be published without exposing any user's recent activity. A standard scheme guards a sliding window of events, but it assumes every user wants the same level of protection.

Their mechanisms let each user set a personal privacy level at each time slot. Budgets for privacy loss are spread across time, saved when unused, and even borrowed from nearby slots, and users may change their settings as the stream runs. The authors prove the guarantees and bound the errors. In experiments, their methods cut estimation error by more than half against leading rivals.
arxiv-2605-09354:
Scherer and two colleagues study how the spectral radius of an operator tuple depends on the operator space structure. In recent work, Shalit and Shamovich attached a spectral radius function to every operator space structure on C^d. For a commuting operator tuple, the authors show the spectral radius is fixed by the underlying normed space alone, as the largest norm over the joint spectrum.

In contrast, when the dimension is at least 3, the smallest and largest spectral radii already differ for some matrix tuple. For selfadjoint operator spaces, equal spectral radius functions for all tuples force the spaces themselves to be equal. Two proofs are given, one using a characterisation via the invertibility domain of the linear pencil. Two operator spaces sharing a spectral radius function also yield matching algebras of locally uniformly bounded NC functions over the matching NC unit balls.
arxiv-2605-09454:
Dey and two colleagues study the single-index bandit problem, where a reward hinges on a projection onto one unknown direction in high-dimensional contexts, passed through an unknown reward function. The model broadens linear and generalized linear bandits into a nonparametric setting, suiting cases where the reward function is unknown. Optimal regret was known only for monotone reward functions, while the general non-monotone case had a best bound of T to the power 3 over 4.

The authors close that gap with ZoomSIB-UCB, a simple two-phase algorithm. It first estimates the projection direction with a normalized Stein estimator, then turns the problem into a one-dimensional bandit using discretization and UCB. It achieves regret of T to the power 2 over 3, and the authors prove a matching minimax lower bound, showing the upper bound is essentially tight. Empirical results further show the approach is effective and robust.
arxiv-2605-09654:
Lam and five colleagues address bias in sampling from score based diffusion models. Bias comes from both time steps and score approximation. A common fix applies corrector steps from the unadjusted Langevin algorithm at each noise level. But that algorithm is itself biased, since it discretizes a smooth diffusion. The authors instead use adjusted Langevin correctors with Metropolis Hastings or Barker accept reject steps. They compute the right acceptance chance from the score function, since the target density ratio is usually absent.

They give the first exact approach for adjusting Langevin corrections in diffusion models, built on a two coin Bernoulli factory algorithm. They also offer a fast Simpson's rule approximation accurate to order five halves in step size at near zero cost. Both methods improve sample quality on synthetic and image data, with steady Fréchet gains on images. Exact correction, they show, is practical for diffusion sampling.
arxiv-2605-10354:
Balázs Pál and three colleagues build starting conditions for a different kind of cosmic simulation. Standard generators assume fully periodic cubic boxes, but stereographically projected N-body codes such as StePS need non-periodic, observer-centered setups. Their 2026 paper presents stepsic, an open-source generator extending Lagrangian perturbation theory to spherical and cylindrical shapes, plus varied cuboids.

The code builds Gaussian random density fields on clean Fourier grids. It applies first- and second-order perturbation theory for displacements and speeds, then maps them onto particles with B-spline mass assignment and Fourier-space deconvolution. A multiresolution scheme maps fields across the varying particle-mass resolution of the projection. In periodic boxes the recovered spectrum matched linear theory to better than 0.5 percent up to half the Nyquist wavenumber. Full StePS runs confirmed that second-order theory removes a 2 to 3 percent transient excess seen at first order.
arxiv-2605-10454:
Leon Keim and three colleagues present a flexible, low-cost data logger for long-term gas monitoring in karst systems. Carbon dioxide and radon-222 dynamics there reveal ventilation and source terms. Continuous monitoring in remote, underground settings demands a robust, adaptable system for self-running capture, storage, and optional remote sending. Yet commercial loggers are expensive and inflexible. Their 2026 paper describes a Raspberry Pi-based platform for Modbus sensors with Ansible deployment.

Compared with microcontroller systems, the Raspberry Pi offers advanced networking, larger storage, and easier coding as a full computer running Python on Linux. The platform's full description and open code aim to make long-term monitoring feasible and user-friendly. Deployment is automated via Ansible and systemd services ensuring automatic startup after power cuts. Users can add sensors by writing a Python driver of roughly 100 lines, though the platform does not prescribe a power supply or enclosure.

arxiv-2606-04154:
Mansoor Ahmed and colleagues present EpiFormer in 2026, a geometric deep learning system that predicts epitopes, the surface patches where antibodies latch onto a foreign protein. Knowing these patches guides vaccine and antibody design, but labeled examples are scarce and lopsided.

Older models encode the antibody's two chains separately and merge them late, missing how the pair shapes the binding surface together. EpiFormer instead interleaves cross-attention inside its graph network layers, so antigen and antibody information flows both ways from the start. Paired with sparsity-aware training goals, it improved the F1 score over the previous best method by more than forty percent on standard benchmarks. Its learned attention even rediscovered known biology about which chain leads the interaction.
arxiv-2606-04454:
Zhang and colleagues propose a framework that helps large language models reason in steps by feeding them small, relevant pieces of a knowledge graph, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Language models often lose logical consistency and factual grounding on complex multi-step questions. Their system, SGR, extracts the key entities, relations, and constraints from a question into a structured schema, then retrieves compact subgraphs matching it, giving the model explicit relational evidence for each step.

SGR also combines direct database-style reasoning over the graph with a collaborative mode that validates candidate answers from several paths, merging them by model confidence and graph consistency. On the CWQ, WebQSP, GrailQA, and KQA Pro benchmarks, SGR improved accuracy and top-answer performance over standard prompting and knowledge-enhanced baselines. Ablation tests showed both schema guidance and graph retrieval were crucial.
arxiv-2606-04554:
Futorny and Tantubay construct and test large families of Whittaker modules, in a 2026 arXiv mathematics paper. The authors revisit the construction for untwisted affine Kac-Moody algebras. They focus on a subtle condition. The Whittaker functions on the Heisenberg algebra must have infinite support. Only then is the resulting module irreducible, meaning it has no smaller submodules.

When support is finite, they show the modules become reducible. This produces infinite chains of submodules. They establish an irreducibility criterion for the induced modules. They construct a large family satisfying it. They then build quantum analogues and prove irreducibility for a family of them. They also give modules over the quantum affine algebra of type A that are not deformations of classical irreducible modules. This suggests a route toward classification.
arxiv-2606-04754:
Bürgin, Herbst, Lin, and Jegelka look past symmetries to explain why separately trained neural networks can often be merged, in a 2026 arXiv machine learning theory paper. Phenomena like linear mode connectivity, where a low-loss straight path joins two solutions, are tied to parameter symmetries. The authors develop a framework of effective function classes: the set of functions a single neuron can actually realize on its input data.

They formalize effective symmetry breaking through neuron identifiability across independent training runs. Their analysis shows networks can admit large families of equivalent solutions even when the model is asymmetric, so equivalence lives in the data-dependent function class, not just the architecture. Identifiability then enables merging representations from different runs without prior alignment, and they characterize when such merging admits a linear low-loss path. The findings recast loss-landscape geometry as a property of parameters, data, and representations.
arxiv-2606-04954:
Seeyangnok, Pinsook, and Ackland find that a structural distortion which usually kills superconductivity instead rescues it in hydrogenated monolayers, in a 2026 arXiv condensed matter paper. Hydrogenation boosts electron-phonon coupling and superconductivity in two-dimensional materials. Using first-principles calculations on the Janus chalcogenide hydrides 1T-WSH and 1T-WSeH, they find the high-symmetry phases soften phonons strongly, driving a transition to a distorted structure with an emergent triangular charge-density-wave pattern.

The instability comes not from Fermi-surface nesting but from strong momentum-dependent coupling. The distortion reconstructs the electronic structure, lowers the Fermi-level density of states, and renormalizes the coupling down, from 2.04 to 1.50 in one compound and from 3.94 to 1.06 in the other, while superconductivity survives. This establishes a universal mechanism in the family: the charge-density wave's primary role is self-stabilization, relieving excessive coupling while preserving phonon-mediated superconductivity rather than eliminating it.
arxiv-2606-05054:
Maria Marina and co-authors improve self-consistency for large language models with a ranking method called RISC in this 2026 arXiv paper. Self-consistency samples several reasoning paths and picks the most frequent answer, but majority voting often fails to recover a correct answer that already sits among the samples. RISC reframes the final choice as a ranking problem rather than a vote.

A lightweight LambdaRank model scores each candidate answer using five features that capture answer frequency, semantic centrality, and consistency of the reasoning traces. Evaluated on three datasets across a range of test-time budgets, RISC gave a better accuracy-efficiency trade-off than standard self-consistency and strong baselines, with especially large gains on question answering. With only 18 samples it already surpassed self-consistency using 99 samples, and the analysis shows the five features are individually useful and complementary.
arxiv-2606-05254:
Arman Akbari and co-authors present Flash-WAM in this 2026 arXiv paper, a distillation method that makes world action models fast enough for real-time robot control. World action models generate future video and robot actions through iterative diffusion, but they need tens of denoising steps per decision, far too slow for live control. Generic step distillation breaks down here because the video and action streams follow different noise schedules.

Flash-WAM is modality-aware: it picks a consistency function for each stream to match its noise regime. Built on the LingBot-VA model, it compresses inference to a single step in each modality, cutting per-chunk latency on RoboTwin 2.0 from 8.1 seconds to 348 milliseconds, a 23-fold speedup. Task success stayed high in simulation, at 85.5 percent on RoboTwin 2.0 and 95.7 percent on LIBERO. It recovered 60 percent success on a humanoid robot where naive distillation managed only 24 percent.
arxiv-2606-05554:
Andrew Chen and Palomino prove a limit on what risk can explain in economic models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Macro models often add fear of risk and shifting risk levels to match asset prices. A classic result by Tallarini hinted that such additions may change little in such economies. The authors sharpen that hint into a clear theorem. Three conditions drive it: split tastes for timing and risk, split drivers of averages and spreads, and near-linear limits.

Under those conditions, risk attitudes and changing risk do not move key responses. The response of any model variable to calm state changes stays fixed. The paper then shows how modelers get bigger roles for risk. They must break or adapt one of the three assumptions. The theorem thus maps exactly where risk can matter and where it cannot. The map helps judge which price puzzles risk stories can truly solve.
arxiv-2606-05654:
Krishnaram and co-authors show mixed-language posts unsettle hate moderation in a 2026 arXiv paper. Live systems do not just label posts; they allow, flag, or send them for human review. Tests, though, usually run on clean English. The team built paired posts with identical content in clean English and Tamil-English code-mix. Thresholds tuned on English were then applied to both forms.

About twenty-seven percent of decisions flipped between the paired forms. Review load more than doubled, rising from about fourteen to about thirty percent. False flags on harmless posts also climbed, from about seven to about ten percent. Tamil-only posts fared worse still, pointing to a broad coverage gap. A simple rule that defers when two scorers disagree cut automatic errors. It did so only by adding reviewer work. Workflow-level tests, the authors argue, expose failures that label scores hide.
arxiv-2606-05754:
Weiguang Wang and colleagues harden fiber-optic listening systems against signal fading in a 2026 arXiv paper. Phase-sensitive reflectometry turns a fiber into a long microphone for roads, rails, and pipelines. Polarization fading blinds random stretches of the fiber, and outdoor noise muddies the rest. The team adds a Sagnac interferometer channel whose steady phase response fills the gaps. An FPGA board aligns the two channels by cross-correlation.

A standard benchmark protocol compares old feature methods, shallow classifiers, and deep models. Tests ran on a ten-kilometer fiber with six acoustic event classes. A dual-branch fusion model, reading both channels, gave the best balance of scores. It reached about ninety percent accuracy with a nuisance alarm rate of five percent. How channels are grouped changed fusion scores strongly. The authors urge judging such systems on alarms, misses, and latency, not accuracy alone.
arxiv-2606-06054:
Jiawen Zhang and colleagues warn that a personal agent's memory is a control channel, not a filing cabinet in a 2026 arXiv paper. Long-term memory personalizes agents across sessions. Today's pipelines retrieve whatever is semantically closest to the query and inject it. Similar is not the same as appropriate: leakage across domains, sycophancy, tool-call drift, and memory-triggered jailbreaks follow. The team evaluated memory frameworks and a personal-agent environment.

Memory proved able to durably reshape how agents interpret tasks and act. That persistence makes poisoned or misplaced memories a threat. Their defense, MemGate, is a neural gate of nine million parameters. It sits between the vector store and the model, admitting memories conditioned on the task. No model surgery or database rewrite is needed. Across frameworks and backbones it reduced such threats while preserving memory's usefulness. Trustworthy retrieval, the authors argue, must judge context, not similarity.
arxiv-2606-06154:
Sunny Gupta, Shambhavi Shanker, and Amit Sethi propose HyperLoRA in this 2026 arXiv paper on federated learning, where many devices train a shared model without sending their raw data to a server. LoRA fine-tunes large models by learning small low-rank updates instead of changing every weight. In federated settings, averaging those small updates factor by factor distorts the combined update, and clients waste rounds restarting their adaptation from scratch.

HyperLoRA replaces both weak points with learned components. A hypernetwork, a network that generates weights for another network, reads a summary of each client's data and produces its starting LoRA update directly. On the server, a learned module merges updates in the full product space rather than averaging factors, with a small correction step for stability. On DomainNet and NICO++ benchmarks, the method matched full-budget accuracy with five times fewer local training rounds.
arxiv-2606-06254:
Parsa Memarzadehsaghezi, Pooria Madani, and Khalil El-Khatib ask a pointed security question in this 2026 arXiv paper. Large code models can rewrite a program while keeping it working, which lets malware authors spawn endless variants that dodge signature based scanners. Shrinking such a model by pruning, removing parts of it, would make that misuse cheaper to run. The authors test whether the mutation skill survives pruning.

Their method, SecRL Prune, learns which feed forward channels to cut, layer by layer, using reinforcement learning. The reward keeps the small student's answers close to the teacher's. A caching trick stores the teacher's top predictions once, cutting peak GPU memory by over half. Across three seven billion parameter code models pruned by ten to thirty percent, the results kept higher code correctness and mutation diversity than rival methods. Mutations from a twenty percent pruned model sharply reduced malware detection in a case study.
arxiv-2606-06554:
Roshni Mahtani and co-authors sort plastics with invisible light and deep learning in this 2026 arXiv paper. Recycling quality depends on telling polymers apart, and conventional sorting struggles with blends and multilayer films. Terahertz spectroscopy probes materials with rays between microwaves and infrared. It is non destructive and finely detailed. The team classifies twelve polymer types this way, including pure polymers, multilayer films, commercial blends, and biopolymers.

Their Multi Scale Feature Attention Network is built for spectral data. Feature gating recalibrates the raw signal. Parallel convolutions at several scales catch frequency patterns of different widths. Cross feature attention then highlights the most informative bands. The network reached a classification accuracy of eighty five point two percent, beating leading comparison models. It also shows which bands distinguish each polymer class. That makes its sorting decisions open to audit.
arxiv-2606-06754:
Grading student essays trait by trait is slow, and human raters often disagree by more than a point. Keramati, Zhou, Mehrotra, and Warschauer build an automated grader that argues with itself in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system, MADRAG, needs no task specific training, a relief for schools that cannot supply thousands of scored examples.

Three agent roles drive the scoring. An Advocate lists an essay's strengths, a Skeptic attacks its weaknesses, and a Judge weighs both arguments into a final trait score. The Judge also retrieves scored example essays matched to the grading rubric, anchoring its standards against real work. Tests showed the system clearly beating plain prompt based judging and approaching supervised systems trained for the job. Breakdown experiments found that retrieval did most of the calibration work, while the debate sharpened judgment on higher level traits like organization and argument.
arxiv-2606-07254:
Lee proposes a strict test for whether sequence models truly track hidden state over very long inputs, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The task uses a non-Abelian group, a set of operations where order matters, so step A then B differs from B then A. Models must accumulate the ordered product of many operations. Selected pairs of consecutive operations are withheld from training yet required at test time, blocking simple memorization of local patterns.

His model, trained only on sequences of length eight, predicted final states perfectly across five random seeds at lengths up to about one million tokens. Matched baselines, including recurrent and state-space models, stayed near chance under the same split. Diagnostics linked success to a hard projection step that keeps the internal state aligned with valid group elements. Softening that projection collapsed accuracy, supporting the claim that explicit non-commutative composition is the active ingredient.
arxiv-2606-07954:
Prayas Agrawal and co-authors at IIT Bombay and Microsoft tackle a quiet inefficiency in language model training: choosing which examples go into each minibatch, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Training data mixes many domains, and a good batch should both speed convergence and cover the domains fairly. Picking examples independently per domain wastes the budget on near-duplicates across domains, while learned domain weights need expensive proxy models.

Their method, PartitionSel, chooses the whole batch at once. It maximises a gradient-matching score: how well the batch's combined gradient mimics the gradient on held-out data. A partition matroid constraint gives each domain its own budget. The objective is weakly submodular, so an orthogonal matching pursuit algorithm selects the batch with provable approximation guarantees. Coupling through one shared score is the point: cross-domain redundancy is priced in, so each step covers more distinct signal.
arxiv-2606-08054:
Jiang-Chao Wan and Yi Wang settle a fifteen-year-old conjecture on matching polynomials, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A matching pairs up vertices with disjoint edges. The matching polynomial's largest root measures how matching-rich the graph is. Csikvári proved in twenty eleven that a threshold graph maximises the root among graphs with fixed edges, and conjectured the extremal graph should be as star-like as possible.

Wan and Wang confirm it and extend it to uniform hypergraphs, whose edges join k vertices at once. For any k-graph with m edges, the largest root is at most the k-th root of m. Equality holds exactly for intersecting hypergraphs, where every two edges share a vertex. In the graph case, deleting isolated vertices leaves only the star or the triangle. A sharper bound holds when the matching number is at least two. Star-like concentration is optimal.
arxiv-2606-08154:
Cheng Qian and co-authors train a robot imitator entirely inside a computer, then hand it real tasks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In-context imitation learning lets a robot learn a new task from a few demonstrations given at test time, with no retraining. The bottleneck is training data: generalisable policies need lots of it, and real demonstrations are expensive.

Their framework, SynthICL, generates high-fidelity training data synthetically, from ordinary colour images only: no depth sensing, precise calibration, or real-world collection. A flow-matching transformer policy trains on the synthetic stream, and also learns to predict the next subgoal image, keeping control grounded in intermediate aims. On sixteen unseen real-world manipulation tasks, SynthICL averaged about seventy-nine percent success with one demonstration at test time, outperforming prior methods. Policies, it suggests, need not be raised on real data to survive the real world.
arxiv-2606-08254:
Lan and colleagues teach simulated patients to show self-stigma in this 2026 arXiv paper. Clinicians train by talking with patients played by language models, but those simulations miss a key reality of mental health care. Self-stigma is the internalization of negative stereotypes about one's own condition, and it makes real patients resist in context-sensitive ways, through avoidance, denial, or self-blame. Existing simulated patients instead behave in a static or uniformly compliant manner, which trains the wrong expectations.

The authors build a framework grounded in a psychological model of self-stigmatization and create a dataset of mental health dialogues enriched with internal monologues, private reasoning reflecting stigma-aware thinking. Fine-tuning on this material lets patient agents adjust how much stigma they show as triggers change. Evaluations show the approach significantly outperforming standard simulation methods.
arxiv-2606-08354:
Shestakov and Zelmanov classify a family of non-associative algebras in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Jordan algebra uses a commutative product that satisfies a special identity, a setup first motivated by quantum mechanics. A superalgebra adds a grading that splits elements into even and odd parts. Unital means the algebra has an identity element. The question is which such algebras are simple, having no nontrivial ideals, meaning no proper substructures closed under multiplication.

The main theorem says that a simple unital Jordan superalgebra of any dimension either belongs to the list of known examples or lies inside a certain proper subvariety. A subvariety is a smaller class cut out by extra identities. So any genuinely new example must live in a tightly constrained corner of the theory. Results of this kind tell researchers the known list is nearly complete, and they point at where undiscovered examples could hide.
arxiv-2606-08654:
Weinan Wang, Gang, and Deng attach honest error bars to neural predictions of fluid flow, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neural operators give fast surrogates for costly partial differential equation solvers. By themselves they provide no calibrated uncertainty. The authors propose a perturbation-based conformal method. It wraps any predictor in bands with guaranteed coverage, aimed at the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations where labeled data are scarce.

The local uncertainty scale comes from comparing two models trained on nearly identical datasets. One uses the original labels, the other labels perturbed by small Gaussian noise. Their disagreement measures how much the output moves when the training data shift a bit. On the standard Navier-Stokes benchmark, the new method produces substantially narrower bands than existing methods in the comparisons reported here. In plain terms, it states how far each forecast can be trusted.
arxiv-2606-08954:
Xu, Zhou, and Wang compute a nuclear decay rate carefully, showing the hardest part of the sum can be ignored, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The decay is two-neutrino double beta decay of germanium-76 into selenium-76, a rare process whose rate depends on a nuclear matrix element. Computing it means summing over every excited state of the intermediate nucleus, arsenic-76, whose levels crowd rapidly with energy. The team analyzes how the Gamow-Teller contributions behave as excitation energy rises.

The contributions fragment into many tiny pieces with random signs at high energy, so they cancel out. As a result the matrix element converges by about 5 mega-electronvolts, and higher-lying states contribute negligibly. Including two-body currents, a correction to the transition operator, quenches the result by roughly 10 percent. The findings support truncating the state sum in practice, and matter for calibrating searches for the decay's neutrinoless cousin.
arxiv-2606-09654:
Miles Gould closes a gap in the sorting of a new class of algebras in this 2026 arXiv note. The objects are selfless C-star algebras, paired with states that weight their parts. Past work showed each such algebra falls into one of two camps: stably finite or purely infinite. One case was left open, where the state is not faithful, meaning it can assign zero weight to whole parts.

Gould proves that case lands in the purely infinite camp, and the algebra is simple as well. The proof runs through free products, a way of fusing algebras with little shared structure. He shows wide classes of such fusions, with the stated traits, are purely infinite and simple. With the sort complete, every selfless algebra of this kind is pure. It also makes headway on a conjecture of Choda and Dykema.
arxiv-2606-09754:
Antonio Scala sets out a defence frame against AI-driven manipulation that aims at people, not machines in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such attacks work through trust, attention, and standing. They play out as linked campaigns, not lone false posts. Incident-by-incident review shreds them into weak hints. Blame-first review stalls aid until a culprit is named.

Scala's unit sits between the two: the Information Manipulation Set. A set bundles the tales, accounts, platforms, timing, fake boosts, and mind tricks of one campaign. The pipeline runs from signal spotting and triage to a set sketch, then grades trust in the sketch and the harm at stake. Aid is picked to fit, and the sketch is revised as facts land. A worked case shows what post-level and blame-first views miss. A tabletop test plan grades call quality and fair response.
arxiv-2606-09854:
Juergen Dietrich tests whether language models can name which model wrote a text, even when names are stripped in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is political statement scoring by teams of models. Past work found models shield their peers from shutdown, and that hiding names only partly cuts the bias. Style marks may leak through the text itself.

Three judges faced a five-way sorting task: four known model families plus an unknown class. Two were big models used cold or with a few samples. The third was a fine-tuned T5. A strict split kept test statements out of training, so wins could not ride on shared content. T5 hit a macro F1 of zero point nine nine one, and held near that on fresh statements. Style, it turns out, survives name-hiding with ease. Only rewriting the output itself could scrub the mark.
arxiv-2606-10054:
Watanabe and colleagues establish a universal scaling law for charging quantum batteries together, in a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum thermodynamics. Quantum batteries store energy in quantum systems, and ergotropy measures how much of that energy can actually be extracted as work. Charging many batteries collectively, rather than one by one, is known to help. The team asks how the extractable fraction behaves as the number of batteries grows.

They prove the ratio of ergotropy to stored energy approaches unity at least as fast as one over N, where N is the battery count, regardless of microscopic details. They call this generic behavior asymptotic freedom. The universal rate can be beaten when the battery state becomes asymptotically pure, giving faster power-law or even exponential convergence. Rigorous upper and lower bounds for finite N back the asymptotic claim. The law gives designers a detail-free guarantee for collective charging schemes.
arxiv-2606-10154:
Kadadekar audits a common shortcut in releasing compressed language models, in a 2026 arXiv paper on AI safety. Quantized checkpoints, models shrunk to fewer bits for cheaper deployment, are often screened first with quality metrics and only later, if ever, with direct safety tests. His matched matrix covers fifty-one model rows across six models, four families, a seven-level GGUF quantization ladder, and AWQ and GPTQ four-bit checkpoints.

All thirty-six quality-safety pairings split direction across models, meaning quality and refusal behavior moved independently. Nine hidden-danger rows, plus one near case, kept stable or improved quality while refusal rates fell by twelve to sixty-eight percentage points, and seven of eleven AWQ and GPTQ rows were hidden-danger. A behavioral screen he calibrates, the Refusal Template Stability Index, routed all ten dangerous rows to direct safety testing.
arxiv-2606-10554:
Ngoli and colleagues introduce a tougher test for editing facts inside language models in this 2026 arXiv paper. Knowledge editing rewrites one stored fact without retraining the whole model, but benchmarks mostly check recall of the edited fact itself. They rarely check logical consequences: learn a new president, and the model should also update who the president's spouse is. The new benchmark pulls logical rules from a knowledge graph for each edit and generates multi-hop questions that probe those consequences.

The results expose a real weakness. Popular methods such as ROME and fine-tuning insert direct assertions accurately, yet often fail to inject the entailed knowledge that should follow. The gap between directly edited facts and their consequences reaches up to twenty-four percent in the reported experiments. One older method, KN, generalises correlated knowledge better. Editing research, they conclude, needs semantics-aware evaluation.
arxiv-2606-10654:
Herron and colleagues probe what speech models secretly learn about speakers in this 2026 arXiv paper on speech technology. Self-supervised speech models learn rich sound representations from raw audio. The team asks how much speaker group information those representations carry, probing gender, age, dialect, ethnicity, and native-speaker status. They inspect models in four states: pretrained, fine-tuned for speaker identification, fine-tuned for recognition, and fine-tuned with a fairness algorithm.

The information is clearly there, spread across layers and embedding dimensions. Fine-tuning for speaker identification amplifies group signals whose variation is phonetic, but not those carried more by meaning. Fine-tuning for recognition discards phonetically variant group information while retaining semantic variants. Fairness training shifts the encoding mainly for phonetic categories. Knowing where group information lives could help design recognisers that treat groups more even-handedly.
arxiv-2606-10754:
Williams and colleagues read the spin of a quantum Hall system with light in this 2026 arXiv paper on condensed matter physics. In fractional quantum Hall states, electrons in a strong magnetic field form exotic phases at fractional fillings, and their spin polarisation reveals what the excitations are. The team uses cavity-polariton spectroscopy on gallium arsenide wells, measuring optical coupling across fillings from one third to one. From the coupling they extract polarisation versus filling.

The coupling to the excitation is suppressed below filling one, the signature of negative trions in a fully polarised system, a first in this regime. Away from the fully polarised fillings, depolarisation is symmetric and follows a law: spin flips per flux quantum equal the composite-fermion filling. Single quasiparticles cannot explain that scaling; collective spin-reversal excitations, minimal fractionally charged skyrmions, can. The work establishes the method as a probe of Hall physics.
arxiv-2606-10954:
Comellas reports new optimal Cayley graphs in this 2026 arXiv paper. In the degree-diameter problem, one wants the largest graph with bounded degree and diameter; Cayley graphs, built from groups and generating sets, supply many record holders. Using SageMath programs, some drafted with AI help and fixed by hand, Comellas searched group libraries and graph databases for alternatives.

The search turned up numerous optimal graphs not isomorphic to those catalogued by Marston Conder, differing in girth, algebraic connectivity, automorphism groups, and cycle counts despite matching order, degree, and diameter. Since parts of the search were randomized, the new collection is not exhaustive. Such twins give extremal graph theory fresh test cases.
arxiv-2606-11254:
Kim and Margarint run numerical experiments on Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) in a 2026 arXiv paper. It is a family of fractal curves arising as scaling limits of planar statistical physics models, generated by Loewner's equation with a Brownian driver. Rather than the curves themselves, they study the spread of the dynamics from its average behavior at fixed time, giving theorists concrete predictions.

Using Euler's method, they track how far individual runs stray from the sample average. In the single SLE case, their experiments predict the spread distribution is bimodal when the dynamics starts close to the origin. Started further away, it can turn bell-shaped. They then tackle Multiple SLE, whose driver is Dyson Brownian motion, harder to compute because of singularities and data volume. There the spread distribution is predicted bell-shaped in all cases. They also check how the distributions change as the parameters kappa and beta vary.
arxiv-2606-11354:
Yuqi Wang, Shen, and Mehmani build a language-model system for talking to buildings in a 2026 arXiv paper, from Nantum AI and Harvard. Talking to buildings could be more direct through natural dialogs. But building data spans many formats, shareable information is scarce, and reading it needs domain expertise. Limited training data makes fine-tuning impractical, and different models align differently.

Their multi-agent framework uses semantic routing and programmatic reasoning to separate language understanding from building analytics. Instead of standard retrieval-augmented generation, a Doorman mechanism decomposes tasks. Specialized coding agents then generate executable Python scripts for precise arithmetic. The system needs no task-specific training, a zero-shot design. They validate it on data from more than 200 commercial buildings. It gave accurate, contextual responses for users from tenants to building managers, across building applications. The authors argue this split is what such domains require.
arxiv-2606-11554:
Beiji Chen and Kui Ren study an inverse problem for tumour growth in this 2026 arXiv paper. Inverse problems work backwards from measurements to unknown causes. Their model is a reaction-diffusion equation, which describes how a cell density spreads and multiplies over time. From limited observations they want to recover three things at once: the local proliferation rate, a competition coefficient limiting growth, and the starting cell distribution.

Using Carleman estimates, weighted inequalities controlling a solution from partial data, they prove the two coefficients are uniquely determined. The bound is of Lipschitz type, meaning errors grow at most in direct proportion. The starting condition gets a weaker logarithmic stability bound. Their two-stage numerical method first separates the coefficients from the starting state using a time shift. Computer tests show accurate, robust recovery, and measurements taken nearer the start time give better reconstructions of the initial state.
arxiv-2606-11654:
Kazuki Nakayashiki and Keisuke Watanabe ask whether a document's future highlights can be predicted before anyone reads it in this 2026 arXiv paper. On their social highlighting platform, the passages a crowd marks are a valuable signal, but new documents have no marks yet. Earlier tests found off-the-shelf language models do worse than a trivial baseline that simply favours the opening passages, called the lead baseline.

The authors train a logistic ranker, a scoring model, on real reader marks, using sentence embeddings and position features. It beats the lead baseline by a small but robust margin, clearing their pre-registered threshold in ninety-seven percent of resamples. The share of correct picks among the top three passages rises from one quarter to nearly two fifths. Two standard unsupervised methods lose to the lead baseline. The edge is biggest on unpopular documents, the long tail where prediction matters most.
arxiv-2606-11854:
Michal Chudoba and three colleagues fine-tune multimodal models through pictures alone in this 2026 arXiv paper. Adapting a language model usually means adding weights, as in LoRA, or adding special input tokens, as in soft prompting. Both change the model's computational graph, which high-throughput serving engines such as vLLM do not fully support.

Their method, ART, leaves a frozen multimodal model untouched and optimises only a raw image fed to it. Gradients flow back into the pixel array, so any fine-tuning objective works, and the learned information settles into high-frequency patterns inside the image. The tuned images can even be styled as task-relevant artwork. Across sizes of the open Qwen architecture, ART reaches accuracy competitive with LoRA on mathematics and tool-use benchmarks, while being cheaper at training and inference time. The authors frame the stored image as a kind of steganography for AI.
arxiv-2606-12054:
Benjamin Leblanc and three colleagues ask how simple noise injection into neural network training can be in this 2026 arXiv paper. Adding random noise to a model's parameters during stochastic gradient descent improves training and generalisation, but designs vary widely in complexity. Two questions matter: how to give each training example its own perturbation efficiently, and whether fancy noise schemes beat plain ones.

For the first, a distributional identity for linear layers lets per-example noise ride along with normal batched computation. Their method, ENSGD, uses it directly. For the second, they systematically compare diagonal Gaussian noise schemes against a simple isotropic baseline across noise levels on the CIFAR-100 image benchmark and text tasks. The verdict is consistent: isotropic noise with one perturbed forward pass per update recovers most of the benefit. Multi-sample gradient averaging and learned per-parameter noise scales add real computational cost for marginal gains, if any.
arxiv-2606-12154:
Jo reports what happens when a large language model is removed from the answering path, in this 2026 arXiv paper. His earlier setup ran a large model on a laptop with eight gigabytes of graphics memory, yet took about four seconds per answer. In the new design, the large model works offline, reading documents and writing checked answers into a structured knowledge store. At question time, only a small router, a fixed renderer, and a billion-parameter model stay active.

Response time fell from 4,465 milliseconds to 518 milliseconds on the same laptop. Throughput rose from 15.7 to 131 tokens per second. On a 563-entry store, keyword routing scored 1.5 percent top-one accuracy, while BM25 ranking, a standard text-matching score, reached 92.8 percent. A confidence gate lifted effective accuracy to 98 percent by escalating only 12.3 percent of queries.
arxiv-2606-12254:
Gairola Shashank and co-authors catalog about twenty-five thousand newborn star clusters across seventeen nearby galaxies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The data come from the UltraViolet Imaging Telescope, since young stars shine brightly in ultraviolet light. Its sharpness resolves clusters at a mean scale of about 54 parsecs. The sample spans 8 massive classic spirals, 6 flocculent spirals with patchy arms, and 3 dwarf irregulars. All clumps formed within the last 400 million years.

Ages come from matching ultraviolet colors against Starburst99 population models, after correcting each region for dust dimming. The age patterns echo known stories. Disc galaxies show inside-out formation, with younger clumps farther out. Flocculent arms match local gravitational instabilities triggering patchy birth. Dwarf galaxies form stars stochastically, in irregular bursts. Because far-ultraviolet coverage spans whole galaxies, the catalog complements optical cluster lists. The clump catalog and dust maps for all 17 galaxies are released publicly with the paper.
arxiv-2606-12454:
Boumali stress-tests two frameworks on toy oscillators, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Klein-Gordon and Dirac oscillators are relativistic cousins of the harmonic oscillator. When temperature-like quantities fluctuate, the Boltzmann weight must be replaced by a wider one. Beck's superstatistics averages over the fluctuations; hyperstatistics does so at the level of domains. It yields a closed-form generalized Boltzmann factor, a q-exponential formula.

Computing partition functions, entropy, and specific heat for both, Boumali finds the new framework behaves well everywhere: positive, smooth, recovering the limit. It separates the two oscillators through the Dirac spectrum's spin doubling, which raises entropy and shifts specific heat. Beck's expansion matches only when the deformation is tiny; outside that corner its brackets can turn negative or grow absurdly. Beck's exact version wins when the underlying fluctuation law is known. For sums, the new framework is the robust workhorse.
arxiv-2606-12554:
Monreal makes a stratification of singularities canonical, and frees it from the machinery that birthed it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Slicing a space into smooth pieces records how singular each point is. Such slicings guide resolution algorithms, but most constructions depend on choices, like the coordinates used to embed the space. Riso-stratifications, built by Bradley-Williams and Halupczok using model theory, promised an alternative.

Monreal proves their riso-stratifications of affine algebraic sets are embedding independent: the answer does not depend on how the set sits in ambient space. They can also be computed étale locally. Building on this, he upgrades the process for schemes of finite type over fields of characteristic zero. The upgrade lets geometers compare riso-stratifications with classical approaches, Whitney conditions and Hironaka's resolution among them.
arxiv-2606-12654:
Ramsay presents the balloon mean, a new estimator for computing averages under differential privacy that stays accurate when data contain outliers, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Differential privacy means the output must barely change if any single person's data changes, which is usually enforced by clipping extreme values and adding noise. Existing private mean estimators that resist contamination tend to be heavy to compute.

The balloon mean instead clips data in steps to growing Mahalanobis balls, ellipsoidal regions shaped by the data's covariance. It privately inflates each ball until it holds most observations before recomputing a noisy average. The method satisfies zero-concentrated differential privacy and uses only simple linear algebra. Ramsay proves finite-sample error bounds under heavy-tailed and adversarially contaminated models, including the minimax-optimal convergence rate for heavy-tailed data. Simulations show it outperforms existing tractable private estimators in contaminated settings.
arxiv-2606-12854:
Kumar shows that small, fine-tuned language models can beat proprietary models at biomedical claim verification, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The task judges whether a claim is supported, refuted, or undetermined by evidence. GPT-4o and GPT-5 do well zero-shot, but API cost, opacity, and the impossibility of deployment in privacy-sensitive clinical settings limit their use.

Kumar fine-tunes 3 models, Phi-3-mini, Qwen2.5-3B, and Mistral-7B, with QLoRA, a 4-bit low-rank adaptation method, on the SciFact and HealthVer datasets, using 1,008 examples. Mistral-7B reaches a macro-F1 of 88.4 percent on SciFact and 65.2 percent on HealthVer. It beats GPT-4o, which scores 85.6 percent on SciFact and 53.2 percent on HealthVer, and GPT-5, at 77.9 percent and 42.4 percent, at 44.5 times lower cost. The study exposes an artifact in SciFact: all 243 not-enough-info training examples have empty evidence fields, making that label trivially detectable and inflating in-domain scores.
arxiv-2606-13154:
Biagioli and Perrone present an algorithm for computing the join of 2 elements in the weak order of the Coxeter group of type B, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Type B Coxeter groups have a combinatorial interpretation as signed permutations, bijections of the signed integers that respect the sign symmetry. Their weak order is a lattice-like partial order defined by the prefix property. Computing joins, the least upper bounds of pairs of elements, is hard beyond small cases.

The new algorithm extends Markowsky's algorithm for computing joins of ordinary permutations to the signed setting. The signed case brings reflection types, including sign-change transpositions, which the extension handles while keeping the structure of the original method. Beyond the computation itself, running the algorithm allowed the authors to confirm Dyer's conjecture on a geometric reading of these joins.
arxiv-2606-13254:
Majer, Šnajder, and Tutek ask whether language models express a fair range of viewpoints in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pluralism here means generated text should reflect the diversity of views people actually hold. Earlier studies used multiple-choice questionnaires or text statistics, which miss the views stated inside free writing. The authors build a layered framework that extracts latent perspectives, the underlying stances expressed in a text, without needing labelled examples. It works across domains rather than tuned to one topic.

They test it on book reviews, rich in varied opinions. Models and prompting styles are compared against the spread in human reviews. Some combinations came close to covering the middle of human opinion. Rarer perspectives, however, remained underrepresented in model output, so the spread of viewpoints in generated text diverged from the human spread. The authors offer the framework as a way to measure this pluralistic gap.
arxiv-2606-13454:
Vanden Abeele and colleagues implement a learning rule on an optical computer in this 2026 arXiv paper. Equilibrium Propagation trains energy-based networks by comparing two states of the system, offering an alternative to the backpropagation used in deep learning. Their hardware is a Spatial Photonic Ising Machine, which encodes neuron states and patterns as phase modulations of light using a spatial light modulator. Inference runs optically through a finite difference scheme, while a digital computer handles the loop, making the system a hybrid.

The system is evaluated on the Wine classification dataset, a standard benchmark. Numerical studies on the harder MNIST digit dataset explore the approach's potential, including continuous couplings and coupling matrices beyond the setup. Implementations like this one promise energy savings over electronic processors, since the optical interference does the computing. The work provides a pathway toward energy-efficient hardware for equilibrium-based learning.
arxiv-2606-13654:
Restaino, Gamboni, Selenius, and Levi review orbital-optimised density functional methods for excited states in this 2026 arXiv paper. Density functional theory is chemistry's workhorse for computing structure. Excited states are handled by its time-dependent extension, but that approach has limits for states of differing character. Orbital-optimised calculations take a different, time-independent route: each excited state gets its own optimised orbitals as a saddle point on the energy surface. Recent method developments for finding them have matured the approach into an active field.

The review clarifies the theory and surveys method developments for excited-state orbital tuning. It gives an overview of methods for open-shell singlet excited states, a tricky case where two electrons' spins couple to zero total spin. By optimising orbitals state by state, the methods describe states of different character. The authors aim the review at users choosing between approaches for photochemistry and spectroscopy.
arxiv-2606-13854:
Qayyum and colleagues present SpheriCity, a chatbot built to help experts search long sustainability reports without losing track of sources. City circularity reports, which track how materials are reused and waste is cut, run to hundreds of pages. Comparing cities across them is slow by hand. Ordinary chatbots answer faster but hide their reasoning and sometimes invent facts. Their 2026 arXiv paper describes a provenance-first design, where every answer stays tied to its evidence.

Six sustainability experts tested the prototype on tasks such as cross-city comparison and policy summaries. They rated answers for relevance, fit, accuracy, neutrality, and depth. Transparent sourcing, clear context, and fit with expert workflow shaped trust most strongly. Experts treated the system as an aid for finding evidence, not a decision maker. Such tools, the authors argue, should support expert judgment rather than replace it.
arxiv-2606-14054:
Parreira and colleagues track how students in one course credited AI help over three years, using code repositories as the record. The course is a graduate HCI prototyping class at Cornell Tech, run in fall 2022, 2023, and 2025. The authors distinguish disclosure, naming that an AI tool was used, from attribution, crediting a specific artifact to it. Their 2026 arXiv paper analyzes two hundred three GitHub repositories with twenty-three thousand sixty-five commits.

Disclosure grew sharply, from zero percent of repositories in 2022 to sixty-six percent by 2025. Explicit attribution remained a minority practice even among students who disclosed. Commit frequency and code volume rose in ways consistent with AI-agent involvement, without being attributable. By 2025 AI was infrastructure, embedded in course templates and student devices. Disclosure frameworks built for episodic tool use, the authors argue, cannot capture this continuous co-creation. Students name their tools but rarely say what they contributed.
arxiv-2606-14854:
Rob Verheyen speeds up event generation for collider physics in a 2026 arXiv paper. Event generation means simulating particle collisions event by event. Precision studies need huge numbers of events. But each event's odds require costly matrix-element calculations. Standard rejection sampling wastes most of that effort. Verheyen tries a sampling method built on Langevin dynamics, where random walks drift toward high-odds regions.

Many chains run in parallel. One final state is kept from each chain, giving unweighted events with no chain-internal correlation. A learned Stein discrepancy watches convergence. It estimates how long the chains need to relax. Tests on a quark-antiquark process making a Z boson plus jets showed modest relaxation needs. The count of exact steps grew only mildly with jet count. A neural surrogate start cut the costly evaluations further.
arxiv-2606-15054:
Naihin and Stambler change how sparse autoencoders score features, from inner product to cosine, in a 2026 study. Standard encoders fire in proportion to both direction match and input size. Features can thus win dictionary slots by tracking token magnitude alone. That is wasteful, since layer normalization discards that magnitude before the model reads it.
