Their encoder blends cosine similarity with a learnable amount of input norm, globally or per feature. Training never returns to the inner product: no feature chooses more than half norm dependence. At matched reconstruction quality, cosine features match human-recognizable concepts far more often. Unmatched standard features fire many times more on high-norm tokens, confirming they encode size, not content. Gradient reweighting barely closes the gap, pointing to forward-pass scoring geometry as the cause. The authors recommend cosine scoring as the default for dictionary learning on normalized activations.
arxiv-2606-15454:
Chhibber and coauthors make speech deepfake detection explain itself through phonetics in a 2026 paper. Detectors usually emit one opaque score per recording, pooling all sound frames equally. Yet sound classes differ in how much evidence they carry: crisp consonants are harder for generators to fake than smooth vowels. The authors build a phoneme-guided cross-attention model in which phonetic anchors, drawn from an estimated phonetic breakdown, query the acoustic features.

A probabilistic factorization shows the score is a weighted sum of per-sound-class spoofing evidence, so each verdict comes with an inspectable breakdown. Across three datasets, from a controlled corpus to in-the-wild deepfakes, importance rankings agree: stops, fricatives, affricates, nasals, and silence closures expose fakes best, while vowels and semivowels matter least. Training detectors per sound group confirms the ordering. Explainable detection suits forensic work, where an analyst must defend the verdict.
arxiv-2606-15754:
Mandel and Rodan ask when tighter causal bounds for ordinal outcomes can be trusted in 2026. Ordinal outcomes, like questionnaire scales or disease stages, have ordered categories without meaningful distances, so average treatment effects do not apply. Natural alternatives, such as the probability that treatment beats control, are not identifiable from data alone, and known sharp bounds are wide.

Bounds computed under a working independence assumption are much tighter, and earlier work hinted they might hold under positive dependence. The authors show that common positive dependence notions, positive quadrant dependence and positive regression dependence, are not sufficient to justify them. They propose a new condition, diagonal tail dominance, under which the independence-based bounds are guaranteed. That condition is strong, so they develop a local version yielding improved bounds that assume independence only on parts of the probability table. A stroke-treatment trial illustrates how the bounds behave in practice.
arxiv-2606-15854:
Adhikary and colleagues propose a sensing method in 2026 that reads a drug mixture's enantiomeric excess from a magnetic field it generates under laser light. The balance between mirror-image molecules matters because opposite enantiomers act very differently in the body. Established optical techniques need large samples, blocking chip-scale sensing.

The method fills a micro-capillary with the chiral solution, down to about ten nanolitres, and excites it with intense laser light. Through the inverse Faraday effect, the mixture develops a static magnetisation whose size and direction encode the excess. Measuring the field near the micro-tube then retrieves the excess directly. Quantum chemistry and density-matrix modelling support the effect in a realistic drug solution, solvated reparixin. The response survives orientational averaging, which makes a liquid sample usable at all. It suits lab-on-chip tests and drug quality control, where samples are precious.
arxiv-2606-15954:
Besanson presents Green SARC in 2026, a framework moving cost and carbon control for agentic AI from dashboards into the agent loop, where four enforcement sites act before money is spent. Its core object is the State Snowball: unconstrained, an agent's state grows quadratically with loop depth, so costs compound rather than merely add. The theory and its gate are tested against real workloads.

On three thousand real multi-step plans, the quadratic law always holds, and plans accrete state faster than the linear model predicts. A predictive gate, calibrated conformally, holds its coverage where a normal-based gate under-covers. A soft Lagrangian penalty, tuned to meet the budget on average, breaches it on over ninety percent of seeds. The architectural gate breaches it on none, across synthetic and real traces. Savings near fifty percent on tokens, dollars, and carbon follow, though their size is policy-dependent.
arxiv-2606-16454:
Oh and co-authors find a geometric flaw in 2026 in LoRA, the low-rank method for adapting large pretrained models, and repair it. In LoRA, weight updates factor into two low-rank matrices. When the full fine-tuning gradient flows back into those matrices, it is scaled anisotropically, unevenly, by their singular values. The update skews toward dominant singular directions and suppresses the rest, shrinking the effective rank of the gradient and pulling the low-rank approximation away from the true gradient.

Their fix, SDS-LoRA, structurally decouples the singular values from the backward pass, so the full gradient propagates only through the orthonormal factors. The parameterization preserves what full fine-tuning would have said. Convergence analysis shows the method's rate no longer depends on the condition number of the LoRA matrices. Experiments across benchmarks and pretrained models show consistent improvements over standard LoRA, per the report.
arxiv-2606-16554:
Muranova extends the theory of electrical networks to graphs whose wires carry complex weights in 2026, asking when such networks keep returning. The graphs have edge weights inside a sector of the complex plane, a sector condition that keeps the energies under control. She shows that the Dirichlet Laplacian is m-sectorial and therefore yields a contractive holomorphic semigroup, the discrete cousin of well-behaved heat flow.

Every sectorial complex-weighted graph can be extended to an electrical network whose weights are holomorphic functions arising from physical admittances, grounding the idea in circuit theory. That bridge yields convergence results for endless graphs, for both Dirichlet problem solutions and complex-valued capacities. Recurrence for complex-weighted graphs is defined and described in several equivalent ways: through function spaces, capacity, Green's functions, resolvents, and the Neumann operator. Recurrence decides whether a random walker returns forever or escapes.
arxiv-2606-17054:
Wu and colleagues learn robot grasping purely from human hands in a 2026 robotics paper. People pick up thousands of objects daily with effortless generality, while multi-fingered robot hands remain narrow. The authors argue the best grasping data source is humans themselves.

With smart glasses, they collect an egocentric dataset of a million grasp frames over thousands of objects in dozens of buildings. Their model, HUG, is a flow-matching network that reads one depth-camera image and generates diverse human grasps for the chosen object. Each grasp is parameterized by wrist position, wrist rotation and a standard hand-pose model. Predicted grasps retarget to various robot hands, enabling zero-shot grasping with no robot data at all. A new benchmark of unseen objects standardizes evaluation. On the real-world test set, HUG beats prior systems by wide margins across cameras, robot bodies and homes.
arxiv-2606-17154:
Powell presents a 2026 arXiv paper on the classical dimer model, a toy system in which paired sites, called dimers, tile a lattice with each site covered exactly once. On bipartite lattices the model hosts a Coulomb phase with slow, algebraic correlations. Its long-range behaviour is known to match a continuum height model, but a constructive derivation of that match was missing.

Powell starts from an exact Grassmann-integral form of the model on square and honeycomb lattices. Taking the continuum limit yields a massless Dirac fermion in two dimensions, described in plain terms as a free relativistic particle theory. Bosonization then maps that theory exactly onto the known height field theory, tilt and flux included. Adding source terms for flux density and local order gives formulas for dimer observables in height terms.
arxiv-2606-17254:
Girish and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on detecting Alzheimer's disease from speech in languages a system has never been trained on. Speech carries both sound cues and language cues of cognitive decline, so the team argues a good detector should fuse both. Their framework, called ORBIT, aims to learn representations that stay the same across languages while suppressing language-specific confounds through adversarial training.

ORBIT combines cross-attentive fusion of speech and text models with multi-tap language adversaries. It also mixes spherical and hyperbolic geometry learning, two ways of shaping the representation space, plus consensus clustering. In zero-shot cross-lingual tests, the multimodal fusion beat single-modality baselines across the settings tried. ORBIT itself achieved the strongest results against both unimodal models and simple concatenation-based fusion, supporting the claim that language-invariant features aid transfer.
arxiv-2606-17354:
Bremerman and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on untranslatability, the cases where no translation can carry all of a sentence's meaning across languages. Language scholars have studied such cases for decades, but natural language processing has largely ignored them as a class. As translation systems ace standard benchmarks, their remaining failures cluster exactly here, in idioms, wordplay, and cultural references with no direct equivalent in the target language.

The authors build a structured map of such cases, paired with a list of workaround strategies for conveying meaning anyway. That framework becomes a data set in many languages, holding hard sentences with strategy-based translations for controlled study. Early human preference studies suggest quality depends on the strategy chosen for a given case. Translations that add brief explanatory context, the annotation strategy, were consistently preferred by the human judges.
arxiv-2606-17454:
Gupta and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper arguing that agent performance is a systems problem, not just a modelling one, because a model's skill only shows through its harness. The harness runs every tool call and feeds results back, so any mismatch between what the model intends and what the harness executes wastes capability. The authors name that mismatch the intent-execution gap and argue closing it matters as much as tools or execution loops in harness design.

Their simple, customisable harness hunts for patterns shared across model families, plus a few model-specific preferences worth honouring. It matched or beat provider-reported scores on popular agentic coding benchmarks in their runs. An analysis of well over a hundred thousand agent trajectories then looked past headline scores. Models differed in edit frequency, testing habits, and phase shifts, revealing distinct problem-solving styles beneath similar totals.
arxiv-2606-17554:
Dutta and Saha present a 2026 arXiv paper on Brownian gyration, the steady swirling of a tiny trapped particle driven out of equilibrium by two heat baths at different temperatures. Past work used round particles in the overdamped limit, where inertia is ignored entirely. This study takes an inertial ellipsoid, a stretched tiny particle, held in an asymmetric trap and coupled to two heat baths. It asks how shape and orientation change the gyration the particle settles into.

Using inertial Langevin dynamics, the authors track the mean and spread of the particle's specific angular momentum. Gyration depends not only on trap asymmetry and the temperature gap, but also on shape, axial orientation, and inertia. Clear differences emerge between round and stretched particles in both the overdamped and underdamped regimes. The findings widen the knobs available for tuning such microscopic heat-driven machines.
arxiv-2606-17854:
Ajwani and colleagues settle a geometry question that stood open for six decades, in a 2026 paper. In 1965 Wegner conjectured that for any family of axis-parallel rectangles, the points needed to pierce every rectangle number at most twice the largest set of disjoint rectangles, minus one. The claim was proven for special families and the bounds kept improving, but the general case resisted.

The authors give an explicit counterexample. They build a rectangle family whose intersection graph has no triangles and a small independence number, so each piercing point can hit at most two rectangles while many points are forced. The ratio of piercing points to disjoint rectangles passes the conjectured limit, and a refined version pushes it higher still. Exact computer checks, included with the paper, verify the construction's counts.
arxiv-2606-18054:
Xu and colleagues ask language models to grade the speech of people describing a picture, as a route to dementia screening, in a 2026 study. The Cookie Theft picture task is a classic probe of cognitive and language ability, but turning its clinical ideas into numbers has been slow and expert-bound. The team defined seven task-specific constructs and prompted several large models to score each one, with examples to back each score.

Claude 3.5 Sonnet performed best, and its severity scores separated cognitively impaired speakers from healthy controls clearly, reaching high accuracy on the ADReSS benchmark dataset. Speech experts reviewing the scores and rationales agreed with them at a strong rate on a five-point scale. The authors present the approach as an interpretable, accessible screening aid, while noting that local models were barely tested and validation remains early.
arxiv-2606-18154:
Zhou and colleagues let a language model agent design patient-specific models of the heart's electrical system, in a 2026 paper. A cardiac electrophysiology digital twin must match each patient's physiology, and the hard part is choosing the model's structure, not just fitting its numbers. Experts traditionally hand-build hybrid physics and neural architectures, work that is slow and does not transfer between patients. Pure language model attempts lack the structural priors that keep heart simulations stable.

Their framework, LEADS, hands the agent a catalog of domain-grounded diffusion and reaction components as its action space. The agent reasons, selects, combines, and refines candidate hybrids in a loop, while gradient descent fits parameters. On synthetic data with known ground truth and on real clinical electrogram recordings, the discovered models beat human-designed hybrids on activation time accuracy.
arxiv-2606-18354:
Zhang and colleagues teach a diffusion model to fabricate brain scans showing Alzheimer's disease, in a paper presented at the 2025 IEEE MIPR conference. Synthetic structural MRI could augment scarce data, protect patient privacy, and harden diagnostic models, but Alzheimer's changes are subtle, region-specific, and progressive, exactly what generative models tend to blur away. The team extends Med-DDPM, a conditional diffusion model first built for brain tumor synthesis, to this harder target.

Generation is conditioned on anatomical segmentation masks drawn from the ADNI dataset, so the model paints tissue into a specified anatomy that already encodes the relevant structures. The synthetic scans captured disease-specific changes well enough to prove useful downstream. Segmentation models trained on synthetic data matched those trained on real scans, and a hybrid of synthetic plus real data did better still. The work points toward shareable, privacy-safe stand-ins for sensitive neuroimaging cohorts.
arxiv-2606-18454:
Deshmukh, Savin, and Arya present Veriphi, a graphics-processor-accelerated system for verifying that neural networks behave safely within set input bounds, in a 2026 paper from TU Wien. The system pairs fast adversarial attacks, which quickly falsify fragile inputs, with formal bound certification, and asks which training style practitioners should actually choose.

Their experiments on two image benchmarks with three training methods deliver a dataset-dependent verdict. Interval bound propagation, a certified training method, reached high certified accuracy on the simpler handwritten-digit data. It collapsed to almost nothing on the harder color-image data, where adversarial training dominated and certified most inputs at small perturbations. Attack-guided falsification sped verification about fivefold, and the approach scaled to a production model with over one hundred million parameters used in aerospace logistics. The authors warn against assuming certified training always wins.
arxiv-2606-18654:
Newman studies infinite exchangeable random sequences whose individual terms are Gaussian, in a 2026 probability paper. He asks how little joint Gaussian pattern forces the whole sequence to be a Gaussian process. Exchangeability, invariance under finite permutations, is the standard loosening of independent sampling. De Finetti's theorem shows such sequences as mixtures. Counterexamples show Gaussian marginals alone do not force a Gaussian process.

Newman says joint Gaussianity of a single pair of coordinates would already suffice. That remains open, but the paper proves the same statement with four coordinates. If the first four terms are jointly Gaussian, the entire sequence is a Gaussian process. Under an extra assumption, the two-coordinate criterion is also shown. That is, the directing random measure is almost surely infinitely divisible. The result sharpens the boundary between rigid and non-rigid exchangeable families.
arxiv-2606-18954:
Zhan and colleagues propose GraphPO in 2026, a reinforcement learning method for improving how large reasoning models solve problems step by step. Standard training with verifiable rewards samples answers independently, so many rollouts repeat similar middle steps and waste computation. Tree-based methods share prefixes and compare branches, yet separate branches that reach similar states still cannot share what they learn with each other.

GraphPO instead arranges rollouts as a directed graph, with reasoning steps as edges and summarized semantic states as nodes. Semantically equivalent paths merge into shared classes, freeing budget for more diverse exploration instead of repetition. Separate advantage signals reward efficient incoming steps and correct outgoing steps, giving process guidance from final outcomes alone. Theory shows lower variance in advantage estimates, and experiments on three language models across reasoning and agentic search benchmarks show consistent gains in both accuracy and inference efficiency.
arxiv-2606-19154:
Kubelka and colleagues introduce the Viking Hill Dataset in 2026, a multi-sensor forest dataset for robot perception. Robots under forest canopy must detect trees and vegetation robustly across seasons. Past forestry datasets offer lidar or camera data with per-tree labels, but none include co-registered four-dimensional imaging radar. Radar is attractive because it resists visual degradation, surface dirt, and occlusion by leaves that defeat cameras and lidar in dense woods.

Data were collected by a mobile robot with imaging radar, lidar, a color camera, inertial sensing, and precise satellite positioning. The site was recorded twice under contrasting vegetation states. Three-dimensional box labels, with per-tree diameter estimates, are shared across all three perception modes. Baseline segmentation with a standard network shows radar scores rival lidar on ground and canopy classes. Radar lags on fine structures like trunks.
arxiv-2606-19254:
Luis Elcoro, Jesus Etxebarria, J Manuel Perez-Mato, and Emre Tasci classify spin splitting in magnetic crystals in 2026. Non-relativistic spin splitting means electron bands split by spin without relativity driving the effect. The classification rests on spin point groups, symmetry groups that treat spin and space rotations separately.

The four authors list every distinct spin point group of the studied form, 1,249 in total. The catalogue, with symmetry operations for each group, sits in the SPGENPOS database on the Bilbao Crystallographic Server. Unlike older lists, it counts groups whose magnetic point group includes time reversal. A companion program, STENSOR, then checks which splitting each group allows. Lowest splitting orders run from zero to nine, except eight, with new types at orders five, seven, and nine. One real material, LaMnAu5, shows the order-five case. The map guides the hunt for spintronic materials with tailored spin textures.
arxiv-2606-19554:
Chong Qi proposes a new bracket for the 48-team football World Cup in 2026. FIFA's expansion to 48 teams fills a 32-team knockout round from twelve groups of four. Current rules pick the eight best third-placed teams by one global ranking across all groups.

That global coupling spawns 495 possible bracket layouts and biased picks among third-placed teams. Group winners lack a clear path, collusion risks grow, and same-group rivals can meet again too soon. Qi's four-section bracket splits the twelve groups into four sections of three. Winners, runners-up, and the two best third-placed teams in each section advance. Winners stay home as anchors, while lower qualifiers move sections under a fixed symmetric rule. Same-group separation then holds until the semifinal round. One fixed topology per section restores the tidy symmetry of the old 32-team format.
arxiv-2606-19654:
Shangzhi Xu and seven colleagues build PufferDoS in 2026, a generator of attack strings for regex denial-of-service flaws. ReDoS attacks exploit regex engines whose worst-case runtime explodes on crafted input. Defenders generate attack strings early to expose and fix such flaws.

Older generators assume unrealistic input lengths and skip program-level checks. Many of their strings then fail against real programs. PufferDoS defines three vulnerable patterns from observation and formal verification. Synthesis builds strings to those patterns within realistic length budgets. ReDoS-specific concolic execution then refines and validates each string in place. On 17,962 real vulnerable regexes, efficiency gains over the leading tool RENGAR run from 97 to over 3,800 times. PufferDoS also found 59 exploitable cases across twelve popular projects, 25 more than RENGAR.
arxiv-2606-20054:
Tanumoy Mandal, Stefano Moretti, and Rachit Sharma hunt non-standard decays of vector-like top partners at the high-luminosity LHC in 2026. Models with extra Higgs bosons and vector-like quarks predict top partners that decay through a charged Higgs into a tau and a neutrino, a signature current searches barely touch. The final state holds two taus, two b-jets, and missing energy.

Global kinematic variables built from visible objects and missing momentum suppress the main backgrounds. Polarization-sensitive observables from hadronic tau decays add a check on the spin-zero origin of the taus. Discovery-level sensitivity reaches top partner masses near the top of the studied range at the full planned luminosity. Extended Higgs sectors gain a largely orthogonal search channel.
arxiv-2606-20154:
Pradip Kumar, Sai Rasmi Ranjan Mohanty, Savita Rani, and Rahul Kumar Singh relate the Atiyah class of a Higgs bundle to simpler data on its spectral curve. Their 2026 paper works in algebraic geometry, where the Atiyah class measures the obstruction to giving a holomorphic bundle a holomorphic connection. For a regular semisimple Higgs bundle with a smooth spectral curve, they prove the bundle's Atiyah class comes from that of the spectral line bundle. It also takes values in the centralizer of the Higgs field.

The second result handles rougher geometry. When the discriminant is reduced, the authors build a logarithmic refinement across the branch divisor, so the class extends with logarithmic poles into a regularized centralizer sheaf. Reducing a higher-rank problem to a line bundle on a curve is a powerful simplification. The results give geometers new control over deformation and obstruction questions for Higgs bundles.
arxiv-2606-20254:
Kaihsun Yang, Min-Yan Tsai, and Chia-Mu Yu defend neural networks against backdoors that wake up only after quantization. Their 2026 paper studies quantization-conditioned backdoors, where a model behaves normally at full precision but turns hostile once compressed for deployment. Existing defenses modify the compression procedure or correct activation stats, adding overhead or tying themselves to specific settings.

Their method, QVec, takes a weight-space view. The weight difference between the full-precision model and its compressed counterpart encodes a structured shift, readable as a malicious task vector rather than random noise. QVec counteracts that direction with a controlled correction of the weights before release. It needs no retraining, no trigger samples, and only one compression pass, plus a light tuning search. Across image benchmarks and several LLM attack setups, QVec suppresses the backdoor while keeping clean performance.
arxiv-2606-20354:
Geena Benga and eight colleagues measure the intrinsic mechanical quality factor of silicon nitride resonators, the loss no design trick can dilute away. Their 2026 paper notes that dissipation dilution and mode-shape engineering have pushed measured quality factors to ultra-high values, but neither changes the material's intrinsic loss. Targeting that loss could raise quality factors further, yet quantifying it reliably has been hard. The team combines automated mode identification with ringdown measurements over many modes.

Applied to high-stress silicon nitride membranes, the method reveals a thickness dependence that established models cannot describe, especially in the ultra-thin limit. A phenomenological model with a thickness-dependent loss channel accounts for the trend. Quality factor governs how long a resonator rings, which sets sensitivity for force sensing and quantum optomechanics. A trustworthy map of intrinsic loss points toward mitigating the channels that drain energy.
arxiv-2606-20854:
Peijin Zhang and five colleagues combine radio imaging with magnetohydrodynamic modeling in 2026 to explain a solar type II radio burst. Type II bursts signal shock waves moving through the Sun's corona. They matter for understanding how shocks accelerate particles. Their multi-lane and split-band features remain poorly explained. Spatially resolved data and knowledge of shock shape have been lacking.

One burst event is imaged with radio spectroscopy. A three-dimensional global simulation models the coronal mass ejection shock that drove it. In the event, burst intensity shifts from fundamental to harmonic emission over time. The favored source region moves from the Earth-facing side of the shock to another part. Linking emission lanes to shock surface geometry and magnetic context helps decode burst spectra. Better decoding could improve space weather warnings, because type II bursts trace shocks that may later disturb Earth.
arxiv-2606-20954:
Nusrat Lia and Aritra Mazumder present LRE in 2026, a tiny learned system that decides what long-running language model agents should keep in memory. Long systems gather history that outgrows the context window. Something must be evicted. Dropping a load-bearing detail, such as a login token or a needed file path, breaks the next action. LRE is a small scorer that runs on CPU alone, with no language model.

LRE learns which history units are load-bearing and keeps them by verbatim extraction. Under matched budgets, no baseline dominates it on the accuracy and cost balance. On agent tasks, it matches the accuracy of keeping everything. Peak context size falls by up to about half. A trace study shows tasks completed where other policies loop. Learning what not to forget, in a few kilobytes, could make long agents cheaper without making them careless.
arxiv-2606-21454:
Rohan Juneja, Vishruti Ranjan, Rakshith Harish, and Li-Shiuan Peh introduce COMPOSE in 2026, a reconfigurable chip architecture for loops whose iterations depend on each other. Coarse-grained reconfigurable arrays map operations onto a grid of processing elements, but fixed elements force dependent iterations to run one after another, wasting time and shuttling intermediate values through registers. COMPOSE instead forms its processing elements dynamically at compile time, guided by static timing information.

Fusing operations across iterations spatially resolves the dependencies that cap throughput, and slack between operations gets used rather than wasted. Deferring registration of values that are consumed nearby cuts memory traffic further. Across varied workloads, COMPOSE averages 1.6 times the performance of leading designs and cuts the energy-delay product by 2.9 times, at minimal extra area and power.
arxiv-2606-21554:
Kun Zhang, Zhanwen Wang, and Lailai Zhu revisit a long-standing fluid mechanics puzzle in 2026: why cross-slot flow of a viscoelastic fluid goes unstable. In a cross-slot, two streams collide head-on and exit sideways, stretching dissolved polymers hard at the center. The instability appeared in experiments nearly fifty years ago and in simulations twenty years ago, yet its origin stayed disputed. The team combines direct simulation, global stability analysis, structural sensitivity, and energy budgets for creeping Oldroyd-B flow.

Simulations reproduce the classic pitchfork bifurcation, and the stability analysis predicts its threshold and growth rates. The unstable mode is a chiral swirl of velocity and stress that tilts the birefringent strand at the center. Narrow ridges of high extension rate act as the wavemaker, releasing stored elastic energy into the disturbance, while neither sharp corners nor the central stagnation point is essential.
arxiv-2606-21654:
Vincent Siu, Manasi Sharma, Dawn Song, Daniel Yue Zhang, and Chenguang Wang argue in 2026 that desktop agents are graded on the wrong unit of work. Benchmarks test one atomic task at a time, but real desktop work means carrying state across several objectives. ChainWorld composes atomic OSWorld tasks into long-horizon workloads through directional compatibility search, keeping the original evaluators intact.

The workload holds 347 chains of two to four tasks, each run two ways: all tasks in one prompt, or revealed one at a time across turns. Across four current computer-use agents, the best chain completion is only 31 percent. Multi-turn helps three of the four models, yet the failure profiles differ: single-turn runs stumble on artifact precision, multi-turn runs on session management, fragmented progress, and disengagement in later turns.
arxiv-2606-21854:
Someki and colleagues announce ESPnet3 in 2026, a rebuilt framework for speech and audio research in the era of foundation models. Modern speech experiments juggle huge datasets, complex models, and tangled workflows, and older toolkits demand heavy engineering for each new study. ESPnet3 reorganizes that work around a modular design with configuration-driven data handling and unified Python workflows.

A new DataOrganizer component makes datasets easier to combine, while sharding keeps memory use manageable during large-scale training, and small stage overrides allow recipe-specific logic. In pretraining experiments with the OWSM model family, ESPnet3 cut 21.1 minutes from each training epoch compared with its predecessor, while holding GPU use above eighty percent across multiple machines. Fine-tuning trials showed new models and datasets could be added with around forty-six lines of extra code. The toolkit is released openly with checkpoints and training logs.
arxiv-2606-21954:
Bajpai and colleagues question, in 2026, whether rising multilingual benchmark scores really mean models are getting better at cross-lingual transfer. That is the skill of carrying ability from a rich language into a poor one. Standard measures mix two things together: better transfer, and simply better performance in the source language itself. The authors propose separating them with a new metric, the Hardness Adjusted Transfer Score, which accounts for how hard each target item is.

Applying the metric to twenty diverse language models on three mainstream multilingual benchmarks produced three conclusions. Transfer in small models is not broken, contrary to a common worry. Progress in transfer strength as models grow is slower than headline scores suggest. And progress over time is still visible once the adjustment is made. The paper argues that honest measurement matters, because inflated claims hide the gap faced by speakers of under-represented languages.
arxiv-2606-22054:
Baweja examines, in 2026, the optimism gap in detectors for radio-frequency impairments such as jamming and spoofing of navigation signals. Such detectors are usually graded on the data they were tuned on, and their scores drop when conditions shift. Using an open synthetic testbed with a tunable severity shift, Baweja evaluated thirteen detectors across four impairment classes.

The gap between tuned-on and shifted performance grew steadily as the shift deepened. What drove the gap was how many signals a detector used, not whether it was learned: single-feature tools degraded alike, while those combining all five signals degraded far less. Most strikingly, a simple ridge model built only from score data gathered before any shift predicted the gap for unseen tools and unseen classes with real accuracy. A pre-registered run on field data from the Jammertest 2024 campaign confirmed the cross-detector prediction holds outside simulation.
arxiv-2606-22254:
Weng and Lee study, in 2026, how peer networks diffuse clinical guidelines into opioid prescribing. Large regional differences in prescribing resist explanation by patient or doctor traits alone. Their framework has prescribing evolve through persistence, peer exposure, and responses to a shared policy signal that vary with how central a doctor is.

Using nationwide Medicare Part D data from 2013 to 2020, over two million doctor-year observations, they test three claims. Doctors whose peers prescribe more later prescribe more themselves. More central doctors cut back more after the 2016 CDC guideline, with no differing pre-trends. By 2020, doctors at the ninetieth percentile of centrality showed cuts 0.30 points larger than those at the tenth percentile. Engaging highly connected doctors could extend stewardship programs' reach.
arxiv-2606-22454:
Anneliese Brei, Abhisheik Sharma, Nicholas Sanaie, Lu Wang, and Snigdha Chaturvedi compare characters in machine-written and human-written fiction in this 2026 paper. As language models produce more stories, the authors ask whether their characters resemble human ones and whether the cast is varied. They borrow tools from narratology, the study of how stories are built.

The team define eight intricate pairs of character categories, such as stylization and wholeness, which judge how a character is portrayed rather than surface traits. They infer these categories automatically in both model-generated and recently published human stories. The comparison then asks two questions: do the two kinds of stories have similar characters, and do models generate stories with a variety of characters? The paper reports a set of similarities and differences between the two collections, with takeaways for how model fiction is evaluated. All code and annotated data are released publicly.
arxiv-2606-22554:
Mohamad Maassarani connects two algebraic structures in this 2026 mathematics paper. The first is isoclinism, an equivalence between groups that is weaker than isomorphism but preserves much of their commutator structure. The second is the conjugacy quandle, an algebraic gadget built from a group's conjugacy classes and their conjugation action.

Maassarani shows that two finite isoclinic groups of the same order always have isomorphic conjugacy quandles. The converse also holds under some extra assumptions on the groups. Combining the directions, isoclinism turns out to be exactly equivalent to having isomorphic quandles for all groups of order below one hundred twenty-eight. That threshold is sharp. The paper constructs two groups of order one hundred twenty-eight that are not isoclinic, yet whose conjugacy quandles are isomorphic. So the quandle detects isoclinism faithfully for small groups and provably fails at the boundary case.
arxiv-2606-22754:
Kaifang Liu, Matthias Schlottbom, J.J.W. van der Vegt, and Yan Xu analyze boundary conditions for Maxwell's equations in this 2026 paper. Simulations of electromagnetic waves need boundaries that let waves leave without reflecting. The Hagstrom-Warburton conditions achieve tiny reflection coefficients without high-order derivatives or nonlocal operators, suiting them to high-order numerical methods, but their stability needed proof.

The authors' main result is an a priori bound: the solution's size is controlled by the initial data, boundary data, and volume sources in a half-space. They first build a mapping from outgoing to ingoing solution components, which shows the classic Kreiss condition does not hold uniformly here. They then construct several symmetrizers, special multipliers that restore energy control, to prove stability anyway. The boundary conditions are thereby shown well-posed in a generalized sense, putting their practical use on firmer theoretical ground.
arxiv-2606-22854:
Wentao Liu and Anqiang Zhu prove comparison results for a boundary value problem in this 2026 paper. Their equation is the p-Laplace equation, a nonlinear diffusion model, posed on a Riemannian manifold with non-negative Ricci curvature. The boundary condition is Neumann type, fixing the flux across the boundary rather than the value on it.

Using spherical symmetrization under suitable constraints, the authors derive Talenti-type comparison results in Lorentz spaces. Such results bound a solution by the solution of a simpler, symmetrized problem, transferring estimates from the simple case to the hard one. They show the Neumann setting needs weaker constraints than the Robin case, a mixed boundary condition studied earlier. Weaker constraints in turn yield stronger comparison principles. The paper thus sharpens what symmetrization can deliver for this class of problems on curved spaces.
arxiv-2606-22954:
Jiayao Ma, Boran Zhang, and Jiefeng Liu extend two linked algebraic structures in a 2026 mathematics paper. Rota-Baxter groups and skew braces both supply set-based solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation, a key equation from mathematical physics. The authors move both structures into the world of affine schemes, a geometric language built from rings and their spectra. Working there lets algebra and geometry describe the same objects from two sides.

Ma and colleagues first define affine Rota-Baxter groups. Using the mirror between affine groups and Hopf algebras, they prove the two notions match exactly. They then show these groups naturally produce the affine skew braces defined by other authors. Every affine skew brace also embeds back into such a group. The circle of links yields fresh ties to Hopf co-braces and new Yang-Baxter solutions.
arxiv-2606-23254:
Kai Zeng and colleagues edit text inside videos while keeping its look intact in a 2026 paper. Visual text editing swaps words in images or footage while preserving style and realism. Video adds hard constraints: the edit needs stroke-level precision in small regions, consistency across frames, and faithful style. Their framework, SteerVTE, steers a frozen video diffusion model rather than retraining it. A lightweight adapter attaches two kinds of control: a style encoder reading the original text's appearance, and glyph encoders spelling the target text at line and character levels.

Zeng and colleagues add a glyph-aware loss that focuses training on the text region, plus a three-stage curriculum growing from images to video. An automatic synthesis pipeline builds a training set of one million triplets across scenes, fonts, and effects. In experiments, SteerVTE beat existing video editing baselines on text accuracy, style consistency, and temporal coherence.
arxiv-2606-23354:
Tom Hodemon and colleagues ground the visual reasoning of multimodal language models in a 2026 paper. Such models answer questions about images well, but their black-box reasoning blocks use in critical domains. Grounded methods attach coordinates to each reasoning step. Text coordinates lack a learnable link to image features, so models hallucinate positions matching nothing in the picture. Their model, Composer, swaps coordinates for learned proxy-tokens. These discrete pointers index the image's latent space directly. The model can then treat regions of the image as addressable sets inside its reasoning.

Hodemon and colleagues build a dedicated dataset to test reasoning consistency and grounding accuracy together. Composer matches its coordinate-based rival on final answer accuracy. Its grounding accuracy is nine points higher. The authors conclude that grounding with learnable links is a promising path to more trustworthy models.
arxiv-2606-23654:
Zhong and colleagues build a benchmark for AI agents from real workplace sessions, in a 2026 paper on agent evaluation. Enterprise agents now work inside office spaces, reading mixed files, calling tools, and delivering business documents. Judging them by chat answers alone misses most of that work. A session can fail by losing files, breaking workspace state, or producing an unusable artifact, even when the final message sounds right.

The pipeline turns a large archive of real sessions into eight hundred fifty two reproducible tasks. Each task carries recovered input files, rewritten prompts, role classes, and scoring rubrics. Because sessions contain private company content, the data itself is not released; the reusable contribution is the protocol. On a hand audited subset of one hundred twenty tasks, the best setup, Codex with a top model, scores only about two thirds. Results, they argue, must report cost, runtime, artifact quality, and skill transfer.
arxiv-2606-24354:
Pariat and a large group of contributing and co-signing French researchers make the case for the European Solar Telescope, within their national community. The planned four-metre-class telescope would study the Sun and its influence on Earth and the heliosphere. It pairs multi-conjugate adaptive optics, correcting atmospheric blur across a wide field, with a light-polarisation analyser. Imaging plus integral-field spectrographs work together.

Such gear promises new views of the solar photosphere and chromosphere. Those are the layers where magnetic activity driving space weather is born. The 2026 white paper surveys what the facility offers French heliophysics. It lists the science questions its community could answer, from small-scale magnetic structures to the dynamics coupling the Sun's surface to its atmosphere. The long co-signer list itself is part of the argument. It shows breadth of support across French solar physics, ahead of building decisions.
arxiv-2606-24854:
Blade Frisch and six colleagues examine how to design and judge AI powered communication aids. Augmentative and alternative communication systems help people who cannot rely on speech to express themselves. AI features promise to widen what users can do with these systems. Standard evaluation metrics, though, capture efficiency better than desire. People are intersectional, with layered identities and nuanced wants for their tools. A metric that misses those wants can steer design the wrong way.

Six problem spaces within AAC are explored one by one. For each, the authors consider how AI might help and how success should be measured instead. They propose more robust evaluation methods that build users' intersectional nuances into the score. Wider issues recur across the spaces, and the proposed methods are offered as a way to address them. The paper addresses a CHI 2026 workshop on speech AI measurement.
arxiv-2606-25654:
Some active galaxies flip their spectral identity within months, far faster than a standard accretion disk should be able to change. Marios Kouzis, Agata Różańska, Debora Lančová, Bożena Czerny, and Dominik Gronkiewicz model those changing look transitions in 2026 with a disk held up partly by magnetic pressure, topped by a warm corona. Their code solves the disk's vertical structure with gas, radiation, and magnetic support together, tracing the S shaped curves that govern thermal instability cycles.

Magnetised disks moved the instability threshold down to the low feeding rates where real transitions are seen, and added a stable bright branch. Cycle times landed in the observed months to years range for black holes between ten million and a billion suns. Five known changing look galaxies matched jointly in rate and duration only when the inner disk was strongly magnetised.
arxiv-2606-25754:
Polishing runs through stages, coarse to fine. A robot that cannot tell its current stage will apply the wrong pressure at the wrong time. Shuai Ke and colleagues propose a stage aware diffusion policy in 2026. It learns polishing from demonstrations. The system infers a probability distribution over stages from recent multimodal observations. That belief conditions the denoising process that generates actions. Long action sequences then stay consistent with the current stage. Nobody labels stages during execution. A second ingredient constrains the sampling itself. Feed speed and contact force are generated under roughness targets and feasibility limits. Spindle speeds are preset per stage.

Trials covered spacecraft cabin coating surfaces and inner cavity finishing. Real robot runs were included. The method showed steadier stage transitions than advanced baselines. Process parameters stayed more consistent. Final surface quality was better. Stage awareness, the results suggest, is what long horizon finishing tasks have been missing.
arxiv-2606-25854:
Raphaël Tinarrage studies Delaunay refinement. The process builds meshes in geometry software by splitting a region into simplices. A simplex is the simplest shape in each dimension. Unlike plain subdivision, a refined Delaunay mesh need not nest inside the previous one, so it is not obvious that the pieces keep shrinking. Tinarrage asks how fast simplex diameters fall under repeated refinement for several choices of inserted Steiner points.

Shrink bounds come out explicitly for several families. They include Delaunay versions of barycentric and edgewise subdivision. The proofs reduce the geometry to covering estimates for flat simplices. Those estimates come from a sharpened approximate Carathéodory theorem. The proof uses a pivotal sampling twist on Maurey's empirical method. Theory and numerical tests agree on the outcome. Delaunay refinements contract more strongly than plain subdivision does. That is welcome news for methods that approximate maps between meshes.
arxiv-2606-25954:
Lawrence Moss and Arthur Paul Pedersen write a theoretical note on majority reasoning in groups. A coherence test is known that decides exactly when qualitative majority judgments, statements about which blocs form a majority, can be represented by a finitely additive measure. Their question is whether some fixed finite list of forbidden patterns could replace that test in finite social decision frames.

No such shortcut exists, they prove. For every whole number k, they build a maximal standard frame in which the shortest coherence violation has length exactly twice k plus two, so violations can hide at any depth. The construction is geometric, built from orthogonality in rational vector spaces, and grows from a symmetric family of voting blocs at half size. Together with a known soundness and completeness result, the frames show measurable majority systems are not finitely axiomatizable.
arxiv-2606-26054:
C. Yao leads a large laser-plasma team reporting experiments on the Kunwu facility in China. Broadband laser pulses were meant to tame laser-plasma instabilities. One instability, two-plasmon decay, spawns hot electrons that preheat fusion fuel. Early theory said bandwidth should suppress such instabilities. Moderate-bandwidth pulses at Kunwu told a different story for this one.

Direct-drive experiments identify two-plasmon decay as the main hot electron source. Broadband pulses actually enhance the instability here. Particle-in-cell simulations explain why. Broadband fields carry random intensity spikes. Those spikes feed the decay instability in both weak and strong driving regimes. Hot electron output follows the spikes. The practical lesson cuts against the original hope. Suppressing hot electrons now means suppressing the spikes themselves. Bandwidth alone does not deliver the promised protection for inertial fusion targets.
arxiv-2606-26154:
Jannik Drotleff and colleagues train microrobots to swim through blood capillaries, in simulation. Tiny robots could one day deliver drugs to exact spots or dissolve clots. Real capillaries are hostile classrooms: twisting flow fields, branching walls, and crowds of red blood cells. Their simulator includes all three, with branching geometry drawn from anatomy. Deep reinforcement learning agents learn navigation there by chemotaxis, following chemical gradients.

Physical limits map out clearly. Across robot sizes and swimming speeds, a forbidden zone appears where Brownian jitter and flow beat propulsion. No policy can cross it. Successful agents discover shared strategies on their own. Run-and-rotate and search-and-sit styles emerge regardless of robot parameters. One search style is notably energy-thrifty. Without retraining, agents then block and unblock capillary flow on demand. Throughput returns to healthy baseline levels, a first step toward robotic intervention in the bloodstream.
arxiv-2606-26254:
Quan Do and colleagues survey the tools programmers use to write quantum software. Quantum hardware has passed a thousand qubits, and high-level languages are how algorithms get expressed and checked. Their classification framework organizes the design space first. Ten actively maintained open-source languages then face review under it. Industry entries include Qiskit, Cirq, PennyLane, and Q sharp. Academic entries include Qrisp and others.

Hands-on and conceptual comparisons fill the survey. Strengths, weaknesses, and design trade-offs emerge for each language. The exercise ends with a list of challenges for future language designers. Integration with classical software is one pressure point. Correctness reasoning is another. The survey gives newcomers a map of a crowded field and gives designers a shared vocabulary for arguing about what comes next.
arxiv-2606-26354:
Andreas Bluhm and four colleagues study non-local quantum computation. Two partners must jointly apply an operation to a split quantum system. They cannot communicate during the task. They rely on shared entanglement, a link between particles prepared beforehand. Such tasks underpin quantum position verification. That technique uses quantum rules to prove where someone is. The team asks which tasks can substitute for each other.

The authors focus on tasks with large classical inputs and small quantum inputs. Those are the most practical kind for position verification. Bluhm and colleagues prove many new reductions. A reduction builds one task from another. Redirecting a quantum system under classical control implies controlled measurements. It also implies controlled Clifford operations and a wider family of controlled operations. Many position-verification schemes therefore share the same entanglement cost growth. They also share a similar security level.
arxiv-2606-26454:
Tiansi Dong, Mateja Jamnik, and Pietro Liò ask whether simply scaling up data-driven machine learning could ever deliver rigorous logical reasoning. Their test case is the syllogism, the classic two-premise argument form behind much formal logic. A rival approach using sphere-based neural networks reaches symbolic-level reasoning by building models explicitly, without training data, which raises the question of whether ordinary training could get there with enough examples.

Dong and colleagues identify two obstacles for systems that treat syllogisms as image recognition, an approach recently reporting near-perfect accuracy. First, training data alone cannot separate all twenty-four valid argument forms, because validity comes from logical structure, not statistical patterns. Second, mapping premises straight to conclusions mixes conflicting goals inside the learner. Their conclusion is that no amount of extra data or computing removes these barriers for purely data-driven systems.
arxiv-2606-26654:
Qinkai Zhang and five colleagues introduce SocialPersona, a benchmark for personal AI assistants. Assistants are usually tested on recalling preferences users stated outright. Real personalisation is harder: inferring interests from the traces people naturally leave online. SocialPersona uses long social-media timelines from one hundred seventy-one ordinary users. Text, images, and timestamps come with thousands of human-checked interest tags across seven interest areas.

Two tasks are tested. One builds a structured user profile from the timeline. The other writes replies fitted to that profile. Leading large models that read text and images spotted broad interest areas well. Their accuracy dropped on fine-grained interests and on recent interests. Performance fell further when inferred profiles had to drive personalised replies. Text and image cues proved to complete each other, each catching likes the other missed.
arxiv-2606-26854:
Magnus F Ivarsen, Kaili Song, Jean-Pierre St-Maurice, and Glenn C Hussey read the aurora's electric field through radar echoes. Coherent radar echoes bounce off auroral plasma structures. Echoes appear only where electron drifts beat the ion-acoustic speed, a sharp threshold. The echo pattern is thus a sampled outline, an excursion set, of the electric field above the threshold.

The authors treat the echoes as a point process and measure its structure factor, a spectrum built from echo separations. Theory says that spectrum mirrors the field's own spectrum. Tests against direct satellite observations matched: in frames moving with the plasma, the radar spectrum followed the same scale-free slope as the in-situ one. The auroral electric field can therefore be imaged from the ground by its threshold crossings.
arxiv-2606-27254:
West, Cerezo, and Larocca sharpen how few samples a fermionic shadow scheme needs. Classical shadows estimate many properties of an unknown quantum state from few measured copies. For fermion systems that keep particle count fixed, key targets are overlaps with Slater determinant states. Average-case costs were known to be flat, but the worst-case bound grew with the number of modes. In 2026, their procedure cuts that growth, tying cost to particle count instead.

Sample needs now scale with the particle count times its logarithm, free of the mode count. Post-processing stays efficient on ordinary computers. A second result bounds samples for general particle-preserving quadratic observables by the size of their traceless part. The proof routes through harmonic analysis on a symmetric space and Jacobi ensemble tools. Fermionic learning gets cheaper exactly where modes pile up.
arxiv-2606-27454:
Cao and Petriello define a one-point charge correlator for deep-inelastic scattering, tailored to the Breit frame where the struck quark flips. These observables track how electric charge is distributed among the particles produced. It is shown safe from infrared and collinear blow-ups, so theory can compute it. Soft-collinear effective theory covers two limits. In the forward limit a new non-perturbative object, the nucleon charge correlator, encodes the nucleon's multi-part structure, in a particle physics paper appearing in 2026.

In the back-to-back limit, the observable matches transverse momentum-dependent distributions, the standard maps of nucleon interiors. Singular terms derived this way match full calculations through second order in the strong coupling. Large logarithms are resummed to high stated accuracy for both unpolarised and spin cases. A bridge is built to existing nucleon tomography.
arxiv-2606-27654:
Data on schools are hard to model with plain regression. The records are wide and sparse, and many measures come in groups that move together. Brianna Reed and Paramahansa Pramanik propose a specialised estimator in 2026 to handle this. Its name is the Adaptive Weighted Group Fused LASSO. It works inside a single penalised regression frame. It picks variables, shrinks whole groups, and fuses like coefficients toward each other at the same time.

An efficient ADMM algorithm computes the estimator. The authors prove its large-sample behaviour, including consistency and a debiased form of asymptotic normality. In simulation studies, it estimated and predicted better than existing penalised methods. A real test uses Alabama public school data, with mathematics proficiency as the outcome. There the method gave a more readable model with better predictive accuracy. It also picked out the school-level factors that matter most for proficiency.
arxiv-2606-27754:
Liviu Ornea, Misha Verbitsky, and Victor Vuletescu study locally conformally Kähler manifolds in 2026. Such manifolds, called LCK for short, are complex spaces that look Kähler up to local rescaling. The paper treats those with algebraic codimension one. For surfaces, this class is fully understood. Non-Kähler compact surfaces of this kind are all elliptic fibrations. Extending the picture to higher dimensions is the driving question.

The main theorem answers it for LCK manifolds of any dimension. A non-Kähler compact LCK manifold of algebraic codimension one is bimeromorphic to one carrying an isotrivial family of elliptic curves. That family maps onto a smooth projective base. An earlier result covered threefolds only under two unproven assumptions. One was the Strong Factorization Conjecture. The other was the existence of minimal smooth models for elliptic non-Kähler threefolds. The present proof avoids both conjectures.
arxiv-2606-28054:
Classifying mixed-state phases needs more than two-point correlations. Mutual information decay and conditional mutual information, through the Markov length, give sharper criteria. Paul Rosa-Ruiz and three colleagues derive such static properties from dynamics in 2026. The generators are Lindbladians, which govern open quantum systems. Rapid mixing and frustration-freeness are the key dynamical features. Long-range interactions are the focus.

Two results are proved. Rapid mixing plus frustration-freeness makes the fixed point's conditional mutual information decay with shielding distance. Rapid mixing with primitivity and regularity gives global decay of mutual information. For power-law long-range interactions, both decays are polynomial, not exponential as short-range systems expect. Gibbs states of long-range non-commuting Hamiltonians also satisfy a local Markov property at any temperature. That extends recent short-range results. Numerical work on the long-range Ising model finds regimes matching the proven bounds.
arxiv-2606-28154:
Georgia Acton, Eduardo Rodríguez, Gareth Roberg-Clark, and Alessandro Zocco study zonal flows in plasma turbulence. Zonal flows are large, belt-like streams that form inside a turbulent plasma and help regulate it. They are a topic of direct interest for fusion energy research using gyrokinetics, the standard theory of magnetized plasma motion.

Acton and colleagues build a weakly nonlinear theory that tracks just three interacting waves. Their scheme predicts the spectrum of the growing zonal flow during the early phase of full simulations. It recovers the known growth rate, where the flow grows twice as fast as the waves driving it, without assuming the plasma sits near a stability threshold. The flow's phase-space shape, they show, is tightly fixed by the fluctuations that force it.
arxiv-2606-28454:
Marouan Mizmizi and Sanzhar Yergaliev overturn a received recipe for near-field wireless links. When a large antenna array serves a single-antenna user, beamfocusing, aiming every element at the user's position, is the standard strategy. Their setting differs: the user also carries an extended aperture, and there is no multipath to exploit.

Deriving closed-form gains for focusing and for plain far-field steering, Mizmizi and Yergaliev show the contest turns on two dimensionless quantities alone: the link's Fresnel number and the aperture ratio. For equal apertures the strategies cross exactly once, at a universal Fresnel value, and beyond it focusing loses ground steadily. Their order-optimal strategy, con-focusing, aims both apertures at the point where they subtend equal angles. It needs no channel knowledge and can be acquired in one refinement round.
arxiv-2606-28554:
The NANOGrav Collaboration, with Nikita Agarwal as lead author among its many members, re-analyzes fifteen years of pulsar timing with better noise models. The collaboration listens for nanohertz gravitational waves, spacetime ripples so slow that only the galaxy's most precise clocks, millisecond pulsars, can register them. Stray noise in each pulsar's signal can mimic or mask the wave background.

Customized chromatic noise models, tuned per pulsar, sharpen the evidence for the Hellings-Downs correlation pattern, the signature of a genuine background. The Bayes factor for that pattern grew roughly eightfold, to well over a thousand. The inferred background amplitude came down slightly and its spectrum steepened. The search volume for individual continuous waves grew more than threefold, while evidence for an exotic scalar polarization mode of gravity faded. Interpretations from black hole binaries to cosmic strings shifted only marginally.
arxiv-2606-28754:
Delavari, Popryho, Partin-Vaisband and Vaisband present SHIFT, a system for moving computing work around inside chiplet-based machines. Chiplets are small separate chips linked together, and in very large systems the links between them slow work down. Instead of only moving data toward a fixed processor, SHIFT moves the computing job itself, with its context, to a better placed node.

Simulations on a wafer-scale design, meaning a system built across a whole silicon wafer, showed relocation succeeding in most trials across setups. Success rates ranged from about three quarters to nearly all attempts. Average delays fell by roughly a sixth to nearly two thirds. Throughput, meaning work completed per second, rose by up to twelve and a half times, and energy used per bit of data dropped by well over half. Tests on standard language model workloads also showed clear gains in speed and efficiency.
arxiv-2606-28954:
Mathieu constructs hyperbolic surfaces that are filled by their systoles while using remarkably few of them. A systole is the shortest closed geodesic on a surface, its tightest loop. A filling set of systoles covers the surface so thoroughly that no other curve avoids them all. His surfaces, indexed by genus, the number of handles, need a systole count matching a known lower bound.

Several earlier papers attacked the same question with more complex methods. The best previously known upper bounds were larger by a factor involving the square root of the logarithm of the genus. Mathieu's count is smaller, matching the lower bound proved by Anderson, Parlier and Pittet up to the stated equivalence. He notes, in his own assessment, that his approach is much simpler than earlier methods. The construction closes the gap between the best construction and the best impossibility result.
arxiv-2606-29054:
Kotte asks when a statistical method called conformal risk control can certify the outputs of language models used for structured tasks like extracting names or filling JSON forms. Such models lack formal reliability guarantees, and common abstention rules miss user-set risk targets widely. He characterises both where certification works and where it provably cannot.

First comes an impossibility result. If a model's base risk exceeds the target, any distribution-free method must abstain on a minimum share of examples, which he computes in closed form. That gives a feasibility test to run before attempting certification. He then ranks three certification bounds. The middle one delivers the largest gain in certified configurations, while a betting-based bound helps when calibration data is scarce. Under dataset shift, an adaptive method cut risk-target violations from 71 to 21 percent. Hard tasks stayed uncertifiable at strict risk levels but opened up at looser ones.
arxiv-2606-29354:
Pei, Huang and Wang let language-model agents invent their own compact languages for reasoning. Chain-of-thought prompting improves hard reasoning, but its long natural-language explanations are costly and poorly matched to how machines reason best. Their framework has several agents autonomously create, refine and share Language Symbolism Frameworks: compact symbolic protocols with their own symbols, usage rules and message-passing contracts.

An evolutionary loop improves these mini-languages, scoring them on correctness and token cost. At use time, a router picks a single cheap framework, combines several, or composes them over multiple rounds for harder queries, trading accuracy against tokens per question. On challenging benchmarks the method cut generated tokens three to six fold compared with standard chain-of-thought, while holding accuracy. The authors also derive a lower bound on token cost, from information theory, that holds under any such symbolism.
arxiv-2606-29554:
Sweeney shows that the order in which training examples are shuffled can be a major source of noise when fine-tuning a model. A memoryless view predicts that reordering the same set of examples should matter only slightly. Optimizers with memory, such as AdamW, break that intuition. Their moment buffers and counters advance with the step index, not with learning-rate-scaled time, so the same gradient receives a position-dependent weight.

Replaying deterministically from a single warmed optimizer state isolates the mechanism. Order-variance slopes differ sharply by optimizer, and matching the memory clock to scaled time restores regular behaviour. For AdamW with a frozen preconditioner, Sweeney derives a closed-form floor for the order variance with no fitted coefficients. The effect is local to each measurement window, since reshuffling averages it across windows. Outputs include order-noise error bars and a seed-budget rule for close comparisons.
arxiv-2606-29654:
Wang and four colleagues address a deployment question for multi-agent language model deliberation: when is the current answer reliable enough to act on, and when should a human review it? Deliberation among models can improve reasoning, but acting on every answer is risky. They formulate budgeted act-or-defer decision making, with a user-declared wrong-action budget.

Each round, the system maps the debate so far to a low-dimensional state. A k-nearest-neighbor lower confidence bound on correctness, computed from calibration data, gates the decision: the system acts only once the bound exceeds a user-set reliability threshold. The guarantee is conditional, relying on stated assumptions with diagnostics. On six benchmarks, the method uses only a small share of its declared budget, reaching high automation and acted-on accuracy. On stress tests it defers instead.
arxiv-2606-29754:
Zheng writes a discussion of a major review by Ji and colleagues that introduces large language models to statistics readers. Her piece argues the review deserves a place in statistics teaching. The review spans training, alignment, uncertainty, watermarking, fairness, and interpretability.

Her central observation is that a language model is a system we built whose behaviour we do not yet fully understand. In-context learning and chain-of-thought reasoning are explained only in part. Formally, these models are stochastic systems. Zheng concludes that such systems are exactly what statistics is equipped to study, and that probing model behaviour should anchor AI education.
arxiv-2606-30054:
Chonghuinan Wang and eleven colleagues build a model that writes text and images in any mix. Free-form interleaved generation means the output can alternate freely. Storytelling, style transfer, and image decomposition all need this skill. Earlier unified models handled such tasks only with difficulty. Their model, ILLUME-X, aims at high quality and stable training.

Three components carry the design of ILLUME-X. An expanded data pipeline prepares training material for interleaved output. A progressive training strategy uses self-adaptive objectives for sequences of any length. A new evaluation method, ILScore, grades interleaved text-image sequences objectively. Together these parts improve data efficiency and stabilize multimodal training. Tests show ILLUME-X beating previous unified models on several tasks. Style transfer, image decomposition, and storytelling all improve. The authors present the system as a step toward fuller multimodal intelligence.
arxiv-2606-30154:
Kadambini Menduli and Md. Nasim study how rescattering distorts a short-lived particle signal in heavy-ion collisions. The particle is the K-star-zero resonance, which decays inside the hot medium. Its daughter particles can bounce off other hadrons before escaping. Those bounces depend on the decay angle in a lopsided way. The authors use the AMPT transport model to quantify this.

Their simulations cover gold-gold collisions at two hundred GeV. Lorentz boost effects make some daughters slow in the laboratory frame. Slow daughters rescatter more, so reconstructed yields vary with decay angle. The loss also warps angular distributions used for spin alignment. Even with zero true polarization in the model, the signal deviates. The alignment parameter moves away from the unpolarized value in both frames. The two reference frames show opposite trends, a warning for experiments.
arxiv-2606-30354:
Michał Czakon and Lorenzo Tancredi remove a roadblock in computing multi-loop scattering amplitudes for particle physics. Feynman integrals reduce to a small set of master integrals. Canonical differential equations then fix those masters elegantly. The catch is exotic functions tied to shapes like Calabi-Yau manifolds. No closed forms for them blocked numerical use in practice.

The obstruction turns out to be only apparent, they show. They obey linear relations with rational coefficients throughout. Any function in the canonical transformation must therefore obey rational ones too. Solving those auxiliary ones enlarges the system, but keeps it simple. Numerical use of the canonical system then proceeds directly. A C++ package implements the whole strategy for users. Applications include two-loop cases for di-jet production. Photon-plus-jet output through a heavy-quark loop is also computed.
arxiv-2606-30854:
Jun Tan and Guannan Wei ask when staging annotations in a programming language can be trusted not to change a program's meaning. Multi-stage programming treats code as data: an early stage generates specialised code for a later one. Typed languages guarantee the generated code is well typed, yet rearranging fragments can subtly change evaluation order, so the staged program may drift from its unstaged reference version. The pair design two statically typed two-stage calculi, the second adding mutable references in the later stage.

Their semantics models automatic let-insertion as a control effect inside a lightweight type-and-effect system. Using binary logical relations, they prove strong preservation theorems: any generated code is contextually equivalent to the stage-erased original. The mechanised theory gives a definitive answer and a base for future language design.
arxiv-2606-30954:
Mujahid Abbas, Alemayehu Negashs and Meaza Bogale study maps whose strength is measured on triangles rather than pairs of points. A perimeter-contracting map shrinks the perimeter of every triangle formed by three points and their images. The authors work in b-metric spaces, where the triangle inequality is loosened by a factor s. They ask what the iterates of such a map do. In the first scenario, where no orbit has prime period two, the iterates behave as graphic contractions once a parameter condition holds.

That makes the map a weakly Picard operator. A theorem bounds its fixed-point set to between one and two points. In the second scenario, a period-two orbit does exist. The even iterates then collapse into continuous graphic contractions. The map has two periodic points, forming one isolated two-cycle. Examples show this class is strictly larger than the graphic contractions.
arxiv-2606-31054:
Yao and five colleagues study hallucination in multimodal large language models, systems that answer questions about images but sometimes describe things that are not there. The team traces the failure to an internal signal: as generation proceeds, the model's text-to-image cross-attention, which should keep words tied to picture regions, progressively degrades into unfocused or biased patterns. Most existing fixes judge only the final output and never touch this drift.

Their framework, ADAPT, intervenes on attention directly. A visual anchor taken from early decoding stabilizes grounding, an inference-time mechanism detects and corrects attention drift, and a preference-tuning step rewards visually grounded answers. Across several hallucination benchmarks, ADAPT cuts hallucination rates by 40 to 60 percent on mainstream model backbones while keeping general multimodal ability intact.
arxiv-2606-31154:
Gandhi and eight colleagues introduce PPT-Eval, a benchmark for computer-use agents that work inside Microsoft PowerPoint. Making and editing slides is a rich, multimodal job, common across offices and classrooms. The benchmark holds 120 tasks across 12 files. Tasks cover both creating content and editing presentations, sorted by difficulty.

Scoring such work is the hard part. Many solutions are valid, and agents often make only partial progress, which pass-fail metrics miss. The team builds task-specific rubrics that award credit for intermediate steps. Rubrics also penalize needless changes and poor aesthetics, and they return written feedback. Their scores correlate with human judgments at 0.77 on Kendall's tau-b. Frontier agents still struggle: a strong model, Claude-4.5-Opus, solved only 45 percent of tasks, with an average partial score of 57 percent.
arxiv-2606-31454:
Kurek and Hajič build one shared model that reads diastematic Gregorian chant notation across four datasets. Chant was the first music written on a staff, and tens of thousands of manuscripts survive. Optical recognition has been tried end to end, but each dataset used its own encoding, so models could not learn from all of them at once.

The pair create a shared encoding based on the S-GABC proposal and convert all four datasets into it. A single end-to-end foundational model trained on the merged data then sets a new state of the art on every dataset. The shared encoding turns scattered chant collections into one training pool, a step toward machine reading of the full chant heritage.
arxiv-2606-31854:
Almeida and De Berardinis revisit coequivalence relations, formulas that a logic proves to be equivalence relations on tuples of unknowns. Ghilardi and Zawadowski brought them in for the categorical study of non-classical logics. When every such relation splits into plain formulas that define them, quotients can be worked out. That separation trait already fails for intuitionistic logic and even for S5.

A weaker trait put forward, phrased through descent theory, was left open. The authors pin down its logical content by adding local coequivalence relations, which carry a transition term for elements in the same fiber. Their local separation trait proves the same, in good cases, as almost Barr-exactness of the mirror category of finitely presented algebras. S5 is shown to enjoy the local trait.
arxiv-2608-00054: RAG-Tester: Automated End-to-End Testing of Retrieval-Augmented Large Language, arXiv 2608-00054. The RAG testing. Researchers may consult the paper. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
arxiv-2608-00454: Cache-Consistent Dynamic Load Balancing for Kubernetes Controllers, arXiv 2608-00454. The K8s balancing. Readers can access the paper here. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
bentivoglio-wars-of-flanders-1654:
Guido Bentivoglio, a cardinal who had served as papal nuncio at Brussels, wrote Della guerra di Fiandra in 1632. Henry Carey's English translation of 1654 gives it as The Compleat History of the Warrs of Flanders. The war in question is the Dutch Revolt, the Eighty Years' War of the Netherlands against Spain.

Bentivoglio watched that war from the Spanish side of the lines, with a diplomat's access to councils and commanders. His history tells the Counter-Reformation case with grace, fairness, and rare inside knowledge. He praises brave foes and blames folly on his own side. The work stands as the great Catholic history of the revolt, and a model of the historian's craft.
bibliotheque-des-philosophes-alchimiques: Bibliotheque des philosophes alchimiques, tome quatrième, 1754. The fourth volume. This book preserves that collection. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
boole-laws-of-thought-1854:
Seven years after his first pamphlet, George Boole issued An Investigation of the Laws of Thought in 1854. The longer book gives the mathematical theories of logic and of probabilities. Boole widens his calculus from classes to whole statements that can be true or false. Reasoning and chance both come under his symbols.

He works out how to test arguments and how to weigh uncertain evidence. The system lets a reader compute with thought itself, in a strict sense. Later logicians refined his tools, but the leap was his. The book made logic a branch of mathematics. Its effects reached far past philosophy. Modern computing descends from it.
borlase-antiquities-cornwall-1754:
Cornwall's oldest stones drew William Borlase to write a county history unlike most others of its time. His Antiquities, Historical and Monumental, of the County of Cornwall came out in 1754. Borlase, a clergyman and keen observer of nature, spent years visiting sites across the far west of England.

Stone circles, cromlechs, and carved stones fill his pages, each one noted, drawn, and placed in its setting. Borlase linked many of these remains to the Druids, as writers of his age often did. Later students of old monuments still start with his record, since some sites have since changed or vanished.
brewster-more-worlds-one-1854:
