Guidelines urge a lipid panel for every child aged 9 to 11, yet only about one child in nine nationwide actually gets one. Two inherited disorders, familial hypercholesterolemia and raised lipoprotein(a), quietly raise lifetime heart risk and can be caught by that single blood draw long before symptoms.

Their twist is generational: finding the disorder in a child should trigger reverse cascade testing of parents and relatives. Adults who drift outside routine care may meet their risk for the first time through their child's result, while prevention can still change outcomes. Adding lipoprotein(a) to the standard panel, they contend, turns a neglected childhood test into a rescue line for the whole family.
pmc-13287154:
Julia Werner and colleagues describe a 2026 method for testing medicines on thin slices grown from gut biopsy tissue taken during routine endoscopy. Samples came from people with ulcerative colitis, people with Crohn disease, and a small control group without bowel inflammation.

Slices stayed largely intact for one day, though condition fell by the second day. Each illness kept its own pattern of immune cells and released signals. A steroid drug lowered many inflammatory signals, and plant myrrh extracts gave dose-related responses. Because results differed between donors, the authors propose the setup for comparing how individual patients might react before treatment choices are made.
pmc-13287254:
Federica Cimmelli and colleagues review in 2026 how hearing shapes balance and walking, beyond simply telling people where things are. Sound gives steady cues about body position, motion, and surroundings, and the brain merges those cues with sight, touch, and balance signals from the inner ear.

Work covered in the review shows that spatial sound, rhythm, and sound feedback can shift step timing, path control, and recovery from a stumble. Shared brain pathways for hearing and balance are described, along with weaker sound-movement links in conditions such as Parkinson disease. The authors see promise for sound-based training, fall prevention work, and assistive device design.
pmc-13287354:
Nieke N P M Smeins and co-authors reviewed scan studies in 2026 on dead fat that can form after breast surgery. They compared flap surgery with fat transfer by injection. Seventeen studies were gathered, using sound scans, X-ray scans, and magnet scans.

The scan signs of dead fat looked much the same for both methods. Oil cysts, specks of calcium, and dark areas that did not light up were common. Place differed: flap cases sat at flap edges, while injected cases spread more widely. Rates varied a lot between studies. The authors say the proof base is thin and a shared, sharper scan definition is needed.
pmc-13287554:
Zefeng Wu and co-authors review deep learning in crop research in a 2026 article that spans genomics and phenomics. Phenomics means measuring plant traits such as growth, yield, and stress damage at large scale. The review covers network types including convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and transformers. It explains where each design fits tasks from gene activity prediction to field imaging.

In genomics, the models predict gene expression, splicing choices, and regulatory DNA regions, and they forecast traits from genome data. In phenomics, they pull trait measures from drone, multispectral, and ground images for yield forecasts and disease checks. The authors weigh accuracy against model size and how clearly a model can explain itself. They close with problems of scarce data, heavy computing needs, and weak transfer between settings, plus paths toward smarter breeding.
pmc-13288054:
Hajime Tsuruoka and colleagues used moving X-ray imaging in 2026 to watch breathing in a woman aged 75 whose left main airway was nearly blocked by a small tumour. Standard lung tests cannot split function by side, so the team filmed the full breath cycle before and after treatment.

Before treatment the left lung barely expanded as she breathed in, and the chest centre shifted as she breathed out. A scope procedure snared out the growth, which proved to be a slow cancer type with no spread. After treatment expansion returned, the shift vanished, and both lungs moved together. Ordinary lung tests also improved.
pmc-13288454:
Subbareddy Mekapothula and co-authors enrich black soldier fly larvae with nano-sized minerals in a 2026 feeding study. The larvae turn organic waste into protein for farm animals, yet their mineral content can be low. The team made tiny particles of zinc, manganese, and copper oxides plus selenium. Larvae ate standard feed or brewery spent grain, each with or without the added minerals.

Mineral dosing raised larval protein to near 41 percent and fat to near 30 percent in the best groups. Gel carriers boosted zinc and selenium uptake, while water dispersions favored manganese and copper. Larvae on brewery grain gathered more zinc and manganese than those on standard feed. Mixed minerals showed no blocking effects between elements. In finished broiler feed, larva-grown zinc reached chickens better than a standard zinc additive. The authors present the method as a scalable way to upgrade insect meal.
pmc-13289154:
Charlotte Johnstone and colleagues announce a 2026 pilot trial plan in Australia. The PROSPER trial deals with pain after major pelvic surgery. The surgery is called pelvic exenteration. Three large referral centers will host it. Pain control for seven days is the test.

Patients will be split by chance in two groups. One gets oral oxycodone with a dummy tongue dose. One gets tongue buprenorphine with a dummy oral dose. Neither side will know their true drug. Join rate over six months is the main check. Missing data and rule keeping will also be logged. Patient views on the trial will be sought.
pmc-13289354:
Carlos Alfredo Fraile Olivero led a 2026 trial protocol, called FPoC, on breathing physiotherapy after lung cancer surgery. Breathing training as part of wider physical training may cut complications after removal of part of the lung for non-small cell lung cancer. Past programs varied a lot in design and testing, making results hard to compare across hospitals.

The multicenter randomized trial compares face-to-face breathing physiotherapy alone with the same care plus the Fissios App, which holds a standard program. Usage data, patient history, surgical details, and recovery course will be tracked together. The goal is to test whether sticking with the standard program links to fewer lung complications after surgery. A shared digital program could make rehab more even across sites.
pmc-13290454:
Where lung macrophages sit shapes what they do, Xin Li and Claudia Jakubzick show in a 2026 study of mouse interstitial macrophages. These tissue-resident immune cells help keep the lung in balance and organize its defenses, and earlier work had split them into CD206-high and CD206-low families.

Combining full transcript profiles with Xenium spatial mapping, the pair charted the gene programs of each subset and where each one lives. The two families carried distinct cytokine, receptor, and innate-defense signatures, plus a predicted self-signaling network. In tissue, the cells clustered in bronchovascular bundles, the interstitium, and the lung periphery, each subset favoring its own niche and showing matching adhesion and enzyme patterns. Chemokine production also varied by location, lining up with where T and B cells position themselves.
pmc-13290554:
Two rare inherited diseases that pull potassium in opposite directions shared one newborn, in a 2026 case report by Ruiping Zhang and colleagues. The boy was admitted to Tianjin Children's Hospital after ten days of intermittent convulsions.

Tests found dangerously low sodium, 88 mmol/L, which explained the seizures, plus hormone levels far above range that pointed to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Genetic testing then confirmed a second condition: variants in both CYP21A2 and the SLC12A3 gene of Gitelman syndrome, a kidney tubule disorder. One disease tends to raise potassium and the other to lower it, which can mask the picture. Zhang and colleagues use the case to show the worth of genetic testing when a baby's chemistry does not add up.
pmc-13290754:
Studies judging hospital efficiency lean on an old workhorse and are only starting to pair it with machine learning, Nesrin Alkan and colleagues find in a systematic review from 2026. They examined work from 2020 to 2025 that used Data Envelopment Analysis, a method that scores units handling many inputs and outputs at once.

Classic CCR and BCC models still dominate, typically fed with staff and money inputs and judged on service outputs. Where learning methods join in, the pairing is usually a two-stage setup aimed at classification or prediction, including work borrowed from outside health care for comparison. Coding the studies and running correspondence analysis, the authors found the hybrids rarely explain their scores or guide managers directly. They point to explainable, decision-ready hybrids as the open opportunity for fairer benchmarking and resource allocation.
pmc-13290854:
Peru's coast hosted a changing cast of respiratory syncytial virus A strains over a decade, Wilmer Silva-Caso and colleagues report in a molecular study from 2026. RSV is a leading cause of severe breathing infections in children, and the team traced which HRSV-A genotypes circulated there from 2009 to 2020.

Of 1,694 samples from hospitalized children, about a fifth tested positive for the virus, and most positives were type A. Sequencing the G gene's variable region in 53 samples revealed two genotype families, NA1 and ON1, sometimes circulating in the same year. One ON1 branch carried three distinctive mutations found only locally, suggesting a homegrown variant. Dating placed the Peruvian ON1 ancestor around 2008, shortly before its first detection. The authors argue such surveillance maps how the virus evolves between epidemics.
pmc-13290954:
A biodegradable mask filter can hit N95 performance without static charge, Nathan Ewell and colleagues demonstrate in a materials study from 2026. Standard respirator layers rely on charged meltblown plastic that never breaks down. Spun nanofibers filter by fineness instead, and they can be made from greener materials.

The team spun polycaprolactone, a degradable polymer, from a relatively benign solvent, tuning fiber widths between 60 and 300 nanometers. The media met N95 targets for filtering power and breathing ease in lab tests. The finest fibers performed best with the least material, and they degraded fastest too. Duckbill-style prototype masks, with the PCL layer between polylactic acid supports, also passed the N95 criteria tested. Ewell and colleagues map the fiber recipes other makers can copy.
pmc-13291254:
Ultrasound you can wear may change heart watch for good. Mengxue Yan leads a 2026 review of this new device class. Normal ultrasound needs a clinic and a skilled hand. Wearable versions stick to skin and watch deep tissue live.

A full system has three core parts. Soft probes must bend with skin yet sound well. Small circuits must balance power, heat, and size. Smart software must clean data while the wearer moves. Heart uses show the stack at its best. The review maps hard trade-offs in each part. It charts a path toward round-the-clock, personal heart care.
pmc-13291354:
A soil fungus can make an enzyme for greener textile work. Sara H. Mansour leads a 2026 study of pectinase production. Mills now use harsh chemicals to strip cloth sizing. A stable enzyme could replace that step.

The best local fungus was named Aspergillus foetidus by gene tests. Broth growth peaked under warm, acidic settings. Wheat bran with yeast extract fed the best yield. The enzyme held up well in acid and heat. Heat math confirmed strong thermal stability. Trial cloth lost its starch sizing under enzyme care. Weight loss matched the sizing share removed. Mills gain a cleaner option for fabric prep.
pmc-13291554:
Bright days may lower dementia risk in later life. Nana Zheng leads a 2026 study of wrist-measured light in older adults. Light sets body clock rhythms that shape brain health. Proof linking real light habits to dementia was thin.

The group held 87,577 dementia-free adults. Wrist sensors logged day and night light for a week. Over about eight years, 741 people developed dementia. More bright daytime light linked to lower risk. Longer time in very bright light helped more. Body rhythms and brain scans explained part of the link. Night light patterns were also examined. Simple daylight habits may be a cheap brain guard.
pmc-13291754:
Andreasen and co-authors publish the protocol for testing dexamethasone after cardiac arrest in this 2026 paper. Survivors revived from out of hospital cardiac arrest often stay comatose, and body wide inflammation after circulation stops drives further organ damage. A strong steroid might blunt that response. This comparison sits inside the Danish DANOHCA trial, which tests four post resuscitation treatments.

Comatose adults with a presumed cardiac cause will be randomised to 20 milligrams of dexamethasone or a salt water placebo. Three doses are given, one at enrolment and one on each following morning. The main measure is death from any cause within 90 days. Enrolment began in June 2023 and aims for 1000 patients at five sites. Andreasen notes the result will guide post resuscitation care either way.
pmc-13292054:
Irene Bernal-Florindo and co-authors review a 2026 body of work on reading prognosis in classic Hodgkin lymphoma from the tumor microenvironment's layout. Between 10 and 20 percent of patients never reach complete response, and standard clinical variables do not explain why. The review follows the shift from manual pathology toward digital image analysis and computational pathology.

Software now counts tumor and immune cells objectively and maps how they sit in relation to one another. The authors argue that spatial and topological features carry prognostic value beyond cell counts alone. They sketch future models blending those features with liquid biopsy sequencing, single-cell data, spatial transcriptomics, and PET/CT imaging. The goal is sharper risk groups and treatments matched to each patient's tumor ecology.
pmc-13292154:
Arturo J Martí-Carvajal and David L Streiner take aim at a 2026 methods target: the Cochrane Handbook's bands for reading the I2 heterogeneity statistic in meta-analysis. The bands label 0 to 25 percent as low, 25 to 75 percent as moderate, and 50 percent or more as high. The authors traced the scheme's history and tested its logic against formal classification principles.

They show the bands overlap: a value of 50 percent counts as both moderate and high at once, so single results land in two categories. Little explicit theory or evidence backs the chosen cutoffs, they argue, and the scheme treats I2 as a verdict rather than a prompt to explore differences. They propose a context-specific framework, named PIOHA, that ties interpretation to outcome type and expected variability.
pmc-13292554:
Genesis D Flores and a large team lay out the Teen Bugs study protocol in a 2026 paper. The study asks how early caregiving adversity shapes teenage mental health through gut microbes and brain reward circuits. Teens aged twelve to fifteen, with and without such adversity histories, will be followed for five years. Three waves combine clinical interviews, reward choice tasks, and questionnaires. Brain imaging uses magnetic resonance markers tied to dopamine biology.

Stool samples will feed microbe gene checks, and blood samples will feed metabolite checks. The data should reveal metabolic pathways linking early adversity to reward-system function and symptoms like depression and anxiety. Teens are understudied in microbiome research despite high rates of emerging illness. The protocol's integrative design aims at mechanisms that could become treatment targets. The paper reports a plan, not results. Its value lies in the joint gut-brain plan it sets out.
pmc-13292754:
Karl Nadolsky writes a 2026 letter disputing a review that filed nonnutritive sweeteners under evidence of harm for heart health. The review leaned on large cohort studies tying artificially sweetened drinks to higher disease rates. Nadolsky argues those observational links are poisoned by reverse causation: people switch to diet drinks because they are already sick or gaining weight, which manufactures the association.

Against that, he marshals randomized trial evidence. Intervention studies repeatedly show sweetened-without-sugar drinks beating sugary ones, sometimes matching or beating water, and meal replacements using these sweeteners aiding weight loss and diabetes remission. A cited meta-analysis of trials by Qin and colleagues anchors the safety case. His plea: let controlled evidence, not confounded correlations, steer what clinicians tell patients about sweeteners.
pmc-13292854:
Narjes Morovati Moez leads a 2026 lab study packing three drugs into tiny fat carriers to fight Brucella melitensis. The bacterium hides inside macrophages, the very cells meant to kill it, so drugs often fail to reach it in full strength.

Carriers holding doxycycline, gentamicin, and thymol together measured about 398 nanometers across and held most of their drug load. They released drugs slowly over 80 hours, unlike free drugs that spread fast. Inside infected cells, the packed form cut bacterial counts far more than free drugs while keeping most host cells alive. Tests in animals are the next step.
pmc-13293154:
Naseer Mohammed Abdul and colleagues compare, in a 2026 pooled analysis, two bearing designs for total knee replacement: fixed and rotating platform. Rotating inserts should help motion in theory, yet trials have not shown a clear edge.

Data merged two large studies from the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom, covering 1,718 patients at 27 centers. Scores from several patient surveys were checked at start and at two years. Without adjustment, change over two years did not differ between designs on any survey the team used. Once body mass was factored in, some scores favored the rotating design, a nuance for surgeons.
pmc-13293754:
Wesley Chorney and Michael Lisi ask, in a 2026 study, whether two standard illness burden scores can predict delirium after belly surgery. Delirium after surgery is common and costly, and a simple pre-surgery flag could focus prevention on high-risk patients.

Using a large intensive care database, the team scored 8022 operations in 7212 adults with both the Charlson and Elixhauser indices. Each score alone predicted delirium within 30 days with modest accuracy, the Elixhauser slightly ahead. Adding other known delirium factors lifted accuracy further in their models. Burden scores help, the authors conclude, but fuller models predict best.
pmc-13294154:
Silvânia da Veiga Leal and coauthors measure late HIV diagnosis in Cabo Verde in 2026, using a cross-sectional design. Testing and treatment are free, yet delays persist and raise illness, death, and spread. Newly diagnosed, untreated adults on four islands gave interviews and clinical data between 2018 and 2019, totaling 135 people. Late meant CD4 under 350 cells per microliter or an AIDS-defining illness.

Overall 56.3% were diagnosed late. Being single and having viral load at or above 5.0 log copies per milliliter each independently raised the odds of late status. Genetic ambiguity suggested most infections were recent, at 68.3%, yet agreement with CD4 staging was low. Outreach to single adults may catch cases sooner.
pmc-13294254:
Dorota Długopolska and colleagues review blood and airway markers for horse asthma in a 2026 synthesis. Diagnosis now leans on lung wash cell counts, an invasive step that field vets cannot always do. Studies in mild to severe disease were gathered from three databases, covering lung wash, blood, tracheal wash, saliva, and breath condensate.

Across 57 studies, blood markers alone proved patchy, though combos improved accuracy. Lung wash markers tracked local inflammation more faithfully. Neutrophil trap markers, NGAL, and allergy antibody profiles looked most promising, above all in combined panels split by disease type. Large validation cohorts are still needed before routine use.
pmc-13294354:
Elisa Vanessa Osterode and coauthors give long follow-up on platelet-rich plasma aided surgery for lamellar macular holes in a 2026 prospective case study. Twenty eyes from 20 patients had vitrectomy with membrane peeling plus concentrated plasma from their own blood, and follow-up ran at least 24 months with mean near 40 months.

Foveal shape was restored in every eye at first check. Vision scores improved clearly by final visit, and central retinal thickness rose as tissue rebuilt. Light-sensing layer defects, present in 80% at start, fully closed in 62.5% of that group in the reported share. Three eyes regrew defects, with no other major complications.
pmc-13294854:
Ting Wang and colleagues use genetics to probe whether vitamin D causes changes in anxiety or depression in a 2026 study. Ordinary comparisons cannot separate cause from coincidence, so the team applied Mendelian randomization in both directions. Genetic data came from large public genome study collections.

Using 32 genetic markers for vitamin D levels, the analysis linked higher levels with lower depression risk across most methods. No clear causal link appeared between vitamin D and anxiety in either direction. Looking backward, genetic liability to depression hinted at slightly lower vitamin D levels, leading the authors to float vitamin D checks as one possible aid in depression prevention work.
pmc-13294954:
Paweł Ręka and colleagues extend a selective recipe for building phenazine dyes and test the results on cancer cells, in a 2026 study. Phenazines are ring systems found in bacterial pigments, with a long record of killing microbes and tumors. The team's method places up to four unlike groups at chosen spots while forming only the wanted isomer, widening one branch of the family.

New compounds joined older kin in tests on mouse mammary cancer cells and human colon cancer cells. Three stood out with strong force in both lines. Tests on normal mouse mammary cells gave a best safety margin near two, which is modest. Chosen members were then checked against a folded DNA stretch from a cancer gene switch, and each one tested loosened that fold.
pmc-13295054:
José Luiz Martins do Nascimento and colleagues propose an enzyme's slowdown as a warning sign of mercury poisoning, in a 2026 study from the Amazon. Riverside communities there eat fish carrying mercury, a metal that attacks the developing brain. The candidate marker is biotinidase, an enzyme that recycles a B vitamin fragment, and the team checked it three ways: computer docking, lab assays, and blood from exposed and unexposed residents.

Blood from mercury-exposed people showed lower biotinidase activity, while other metals tested in the lab left the enzyme alone, pointing to a specific effect. Docking simulations showed methylmercury gripping the enzyme's active site through sulfur and selenium atoms, with a cysteine residue the likely anchor. A cheap blood test for the enzyme, the authors argue, could flag intoxication early in remote regions where exposure monitoring is scarce.
pmc-13295254:
Lindsay Howard and co-authors put a questionnaire about hiding eating problems under the microscope, in a 2026 psychometric study. People with disordered eating often deny or conceal their behaviors, which can keep problems going, yet few tools measure that denial. The team retested a twelve-item scale in more than three thousand undergraduates, checking its structure and whether it means the same thing across gender, race, and symptom severity.

The original single-score design failed statistical tests. A trimmed seven-item version focused on denying dietary restriction fit well, hung together reliably, and lined up sensibly with related measures of concealment and restraint. Scores compared fairly across men and women and across Black and White students, though the scale's zero point shifted with symptom severity, complicating direct group comparisons there. The authors renamed the short form and call for testing beyond college samples.
pmc-13295354:
Nishadi Jayathilaka and colleagues hunt the resistance genes inside urinary bacteria that shrug off last-resort antibiotics, in a 2026 study from two Sri Lankan hospitals. Carbapenem-resistant organisms are spreading in urinary infections, and knowing which carbapenemase genes they carry guides both treatment and infection control. From more than seven thousand urine samples collected through 2023, the team gathered about one hundred resistant isolates and ran a multiplex gene test covering eight carbapenemase genes.

Klebsiella pneumoniae was the most common species and carried the widest mix of genes. About a third of tested isolates held a single resistance gene, while nearly two fifths held two or more together. Two OXA-family genes dominated the tally. Most patients improved within a week of treatment, yet three quarters of those followed for three months suffered at least one mild recurrence. The authors press for continuous surveillance and targeted control programs.
pmc-13295454:
Davide Orsini, Anna Maria Spagnolo, and Mariano Martini call antimicrobial resistance a silent pandemic and trace its roots to medicine's first drug era, in a 2026 review. Resistance already kills more than a million people each year, and some forecasts rank it first among causes of death by 2050. Rather than treat it as a modern mishap, the authors revisit the first sightings of the pattern.

Microbes adapted to Salvarsan, the arsenic drug used before antibiotics, and early failures soon hit sulfonamides and penicillin too. Some reports came before Fleming's penicillin news reached the world. The pattern drawn is of resistance as a built-in answer to selective pressure. Each use of a drug trains its targets, and the training compounds as use spreads, so stewardship, not shock, is the reply the authors urge.
pmc-13295754:
Andrei Scripcaru and colleagues compare three ways of fixing a badly broken upper arm bone near the shoulder, in a 2026 study. Such breaks are hard to treat, since bone quality and shape vary by patient. The team built a four-part break in lab models of the humerus and fixed it with polyaxial locking plates, monoaxial locking plates, or a nail down the bone's core.

Pressing tests, computer models, and close surface checks gave the verdict. The two plates behaved much alike, bending at like stiffness before the metal gave way. The nail build was far stiffer, near nine and a half times the plates, yet it failed by cracking the bone instead. Which choice is best, the authors say, leans on the patient's bone.
pmc-13295854:
Stefan Knippen and colleagues test how user choices sway deformable image registration in breast radiotherapy planning, in a 2026 study. The method warps one scan onto another so dose plans can follow the body, here scans taken breathing freely and holding a deep breath. Seventy-three women with left-sided breast cancer had both scans, and one doctor drew the target and organs on each.

Where the user told the software to focus changed the result a lot. Focus on the target gave the best target match but hurt other organs, while focus on the heart did the reverse. Which way the warp ran mattered little for volumes. Breath size swayed both target and heart scores in opposed ways. Hand fixes stayed needed in every case, the authors say.
pmc-13296054:
Ahmed Ali and Derar Derar review, in 2026, sudden reproductive emergencies in male dromedary camels. Conditions range from testicle and penis injuries to cord twisting, trapped erections, blocked urine flow and problems after castration, many of them poorly documented in camels.

The authors set out how each problem presents and how vets can confirm it, stressing examination and ultrasound early. Treatments span drugs, surgery and removal of damaged parts, with prompt action sometimes saving breeding ability. Delays often end in lasting infertility or death. The review aims to give vets a practical guide for a high-value desert animal.
pmc-13296754:
Bhagath Kumar Potu and colleagues test whether the antipsychotic aripiprazole, given during pregnancy, slows fetal bone growth in a 2026 rat study. The drug crosses the placenta, yet its effects on the developing skeleton were unexplored. Forty pregnant rats received one of three daily doses, or none, through most of pregnancy.

Fetuses exposed to the drug showed fewer fully hardened bone centres, and the effect grew with dose. Ossified parts of the long bones were significantly shorter in treated groups. Microscopic measures of thigh bone confirmed thinner hardened bone and a shorter growth-plate zone. The authors call for work on the molecular mechanism and on what the delay means after birth.
pmc-13297054:
Su-Kiat Chua and co-authors trace, in 2026, how rapid electrical pacing of human atrial fibroblasts switches on self-eating through a long RNA signal. Paced cells shed tiny packets rich in MALAT1, a regulatory RNA tied to atrial fibrillation scarring.

Reporter tests and gain-and-loss experiments confirm a chain: MALAT1 soaks up a small RNA, freeing a self-eating protein to rise and activate the process. Blocking any link in the chain damped the response. The authors name the axis a possible drug target for limiting structural damage in fibrillating atria and related rhythm care.
pmc-13297554:
Emilia Georgiana Prisăcariu and a large team study a flapping wing built for thin air, such as the Martian atmosphere, in a 2026 paper. Rotor craft struggle where air is sparse, while flapping wings promise lift at the slow, small scales involved. High-speed cameras captured the wing's motion, and a scaled model was tested in computer models of structure and airflow.

Bending and twisting of the wing proved tightly coupled. When flapping neared the wing's natural rhythm, warping grew large and phase patterns shifted. Airflow models showed lift coming mainly from swirling vortices, as in insect flight. The results give designers a physics base for flapping machines in thin-air flight.
pmc-13299454:
Mirfat Mohamed Labib Elkashif and others assess sustainable healthcare knowledge among obstetric and maternity nurses in Egypt, in a 2026 one-time study. Maternity services contribute pollution and emissions, so nurse practice matters. A purpose-built survey reached 120 nurses across a university hospital and family medicine centres in one governorate.

About half reported having heard of sustainability and received training. Good knowledge appeared in roughly half the group, good practice in fewer, while positive attitudes were held by nearly all. Trained nurses scored clearly higher on knowledge, attitudes, and eco-conscious practice across every domain. The authors advise embedding sustainability in training and institutional policy.
pmc-13299854:
Carpet beetles quietly eat museum collections, and Peter Brimblecombe with co-authors census them across Austrian heritage buildings in a 2026 study. Traps in 31 museums, libraries, and storerooms caught the two main pest genera, Anthrenus and Attagenus, in roughly proportionate numbers.

Colder buildings favored species such as Anthrenus fuscus, while Anthrenus olgae, frequent in Austria, appears uncommon elsewhere in Europe, hinting that ranges differ by country. The authors connect the pattern to climate and the movement of goods and loans that ferry pests between institutions. A warming future, they warn, will likely widen the roster of species threatening wool, specimens, and furnishings.
pmc-13300854:
O Bastidas and a large co-author team describe a simplified pulmonary vein isolation strategy built on tight lesion spacing, in a 2026 study. Their protocol spaces radiofrequency burns three millimeters apart and skips the usual waiting period, adenosine testing, and remapping steps. The series covered 771 first-time ablation patients treated between January 2022 and May 2025, followed with rhythm monitors or device checks for at least a year.

Median procedure time was one hundred minutes, and nearly half the cases used no fluoroscopy at all. Safety events were rare: no esophageal fistula occurred, and three patients developed vein narrowing that needed no treatment. At one year, eighty-six percent of patients remained free of any atrial arrhythmia recurrence. Results did not depend on operator experience or on whether a trainee fellow took part. The authors present the stripped down protocol as safe, effective, and easy to reproduce.
pmc-13301254:
Débora Andrea Castiglioni Alves and co-authors relate severe obesity, blood pressure, and activity to day long heart rhythm variability in a 2026 cross sectional study. The group covered 1,048 adults being evaluated for weight loss surgery, sorted by obesity class, hypertension diagnosis, and activity level. Variability between heartbeats over twenty-four hours served as the readout of autonomic control.

Severe obesity came with lower variability throughout and roughly double the odds of hypertension and of blood pressure medication compared with class II obesity. Hypertension itself tracked with lower variability, much higher odds of diabetes and lipid disorders, and less physical activity. Activity pointed the other way: active patients showed higher variability and lower odds of hypertension and its treatment. The authors read the pattern as support for movement as a practical lever on cardiovascular risk in this surgical population, while noting the design shows association, not cause.
pmc-13302154:
Yashraj Srivastava and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, whether weakened immune states raise danger from disease of the chest aorta. Aneurysms there can grow silently until the wall tears, and immune dysfunction plausibly harms the wall through inflammation and poor repair. Evidence comes from transplant recipients, autoimmune disease, HIV, and cancer treatment.

Recurring themes included damaged vessel lining, enzymes chewing through the wall's support matrix, and reduced repair capacity. Direct growth data for the chest segment stayed scarce and often mixed with other vessels. Cancer therapy showed no uniform effect on aneurysm growth, though single drugs may still matter. The authors advise exposure-aware monitoring and call for standardised long-term imaging studies.
pmc-13305454:
Irene Dini introduces a 2026 special issue on turning farm and food leftovers into valued health ingredients through fermentation and smart processing. Stalks, peels, pomace, and off-grade fruit once counted as waste now look like stores of fiber and protective plant compounds.

Studies in the collection add broccoli stalk powder to bread, raising fiber and antioxidant scores. Others fortify gluten-free loaves with treated artichoke and broccoli scraps, easing starch digestion and expected sugar impact. Mango leaf screening and similar work map which residues deserve scale-up in a circular food economy.
pmc-13305854:
Tim Bozic and colleagues set out a 2026 laboratory protocol for profiling mouse lymph node cells with 14-colour flow cytometry. Lymph nodes guide immune responses, so detailed maps of their resident cells help explain how immunity is organised.

Steps cover finding nodes by anatomy, breaking tissue apart by hand and with enzymes, then staining and gating to separate helper and killer T cells by maturity stage. Killer-cell relatives called natural killer cells are also sorted by development stage. Although tuned for response after a bacterial challenge agent, the panel offers a reusable route for wider immune studies.
pmc-13305954:
Ziwei Yan and colleagues report in 2026 that muscone, a natural compound from musk, calms a powerful inflammatory switch in immune cells. The switch, called the NLRP3 inflammasome, drives harmful inflammation in sepsis-like states. Experiments used stimulated macrophages in culture and a mouse model of endotoxin poisoning.

Muscone weakened both the priming and firing stages of the inflammasome, cutting interleukin-1 beta release by about sixty percent at the best dose. It also boosted a clean-up process that removes damaged mitochondria, which lowered reactive oxygen from those organelles. In mice, treated animals survived longer than untreated controls after endotoxin exposure. The authors argue that muscone's ring-shaped structure, which can cross into the brain, makes it a useful starting point for new anti-inflammatory drugs.
pmc-13306054: A 2026 correction in Age and Ageing concerns a study of an unsupervised, adapted physical activity programme, called the PACE tool, used as pragmatic care in an outpatient clinic for older adults. The notice is a correction only: in the original version, the authors' first and last names, led by Fabien Jean Manuel Ruiz, were transposed by mistake. Those names have now been reordered in the published paper. No findings, data, or conclusions are altered by the change.
pmc-13306754:
Jing Liu and co-authors clean noisy fibre-optic strain data from underwater riverbed mattresses in a 2026 study set on the Yangtze River. Flexible mattresses protect shorelines, and distributed sensing tracks their deformation, but field readings arrive heavily contaminated with no clean reference. Their TrendBlend-BSFormer system learns to denoise without supervision.

Blind-spot masking hides points so the network must infer them from neighbours, and a transformer section captures long-range patterns along the fibre. Two field datasets, each with over nine thousand valid points, were used for validation. The system beat a published benchmark on signal quality and sharply cut high-frequency noise energy. Spikes vanished while real peaks and valleys survived. The authors argue that such cleaning makes fibre monitoring physically credible for hard-to-inspect underwater works.
pmc-13306854:
Hairong Gu rebuilt large rescue shafts in 3D from photos using neural radiance fields in a 2026 study. Such shafts carry rescue capsules after mine disasters, so wall bending must be measured before anyone rides through.

A pipeline filters photos by a no-reference quality score, estimates camera poses, builds the radiance model, then exports a dense point cloud for circle fitting. Keeping about 35% of top photos balanced speed and detail in reported trials on a simulated shaft. Radius errors and fit residuals judged how well the rebuild supports safety checks.
pmc-13307354:
Jonnathan Santos and colleagues measure in 2026 how hard it is to split apart layers of a 3D-printed glass fibre composite. Specimens of continuous glass fibre in polyamide 6 were printed on a commercial machine and pulled apart in a standard beam test. Two calculation methods checked each other's readings.

Both methods agreed well, and repeat tests gave consistent values. Resistance rose as the crack advanced, a pattern shown by the resistance curve. Microscopy revealed uneven mixes of fibre, matrix, and voids between printed lines. Against earlier printed systems, the material sat mid-range for starting toughness but lower for propagation toughness. The authors say the data fill a gap for designers. Knowing delamination behaviour matters before printed composites carry structural loads.
pmc-13307454:
Ramon Hernany Martins Gomes and co-authors test in 2026 whether water plants pulled from Brazilian reservoirs can serve as fertiliser for soil and grass. Four plant species from the Santana Reservoir were mixed into pots at three doses, and seedlings of Urochloa decumbens were grown in them.

Two joint scores, one for soil quality and one for plant growth, both rose when plant matter was added, though gains varied by species and dose. The two scores moved together closely, with an R squared value near 0.73 in the data set. One high dose raised soil score without a matching plant gain, so field trials and safety checks must come before farm advice.
pmc-13307654:
Tamara Barnett and colleagues update evidence in 2026 on HIV prevention pills for women, a group whose needs prevention programmes often miss. Their review covers cisgender and transgender women, including teenagers, women who use drugs, sex workers, migrants, and women leaving prison. Findings focus on daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis.

Themes include barriers to starting, reasons for stopping, and the idea of seasons of risk when perceived danger dips. Partner violence, trust inside relationships, and preferred access points all shaped use. Peer supporters and navigators created safe spaces that improved trust and persistence. Regional differences in services and messaging also mattered. The authors call for women-centred programmes that attack clinical, social, and structural barriers together, tailored to each setting.
pmc-13308554:
Peng Chen and co-authors probe in 2026 a uric acid carrier, SLC2A9, in triple negative breast cancer, the most aggressive common breast form. Lab data showed far less of the carrier in tumour tissue and in most cell lines than in normal tissue.

Raising the carrier in cells slowed growth, spread, and invasion, while it pushed more cells into planned death in dish tests. It also moved uric acid out of cells and cut the load kept inside each cell. Lowering the carrier flipped each of those effects in turn. The carrier may thus serve as a sign of outlook and as a fresh metabolic target for drug work.
pmc-13308754:
Trevor Binedell and co-authors test in 2026 a knitted prosthetic liner, Flexoknit, shaped by digital maps of skin stretch for people with below knee limb loss. Stiff heat set yarns form support zones, while stretch yarns form cool, soft zones, all woven in one piece by a programmed machine.

Bench pulls showed near tenfold gaps in stiffness across yarn and stitch blends in the lab runs. In wear tests against a standard silicone liner, the knit gave 22.5 percent more joint range and cut liner weight by 37.5 percent for the user. Breath and heat control also beat the old liner in hot, damp air. Comfort first users may gain most.
pmc-13309054:
Jingxian Zhao and co-authors test in 2026 dimethyl itaconate, a cell signal kin, against Toxoplasma gondii in dishes and in infected mice, as current drugs harm many and face resistant strains. Dish work used scope views, plaque counts, gene counts, and energy checks to trace how the compound hits the parasite.

Treated parasites showed wrecked inner parts, torn skins, and dose tied growth cuts across the dish tests run here. Energy hubs failed, with low charge and fuel stores plus a surge of harsh oxygen by products in the cells. In mice, the drug raised survival, cut loads in key organs, and eased tissue harm and swelling. A fresh drug path may open.
pmc-13309554:
Craig MacLean argues in a 2026 perspective that two classic labels for bacterial survival under antibiotics need rethinking. Resistance and tolerance were defined from whole-culture tests dating to the 1920s. New single-cell work shows culture outcomes grow out of shifting birth and death among cells, which the old labels blur.

An ecology-style growth model links culture-level growth rates to single-cell birth and death rates. In that frame, resistance and tolerance appear as side effects of selection on birth and death, not as fixed cell traits. The author urges researchers to measure cell-level rates directly. The piece aims to reset how drug response in bacteria is taught and studied.
pmc-13310754:
Guillermo Yepes led a 2026 study on urine markers for repeat bladder infections in girls and teens. Repeat infections are hard to predict, and weak natural defenses in the urine tract may raise risk. The team measured defense proteins and signal proteins in urine and asked if the pattern could flag past repeat illness.

Urine came from 42 patients with a history of repeat infection and 37 healthy controls at a children hospital in Ohio. Repeat cases showed lower levels of some defense proteins and higher levels of signal proteins. A model that mixed urine results with health facts sorted the groups well. Wider tests must confirm the value.
pmc-13310854:
Ali S. Aljumah and colleagues present a new optimizer for running power grids at lowest safe cost in a 2026 study. Grid operators must meet demand without breaking voltage or flow limits, while adding solar power adds fresh strain. The team upgraded a Newton based search method with two adaptive tricks.

One trick lets trial solutions swap useful parts to keep variety high. The other shifts the search slowly from wide scanning to fine tuning. Tests on the standard IEEE 30 bus grid covered fuel cost, loss cuts, and barred zones under light, normal, and peak loads. The new method beat the base method and rivals on cost, speed, and steadiness.
pmc-13310954:
Alessia Marialydia Lavigne and colleagues report low hatching success in Aldabra giant tortoises in a 2026 study. Tortoises face high threat, yet breeding traits and early life stages are poorly tracked. Adult counts can hide breeding failure for decades in long lived species, so egg outcomes in natural and moved groups were checked.

Eggs totaled 317 in number from 24 clutches across one natural and five moved groups in the Seychelles. Only a small share hatched, and most failed eggs never developed. Whole clutch failure was common. Moved groups hatched far less than the natural group and far below rates from fifty years ago. Breeding checks should join adult counts.
pmc-13311154:
Ruida Li and co-authors identify in 2026 the enzyme policing levels of N-acetyl-β-alanine, a metabolite linked to obesity and type 2 diabetes whose regulation was unknown. The enzyme, PTER, was already known for breaking down a related taurine compound. Lab tests compared its speed on several similar molecules, and mice lacking the gene showed where control actually sits.

Purified PTER split N-acetyl-β-alanine into free β-alanine far faster than it handled its older known substrate, and ignored two close chemical cousins entirely. In knockout mice, breakdown activity fell in a tissue-dependent pattern, and metabolite levels shifted in both directions depending on the tissue. Carnosine and other pathway members stayed unchanged, while the taurine compound rose everywhere. Raising N-acetyl-β-alanine pharmacologically curbed feeding and weight gain in obese mice. The enzyme emerges as a control node in β-amino acid metabolism worth drug attention.
pmc-13311254:
Mahsa Asadi Anar and co-authors present a 2026 test of Recursive Informational Curvature, a math lens for reading brain state changes, in macaque brain recordings. The scalar term K is the measure put to work.

Two open datasets were used: a 128-channel set comparing eyes open and closed, and a 64-channel set recorded during food tracking with motion capture. Entropy, recursive gain, and curvature were drawn from each channel and time window. Curvature features from many channels split the eye states almost perfectly, and pairing curvature with signal size worked best in the food task. Entropy alone was weak throughout.
pmc-13311454:
Anastasia Matchanova and co-authors compare ways of defining mild cognitive impairment in Vietnam-era veterans in a 2026 study. Three rule sets were tested against brain scan markers of vessel damage and shrinkage.

The study classified 228 veterans, average age 69.65 years, by standard ADNI rules, by broader test-based rules, and by a typical clinical rule set. Only the test-based rules tied to greater white matter damage on scans. Links with memory-related brain measures also differed by rule set and by memory subtype. The authors argue that test-based rules best match the brain risk picture in this group.
pmc-13311654:
Daniel C Brock and colleagues analyze their 2026 national trauma database study on alcohol use and helmet wearing among injured cyclists. Helmets cut head injury risk, yet drinking may loosen the habit.

The study covered 155,766 injured cyclists recorded from 2017 to 2023. Riders were grouped by blood alcohol level, from sober to drunk plus drug-positive. Helmet use fell step by step with drinking, from 45.9 percent in sober riders to 6.2 percent in the heaviest group in this dataset. Drinking also tied to higher death rates and more head and neck injuries. Prevention could pair helmet drives with alcohol counseling.
pmc-13311754:
Carmen A W Dietvorst and co-authors present the MEDFAST trial protocol in a 2026 article. The trial pits an early time-restricted Mediterranean diet against a weight-loss drug pair for liver fibrosis in people with metabolic risk.

Seventy overweight adults with diabetes, high blood pressure, blood fat problems, or obesity and clear liver stiffness will be assigned to one arm. Liver stiffness by elastography is the main measure. Direct head-to-head data on diet timing versus drug treatment are lacking, though both routes can cut weight. The trial will show whether meal timing can stand as a real drug alternative.
pmc-13311954:
Lorelle Bowditch and co-authors analyze 2025-published Australian patient safety investigations for signs of systems thinking. Up to 17 percent of hospital patients suffer a safety incident, and learning from them is vital.

The team coded 300 investigations from 56 health services. Contributing factors were sorted by system level using two frameworks, and recommendations were graded weak, medium, or strong by federal criteria. Half the incidents had factors spread across levels, on the report's account. The study tests whether investigations truly hunt system causes or settle for blaming the sharp end, and whether their fixes are built to last.
pmc-13312054:
Yuan Wang and colleagues present a 2026 study that uses machine learning to predict and control the particle size of metal-organic frameworks. These porous crystals serve in catalysis, separation, and drug delivery, yet their size was usually tuned by trial and error because growth depends on many interacting steps.

The team built a database from published work on the framework ZIF-8, using seven process settings as inputs, and compared several learning algorithms. A categorical boosting model performed best, and explanation analysis singled out the precursor concentration ratio and reaction time as the strongest levers on size. Trials on an automated synthesis platform matched the predictions closely, supporting a shift from guesswork toward data-guided design of these materials.
pmc-13312254:
Niyati Bansal, Steve Thomas, and Sri Gayathri Shanmugam present a 2026 case report of follicular lymphoma that had spilled into the bloodstream, its rare leukemic phase. Follicular lymphoma is usually slow-growing, but the leukemic presentation brings high tumor burden and a worse outlook. Their patient, a 51-year-old woman, arrived with widespread swollen lymph nodes and a high white cell count, and her prognostic index score of 3 placed her in the high-risk band.

She received the bendamustine and rituximab combination, with preventive supportive care and growth factor cover. Across six cycles she tolerated treatment well, improved clinically, and kept stable blood counts. The authors use the case to argue that fast, accurate diagnosis, honest risk scoring, and early risk-adapted chemoimmunotherapy can together produce a favorable outcome even in this uncommon, high-risk presentation. The report adds a documented success to a presentation where published experience is thin.
pmc-13312454:
Fabio Della Sala and colleagues present a 2026 study testing adiabatic connection methods for finding correlation energy in real metals. These methods blend perturbation theory with density functionals built for strongly interacting electrons. They have worked well for molecules, but in metals the perturbation term blows up, so their value for solids, including transition metals, was unknown.

Working from Hartree-Fock ground states built with tuned Gaussian basis sets, the team tried several variants and set lattice constants, cohesive energies, and correlation energies against trusted values. Only one pairing, the density parameter interpolation approach with a strong-interaction functional matching the exact Wigner crystal model, gave the correct gradient coefficient. That variant matched the best density functional methods on lattice constants and bulk correlation energies, and its cohesive energies matched well on their own.
pmc-13312854:
Xi Zhu and co-authors quantify, in a 2026 nine-year study, how much tuberculosis in fast-growing Shenzhen spreads locally rather than arriving with its host. The team collected every culture-positive case diagnosed from 2014 to 2022, sequenced the bacteria, and mapped where clustered, genetically matching cases lived and moved.

Of 4,560 patients, a striking 93.4 percent were internal migrants, and 21.8 percent carried isolates belonging to genomic clusters, evidence of recent transmission inside the city. Hotspots appeared in the central business district and in suburban industrial zones. Spread was likelier between patients of similar age, living close together, or sharing a province of origin, and neighborhoods dense with migrants saw more clustering. The authors argue control programs should shift from static plans toward dynamic efforts aimed at social networks, high-risk communities, and mapped urban hotspots.
pmc-13313154:
Marcos Fanton and co-authors apply, in a 2026 study, an intersectional statistical method to obesity among Brazilian adults. They argue that looking at one social category at a time hides how combined disadvantage shapes health. Using the 2019 National Health Survey's 71,896 respondents, they sorted people into 162 strata woven from race, gender, age, income, and schooling.

Obesity, defined by a body mass index of 30 or more, varied sharply between strata, concentrating most heavily among Brown and Black women with less schooling and lower income. Simply adding the separate effects of each dimension explained only part of the pattern: nearly half the strata-level difference in the reported analysis required interaction effects, where disadvantages multiply rather than add. The authors say the findings show systems of power literally embodied, and that equity policy needs intersectional tools to see it.
pmc-13313254:
Xiaowan Chen and co-workers report in 2026 that a protein called OTUD5 helps acute myeloid leukemia grow by blocking a form of cell death. This blood cancer is fierce and often beats treatment, so new targets are in demand.

OTUD5 was found at high levels in patient samples and leukemia cell lines, and that rise tracked with low rates of ferroptosis, an iron-linked cell death. Lab tests that silenced or boosted OTUD5 in THP-1 and HL-60 cells changed growth, colony forming, and ferroptosis markers such as reactive oxygen, iron, and GSH. Binding tests showed OTUD5 grips SLC7A11 and strips off its ubiquitin tags, keeping it stable and shielding cells from death. Mouse grafts backed the lab findings, marking OTUD5 as a drug target worth testing.
pmc-13313754:
Ali Murat Başak and colleagues compare, in a 2026 retrospective study, two patient positions for balloon kyphoplasty, the cement procedure that stabilizes osteoporotic spinal fractures. Lying face down is standard but impossible for some patients, including the severely obese. Fifty patients over 65 treated with local anesthesia during 2021 to 2024 were split evenly between face-down positioning and side-lying, the latter chosen when face-down was ruled out.

Side-lying patients reported less pain on the first postoperative day, scoring 2.6 against 3.4 on the visual scale used, and their procedures needed less X-ray time, at 81.5 seconds against 95.2 seconds in the comparison. Surgeons also rated the side position more comfortable. Vertebral height loss at six months matched between groups, and the only complication was silent cement leakage in one patient per group. The authors endorse the side-lying approach as a safe, effective alternative for patients who cannot lie prone.
pmc-13314454:
Michaela Reimann-Ayiköz leads a 2026 study of how fetal hormones and mother mood jointly shape baby language. Language growth rests on both biology and home life, and most past work looked at estradiol and testosterone, but DHEA, the main fetal steroid, may be the sharper early marker.

The team measured fetal DHEA and asked about mother mood at eight weeks after birth, then tested the language grasp of the babies at 12 months. Low mother mood after birth, even below illness level, can cut how much mothers talk with babies in the tuned speech babies learn from. The study split results by sex, since hormone effects may differ in boys and girls. Its joint view links womb chemistry and home mood to the first steps toward words.
pmc-13314754:
Jefferson Li and co-workers test whether a half elbow replacement restores the natural slant of the joint, in their 2026 study. For elbow arthritis, a hemiarthroplasty can work only if the implant copies the native anatomy of the arm bone.

The team stripped six cadaver arms and took straight X-rays to map the natural angle of the lower arm bone. They then fitted an uncemented implant held by screws inside the bone canal and took fresh X-rays. Angles were compared between the canal and the joint axis before, and the canal and the implant spin line after. The arms came from five men and one woman, as noted in the report. The check shows whether screw-fixed implants can match the valgus angle the elbow needs to move true.
pmc-13315054:
Jody G. Abrams and co-workers survey people with thyroid eye disease on how it wears down daily life, in a 2026 paper. The disease can harm sight and disfigure the face, and its toll runs past eye signs into work, sleep, and mood.

The ElevaTED survey ran in July and August 2024 with 204 adult US residents who said a doctor had diagnosed the disease, as the design states. Mean age was 50 years and a share of 74 percent were female in the figures given. Nearly all had symptoms in the past month, at a share of 93 percent as reported. Patients classed those symptoms as mild, moderate, or severe at shares of 23, 58, and 18 percent in the report. People juggled a mean of 6 symptoms in all, as counted. The census presses care teams to treat life impact, not just eyes.
pmc-13316254:
Maria Julieta Corazon V. Germar leads a Philippine panel whose 2026 guideline covers screening for disorders that arise before birth. Such conditions are a major cause of newborn deaths in the Philippines and account for a notable share of deaths in young children. The guideline supports the national Universal Health Care Act.

Developed with the GRADE approach and an evidence-to-decision framework, the work drew on systematic searches and appraisals of local and international guidance. De novo reviews were added where needed. A multisectoral panel weighed benefits, harms, cost-effectiveness, patient values, feasibility and equity. Eleven recommendations resulted, aimed at pregnant Filipino women without symptoms, their clinicians, policymakers and health institutions, with a web tool planned for wider use.
pmc-13316454:
Cuiping Shi and colleagues report a 2026 food science study on low-protein cookies, a medical food for people with kidney disease or inherited metabolic faults who must limit protein. Starting from low-protein steamed bun flour, they tuned the recipe and oven heat step by step.

Fish oil and corn oil together gave the firmest dough and cookies in their tests. Mid-range baking from 120 to 160 degrees Celsius gave the best quality overall in the reported ranges. Hardness rose, held, then fell as heat climbed toward 200 degrees. Cookies baked at 160 degrees carried just 0.27 grams of protein per 100 grams in the measured batch. Storage and fat release also shifted with heat, guiding makers toward stable, tasty products.
pmc-13316654:
Daniel Ramos and colleagues present a 2026 method for forecasting building electricity use five minutes at a time, tuned to context. A building's day has many moods, and a single prediction tool rarely wins in all of them, so the system first sorts moments into contexts, then picks its tool per context.

A decision tree reads sensor and energy patterns to name each context, and a learning bandit algorithm chooses between neighbor-based and neural network forecasts for each. In the third context, error rates were 3.54 percent for the neighbor method and 4.79 percent for the network in the reported tests, with the ranking flipping in the fourth. Matching tool to moment, they argue, sharpens control and storage planning.
pmc-13316754:
Jing Qiao and colleagues built, in a 2026 dental study, a three-metal nano coating that protects crowns from germs and biofilms, a common cause of early crown failure. The mix of tin, silver, and aluminum was made with sound waves plus pressure, then blasted onto resin and metal crowns.

Lab checks confirmed even, crystal-structured layers that stuck well to crown surfaces. Germ killing rose with dose, and biofilm growth fell by up to 85.4 percent against E. coli in the reported tests. Human gum cells stayed healthy at working doses, and repeated salt water washing left the layer intact and active. The wash-proof coating could lengthen crown life by guarding the gum line seam.
pmc-13318654:
Qing Xin, Fei Xu, and Jie Wu report a 2026 mouse and cell study of β-caryophyllene. The compound is tested against ischaemic stroke injury. Earlier work suggested it protects the brain, but the mechanism was unclear. The team focused on a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis.

Mice with temporary blocked brain blood flow received the compound. Treated mice showed smaller damaged areas and better movement. In brain tissue and microglial cells, the compound cut pyroptosis and sugar breakdown. It also lowered two lactylation marks on histone proteins, H3K9la and H3K18la. Adding lactate reversed much of the protection. Blocking a related enzyme copied the benefit, pointing to a lactate-to-pyroptosis pathway as the target.
pmc-13318754:
Rongjin Ma and colleagues review, in 2026, how acetylation helps plants remember stress and tolerate new ones. Plants now face repeated and combined stresses such as drought, salt, and heat. A first stress can leave traces that speed later responses. The chemical marks behind that memory are the focus here.

Acetylation is fast, reversible, and tied to cell metabolism. The review covers marks on chromatin that bookmark genes for later use. It also covers acetylation of signalling and energy proteins outside the nucleus. Compartments from chloroplasts to mitochondria each play a part. Enzyme pairs that add and remove marks act differently by crop and context. The authors assess breeding and editing strategies built on these marks.
pmc-13319654:
Fangyuan Long and co-authors review smart software for throat cancer care in a 2026 article on a hard to spot illness. This cancer of the food pipe often grows in secret, varies a lot from case to case, and carries a poor outlook. Early checks, exact diagnosis, and calls on how well treatment works all stay hard in daily care.

Learning software now helps read scope views and scans, and in test settings some tools match expert readers at finding early growths. Models that mix scan traits, lab signs, and case facts also help sort risk and guess drug response. Most proof still comes from past records at single sites, so wide testing and clearer models are still needed.
pmc-13319954:
Sara Merkaj and co-authors review what is known about sexual harm after planned spine surgery in a 2026 article. Spine surgery is among the most common operations in the world, and rates are rising among older adults. Sexual health shapes life quality, yet patients and surgeons rarely raise it, and proof on harm after surgery stays scattered.

Fifteen studies met the rules for a close look, and most were small, single center, and backward looking. Most found no drop or a gain in sexual function after surgery, while a clear minority found a drop. A back pain form was the main tool used, though it misses much of sexual health. Sex specific, forward looking work with fuller scales is badly needed.
pmc-13320254:
Mohammad Badra and co-authors report one case from 2026 in which a benign bone tumor in the chest spine was removed by keyhole surgery. The tumor type is benign but sore, and it rarely sits in a chest facet joint. Wide open surgery there can harm soft tissue and shake spine steadiness, so a full keyhole route through a tiny cut was tried instead.

A 26 year old woman had two years of upper back pain that spread to her front chest wall. Scans showed a small hollow spot at one chest facet joint with no spread to the cord space. Keyhole tools ground the lump away to healthy bleeding bone through a cut about a finger width wide. She felt relief at once, walked the same day, and left hospital the next day pain free.
pmc-13320454:
Satsuki Ito and co-authors model paths from symptoms to work hours in schizophrenia in a 2026 study. Work life often shrinks in this illness, yet how odd beliefs and voices, thinking loss, and daily living skills jointly set work hours was tangled. Data from 396 patients and 1109 healthy peers gave work hours, thinking scores, and social function grades for a path model test.

Patients worked fewer hours and scored lower on thinking and daily skills than peers in the group checks. Thinking loss and social function each tracked weekly hours among patients. The path model found routes from core symptoms to work hours that ran through daily living skills, with or without a thinking loss step between. Care that lifts daily skills may thus lift work life.
pmc-13320554:
Rodolfo Furlan Damiano leads a 2026 long-term cohort study on early signs of later suicide attempts in Brazil. Suicide attempts in youth are common, often repeat, and strongly predict later death, yet early roots are poorly mapped outside rich countries. The Brazilian High-Risk Cohort followed children from ages 6 to 14 for 15 years.

Of 2060 young people with full data, 309, or 15.0 percent, reported an attempt during follow-up. Factors from genes, birth, family life, hardship, thinking skills, and mental health were all tested together for whether attempts occurred, when they began, and how often they recurred. The team also weighed how much changeable risks matter at population level.
pmc-13321454:
Lena M. Lundgren and co-authors evaluate a Swedish training programme for social workers on substance use care in a 2026 study. Municipal social workers in Sweden carry legal duty for assessing substance use disorders and planning care, yet training in proven methods is limited. The study covered 173 workers from 64 municipalities across five cohorts from 2021 to 2023.

Starting skill was rated low to moderate, and longer work experience went with higher self-rated skill. Wide knowledge gaps appeared, above all in psychosocial methods and digital tools for assessment. After training, knowledge rose in every module, with gains from small to very large. The biggest jumps came in technology use and combined bio-psycho-social care.
pmc-13322854:
Rongchen Liu, Jiahui Liu and Linrong Li compare commercial Chinese herbal mixtures for loss of appetite in young children, in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Their search found 141 randomised trials with 16,963 patients and 49 products, drawn from Chinese and international databases up to April 2024.

Different products led on different outcomes, covering overall response, weight gain and haemoglobin levels. Huaji Oral Solution ranked high for overall effect, Erpixing Granules for weight, and Jianbaoling Granules for haemoglobin, in the authors' comparisons against control care. Reported side effects were mostly mild across products. The authors still ask for larger and stronger multi-centre trials before firm advice can rest on these rankings.
pmc-13323154:
Carolin Luisa Kramer and colleagues compare bacterial stress resistance from German schools and the International Space Station, in a 2026 study tied to an antimicrobial surface experiment run in both settings. Habitat shapes how microbes endure stress and swap resistance traits.

Isolates from both sites were tested for antibiotic resistance and wider stress profiles. No detectable rise in antibiotic resistance appeared under the tested conditions in either space or school isolates in their assays. Space adds strain from weightlessness, radiation and drying, plus tight cleaning routines in a closed cabin. The authors argue that multi-stress checks matter for keeping crews safe on longer missions and for designing control methods that hold up off Earth.
pmc-13323854:
Necmiye Şengel leads a rat study comparing ozone delivery routes after spinal cord ischaemia, published in 2026, asking whether remote organs gain protection. Restoring blood flow after aortic clamping can injure not only the cord but also liver, lungs and brain through circulating mediators.

Thirty rats split into five groups: control, injury alone and injury plus ozone given into the spinal canal, the abdomen or the rectum. The injury model clamped the lower aorta for thirty minutes, then released it for two hours of reperfusion. Tissue checks in cord, liver, lung and brain judged which route best limited damage, testing ozone's antioxidant and circulation claims across organs at once.
pmc-13324454:
Lei Feng and co-authors trace how the gene NDRG1 drives oral squamous cell carcinoma growth in a 2026 multiomics study. This cancer of the mouth is highly aggressive, and the forces behind its spread remain partly unclear.

The team combined bulk, single-cell, and spatial gene data with lab and animal tests. A regulatory chain, MSTRG.47889 with miR-1299 and NDRG1, sped tumor growth and invasion while weakening cell adhesion. Cells high in NDRG1 grew in tumors, shifted toward a partial transition state, and sat in low-oxygen niches. Those zones may work with vessel cells through ANGPTL4 and CDH5 signals. NDRG1 stands out as a possible target for diagnosis and treatment.
pmc-13325154:
Liwei Zhao and colleagues trace how heat processing reshapes the chemistry of bitter almond in a 2026 study. The old remedy holds amygdalin, which can release toxic hydrogen cyanide, so heating before use is a safety step.

Two lab routes mapped scent parts and non-scent parts after steaming, boiling, or frying. The scent scan found 30 compounds, with d-limonene and linalool rising under steam. The wider scan found 199 compounds, of which 80 shifted a lot. Steaming broke down the most, with 45 down against 19 for boiling. The cyanide-linked prunasin split into benzaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide gas. That split shows how heat makes the seed safer at the molecular level.
pmc-13325454:
Jiakang Ma and co-authors find a tumor cell group that shields esophageal cancer from immunotherapy in a 2026 study. More than half of patients fail to gain a major response from chemo plus checkpoint drugs.

Multi-omics work spotted cancer cells rich in SPP1, apart from the known SPP1 source in macrophages. These cells raised PD-L1 through mTORC1 and STAT3, tired out killer T cells through CD44 signaling, and bent macrophages toward a suppressive state. Spatial maps showed the cells organizing sheltered niches inside tumors. Blocking SPP1 teamed well with anti-PD-1 therapy in models. Drug screens also flagged microtubule and kinase blockers as weapons against these cells.
pmc-13326354:
Kai Wheeler and team report health research priorities found by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander groups in Queensland, Australia. Their 2026 study, the Indigenous Health Research Priorities study, responds to a history in which Australian health research leaned on deficit-based approaches and overlooked local knowledges and leadership. Using local methodology and a participatory action framework, groups across Far North, North, Central, and South-East Queensland set goals with a focus on early life, perinatal, and family health.

Goals emerged in two phases: initial yarning sessions followed by Delphi workshops in which groups refined their lists. The study centers local voices as the authority on what research should address, arguing that self-determined goals can orient future work toward strengths, kinship, and knowledge systems rather than deficits alone. The authors present the resulting agenda as a foundation for research that serves local wellbeing on local terms.
pmc-13327454:
Dirk Müller and co-authors test whether knee-specific details sharpen risk forecasts after knee replacement in a 2026 machine learning study. Most forecast tools use only age, weight, and other illnesses, ignoring the state of the joint itself. The team compared both approaches on 1,207 operations done at one center between 2018 and 2022.

Models were built with a stacked boosting method that joins XGBoost and CatBoost, aiming at lasting pain, any complication, and major complications one year after surgery. Adding joint measures such as leg alignment and range of motion, taken from X-rays and exams, clearly improved forecasts for complications. Fairer risk adjustment could help hospitals compare results and counsel patients with more honest odds.
pmc-13327654:
Dikai Bei, Kaifeng Gan, and Binhui Chen hunt for gene markers of neck disc wear in a 2026 study, working with Jie Li. Cervical disc degeneration is often caught late, so early gene signs could help. Data came from a public expression database, comparing worn discs with healthy ones.

They found 71 genes with altered activity, 50 raised and 21 lowered, and the changes clustered in inflammation pathways. Machine learning screens plus lab checks on surgical disc samples singled out CDKN3, SLC22A4, and SYDE1 as key marker candidates. Immune cell profiling tied the genes to shifts in which immune cells enter disc tissue, hinting that immune activity helps drive the wear process.
pmc-13327854:
Elena Campione and colleagues report how an allergy drug reshaped skin microbes in a rare skin disease in a 2026 case report and literature review. A 35-year-old woman with Netherton syndrome, present since birth, had eczema, patterned scaly skin, and severe itching. Swabs from sore areas were taken before dupilumab treatment and after one month and one year.

At the start, skin microbe variety was low, with Pantoea and Pseudomonas types dominating. After a year on the drug, variety rose, Staphylococcus types led, and Malassezia grew more common, a mix closer to healthy skin. Her symptoms eased in step with the microbial shift, suggesting the drug restores skin balance as well as calming inflammation.
pmc-13330554:
Pascal Rosendahl and team revived voltage-gated potassium channels as an epilepsy drug target. Their 2026 review recalls that KV7.2/3 channels were later found to be the target of flupirtine and retigabine, whose clinical use ended after decades or six years, before their scope was explored. Market withdrawals across 2017 and 2018 slowed research and left a gap for KV7.2/3 patients and off-label users.

Failure of these drugs might suggest dropping the class, given class toxicity ideas and competitive markets. Yet evidence built up that toxicity of both compounds is not built into KV7.2/3 modulators but comes from an oxidation-sensitive metabophore, and epilepsy from KV7.2/3 channelopathies might be best treated with such modulators. Using retrometabolic design to rebuild the labile carbamate structure and central substituted ring, azetukalner emerged from its unlucky forerunners with better metabolic stability, potency, and blood-brain barrier penetration. The review details its synthesis, properties, and results.
pmc-13331454:
Moez Alnazeer and co-authors report a single-center retrospective study from 2026 comparing two ways of guiding catheter ablation for premature ventricular contractions. One group had robotic magnetic navigation, the other standard hand-guided ablation, in patients treated from 2019 to 2023.

The main comparison covered 86 patients, 67 robotic and 19 manual, after seven robotic cases that switched mid-procedure were set aside. Procedure time, X-ray time, symptom relief at one month, and complication rates were all similar between the two groups. Use of strong rhythm drugs fell in both groups. The authors caution that later heart function and beat counts were not tracked, so the findings mainly address how the procedures run and how patients feel soon after.
pmc-13331954:
Seok Lee and colleagues report 2026 real-world results for ponatinib in Korean patients whose blood cancers had already resisted earlier drugs. The study followed 148 people across 24 sites: most had chronic myeloid leukemia in chronic, accelerated, or blast phase, and 33 had Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Many had failed prior kinase-blocking drugs or carried the T315I mutation. Most started at 45 milligrams once daily, often as third-line therapy.

In chronic-phase leukemia, about four in ten patients reached a major molecular response, and earlier use gave stronger deep responses than later use. Response rates were higher still in the lymphoblastic leukemia group. Rash, high blood pressure, and fever were the most common side effects, and two vascular blockage events occurred. The authors judge the drug usefully effective with manageable safety in this hard-to-treat group, with early high-dose use looking most promising.
pmc-13332154:
Francesca Bernini and colleagues map the gene patterns of Irish Wolfhounds sampled worldwide in a 2026 study. The breed has a tangled past and a small population, which raises worry about lost diversity and inbreeding. The team typed 96 dogs from 23 countries with a canine gene chip and ran several population analyses. Measures of population size, gene mixing, and variation all pointed the same way: diversity is limited.

Runs of identical gene stretches were mostly short, and 40 dogs carried stretches longer than eight megabases, while none passed sixteen. That pattern fits long-term demographic change and past selection better than recent inbreeding alone. Twenty-six shared stretches appeared in at least 85 percent of dogs, marking regions under selection. Breeders gain a genome-wide guide for guarding diversity and health in a breed shaped by closed mating.
pmc-13332854:
Johnny Wang and colleagues study 2026 racial differences in mental health after prostate cancer, using the All of Us Research Program. Life after prostate cancer carries substantial mental distress, yet racial gaps in mental health outcomes are not fully mapped. The team used adjusted regression models to test links between race and depressive episodes after diagnosis, plus patient-reported quality of life, mental health, and social contentment. The cohort came from a diverse national sample.

The cross-sectional study drew on the National Institutes of Health All of Us Controlled Tier Dataset, version 8. Adults with record-documented prostate cancer who completed surveys after diagnosis were included, comparing non-Hispanic White and Black participants. Models adjusted for age, time since diagnosis, and other factors detailed in the full paper. The work helps clinicians see which survivor groups carry heavier mental and social burdens and where support should be targeted after prostate cancer.
pmc-13333154:
