Navid R Reshadi Nezhad and colleagues review 2026 current concepts in platelet-rich plasma therapy for tennis elbow, through tissue and clinical lenses. Lateral epicondylitis is a degenerative tendon disease of the extensor carpi radialis brevis tendon. Most patients improve with conservative care, yet a subset faces chronic, refractory symptoms needing advanced interventions. Platelet-rich plasma has come up as a hopeful biologic treatment, giving a self-sourced pool of growth factors that may boost tendon healing.

Chronic tennis elbow shows few inflammatory cells and increased programmed cell death, suggesting limited intrinsic healing. Plasma therapy delivers growth factors including VEGF, PDGF, IGF, FGF, and TGF-beta, each with pro-healing properties in lab and animal work. The review weighs basic science, animal studies, and clinical outcomes together. Clinicians gain a measured view of when plasma therapy might help a stubborn tendon and where evidence still falls short.
pmc-13333354:
Lise Paprzycki and colleagues used a mouse model in 2026 to ask how repeated low-oxygen episodes reshape leg muscles. The pattern is common in COPD patients whose blood oxygen dips repeatedly rather than staying low. Muscle failure is a burden in lung disease, and this on-off pattern had been little studied.

Mice breathed 10 percent oxygen for 8 hours a day, and the team tracked fiber size, growth regulators, and building genes in the slow-twitch soleus and the fast tibialis anterior. Blood haematocrit rose as expected. By day 35 the soleus had grown, mostly in its slow fibers, while the fast muscle showed no growth and its building genes Myod1 and Myog faded over time. Oxygen sensor HIF1 signals rose early, and the growth brake myostatin fell, though its machinery answered differently in each muscle. The authors conclude the same stress fattens slow muscle while undermining fast muscle upkeep.
pmc-13335154:
Devin M. Saunders and colleagues model 2026 stimulus-induced stress responses in brain immune-like cells using a store-bought stem cell CRISPRi line. One widely sold line, the AICS-0090 dCas9-KRAB line from the Allen Institute, has full checks behind it for genome soundness and stem cell power. Whether it can model special immune cell types like microglia, and gauge their working responses to disease-linked triggers, is still not settled.

The authors tested whether the line can grow into brain immune-like cells, knock genes down well, and react to outside stressors. Growth capacity was checked by gene tests, flow cytometry, and cell staining, which showed steady microglial surface markers at both early and late timepoints. Gene knockdown power held up both for single genes and in pooled CRISPRi screens.
pmc-13336454:
Kang Liu and colleagues present 2026 light-activated TVA lipid nano-bits for boosting immune blockade therapy. Nutrient tuning of tumor immune defense beats making new immune drugs, yet clinic use is slowed by low oral uptake. The authors put forward nano-food care: IR780 packed in lipid nano-bits with a blend of TVA and stearin.

The blend melts at 40.5 degrees Celsius and acts as gated phase-change stuff, fired by near-IR light to release TVA. Versus oral free TVA, these nano-bits increase in-tumor TVA levels by 21.86-fold. These nano-bits show light-heat killing and spark defense. Later, the freed TVA not only cuts CD8-positive T cell tiredness by switching on cAMP-PKA-CREB axis, but lowers PD-1 levels in T cells. It also raises PD-L1 levels in tumor cells, boosting PD-L1 blockade therapy in hot and cold models.
pmc-13337454:
Yan Pan, Fangjian Chen, and Yanzhong Wang test whether immune gene variants predispose people to immune thrombocytopenia in a 2026 evidence synthesis combining systematic review, meta-analysis, and trial sequential checks. In this disorder the immune system destroys platelets. The team searched major databases through December 7, 2025, for studies of CD16, CD32, CD40, and CD152 variants, adding trial sequential analysis to check evidence strength.

Thirty-three articles entered the synthesis. One variant stood out: the FcγRIIIA-158 F/V change was associated with the disease across every genetic model, with the strongest pooled odds ratio of 2.61 in the homozygous comparison. Seven other variants showed no significant link. The result narrows genetic suspicion to a single receptor variant worth deeper study.
pmc-13337754:
Tingru Chen and colleagues review natural products for diabetic eye disease in a 2026 article. Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of vision loss in working-age adults. Damage is framed here as breakdown of the network that controls mitochondrion quality inside retinal cells.

Under lasting high blood sugar, that network moves from strained balance toward collapse, bringing oxidation, inflammation, and injury to the retinal nerve and vessel unit. Natural products act on many targets and may restore fusion and cleanup balance in stage-specific ways. Low uptake and poor passage into the retina limit use, so targeted nano carriers are discussed as a way forward.
pmc-13338254:
Fan Mo, Yan Yi, and Katsuya Yano show how sweet potato unlocks soil potassium for neighbors in a 2026 plant study. Sweet potato needs much potassium yet grew well in vermiculite without added fertilizer. Which soil pool it taps was unknown.

Sweet potato and water spinach, both in the Ipomoea genus, grew normally in vermiculite alone by freeing fixed potassium between mineral layers. Soybean and barley could not do this. Root maps showed sweet potato gathering more potassium within seven days as reported. When soybean grew beside sweet potato, its potassium and growth rose too, revealing a shared benefit from one crop's root activity.
pmc-13338854:
Helen S. Clifford, Aniruddha Seal, and Laura Gagliardi test a new simulation method for light-driven proton jumps in a 2026 study. Excited molecules rearrange bonds in trillionths of a second, and models must stay accurate yet fast. Linearized pair-density functional theory is assessed as that middle path.

Simulations followed 10-hydroxybenzo[h]quinoline, a standard test molecule that moves a proton after absorbing light. The method placed the jump at 16 femtoseconds, matching the latest fluorescence experiments closely as reported. Path analysis showed the proton itself driving the move. Strong agreement suggests the method can handle broader light-driven chemistry in dynamics studies.
pmc-13339054:
Yi Yang and colleagues study how young adults view their future selves alongside mental illness in a 2026 analysis. Feeling connected to a future self and judging that self kindly are two separate outlooks. Both may cut across many disorders rather than belong to one.

Data came from wave 8 of a Zurich youth study with 1,180 people around age 20 as reported. Factor analysis split illness into shared and domain parts. Both future outlooks linked negatively to inner distress, attention, psychosis-like, substance, and aggression dimensions. Single-question measures limit strength, the authors note, so richer tools should test this broad pattern again.
pmc-13339154:
Morgan S. Young and colleagues tune biodegradable plastics through chain geometry in a 2026 study. Polyhydroxyalkanoates could replace low-density polyethylene, but matching its softness, stretch, and heat tolerance is hard. Ring-opening growth of a methyl-bearing monomer gave a tunable family.

New zinc sandwich catalysts varied chain regularity from 45 to 79 percent as reported, with melting points from 141 to 174 degrees. Middle regularity grades near 73 and 75 percent stretched much like polyethylene in the reported tests. Those grades melt higher while still degrading, making them candidate substitutes for a plastic that recycling handles poorly.
pmc-13339754:
Laurens A. van Kleef and co-authors link chemicals in urine that come from volatile organic compounds to fatty liver disease, and test one of them in lab-grown liver tissue. Their 2026 study analyses a United States population survey from 2017 to 2020, using ultrasound-based liver measures in 2,004 participants after exclusions.

Higher combined metabolite levels were associated with higher risk of metabolic fatty liver disease and of its at-risk inflammatory form, driven mainly by two metabolites, while a third showed the opposite pattern. No link appeared with liver stiffness itself, though a ratio between two styrene-related metabolites tracked the stiffer, at-risk groups. In human liver organoids, that metabolite, phenylglyoxylic acid, increased the number and size of fat droplets. The authors suggest poor breakdown of styrene and ethylbenzene may let this compound accumulate inside liver cells and drive fat build-up.
pmc-13341054:
Matias Karvonen and colleagues read five years of incident reports in 2026 from a Finnish forensic psych hospital. Nurses in forensic psych wards face violence that harms health and may hurt safe care. The team read prevention notes in staff reports and counted how often each prevention theme appeared.

Prevention formed layers. They were stable clinical care, staffing and work plans, and early warning routines. Kind talks and de-escalation, safe rooms and tech aids, rules and outside risk control, plus clear notes, debriefs, and learning from events completed the layers. The findings show that clinical, work, and place factors join together in stopping violence on forensic wards.
pmc-13341454:
Less armpit surgery for early breast cancer is tracked across China by Jiang Wu and colleagues in a 2026 multicenter cohort study. The database held 53,758 women with node-negative-looking, stage T1-3 disease treated between 2013 and 2022, comparing sentinel node biopsy against full axillary dissection.

Sentinel biopsy use climbed from 18.8% to 75.3% in node-negative patients. In that group, five-year regional recurrence matched between approaches at about 1%. With positive nodes, recurrence ran higher after sentinel biopsy only in breast-conserving surgery (4.99% versus 1.27%), especially with fast-growing tumors, while mastectomy patients showed no clear difference. De-escalation looks safe for most, with caveats.
pmc-13341554:
Brain scans before treatment predict who gains from magnetic stimulation for tinnitus, in a 2026 study by Zhongling Ding's team. Sixty-four patients got a 2-week course of magnetic stimulation, with 18 healthy controls for contrast and detailed MRI scans first.

Thirty-six of the patients (56.25%) responded to the treatment. Ten local features across four brain networks set responders apart from non-responders, and a machine learning model built on them reached an AUC score of 0.85 in cross-validation testing. Extra analysis showed which features counted most. Pre-screening by scan could spare unlikely responders a useless course of sessions.
pmc-13341654:
CT signs and surgical findings in gut ischemia are compared by Andrea Cavallaro and colleagues in a 2026 single-center cohort. The study gathered 102 adults with CT-confirmed acute mesenteric ischemia admitted from January 2018 through February 2026.

Patients were sorted into arterial, venous, non-occlusive, and mechanical subtypes, and eight set scan findings were scored, from bowel wall gas to free air and poor wall enhancement. The main endpoint was dead or irreversibly damaged bowel found at surgery. Because this emergency kills largely through delay, knowing which scan features truly forecast unsalvageable bowel could sharpen decisions on when and how widely to operate.
pmc-13342854:
Yunus Emre Genc and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, how much doctors agree when reading bladder filling tests in children with spina bifida. Such urodynamic tests guide care for neurogenic bladder problems, yet scoring detrusor overactivity and bladder stretch can depend on who reads the tracing.

Records covered 100 children tested between 2020 and 2025, each read independently by four pediatric urologists and three neuro-urology specialists. Readers reached at least 80 percent agreement in most cases, but kappa scores showed only moderate agreement for overactivity and weak agreement for compliance. The authors call for shared scoring rules and larger multi-center work to make readings more consistent.
pmc-13343154:
Jiaqian Rao and co-authors built a rapid test for avian polyomavirus in 2026, the agent behind budgerigar fledgling disease. Sick nestlings can show swollen abdomens, missing down feathers, and bleeding under the skin, with high death rates, so parrot breeders need fast and accurate screening outside big laboratories.

Their real-time amplification assay targets the viral large T antigen gene and finishes within 25 minutes at 41 degrees. It detects as few as 256 copies per microliter, ignores four other bird viruses, and repeats steadily across runs. On 63 suspected parrot cases the new test matched standard qPCR on every call, offering field-ready screening for flocks.
pmc-13343354:
Silvia Goss and a large team track support needs among people who lost someone during the COVID-19 pandemic, in a 2026 longitudinal UK survey. Grief harms from that period are well known, but how needs changed over time, which help people used, and whether it truly helped remained unclear.

Four survey waves followed participants from 711 at baseline to 185 at 25 months after loss. Early needs ran highest for managing grief, anxiety and low mood, and loneliness, then eased over time except among those with prolonged grief symptoms. Family and friends carried most support, yet a third of the high-risk group used no formal help in year one. Matching varied support types to personal needs is the core lesson.
pmc-13344154:
Richik Chakraborty, Nina Shenoy, and Rahul Bhandary review quantum dots for gum disease care in 2026. Periodontitis destroys ligament and jaw bone as biofilms resist standard cleaning and local drugs. These semiconductor crystals, just 1 to 10 nanometers wide, glow brightly, hold their light, and accept tailored surface chemistry.

Four uses stand out. Clinics can sense spit and gum fluid markers at tiny levels and image germs live. They can deliver drugs such as curcumin on light or chemical cues. They can also coat implants to fight bacteria and knit bone. Carbon-based versions ease the heavy-metal toxicity worry, yet instability in the mouth and missing long-term animal data block clinics. Standard recipes and safety proof must come next.
pmc-13345654:
Shivam Chandra and colleagues compared in 2026 patient education sheets written by artificial intelligence with those from professional societies, across gut, surgery, eye, and anaesthesia topics. Society sheets often read above recommended literacy levels, which can shut out patients who most need clear guidance before a procedure.

The team paired 100 topics, 25 per specialty, and scored each version for reading level, information quality, clarity, and actionability using standard tools. In surgery, the machine-written sheets read at a lower level and scored higher on quality and clarity, while other specialties showed their own patterns. The comparison helps societies decide where machine drafting could widen access, and where expert review must still guard accuracy.
pmc-13345954:
Alexandr Klioutchnikov and colleagues built in 2026 a head-mounted microscope that films brain activity across several cortical layers at once in freely moving mice. Earlier head-mounted multiphoton microscopes could record only one layer at a time, limiting how researchers watch circuits that span the cortex.

Combining two- and three-photon excitation through multiple fibres, the lightweight device images five vertically separated planes near-simultaneously, with remote focusing for fine depth adjustment. Its onboard two-channel detector works in light and darkness and can follow the same cell populations over weeks in the visual cortex. The tool lets scientists link activity across layers to behaviour in animals that move and explore naturally.
pmc-13347154:
Bijin Luo and colleagues reviewed in 2026 biomarkers for sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle mass, strength, and function that erodes independence in later life. Diagnosis remains tricky because guidelines differ in criteria and tools, delaying recognition until weakness is already advanced.

The narrative review groups candidate markers into biochemical, imaging-based, and physical performance categories, weighing which are established and which are still emerging. Good markers could catch muscle decline earlier, track its course, and show whether treatments work. By sorting a fast-growing literature, the review helps clinicians and researchers choose markers that are practical, reliable, and ready for testing in real clinics.
pmc-13347654:
Fan Wu and colleagues model how coal grains handle methane. Their study was published in 2026. It covers both soaking up and releasing the gas. Samples came from the Guobei Mine. Tests ran at steady heat. Pressure and grain size both varied. Maths models were built for two grain shapes. One shape was a cylinder. The other was a sphere. Density-gradient ideas shaped both models.

Smaller grains took up more gas. They also took it up faster. Higher starting pressure raised the soaked limit. It also shortened the time to balance. Both shapes gave near-identical fits. Pressure inside grains followed a shared path. It ran from fast surface response to full balance. The pattern helps gas control and methane recovery planning.
pmc-13348054:
Inne Vanreusel and colleagues link right heart function to fitness and life quality in adults born with heart defects, in a 2026 study. Fifty-five patients had detailed ultrasound of the right ventricle from four walls, a cycling fitness test. Quality surveys, then were split between usual care and a 16-week home program of interval cycling plus strength work.

Right heart measures tracked peak oxygen use and several life quality scores at the start, covering body function, health views, and a visual health scale in the reported links. Fitness, strength, and life quality all rose after home training, though 39 percent of the training group stuck poorly to the plan, a real-world caveat for home rehab.
pmc-13349054:
Elizabeth M Hennen and colleagues test whether high blood pressure deepens bone loss after estrogen loss, in a mouse study published in 2026. Twelve-month-old females had ovaries removed or left intact, then six weeks of angiotensin infusion to raise pressure. Bone density, femur shape, and breaking strength were tracked before and after each stage.

Ovary removal alone cut whole-body density, yet pressure plus removal together thinned thigh cortical bone and weakened both thigh and spine beyond either hit alone in the reported tests. Spongy bone losses added up in the combined group, which hit the lowest values, backing extra fracture care for postmenopausal women with hypertension.
pmc-13349754:
Majd Mohsen and colleagues report a rare itchy skin disease in a man with several long illnesses, in a case report from Palestine issued in 2026. A 55-year-old man admitted with failing heart, type 2 diabetes, kidney failure. Overactive parathyroid glands bore widespread papules, some grown into domed lumps with hard central plugs, and skin samples were stained to trace what pushed through the surface.

Tissue showed cupped surface dips with debris and altered collagen forced out through the skin, sealing a first diagnosis of acquired reactive perforating collagenosis in the account. Creams, allergy drugs, and moisturisers plus body illness care gave only slight itch relief after one month, with lumps unchanged.
pmc-13349854:
Raffaella Greco and co-authors told in 2026 of a landmark year for cellular therapy. The European transplant activity survey passed one million stem cell transplants tallied since 1990 and twenty thousand CAR-T treatments since 2018. The 2024 survey captures a field grown from trial rescue therapy to routine care across dozens of lands.

That year, 47,204 transplants in 43,791 patients at 688 centres across 53 lands were tallied. Allogeneic transplants rose to their top annual total, while autologous activity dipped slightly. CAR-T reached 6,082 patients, up nearly a quarter on 2023. Myeloid cancers led allogeneic uses, followed by lymphoid cancers and non-malignant ills. The survey gives policy makers a bench mark for capacity, access, and growth.
pmc-13349954:
Marcio Roberto Facanali Junior and Everson L A Artifon commented in 2026 on removing oesophageal stromal tumours through an endoscope instead of open surgery. These tumours are exceptionally rare, under 1 percent of all gastrointestinal stromal tumours, and caution has long ruled their care.

They discuss a study comparing oesophageal and stomach tumours and endoscopic versus surgical removal. The oesophageal tumours showed more ulceration, bleeding, and cell division, and patients fared worse than those with stomach tumours. The narrow food pipe, lacking an outer coat and sitting near vital structures, raises procedural risk. Their piece weighs where the gentler approach fits and where its cancer-control limits lie.
pmc-13350454:
Antti Puhakka and co-authors reviewed superficial heat therapy for women's health in a 2026 narrative review drawing on studies from 2010 onward plus clinical experience. Period pain, endometriosis pain, and aches tied to pregnancy, birth, and menopause are common and often undertreated.

Heat applied to the skin widens vessels, improves local blood flow, relaxes muscle, and dulls pain signalling, mechanisms proven in muscle pain care. Evidence gathered suggests meaningful relief for period pain and endometriosis among other conditions. A cheap, drug-free option with few risks deserves a clear place in care plans, and the review maps where proof is solid and where it thins.
pmc-13350754:
A S Kaviya Dharshini and J B Jeeva compared ways to estimate haemoglobin without a blood draw in a 2026 study using light signals from the fingertip. Twenty-one volunteers aged 20 to 54 gave readings twice in one day from a sensor device and from a smartphone camera, checked against laboratory values.

Features describing how light fades through tissue, plus age and sex, fed five machine learning models. The boosted tree model XGBoost won, matching lab values extremely closely for both signal types. Painless, instant haemoglobin checks from a phone could transform anaemia screening where laboratories are scarce.
pmc-13352054:
Jonggyu Baek leads a 2026 methods study building a population-based Z-score for MRI disease activity in knee osteoarthritis. An earlier imaging measure combined bone marrow lesion and effusion-synovitis volumes, but raw values were hard to compare across studies. Data came from Osteoarthritis Initiative projects with 1,084 participants and 6,876 observations.

Most observations, 76 percent, came from knees with scan-proven osteoarthritis. The team targeted a reference population with 25 percent prevalence and used a Box-Cox change to shape the combined metric toward a normal spread. Checks against WOMAC pain levels tested whether the score behaves sensibly over time. Age shifts the score upward, so age handling forms part of fair use.
pmc-13353054:
Kwangho Kim and colleagues set out a 2026 trial protocol comparing short and long needles for deep ultrasound-guided pharmacopuncture in acute low back pain. Early pain often fades fast, but poor early care raises relapse and chronic pain risk. Adults aged 20 to 65 years within 7 days of pain onset will receive one guided session.

Treatment injects polydeoxyribonucleotide into the deep QPI tissue plane under ultrasound, using either a 60 mm short needle or a 100 mm long needle. Group choice follows site practice rather than random draw. Pain change right after treatment is the main outcome, with movement range, felt relief share, and safety as secondary checks across centres.
pmc-13353154:
Faith E. Kidd, Cristian Vásquez Tapia Vera, and Jeffrey S. Bandar report a base-driven route to decorate amides beside their carbonyl group in 2026. Amides with a heteroatom at the alpha spot resemble amino acids and tune binding and shape, yet adding that atom after amide formation is hard. Classic two-step enolate and halogen routes usually fail.

Mild bases plus cheap 2-bromothiophenes as halogen sources run a joined sequence of proton removal, halogenation, and substitution in one flow. Oxygen, sulphur, and nitrogen partners all couple directly at the alpha carbon. The shortcut replaces multi-step builds that first assemble a decorated acid, giving chemists a modular path to varied amide products.
pmc-13354454:
Harshika Khaim Chandani and others surveyed garadacimab, a new preventive care for hereditary angioedema, in 2026. This rare inherited illness causes recurrent, maybe life-risky swelling of skin, gut, and airway driven by bradykinin. Current preventive options help many people, but a more convenient and effective choice was still needed.

Approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration in June 2024, garadacimab is a first-in-class antibody that blocks activated Factor XII, acting upstream in the kallikrein-bradykinin pathway. By intervening earlier in the cascade, it aims to prevent attacks before swelling starts. The review helps doctors and people judge where this upstream approach fits among current prophylaxis options.

pmc-13368954:

pmc-13369954:

pmc-13370754:

pmc-13370854:

pmc-13374154:

pmc-13374254:

pmc-13374854:

pmc-13375254:

pmc-13379854:

pmc-13379954:

pmc-13382754:

pmc-13385954:

pmc-13391354:

pmc-13393154:

pmc-13397054:

pmc-13400654:

pmc-13402254:

pmc-13402754:

pmc-13403054:
Salomé Rigollet and colleagues chart how to coax lignin, the woody plant polymer, toward graphite-like carbon using hydrothermal treatment plus extreme heat, including heat from concentrated sunlight. Biocarbons could replace fossil carbon in energy and environmental uses, but true graphitization demands temperatures above 2000 degrees Celsius, with heavy energy bills. Their route first pre-structures the material in hot pressurized water.

That step already yields small graphitic units of six stacked layers; pyrolysis at 800 degrees then multiplies them, making an ideal precursor. At 1800 degrees, conventional heating gave a turbostratic structure, while solar heating produced a mixed material holding a genuinely graphitic phase with tighter layer spacing alongside the disordered one. Despite sunlight intermittency, the solar route stacked graphene layers higher, a mechanistic clue for greener carbon manufacture.
pmc-13403554:
Masayuki Saito led an 11-author case report in 2026 on breast cancer that spread to the pineal gland, deep in the brain. A 59-year-old woman had surgery, radiation, and hormone therapy for a lobular breast tumor. Nine months later the cancer reached her bones, then her brain, causing headache and double vision.

Scans showed spots in three brain areas, among them the pineal gland. A scope biopsy proved the spread and showed the tumor had switched to a harder type. Gene tests found many mutations, which may open drug options. Whole-brain radiation and drug therapy followed. The case shows why odd brain spots need tissue proof.
pmc-13403754:
Igor Lakhno, Victoria Romaieva, Svitlana Pak, and Iryna Sykal charted in 2026 the push to raise midwifery in Ukraine to a university profession. Village midwives once served births, then formal schools grew in the 1700s. Soviet rule folded midwifery into nursing under doctor control, below degree level.

War since the 2022 invasion has strained services, pushed births into shelters, and raised pregnancy risks. A United Nations review found local course plans cover many core skills yet leave gaps. Ukraine now aims for bachelor, master, and doctor levels, with a Swedish partner project as a bridge. Practice drills help train staff safely amid wartime breaks.
pmc-13403954:
Sarah E. Polk led a 2026 trial that split healthy older adults into language study, exercise, both, or a busy control plan. The group held 142 adults aged 63 to 78, followed over six months. Brain scans tracked a memory area that helps tell similar memories apart.

That area shrank in groups without language study, yet held steady for language learners. Memory test scores rose in groups that exercised, while non-exercise groups stalled. Only the combined group gained both gifts: a steady memory area plus sharper test scores. The two habits seem to help in separate ways, which makes pairing them attractive for aging brains.
pmc-13407454:
Gang Luo and co-authors, in 2026, asked whether checking the heel bone's back knob before surgery helps choose the right operation for shattered heel fractures inside the joint. Gentle keyhole surgery spares soft tissue but leans on that knob, the calcaneal tuberosity, as a lever anchor; if it is itself smashed, the technique can fail.

Reviewing 118 patients treated from 2019 to 2022, the team compared selection by the standard Sanders fracture grading with selection guided by tuberosity integrity. X-ray correction and foot function scores ended up similar under both schemes. Surgery for smashed-knob fractures ran about ten minutes shorter under the new scheme, in a small subgroup. Wound problems clustered where keyhole surgery met a smashed knob, reaching every such case in one tiny subgroup against about a tenth elsewhere. The authors call the check a useful extra, pending bigger studies.
pmc-13408054:
Olivier Janjic and co-authors tell, in a 2026 case report, of a young girl whose hoarse, breathless year traced to a rare benign growth on her vocal fold. Juvenile xanthogranuloma usually appears on infants' skin and almost never in the airway, where it can threaten breathing; laryngoscopy found the growth on her left vocal fold, and it was removed endoscopically.

She remains symptom-free with no recurrence so far. Only eleven cases of upper airway or tracheal involvement have been published, with treatments ranging from tracheostomy to endoscopic excision. The authors stress complete resection and close follow-up given a notable recurrence risk, and offer the case as management guidance for a benign condition that turns dangerous purely by location.
pmc-13408254:
Joost Meijer and a large Dutch team report in 2026 on five pregnant patients treated with dupilumab for a severe blistering rash of pregnancy. The condition, pemphigoid gestationis, brings intense itching and blisters and usually forces reliance on corticosteroids. The group also gathered every published case of this off-label treatment.

All five women began with severe itching, and blistering stopped within one to four weeks in most. Two needed weekly rather than fortnightly injections for control. Steroids were stopped in three patients and cut to low doses in the rest before delivery, and every baby was born healthy. Blood antibody levels were tracked alongside symptoms. The series suggests a steroid-sparing option worth formal study, while stressing that use in pregnancy remains off label.
pmc-13408354:
Jiaqi Zhou, Lu Wu, and co-authors report in 2026 a hidden route by which doubly charged water falls apart. How water breaks up after being charged matters for radiation science and biology. Yet one rare three-piece breakup had resisted a clear account. Electron impact tests, paired with particle imaging that tracks each fragment's path, supplied the proof.

The readings point to highly excited Rydberg states of the charged water steering the breakup. Sums on how electron capture breaks such ions apart support that reading. The same thing showed up in ammonia and in strong laser fields. There, a returning electron re-excites the ion in a flash, freezing the nuclei mid-motion. Readers gain a general breakup route that doubles as an ultrafast clock. It also sharpens how scientists read radiation damage in water.
pmc-13408454:
Chloé Moran, Zeeshan Kazmi, and Stephen Ball report in 2026 a patient they believe is the first ever logged with three major conditions at once. He had a swollen belly aorta, a kidney cancer, and kidneys fused together on one side of the body. Each condition alone is a known problem in blood vessel or urinary surgery. Aneurysm and kidney cancer are also often spotted by chance on scans.

The fused kidney layout made standard planning impossible. Its blood supply and anatomy follow no normal map. Surgeons therefore joined open repair of the aneurysm with removal of part of the fused kidney in one operation. The case gives surgical teams a reference point. It helps them weigh a joined operation against staged ones, when rare anatomy meets two common but serious diagnoses.
pmc-13408954:
Quanlong Lu and colleagues image in 2026, at near-molecular resolution and in three dimensions, the membrane choreography that builds a primary cilium, the cell's antenna. Construction starts when small vesicles dock at the mother centriole and must merge into a platform for the antenna shaft. Isotropic imaging, equally sharp in every direction, let the team measure those fleeting shapes quantitatively.

Docked vesicles first swell, a step requiring the appendage protein CEP164, then fuse into curved tubular sheets and a doughnut-shaped intermediate nobody had described. Trafficking regulators sculpt those tubes, and one of them also clears a blocking cap from the centriole by direct action. As the tubes form, gate proteins of the future cilium arrive. The study rewrites the opening steps of ciliogenesis and showcases the imaging approach for other membrane puzzles.
pmc-13409954:
Kamala Tamirisa and colleagues review in 2026 why diseases of the immune system so often disturb heart rhythm. Swelling signals, stray antibodies, and scar tissue in heart muscle can upset the cells that set each beat. The review covers lupus, joint inflammation, and systemic sclerosis, three very different illnesses with shared heart risks.

Faulty rhythms discussed range from fast upper-chamber beats to dangerous lower-chamber events and slow blocked signals. Certain antibodies stretch the heart's electrical recovery time, raising risk further. Modern heart scans can spot swelling and scarring even when pumping strength looks normal. Care pairs standard rhythm drugs with firm control of the underlying immune disease, though trials aimed at immune-driven rhythm faults are still lacking.
pmc-13410554:
Henrik Fritsch and colleagues build in 2026 cow udder organoids, tiny lab-grown tissue models, to study flu infection in cattle. Flu viruses lately reached cattle, with one bird strain shed heavily in milk during United States outbreaks. The mammary gland looks like a real site of infection, raising farm and health concerns.

Grown from udder cells, the organoids kept the structure, cell types, and milk-making traits of real tissue. Bird, pig, and human flu strains all grew well inside them. Mammal H1N1 strains matched the cattle H5N1 strain, while one mild bird strain grew poorly, showing strain-specific limits. The model offers a workable base for probing udder infection in detail.
pmc-13411154:
Busra Aydin and co-workers hunt in 2026 for recycled drug candidates against breast cancer by reading gene activity networks. Breast cancer varies enormously, and current treatments can be toxic, narrow, or costly. Reusing approved drugs for new purposes offers a shortcut worth mining.

One dataset yielded over four thousand genes whose activity shifted in tumors. Layered networks of protein, gene-switch, and small-RNA links distilled those into hub genes, eleven of which tied to patient survival. The top recycled candidate was niclosamide, an old worm drug. In dish tests it cut breast cancer cell survival sharply at modest doses. A comparison compound needed far higher doses for similar effect, and mixing the two added nothing.
pmc-13413454:
Jianru Wang and colleagues model in 2026 how hidden air pockets of different sizes threaten the strength of solid rocket propellant grains. During service a grain endures cooling after curing, its own weight, and the pressure of combustion; pores left from casting can concentrate stress dangerously. The team built a three-dimensional computer model of propellant, insulation, and mould, testing voids from 30 to 100 millimetres under three load cases.

Pores raised the overall mechanical response compared with flawless grains in the simulations, with peaks near the core hole and wing grooves. Pore size mattered less for the broad pattern than for local hot spots, though an 80-millimetre pore oddly eased stress in one groove through interference. Under gravity, edge stress around pores grew with pore size, informing inspection limits.
pmc-13414554:
Vicente Fajardo-Rosas and co-authors map in 2026 the memory T cells standing guard inside human lungs, overturning a lesson drawn from mice. Mouse lung sentinels fade within months, supposedly forcing constant replenishment. Here, receptor-guided sequencing of over 87,000 T cells from forty donors traced which past pathogens each cell remembers, and whether those clones truly stay put in lung tissue.

Most donors carried resident memory cells aimed at several different pathogens at once. A large share of those clones stayed resident in lung tissue across many months and even years, directly contradicting the rapid mouse fade in this human dataset. The authors argue human lungs hold a stable, varied garrison, so vaccines that plant or boost these resident cells could give durable protection against severe lung infections.
pmc-13416154:
Gang Cheng and co-authors map chromosome folding during sperm formation at record resolution, in 2026. As mouse germ cells enter meiosis, chromosomes line up as loops on a protein axis. Two contact mapping methods tracked the change from spermatogonia to spermatocytes over time.

Large scale genome compartments faded during prophase, while local regulatory contacts survived. Reorganization began before the textbook entry point of meiosis, alongside a swap from mitotic to meiotic cohesin rings. Distinct loop positions were detected for the first time in mammalian meiosis. Their bases sit at selected CTCF anchor sites, suggesting existing loops get remodeled rather than freshly extruded.
pmc-13416754:
Abete and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a man whose heart arteries held several giant aneurysms, balloon-like swellings far wider than the normal vessel. Such giant swellings are rare, and this 62-year-old man had them in the right coronary artery and the circumflex artery. He also lived with long-term heart disease after a past heart attack, plus obesity and high blood fats.

Scans showed clots inside the swollen vessels and pressure on nearby structures. Doctors judged the layout unsafe for both open repair and stent-based repair, so the man was listed for a transplant. He received a donor heart in a standard operation and came through with no major problems. The case suggests transplant can be a workable last option when no safe repair exists.
pmc-13417254:
Kuanjiu Lei and colleagues test data cleaning and fault spotting methods for bridge and road sensors on small edge computers, in a 2026 engineering study. Sensors on structures produce gaps, jumps, drift, and noise, and field devices have little memory or power. Their workflow fills gaps, corrects jumps, reduces noise, separates responses, and flags anomalies.

Test data mixed simulations with real bridge displacement and highway strain records. Three detection methods, from a classic time series model to neural networks, were timed for speed, memory, and processor load. The comparison shows what each method costs on limited hardware, helping engineers pick tools that fit roadside boxes rather than data centres.
pmc-13417854:
Azza G Kamel and colleagues isolate a virus that infects Escherichia coli and test it as a cleaner for fresh poultry meat, in a 2026 study. Such viruses, called phages, attack bacteria with high specificity. The new phage came from poultry samples and was checked by microscopy, genome sequencing, and lab safety tests.

Under the microscope it showed the short tailed podophage form, stayed stable across heat and acidity, and killed bacteria fast in culture. Its genome held no resistance genes. Human cells tolerated high doses. Sprayed on contaminated meat, it cut bacterial counts significantly within two hours, supporting phage use for food safety.
pmc-13418354:
Mancke and colleagues ran a feedyard trial in 2026 on whether shade helps finishing steers after final sorting. Heat stress hurts cattle growth and welfare when heat load beats the body's cooling ability. At a Pacific Northwest commercial feedyard, twelve pens had shade and twelve had none.

Shaded steers drank about 15 percent less water than unshaded steers. Unshaded pens ate less feed after very hot days, while shaded pens held their intake steady. Shade also cut open-mouth breathing, the number of culled steers, and dark-cutting meat, a quality flaw. A slightly higher share of shaded steers graded choice or prime, the top meat grades. The authors present shade as a practical tool against heat stress in finishing cattle. They note gains in welfare, meat quality, and resource use during summer months.
pmc-13418554:
Marva V Foster and colleagues examine which underserved patients with chronic low back pain had used telehealth before joining a telehealth mindfulness trial, in a 2026 survey analysis. The trial recruited through a safety net hospital and a community health centre. Of 244 participants, about 71 percent had prior telehealth experience, and the analysis weighed personal, access, and neighbourhood factors.

Black and Hispanic participants had lower odds of prior telehealth use, as did part time workers. Lower comfort with video software also predicted less use, while home internet access alone did not. Neighbourhood disadvantage and rurality showed no clear links. Recruitment should budget support for first time telehealth users.
pmc-13418754:
Kei Haga and colleagues name the doorway that human sapovirus uses to enter cells. Sapovirus is a leading cause of stomach and bowel illness, yet for years no one knew which cell surface part the virus grabs. The team traced infection to CD36, a scavenger receptor found on many cell types.

Binding tests showed the virus particles grip CD36 with strength in the nanomolar range, a tight hold for such a pairing. Cells lacking the receptor resisted infection, while restoring it brought infection back. Naming the receptor ends a long search and gives drug and vaccine work a clear target. It also helps explain which tissues the virus can reach and why illness takes the form it does.
pmc-13418854:
Angel Luis Orosco-Ttamina and colleagues describe a patient who turned out to carry two slow-growing B-cell lymphomas at once. One type, marginal zone lymphoma, dominated the first picture and drew the treatment. Therapy with a bispecific antibody shrank that main disease and, in doing so, exposed a second hidden growth in the tissue.

Gene tests confirmed a clonal B-cell population, while a later probe found no sign of one common gene swap. Scans and blood tests showed spread at several sites across the body. Putting the pieces together gave a joint diagnosis of composite lymphoma rather than a single disease. The case warns care teams that a strong response in one cancer can reveal a second one hiding behind it.
pmc-13420054:
Azza O Alawad and colleagues review the heart effects of tirzepatide, a diabetes and weight drug whose benefits may reach well past blood sugar control. Type 2 diabetes and obesity raise heart risk through overlapping routes: insulin resistance, poor blood fats, steady inflammation, and vessel lining damage. Their narrative review gathers the clinical and mechanistic record on this dual-action drug.

Double signaling through two gut hormone receptors appears to help vessel lining work, raising nitric oxide supply while cutting oxidative stress. Better pumping, less harmful heart reshaping, and improved salt handling add to the case, partly apart from glucose lowering. Diet and activity remain the base of care in the review's framing. The authors also look ahead to triple-action drugs now in development.
pmc-13420154:
Kalpana Poudel-Tandukar and colleagues run a pilot randomized trial of peer-delivered mental health support for Bhutanese adults resettled in Massachusetts. Refugees carry the heaviest burden of mental illness yet use formal services the least. The program, a peer version of problem management plus, teaches practical coping steps through trained community members.

All 232 recruited participants, drawn from 116 families in the study, stayed through the whole project, a strong retention mark. Stress, anxiety, and depression were scored at the start, at six weeks, and at three months after the program. Models compared change between the peer program and control groups while adjusting for starting scores and background traits. Full retention in a wary population suggests peer delivery earns trust that clinics struggle to build.
pmc-13421254:
Silvana Kaouar leads an eleven-author team examining, in a 2026 study, how well parents and children stay in behavioural sync during play when the child has conduct problems. Synchrony — the pair's moment-to-moment coordination — supports emotional development, and the team compared children with conduct problems alone against two groups marked by callous-unemotional traits.

The study followed 234 children aged two to seven through standard play tasks scored on cooperation, communication and emotional tone. Mothers and children in the group combining callous-unemotional traits with anxiety or low mood showed weaker communication and emotional warmth at the start. Parent training then improved synchrony across all groups, and gains held for mothers at three months.
pmc-13421454:
Zeyu Liu leads a seventeen-author team proposing, in a 2026 paper, a new training principle for artificial intelligence that reads pathology slides. Cancer diagnosis by microscope remains the gold standard, yet algorithms struggle with tumour patterns that vary across patients, tissues and magnifications.

Their framework, called PASS, works with pathoentities — cells, glands and tissue structures — and deliberately shuffles them within and between samples during training. The shuffling forces the network to learn how parts relate, locally and across a whole slide. Theory supports the approach, and tests on ten datasets covering eight diseases and nine organs showed consistent gains. A rapid on-site evaluation trial in gastroenterology hints at clinical use.
pmc-13421754:
Ping Zou and six colleagues formulate, in a 2026 paper, a tablet inside a tablet that releases the painkiller ketorolac in two waves. The drug works well for moderate to severe pain but leaves the body quickly, forcing frequent doses. Their design pairs a fast outer layer for immediate relief with a slow core for the hours after.

The core's polymer blend was tuned with a factorial experiment. The best core released little drug in the first half hour yet about two thirds by twelve hours, through a mixed diffusion-and-erosion mechanism, closely matching the target profile. The finished tablet was hard, barely crumbled, and its outer layer broke apart in under fifty seconds. The authors present the system as a compliance-friendly option.
pmc-13423054:
Grace Knowles leads a team interviewing birthing parents who chose either termination or a hospice birth after a severe heart defect was found in their unborn child. Care took place at a tertiary congenital heart surgical centre between 2019 and 2023. Families there received counselling from several specialties. The study asks how that counselling felt and what shaped the final choice.

Ten of twenty eligible parents completed interviews, analysed in five stages mixing set themes with new ones. Parents valued facts that reached past clinical outcomes to family life and money, and they prized control over the decision. The team also records counsel strengths, weak spots, and the outside voices and emotions that weighed on families.
pmc-13424454:
Yuxin Zhu and three colleagues review the triglyceride–glucose index as a predictor of cardiovascular disease. The index is a simple score built from routine blood fats and sugar. The patients in view carry both type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease. Insulin resistance drives this common pairing and its heart complications, and the index offers a cheap stand-in for measuring that resistance directly.

Study after study, the reviewers find, links a higher index with more cardiovascular disease in this population, though the exact biology connecting them is not fully mapped. The review gathers the proposed mechanisms and the prediction evidence in one place. It aims to sharpen prevention and treatment strategies for a group whose quality of life suffers on several fronts.
pmc-13424554:
Santoro and colleagues test in 2026 what the bioinsecticide azadirachtin, sold as AzaMax, does to the stingless bee Nannotrigona testaceicornis, an important pollinator that meets crop sprays while foraging. A product can look safe if only deaths are counted.

Worker bees took the doses recommended for strawberry crops through contact and through food, and deaths were tracked for three days. Killing was so low that no lethal concentration could be calculated. The damage hid below that threshold: survivors showed disorganized midgut lining, lost digestive cells, fewer regenerative cells, and a vanished protective membrane in the gut. Brain cells showed more condensed chromatin, the packed form of DNA, hinting at disturbed gene regulation. The authors argue that risk checks for bioinsecticides must count such sublethal harm.
pmc-13425654:
Zhewei Ma and Yiquan Ji wrote a 2026 commentary on the translational limits of targeting Txnip, the thioredoxin-interacting protein, to improve bone health. Work they discuss ties Txnip to coordination of glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid cycle in bone, with altered levels linked to defective remodeling and slower fracture healing in older age. Blocking Txnip has been proposed alongside marrow stromal cell regeneration strategies.

Three gaps temper enthusiasm: which bone cell types drive the effect, how broadly metabolism shifts, and whether human tissue behaves like the models. The authors urge cell-specific testing before metabolic modulation enters bone therapy trials.
pmc-13425754:
Pedro Leite and co-authors map the drug-binding pocket of FabI, an enzyme bacteria need to build fatty acids, in two important pathogens. Their 2026 computational study compares FabI from Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli to find features that future antibiotics could exploit.

The team combined pharmacophore modelling, which abstracts the chemical features a drug needs, with hotspot mapping, molecular dynamics simulations, and analysis of crystal structures. Both species shared a conserved binding core involving two tyrosine residues and an alanine. Surface mapping flagged another tyrosine tied to known resistance mutations. Three further residues, differing slightly between species, emerged as unexplored contact sites. The authors propose validated consensus models to guide virtual screening for new FabI inhibitors.
pmc-13426354:
Yiqi Dong and colleagues mined published studies for acupuncture point patterns in discogenic low back pain in a 2026 data study. This pain subtype stems from disc degeneration without nerve root compression, and earlier mining work focused on disc herniation instead. Eight databases were searched for clinical studies from 2016 to 2025, yielding 57 studies using 41 distinct points.

Frequency counts, association rules, and clustering named BL40, BL25, Ashi points, EX-B2, and BL23 as the most used points. Practitioners gain an evidence map of standard prescription patterns specific to discogenic pain rather than borrowed herniation protocols.
pmc-13427554:
Chihiro Fukunaga and a large team recount, in a 2026 case report, an infection that imitated cancer of the fallopian tube. An 87-year-old woman had a routine scan that lit up near her right ovary, and a tumor marker in her blood was high. Doctors suspected tube cancer and removed the tissue in a major operation. Frozen samples during surgery showed dead, inflamed tissue with no cancer cells at all.

Lab cultures then grew Mycobacterium abscessus, a germ from soil and water that rarely infects these organs. Surgeons had already removed all diseased tissue, so she needed no antibiotics afterward. She stayed well for a year of follow-up. The case warns that scans and blood markers alone cannot separate this rare infection from cancer.
pmc-13427954:
Dickers and colleagues simulated in 2026 how bending settings affect the radiation peaks from positrons channeling through periodically bent diamond crystals. Such crystals could become compact gamma-ray light sources. Using relativistic molecular dynamics, the team varied bending amplitude and period for 530 megaelectronvolt positrons and tracked the peak's energy and strength.

Raising the bending amplitude shifted the radiation peak to lower photon energies, while shortening the period shifted it higher. Both changes also knocked more positrons out of their channels, weakening the beam. Lines of constant peak energy mapped out stable operating regions. For settings like recent experiments at the Mainz Mikrotron facility, the simulated peak sat near the expected energy. The authors conclude the peak stays usefully stable across a broad range of bending choices.
pmc-13428154:
N Tran and colleagues tested whether two simple blood ratios can flag stomach cancer that has already spread to distant organs. The ratios compare white blood cells and platelets, the small cells that help blood clot, against lymphocytes, another white cell type.

The team studied 114 patients in Vietnam, of whom about 45 percent had cancer that had spread. Both ratios ran higher in patients whose cancer had spread, and rose as the disease advanced. A model joining the two ratios with tumour location sorted patients far better than clinical details alone. It also spared about 19 of every 100 patients from needless intervention at one risk cut-off, a gain for stretched hospitals.
pmc-13429254:
Leia Heckman and colleagues asked whether the layout of a newborn intensive care unit changes how much mother's milk sick premature babies receive. They compared care before and after one unit switched from open bays to private single-family rooms.

The study covered 276 babies born before 32 weeks in a high-level unit, tracking milk use at discharge and first feeding times. Overall breast milk use at discharge rose after the move, but use of the mother's own milk did not change clearly. Babies in private rooms also made their first oral feeding attempt about a week later than babies in open bays. Heckman concludes that feeding support and daily practice shape milk use more than room design does.
pmc-13430254:
Thomas Theo Brehm and a very large group of experts issue, in a 2026 call to action, a plea to protect tuberculosis drugs from resistance. Their statement came out of the first conference on antimicrobial stewardship in tuberculosis, held in Chişinău, Moldova, in June 2026 with over 60 experts from across the European region. Tuberculosis remains the world's deadliest single-pathogen infection. Drug-resistant forms already fare far worse, and the hardest forms approach pre-antibiotic-era outcomes.

Shorter, all-oral treatment courses have transformed care for resistant disease in recent years. That progress is fragile: resistance to bedaquiline, a cornerstone drug of the new regimens, is already emerging. The signatories argue that every new drug's useful life depends on stewardship, the disciplined use that slows resistance. European programs, carrying a heavy share of resistant disease, are urged to lead and to fund the effort.
pmc-13432854:
Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 study of vaccine hesitancy for the HPV vaccine among female university students in China.  The team ran two large national online surveys, in 2022 and 2025, and matched the samples so the years could be compared fairly. 

Hesitancy more than doubled between the surveys, rising from under one in eleven students to over one in five, even though knowledge about HPV improved and exposure to negative claims fell. What dropped was belief that the vaccine is needed, along with trust in health workers and in both home-made and imported vaccines. Students who saw the vaccine as needed, who had a health worker's advice, or who had paid for other vaccines themselves were less hesitant. Facts alone do not hold trust; clear need and trusted voices do.
pmc-13433254:
Maria Jose Perez J and co-authors strained the power plants of human brain guard cells in 2026, grown from stem cells, to see how the strain warps their talks with nerve cells. Power plants run a stress reply that guards their protein fold. In plain worms, glial stress replies help nerve cells, yet the human brain case stayed open.

Under strain, guard cells rewired their fuel use, lost a key methyl donor, and reshaped their fats, which ended in an aged state. Mixed growths of nerve and glial cells, plus mini-brain balls with guard cells inside, showed the strain break cell talks. Swelling signals lit while fold guards slipped. The authors tie weak power plant care to brain aging and nerve loss disease.
pmc-13434654:
Landry Peyran and coauthors describe a self fixing loop that keeps yeast growth on track in 2026. Yeast cells must grow toward one pole to divide well. A cell cycle driver starts pole growth, then watches whether the pole forms as planned.

When the pole falters, the driver boosts its own action on pole building targets. Longer and rerouted signals buy time for repair. The rescue has a price when harm cannot be fixed. Stuck high driver levels force the cell onward without a daughter, making cells with many nuclei. The loop shows how drive and watchfulness share one switch.
pmc-13437454:
Xuanming Hu and colleagues pooled small trials of exercise snacks, short bursts of movement breaking up long sitting, and their effect on blood sugar after meals. Such snacks may suit people at metabolic risk who cannot fit in full workouts. Their 2026 analysis searched six databases for crossover trials in sedentary adults and kept eight trials with 159 people. Each tested a snack day against a day of unbroken sitting under lab conditions.

Across the trials with full sugar curves, snacks cut the total rise in blood sugar after meals by a clear margin. Results varied a great deal between trials, which tempers the claim. Neither starting metabolic state nor intensity clearly changed the effect, and blood vessel outcomes rested on only three small studies. They warn the findings are too thin and uneven to write them into clinical advice as a set prescription.
pmc-13437654:
Koldemir-Gündüz and colleagues made two new boron-arginine compounds, a monoester and a diester. They tested them against B16-F10 mouse melanoma cells, a fast-growing cancer model short on low-harm treatment options. After 48 hours of contact they tracked cell killing, death-pathway markers, inflammatory signals, and antibacterial activity of both compounds.

The diester was far more potent. Its half-maximal dose was 51.9 micromolar, against 5.97 millimolar for the monoester in the melanoma line. Both compounds raised the Bax to Bcl-2 ratio and raised p53 levels. That pattern matches switching on the cell's death machinery. They also shifted cytokine levels, including tumor necrosis factor alpha and interleukin 6 and 10, in an anti-inflammatory way under some conditions. Antibacterial testing showed minimum inhibitory levels between 3.12 and 12.5 micrograms per milliliter. Those held against Gram-positive and Gram-negative species.
pmc-13437754:
Erkan Kırıs and Nilay Akcay measured trace elements in maize flour sold in Turkey and weighed the health stakes of eating it. Maize flour is a daily staple there, and farming, milling, and storage can all leave metals behind. Their 2026 study ran twenty shop-bought samples through a plasma-based instrument reading element levels with high sensitivity. Certified reference material backed the accuracy of the readings, and standard hazard formulas converted levels into risk scores.

Iron led the list, followed by zinc and manganese, with copper and nickel at low levels. Cadmium and chromium sat below what the instrument could detect. All measured values fit inside international limits, and the combined hazard index stayed in the safe zone, so the flour is unlikely to harm eaters through these elements. The authors offer the numbers as a starting reference for Turkish maize flour.
pmc-13439254:
Jingzhen He and colleagues sort young adults by habits of mind and ask which brain circuits forecast who stays adaptable, in a 2026 longitudinal study. Adaptability balances self-control against impulse and sensitivity to reward or punishment. Grouping people by trait mix may reveal more than studying each trait alone. The team profiled 1,229 young adults, scanned their resting brains, and rechecked 432 of them two years later.

Three profiles emerged, labelled adaptive, moderate, and maladaptive. The adaptive group showed strong links between the medial prefrontal cortex, a control hub, and the striatum, a reward hub. Strength of that circuit at the start forecast steadier adaptation two years on, with the clearest added value in men. The authors present the circuit as a scaffold that helps flexible behaviour endure.
pmc-13439654:
Erin S Rogers and colleagues examine mental distress among low-income food assistance recipients who smoke, reporting in 2026. People receiving food aid smoke at high rates, yet their mental health needs are rarely mapped. The group came from a quitting trial and held 352 adults earning under twice the poverty line, each smoking at least five cigarettes daily. A standard six-item scale sorted distress levels, and questions covered recent care, satisfaction, and whether care might help.

About a quarter of the group scored in the severe distress range, and just over half scored in the moderate range. Severe distress tracked with younger age, money strain, and food insecurity, not with smoking habits or quit drive. Care use rose with distress, and satisfaction stayed high among those treated. Untreated participants, above all the severely distressed, said care would likely help, signalling unmet need.
pmc-13439954:

pmc-13440554:
Alfredo Perez Tagle Tejeda and colleagues recount a near-fatal lupus flare striking heart, kidneys, blood, and brain together, reporting a 2026 case. pmc-13446354:
Lucas Leite Cunha and Laura Sterian Ward revisit Brazil's university quota law a decade on, reversing the worry they voiced when it passed in 2012, in a 2026 essay. pmc-13447154:

Surgery was linked to longer survival in the full group and after careful matching of similar patients. Checks using other transplant rule sets pointed the same way, though the authors call for forward-looking trials to confirm who benefits most.
pmc-13448254:
Xin Zhang and colleagues create crystals that remember mechanical stress and glow later in near-infrared light in 2026 materials work. A material that stores the hit and reveals it on demand could simplify officiating, sensing and interactive devices alike.

Blending two similar hosts tuned both brightness and glow duration. Ball impacts were captured and visualised directly with fast processing and high accuracy in demonstrations. pmc-13448354:

pmc-13448654:
Yongfang Qu and co-authors build a conjugated framework material that captures sulfur dioxide and converts it onward in 2026 work. Sorbents must hold large amounts, pick the gas out of mixtures precisely and survive humidity and corrosive exposure over many cycles.

Capacity reached a very high level under ambient test conditions, with strong selectivity over hydrogen sulfide, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. pmc-13448954:

The authors read the pattern as an access effect reaching the whole clinic population.
pmc-13449354:
Besir Besir and a large team focus in 2026 on anemia in the oldest patients receiving a transcatheter aortic valve replacement, a group where the warning sign is easy to overlook. These procedures typically serve people around eighty, and over half of candidates arrive anemic, often from iron deficiency. Causes tied to the valve disease itself, including acquired bleeding tendencies and gut blood loss, add to the usual burdens of age.

After the valve procedure, anemia tracked with worse long-term outcomes, including higher mortality and more repeat hospitalizations for heart failure. That adverse signal persisted within this oldest group rather than washing out with age. The authors present anemia as both a risk marker worth screening for and a possible treatment target before intervention.
pmc-13449454:
Yalini Guruparan and colleagues track in 2026 five years of antibiotic use at the Teaching Hospital in Jaffna, northern Sri Lanka. Surveillance of consumption is a frontline weapon against drug resistance, yet many low-income health systems lack it. Using the World Health Organization method, the team converted hospital supply records from 2018 to 2022 into defined daily doses and sorted drugs by the Access, Watch, and Reserve stewardship categories.

Total consumption trended downward across the period, dipping except for a 2019 rise, and oral forms made up over eighty percent. Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid stayed the single most used antibiotic throughout. Reassuringly, Access drugs, the ones guidelines favor, supplied over seventy percent of use, with the Access-to-Watch ratio above two every year. Inpatient use did jump significantly in 2021 amid the pandemic. The authors call for routine monitoring to become permanent.
pmc-13451554:
Foster and colleagues examine how the share of breast milk in a baby's diet shapes growth when the mother had diabetes in pregnancy. Their 2026 SWIFT study followed 435 such infants born in Northern California hospitals. Each month of the first year, mothers reported the mix of breast milk and formula over a week, giving a lactation intensity score. The team grouped babies by growth paths for weight, length, and weight for length.

Babies fed a higher share of breast milk were far less likely to follow the rapid growth paths linked to later obesity risk. The link was strongest for weight relative to length in early infancy and held, more mildly, across the whole first year. Skin thickness paths, a direct gauge of body fat, showed no clear link. The authors read the results as support for continued breastfeeding, even alongside formula, for infants exposed to diabetes before birth.
pmc-13451854:
Weida Shi and co-authors test in 2027 whether two genes that now live in the green cell's sun-catching unit can work from the cell core instead. Over ages, most genes of that unit moved to the core, yet a core set stayed behind. The team picked two held genes in the alga Chlamydomonas and placed them in the core of matching mutants.

Both moved genes made proteins that found their way back to the unit and joined its working parts. One strain kept much of its sun-fed growth, while the other grew only in rich carbon air. Protein levels ran far below normal, which capped the rescue. The work frames a path toward a stripped-down sun unit for lab algae.
pmc-13452754:
Paul H McClelland and twelve co-authors check how well scans and blood tests show if drug treatment before surgery is working in pancreatic cancer. Their 2026 study covers 166 people with tumors that surgeons could remove, or nearly remove, at one center between 2008 and 2024. Each person got several drugs before any operation.

Of the group, 148 finished the drug course and 121 went on to surgery. Scans showed shrinkage in only 27 percent, yet 83 percent hit a strong drop in a blood marker called CA 19-9. Under the microscope, 74 percent of removed tumors showed a clear treatment effect, and 8 percent showed none left at all. Only the microscope result lined up with longer life, so the authors warn against trusting scans alone to judge success.
pmc-13453754:
Sirui Zhu, Fangkun Yang, Haoxuan Lu, Jun Jiang, and Wenming He argue that fatty liver disease and clogged heart arteries should be managed as one linked problem. The two conditions feed each other through shared roots: insulin resistance, long term swelling, and faulty vessel linings. Their 2026 review pulls together the overlap in spread, causes, and genes.

Pairing drugs can add further gains, the authors note, and lifestyle change still underpins every plan. pmc-13454054:

Their 2026 proof of concept joins clinic visit data with repeated wearable style readings, keeping the two streams apart until the reading stage. Three data sources play distinct roles: public datasets train the models, while two synthetic generators fake patient records and sensor streams.

The maternal risk model sorted low and high risk cases better than the murky middle class. Diabetes prediction scored high at catching true cases in both data styles. Preeclampsia, a dangerous pressure disorder, proved harder, and wearable blood pressure alone fell well short. The authors stress the framework is a prototype: calibration, richer inputs, and real patient cohorts must come before any clinical use.
pmc-13454654:
Norihito Takahashi and Hiroshi Iwata write, in a 2026 editorial, about the lag between lowering cholesterol and truly calming a dangerous artery plaque. Modern drug stacks cut LDL cholesterol fast and deep, and guidelines urge early, strong treatment. The editorial discusses a case in this journal where a patient with inherited high cholesterol reached an LDL of 51, yet suffered a new heart event seven months later.

Repeat artery imaging in that case showed a thin-capped, fat-rich plaque still carrying clot. The authors call the gap a drug-intervention lag phase: blood numbers improve quickly, while local plaque healing trails behind. Risk during that window stays layered, spanning leftover plaque, lipid, and inflammatory sources. They urge doctors to judge patients by plaque imaging plus overall risk, not by cholesterol alone, when tailoring follow-up care.
pmc-13455054:
Diana A. Martin-Rojas leads a nine-author study, from 2026, of why young white wines lose their fruity sparkle in storage. The sparkle comes from esters, aroma compounds that slowly break down in the bottle. The team tracked 17 esters across 32 commercial wines under forced aging, conditions that speed storage chemistry.

Textbook logic blamed starting ester levels and acidity for the losses. The data disagreed. The wine's overall makeup mattered more, and metals stood out: iron and manganese sped ester breakdown, apparently acting as catalysts. Potassium and magnesium mattered about as much as acidity did. Together, metal content and acidity predicted shelf life better than the starting aroma levels. The authors advise winemakers to watch metal pickup during production if they want young whites to stay fresh and fruity longer.
pmc-13457054:
Hongxia Xue and four colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a prediction model for osteoporosis in older adults using routine health check data. The team analyzed 852 people aged sixty and over from one examination center, of whom about 29 percent had the bone-thinning disease. Nineteen candidate clues, from body mass to blood fats, entered the screen.

A selection method kept twelve features. Five algorithms then competed, from plain logistic regression to boosted trees. The fanciest models looked perfect on training data, a warning sign of overfitting rather than skill. On the held-out group, the simpler regression held up as the robust choice, matching the study's stated aim. The authors argue that honest, well-checked simple models serve clinics better than dazzling ones. Their tool aims to flag high-risk elders early, using numbers any checkup already collects.
pmc-13458154:
Al Jaff and colleagues review eighteen years of end-of-life practice for implanted defibrillators. Their 2026 paper examines records of 1,606 patients with defibrillators or combined resynchronisation devices who died between 2006 and 2022. These devices can fire painful shocks during life's final phase, and guidelines urge switching off the shock function, called tachytherapy, in advance through care planning.

A third of deactivations still occurred on the patient's final day of life, mostly during hospitalisation. Heart failure and cancer were the leading causes of death. The authors call for deactivation talks to become routine earlier in care, particularly for heart failure patients, rather than last-day decisions.
pmc-13458354: Artificial intelligence in spiritual care — explored through a modified Delphi study of experts. Fabian Winiger, C Estelle Smith, Shadi Nourriz, and others convene the panel. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is digital chaplaincy. It asks experts what AI means for the soul.
pmc-13459254:
Mira Miraturrofi'ah and co-authors mapped how information flows, and where it breaks down, in the care of premature babies in Bandung District, Indonesia. Above them, policy, funding, referral pathways, and geography governed access. The authors show fragmented practices undermining unbroken care for these fragile infants.
pmc-13459454:

The condition, metabolic dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease, combines liver fat with metabolic problems. pmc-13459554:

pmc-13459754:

pmc-13459954:

Immune cell mixes inside the valve also shifted, with more resting macrophages and fewer resolving ones. pmc-13460854:

pmc-13461154:

pmc-13462854:

pmc-13463654:

pmc-13464854:

pmc-13465154:

pmc-13465254:

pmc-13466554:

pmc-13467054:

pmc-13467254:

Cleaning left 180 recordings per condition for analysis. Four classic microstate shapes were extracted and compared across groups for their layout and timing. pmc-13467354:

pmc-13467454:

pmc-13468854:
Aldaghi and a team in Iran compared blood antibodies in 2026 between Alzheimer's patients and healthy peers, testing the parasite Toxoplasma gondii. The result ran against the blame story: about 78 percent of patients carried the parasite, against 89 percent of controls. Still, the finding joins a mixed literature and argues for prospective studies that track infection before dementia begins.
pmc-13469354:

A sectioned layout leaves room for a second coil type and cancels sensitivity to fields pointing through the board.

They argue the large area averages the field over more of a sample surface, which should improve accuracy. Measurements stayed usable up to 100 kilohertz despite the coil size.
pmc-13470254:
Ismail and Zafira's 2026 systematic review asks whether artificial intelligence tools can build the emotional side of healthcare training, known as the affective domain, which covers empathy, communication, professionalism, and self-awareness. pmc-13470954:

pmc-13471254:

pmc-13471354:
