The altered genes clustered in mitochondrial energy production, especially respiratory chain complex I, and in purine metabolism, the handling of building blocks for DNA. Stress hormone levels rose briefly under short dosing, then fell below baseline with long use, and behaviour changed only modestly. The authors read the pattern as the brain adapting its energy systems rather than suffering damage.
pmc-13471454:
Yang and co-authors sequenced the complete genome of Streptococcus lingualis, a recently named mouth bacterium, from plaque under the gumline of a healthy adult. Their 2026 data report describes strain KHUD_012, read with a PacBio long-read machine that produced 144,821 high-accuracy reads from a single run.

The genome is one circular chromosome of 2,115,610 base pairs with a G+C content of 42.0% across its length, encoding 1,956 protein-coding genes, four ribosomal RNA operons, and 62 transfer RNAs. A completeness check scored 99.5% of expected genes present, and whole-genome comparison placed the strain closest to the species type strain, with an OrthoANI similarity of 96.44% between them. The pair share 1,717 core gene clusters.
pmc-13471554:
Chen and co-authors review how surgeons can check, during the operation itself, whether a breast-conserving cancer removal got clean margins. Their 2026 survey weighs specimen imaging, frozen sections, and newer fluorescent molecular probes that light up tumor tissue, against pathology results that arrive only days later.

The problem is common: about 15 to 35% of patients need a second operation because cancer cells reach the cut edge of the removed tissue. One device trial with 596 lumpectomy patients cut the false-negative rate to 24.8% from 66.1% in controls, and re-excision fell to 19.8% of patients versus 25.8% without the device. The authors say fluorescence guidance is promising but still at proof-of-concept stage.
pmc-13474254:
Luan and colleagues offer a 2026 hypothesis-driven review on whether exercise eases adolescent depression through a brain chemical called anandamide. Anandamide is an endocannabinoid, a cannabis-like compound the body makes. It acts on CB1 receptors in circuits linking the prefrontal cortex and the amygdala, two regions that manage stress and emotion.

Adult studies show that one bout of aerobic exercise can raise anandamide in the blood. Animal and brain studies show such signaling can shape stress responses and fear learning. Yet no study has tested the full chain, from exercise to anandamide to circuit change to symptom relief, in adolescents. The authors treat the chain as an unproven model and propose combined experiments measuring exercise dose, blood markers, brain circuits, and symptoms together.
pmc-13474654:
Yuansen Yang and colleagues pin down how much linoleic acid nursing sows need in 2026. Linoleic acid is a fat the body cannot make, and modern sows nurse large litters that strain supply. One hundred sows were fed five diets with rising fat levels for four weeks around farrowing. Sow output, piglet growth, and milk and blood markers were tracked.

Sow breeding output did not change across diets. Piglet weaning weight rose step by step as the fat level rose. Litter weight gains leveled off near a mid-range fat level on two check days. Milk antibody peaks also sat near that mid range. The dose curves give feed makers a target that balances cost and litter growth.
pmc-13474754:
Jingyi Li and co-authors sort nurses in southeastern China into skill groups for artificial intelligence in 2026. A survey of 366 nurses from three large hospitals used a literacy scale plus attitude and innovation measures. Group-finding math split scores into hidden profiles rather than forcing a single average. Traits tied to each profile were then tested.

Three profiles emerged, led by a low literacy and low use group at about a fifth of nurses. A middle group paired moderate literacy with high use, and a top group scored high on both. Attitude toward the tools and inventive behavior helped sort who landed where. Training can now target the low group first, where need is plainest.
pmc-13474854:
Zheng and colleagues built a risk score for osteoporosis in 2026 from life exposures rather than genes, using health records from 477,792 UK Biobank participants. The exposome means everything a person encounters, from income and mood to sleep, diet, smoking, and neighborhood. They screened hundreds of non-genetic factors, kept the ones tied to bone thinning, and combined them into one weighted score called Meta-ERS.

The screen kept 41 independent exposures across eight life domains, with socioeconomic status and mental health carrying the strongest links to osteoporosis in this population. The combined score explained 5.1 percent of variation in osteoporosis, roughly matching a gene-based score at 4.8 percent on the same data. Improving bad exposures cut risk most in people with high genetic risk, and a blood protein called GDF15 carried part of the exposure effect on bone.
pmc-13474954:
Yao and colleagues searched for a scan measure that predicts who benefits from surgery for NAION, a sudden optic nerve stroke that steals sight without warning. The operation, done through the nose, widens the bony canal around the nerve to relieve pressure. Their 2026 study covered 71 patients, 30 treated with surgery and 41 with medicines alone, comparing vision and nerve scans at the start and after three months.

Surgery beat medical care overall, but the gain hinged on the starting thickness of the retinal nerve fiber layer, the bundle of fibers leaving the eye. Patients with moderate swelling, a layer under 150 micrometers thick, responded strongly, with odds of improvement at 7.88 times the comparison rate reported. Patients with massive swelling gained little, and blood-flow scans in responders showed restored capillary flow around the nerve head, backing the pressure-relief theory behind the operation.
pmc-13477354:
Giulio Vidotto and coauthors published a 2026 laboratory study mapping how coronary artery lining cells respond to different blood flow patterns. Plaque tends to grow where flow is disturbed, while surface erosion happens where flow runs high. The team grew human coronary endothelial cells for 72 hours under swirling flow, steady normal flow, and elevated flow, then measured gene, microRNA, and protein activity.

Elevated flow switched on a distinct program, with 665 genes responding only to that condition. Flow also changed which gene versions cells used, touching pathways tied to artery disease. Many flow-sensitive genes sat near known disease-linked DNA variants. Protein changes often failed to match gene changes, which the authors flag as a warning against reading gene data alone.
pmc-13479554:
Tayebe Zarekar and coauthors published a 2026 preliminary randomized trial on whether intense interval exercise can push stem cells into the blood of cancer patients preparing for bone marrow transplant. Mobilizing these progenitor cells is essential for transplant success, yet prior cancer treatment can blunt their release. Twenty patients were split evenly between an exercise group and a control group.

Exercise patients first completed a graded test to find peak power, then received a growth factor drug followed by twelve one-minute hard efforts. Blood measures tracked how many progenitor cells entered circulation. Interval exercise raised these cell counts in healthy people in earlier work, so the trial tests whether the same shortcut works in patients whose marrow has been stressed by cancer therapy.
pmc-13480054:
Hsiang-Chin Hsu and co-authors describe a 2026 study of bedside ultrasound as a teaching tool in emergency care. Twenty-eight third- and fourth-year medical students from other countries took part in guided heart and belly scanning practice. After the session each student wrote a reflective account, and the team sorted the accounts for shared patterns in how learning took place.

Four themes emerged from the writing. Seeing organs move in real time helped students grasp how the body works and what may be wrong. Cases tied to clear problems made the scans feel purposeful, while group work and teacher guidance kept students engaged. Students also noted the limits of the tool and the need for steady practice. The study suggests that scanning lessons work best when images, cases, and reflection are woven together.
pmc-13480154:
Ryudo Kawahara and colleagues report a 2026 case of a growing clot in the heart after a closure attempt was called off. A man aged eighty-four, with atrial fibrillation and past clot events, had a planned plug procedure for the left atrial appendage, a small pouch where clots often form. Odd pouch shape forced the team to abort.

A scan the next day hinted at a small clot, even though the man stayed on full blood thinning drugs. Over three months the clot grew large. Surgeons finally removed the clot and cut away the pouch. The team points to a brief pause in thinning drugs, surface injury from the attempt, sluggish flow, and a clot-prone state as likely drivers. They advise close imaging follow-up after aborted attempts in high-risk patients, since early clot signs can be easy to miss.
pmc-13480254:
Manel Ben Fredj and colleagues present a 2026 study of COVID survival across six waves in Monastir, Tunisia. Records covered all patients admitted in the region from March 2020 to March 2022, totalling near 59,000 infections, over 5,000 hospital stays, and more than 1,100 hospital deaths. Survival curves and risk models compared waves and hunted for factors tied to early death.

Thirty-day survival sank lowest in the fourth and fifth waves, near thirty percent, and overall hospital death risk across stays ran high. Age above seventy-five more than tripled death risk, while cancer roughly doubled it, and nerve symptoms added risk as well. Fever and gut symptoms oddly linked to lower death risk in the data. The six-wave view gives planners in like settings a timeline of when wards faced the deadliest strain.
pmc-13480754:
Lei and Liu used in 2026 gene based math to hunt blood proteins that may cause irritable bowel syndrome, a long gut ill with no clear root. The trick, Mendelian randomization, uses gene quirks as stand ins for protein levels. That helps split cause from mere link. They weighed near five thousand proteins from an Iceland bank against gut data from a Finnish pool of three hundred thousand plus people. Checks ran both ways.

Twenty proteins held up as likely causes of the syndrome. Two of them cut risk, acting as guards, while the rest raised it. The back check found no sign that the gut ill moves the proteins, which backs the one way arrow. The hits cluster in cell power plants, nerve end traffic, and cargo sorting paths. The authors pitch the twenty as drug leads for a field short on targets.
pmc-13481754:
Yuhan Hu and co-authors report a 2026 study of a receptor protein that fuels gum disease. Periodontitis rots the tissue and bone that hold teeth, driven by runaway inflammation. The receptor, called GPRC5A, ran high in inflamed human gum tissue. The team silenced it in mice with gum disease and in gum ligament cells stressed with bacterial toxin.

Silencing cut bone loss and disease severity in mice. In cells it lowered inflammatory output and calmed a master inflammation switch. A partner protein fell in step, and its own partner, a protein-building factor, carried less of an activating mark. The chain offers a fresh drug angle for gum disease, though the authors note that direct proof of the full chain still needs work.
pmc-13482154:
Chudyba and colleagues test rubber-like pads fitted under railway sleepers in 2026, measuring how well the pads shield the ground from train vibration. They built a reduced-scale track in the laboratory and shook it at four frequencies, 3, 5, 10, and 20 hertz, recording motion at the sleeper stand-in and at the soil stand-in below. Five pad variants, differing in stiffness and underside pattern, competed against a bare track setup.

Every pad created the same trade-off, letting the sleeper itself move more while passing less vibration down into the ground beneath the track. Softness and surface shape decided the winner, with softer pads and corrugated undersides cutting transmission the most in the transfer measurements taken. One optimized pad, with stiffness near 0.12 newtons per cubic millimeter and a corrugated face, was picked for the next step, a planned trial on Poland's national rail network.
pmc-13482554:
Matsui and colleagues in Japan tested in 2026 a chart tool that sums up care for old patients in five parts, known as the Geriatric 5Ms. The five parts cover mind, movement, drugs, many sided health woes, and what counts most to the patient. Their ward at Nagoya University Hospital built the summary into its electronic record. The team checked how fully staff filled it in for 139 stays over ten months.

Nearly every stay, all but four, had a summary on file. The fullest part was the many sided woes list, filled in for near all patients. The weakest part was what counts most to the patient, filled in for about seven in ten. Across all parts, staff filled in about half of the set sub items on a typical chart. Drug lists were started often but rarely checked for drugs with no clear need.
pmc-13483054:
Ezekiel and colleagues tested cheap ways to firm up swelling clay soil so it can carry roads without cracking. Their 2026 laboratory study mixed expansive clay with fly ash, lime, and granules from waste tyres. Untreated clay swells when wet and shrinks when dry, which breaks road bases. The team measured density, stiffness, and swelling across several mix ratios to find a sweet spot.

A blend using 5 percent combined lime and fly ash cut the soil plasticity index, a swelling measure, by 86 percent in the reported tests. Bearing strength jumped as well, rising from a weak untreated range to a much stronger treated value. Doubling the additives to 10 percent backfired, giving worse results than the smaller dose. Tyre granules raised water demand and lowered density. Ezekiel recommends the modest blend for road subbase work.
pmc-13483454:
Madavi and team grew tiny silver particles using a fungus that lives inside plants, avoiding the harsh chemicals usually used to make them. Their 2026 study confirmed the particles were round, crystalline, and only about six nanometers wide on average. Silver particles at this scale can kill microbes, so the team ran a battery of medical tests on their fungal-made batch.

The particles blocked biofilms, the slimy shields bacteria hide behind, by up to about 74 percent in the reported assays. They neutralized cell-damaging molecules at modest doses and calmed inflammation in a protein test at even lower doses. Lung cancer cells died at doses in the same general range, while a diabetes-linked enzyme was slowed more weakly. Madavi presents the batch as a multi-purpose candidate, though all results so far come from laboratory dishes.
pmc-13483554:
Nadir Bilici and collaborators evaluate a phone-based program meant to soften snap negative judgments toward faces with visible differences. Published in 2026, the work builds on the idea that repeated contact plus personal stories can shift automatic evaluations. Volunteers used an app twice daily for five days, viewing either faces with anomalies or typical faces, each paired with stories of praiseworthy actions.

Automatic evaluations of the faces people saw grew more positive over the sessions, with the clearest targeted gain for faces bearing visible differences. Stated attitudes, measured directly, did not move. People who found it easy to imagine life from a storyteller's viewpoint tended to change most. The authors present the low-cost approach as a promising way to reduce stigma, while noting that durability still needs testing.
pmc-13486654:
Alzabidi and colleagues added a supervised cleaning stage before dropout prediction, arguing that odd student records poison otherwise good models. Their 2026 method, SOD-FE, uses the known outcomes to hunt outliers, trims them, then engineers and selects features before classification. The team tested five classifiers on real student datasets from Portugal and Slovakia, checking whether the cleaning stage lifted every model or just one.

The random forest classifier gained the most, reaching balanced F-scores near 98 percent on both national datasets under cross-validation. Those scores beat the same forest without the cleaning stage by about seven and three percentage points respectively. Other classifiers also improved, though less dramatically. Alzabidi says the gains rival the best published results on these benchmarks, making early-warning lists more trustworthy for advisors deciding whom to contact first.
pmc-13487154:
Said and colleagues built a joint epidemic model for COVID-19 and leishmaniasis, two infections that overlap in some regions, and fitted it to real case data with a self-correcting filter. Co-infections can change how each disease spreads and how sick patients become. Their 2026 model tracks humans and the sandfly vectors of leishmaniasis, including latency, treatment, recovery, and reinfection, while an ensemble Kalman filter continually re-estimates key rates as data arrives.

Fitted separately, the leishmaniasis sub-model showed a slightly lower transmission rate but much faster treatment than the COVID-19 sub-model over twelve months. The combined model matched observed data closely enough to support its structure, according to the authors' checks. Interaction terms revealed how co-circulation alters transmission and outcomes versus either disease alone. Said offers the framework for forecasting in regions fighting both infections at once.
pmc-13487354:
Bischoff and a Dutch team ran in 2026 a feeding trial on E171, the food grade form of titanium dioxide, a white dye once used in sweets and sauces. Europe pulled it from food over fears it could harm genes, but proof in humans was thin. Thirty one adults ate a set daily dose for two weeks. Each person also had a plain phase for contrast. The team checked stool, blood, and gut samples from each phase.

Stool titanium shot up during the dosed phase, as most of the dye passed through. Blood tests hinted at more oxidative stress, the rust like cell strain from stray oxygen forms. Gene readouts from colon samples showed seventy three pathways switched on. Those paths tie to stress, cell fuel use, and colon cancer linked steps. The shifts back the case for care with the dye in food.
pmc-13488054:
Auroni Deep and co-authors show that natural cell chemicals called polyamines can undo a folded DNA structure in a 2026 molecular study. Polyamines carry positive charges and help cells grow, while i-motifs are four-stranded DNA folds found in gene control regions. Computer docking suggested polyamines grip i-motifs tightly, and lab methods using light and binding tests checked the prediction on telomere and gene promoter sequences.

Spermine, spermidine, and putrescine loosened i-motifs while leaving related G-quadruplex folds and ordinary double-stranded DNA largely alone. Cell imaging showed fewer i-motifs inside nuclei after treatment, and gene activity shifted most in genes whose control regions can form i-motifs. The authors propose a new route for gene control.
pmc-13488154:
Martha Funabashi and colleagues map how harms are reported in trials of spinal manipulative therapy in a 2026 scoping review. The treatment uses quick, small thrusts for spinal pain, and clear harm reporting is needed to judge its safety. The team gathered 253 randomized trials from earlier reviews and fresh searches, then checked whether each trial mentioned harms, collected them, and actually reported what happened.

Only a little over half of the trials mentioned harms, and just twenty-eight percent reported whether any occurred. Pain-type problems were most common and usually mild in the reports that gave details. Timing, duration, relatedness, and extra care were often missing. The authors say reporting still falls short of established guidance.
pmc-13488254:
Catalina Ramirez leads a large cohort team studying dental disease in adults with and without HIV in a 2026 cross-sectional analysis of a combined United States cohort. Mouth photographs from 2,927 participants were graded by dentist researchers for missing teeth and untreated decay or leftover roots. Groups included women and men, each split by HIV status, with middle age typical across the sample.

Women carried more tooth loss and untreated decay than men at every age, and older women showed striking rates of total tooth loss in the reported figures. Income predicted untreated decay in women more strongly than age did. HIV status itself showed no independent link with either outcome after adjustment. The authors frame the burden as a story of poverty and access.
pmc-13489154:
Gopidi Aparanji and eleven colleagues published this 2026 case series of three young patients whose heart attacks came not from clogged arteries but from coronary embolism. That is material swept into a heart artery from elsewhere. Such cases are uncommon and easily missed. The series traces each patient's source through history and imaging, and shows how treatment followed the source rather than a standard heart-attack script.

The first patient, a 23-year-old man, suffered a heart attack from an infected embolus thrown by mitral valve endocarditis, and needed valve replacement plus aneurysm repair. The second, a 35-year-old man, was struck by tumour fragments from a left atrial myxoma, treated by mass removal, valve repair and bypass grafting. The third, a 38-year-old woman with severe mitral stenosis, was managed with anticoagulation and a planned valve-opening procedure. The authors urge considering embolism in young patients without atherosclerosis.
pmc-13489554:
Israeli and co-authors uncovered a 2026 two step hormone conversation shaping tomato compound leaves, where leaflets sprout along a central stalk. Auxin, a growth hormone, drives both the starting of leaflets and their later expansion, yet how one signal does both was unclear. Gibberellin, another hormone, turned out to be the switch between stages.

Short auxin exposure switched on genes that break gibberellin down, while longer exposure switched on genes that build it up. Israeli showed leaflet initiation needs lowered gibberellin, since raising it cut leaflet numbers and lowering it locally spawned extra leaflets. Mutants unable to make gibberellin could not expand the leaf blade under auxin treatment as normal plants did. Turning on a breakdown gene in starting leaflets even triggered new leaflets in neighbouring tissue.
pmc-13491654:
Rafael Melo Santos de Serpa Brandão leads a large team reporting a 2026 comparison of kidney transplant allocation eras in Pernambuco, Brazil. Candidates whose immune systems react against many donor types wait longest for a kidney. The state adopted EpViX, a system that uses detailed antibody targets, called epitopes, to run virtual crossmatches before an organ is offered.

The earlier era covered 3,136 candidates from 2005 to 2014, and the EpViX era covered 4,544 from 2016 to 2025. Transplant rates rose from about thirty-six percent to fifty percent, while median waiting time fell from twenty-two months to seven. Highly sensitized candidates gained the most ground in their first-year transplant chances. The virtual test also matched the laboratory crossmatch closely, supporting wider use.
pmc-13491854:
Walter Appati and three colleagues chart in 2026 tuberculosis that strikes outside the lungs at a major Ghanaian teaching hospital. Records from the chest clinic between October 2023 and November 2025 covered 1,098 tuberculosis patients, and the team separated lung disease from disease elsewhere in the body. Outside-lung cases made up about one in six patients.

Spinal tuberculosis dominated at roughly two fifths of outside-lung cases, followed by gland and abdominal disease, with heart sac and brain cases rarer. Patients aged thirty-five to fifty-four had triple the odds of the spinal form compared with other ages. Male sex and HIV infection each independently raised the odds of gland tuberculosis. Outside-lung patients were less often male and less often HIV-positive than lung patients overall, underlining how varied this disease family is.
pmc-13494554:
Pinheiro de Castro and colleagues trace how toxic Heliconiini butterflies gained, refined, and sometimes lost a flexible chemical defense. These butterflies either take up cyanogenic glucosides, poisons stored in their food plants, or make the poisons themselves when plants lack them. Using chemical data from more than 700 insects, the 2026 study rebuilds the family history of this flexible trait across the whole tribe.

The flexible trait was present in the tribe's ancestors but was lost in a few branches, such as the Sapho group, which now only takes poisons from plants. Gene editing in Heliconius erato proved the point: caterpillars with the CYP405 gene knocked out could not make the poisons at all. In the Sapho group, most copies of that gene lack key working parts, which explains the loss. Butterflies and a burnet moth, the authors show, each recruited the same genes for poison making on their own.
pmc-13495154:
Eduardo Aguilar-Bejarano and co-authors benchmark, in a 2026 study, ways to feed chemical data to machine learning for asymmetric catalysis, where a catalyst must favor one mirror form of a product. Labs code molecules in many unlike ways, and no guidance tells newcomers which coding suits small early data sets. The team used 103 palladium-catalyzed reactions with three ligands and many starting materials as their test bed.

They paired eleven codings, from shape and charge measures to fingerprints and language-model embeddings, with five learning methods. Simple fingerprints, one language model, and the hand-built measures proved robust across data sizes. A team of graph networks did best on new starting materials. A key lesson: splitting test data by molecular scaffold, not at random, gives a truer read on skill. Follow-up analysis showed the winning codings carried chemical meaning a chemist can read.
pmc-13496354:
Beyer, Toy, and Burslem set out a protocol for editing proteins inside mammalian cells, in a 2026 methods paper. The technique uses protein trans-splicing, in which two halves of a self-cutting protein called an intein rejoin. They stitch a cargo into a target protein with single-amino-acid precision, in minutes, without antibodies. Edited proteins remain functional, and the method has visualized native proteins, isolated them, and tracked their lifetimes.

First it makes an intein donor carrying a nonstandard amino acid with a chemical handle, then purifies and labels that donor. Then it prepares the mammalian cells and delivers the donor by electroporation so splicing happens. Planning guidance covers choosing splice sites and flanking residues that affect efficiency. The authors present the workflow as a roadmap adaptable to target proteins, cell lines, and cargoes, enabling experiments on proteins in their setting that were out of reach.
pmc-13499954:
Asis A Babun and co-authors review in 2026 how kratom harms the body, a Southeast Asian plant product with opioid-like effects that more people use to self-treat pain or opioid withdrawal. Emergency visits for kratom toxicity are rising, yet its makeup depends heavily on breakdown products in the body, and shop products vary wildly in strength while users often take other drugs too. Their review gathers clinical, lab, and drug reports, with close attention to breathing suppression and response to the reversal drug naloxone.

Published cases show opioid-style poisoning with uneven response to naloxone, likely reflecting differing plant mixes, breakdown products, product strength gaps, and other drugs taken alongside. Delayed or returning slowed breathing after a first response to the drug has been reported, which complicates decisions about observation time and discharge. The authors advise clinicians to expect that pattern and consider longer monitoring for selected patients.
pmc-13500054:
Alan Wu and colleagues describe in 2026 an emergency hidden inside an ear procedure on a young child. Their patient was a five-year-old boy with profound hearing loss in both ears and an unknown inner ear malformation. He was having a small cut in the eardrum, called myringotomy, for repeated middle ear infections. Clear fluid poured out in a high-flow, pulsing stream, raising immediate suspicion of cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid bathing the brain and spine.

Fluid testing confirmed the leak marker. Urgent exploration through the side of the skull found a congenital opening letting fluid escape from the inner ear chamber through the oval window into the middle ear. Surgeons sealed it in layers with tissue packing, cartilage, a muscle flap, ear canal closure, and blocking of the connecting tube. Untreated leaks risk meningitis, so the authors urge imaging before ear procedures in children with profound hearing loss.
pmc-13500854:
Craig and colleagues piggybacked a disease check onto a national health survey in Niue, the tiny Pacific island nation, to confirm a past public health victory still holds. Niue was validated in 2016 as having eliminated lymphatic filariasis, a mosquito-spread worm disease, but nobody had rechecked since. In 2025 the team folded filariasis blood testing into the near-census non-communicable disease survey already visiting households.

Only one participant tested positive for worm antigen, a fraction of a percent of those tested, and no live microfilariae were found, evidence that elimination has been sustained for nine years. Ten people carried antibodies, the footprint of past exposure, which the authors read as a reason for continued vigilance rather than alarm. Staff and residents judged the combined survey efficient and acceptable. They recommend the integrated model to other small island health systems.
pmc-13503454:
Ozates and colleagues study how the standard glioblastoma chemo drug, temozolomide, may sow its own escape, and whether adding a second drug blocks that escape. Glioblastoma stem cells drive this brain tumour's regrowth. In their 2026 cell tests, the team profiled microRNAs, tiny molecules that tune gene activity, after each drug alone and combined. Temozolomide alone raised three cancer-promoting microRNAs, a reaction the authors read as the cells adapting to survive treatment.

Ruxolitinib, a drug that blocks the JAK signal pathway, pushed the same microRNAs down, and the combination cancelled temozolomide's rise in the reported measurements. Analysis of their targets pointed to cancer circuits controlling growth and cell death, including genes such as PTEN and BCL2L11. The authors propose that pairing pathway blockade with chemo could blunt this adaptation behind recurrence.
pmc-13503754:
Movva Naga swapna sri leads a team testing how a mixed aluminum material stands up to rubbing wear, in a 2026 study. The mix adds boron carbide and granite dust to an aluminum alloy and is cast by stirring. Granite dust is a cheap, green filler that may harden the alloy.

Disc tests varied the load and slide speed. The lowest wear came at low load and speed with a small share of granite. Photos of worn faces showed small cracks and little loose debris. Three smart models were trained to predict wear, and one tree-based model fit the data almost exactly. A joint scoring step picked best settings that trade off wear rate and friction together.
pmc-13504054:
Nabil Saouti leads a team reporting the first results of a new Ross program for adults, in a 2026 study. The Ross operation swaps a diseased aortic valve for the patient's own lung valve, an option regaining favor for young and mid-age adults. Substitute valves carry lifelong risks, so the choice matters.

The center treated 32 patients from spring 2024 to late 2025, with a median age of 39. Most had a two-leaflet aortic valve from birth, and narrowing was the main fault. No patient died during surgery or in the first month. Two had major setbacks, one needing a switch to a standard root replacement and one an urgent heart artery procedure. At discharge no patient leaked more than mildly through the new valve.
pmc-13504754:
Bin Luo, Yan Huang, Yongjun Wu, and Shengkang Xu compare robot-guided and freehand X-ray-guided screw placement for severe pelvic breaks, in a 2026 study. The injury type is an unstable break of the back pelvic ring. Screws must pass through narrow bone corridors near nerves, so aim matters.

Records covered 60 patients treated from 2021 to 2023 at one center, split between robot and standard care. Operation time and healing time were alike. The robot group needed far fewer X-ray shots and wire adjustments, and lost less blood. Screw placement rated excellent or good in nearly all robot cases, clearly above the standard group. Final function scores also favored the robot group slightly. The authors call for larger, forward-looking trials.
pmc-13505054:
Álvaro Hernáez leads a large team tracking how sticking to a Mediterranean diet year by year shapes blood fats in older adults, in a 2026 study. The data come from the PREDIMED trial in Spain, with nearly five thousand people aged sixty to eighty at high heart risk. Diet scores were taken yearly over a median of four years.

People with high lasting adherence ran lower triglycerides than low adherers, with the gap widest in those on fat-lowering drugs. Their good cholesterol ran slightly higher and their ratio of bad to good cholesterol lower. High adherence cut the risk of every listed lipid disorder by a fifth to nearly a half. Gains per added diet point were largest for people starting with low adherence.
pmc-13505154:
Selman Arslan and colleagues used computer models of the lower jaw to test how cysts around buried wisdom teeth affect fracture risk at the jaw angle. They built four matching three-dimensional models that differed only in cyst size, from none to large. A fixed load was applied from three directions, and stresses were read at twelve points on the bone surface.

Models with cysts showed higher stresses than the cyst-free model, and the rise grew with cyst volume. Under loading on the same side, some surface regions carried several times the stress seen without a cyst. Loading from the opposite side or the chin raised stress less, and areas beside the cyst weakened most. The authors argue that finding and treating such cysts early may help prevent angle fractures after injury.
pmc-13506154:
Hanae Mezrhab and colleagues report a newborn girl whose left eyelids were partly joined by a thin tissue band, a rare birth defect called ankyloblepharon filiforme adnatum. She was born at term with poor growth before birth, unusual facial features, and a heart defect. Testing of her blood confirmed trisomy 18, also known as Edwards syndrome.

Heart ultrasound suggested a complex defect resembling tetralogy of Fallot. The eyelid band was snipped with scissors at the bedside, without sedation or local anaesthetic, and the eye opened at once with no bleeding. Clearing the visual axis early matters because a blocked view can permanently weaken vision development. The authors use the case to argue that any baby with this eyelid finding deserves a full check for other malformations and chromosome problems. Such a sign can point to a wider syndrome.
pmc-13507054:
Gonzalo G Peraza-Mues and colleagues analyze, in 2026 work, how Mexican cities grew from 1990 to 2020 using census data for 69 metro areas. Their model tracks population size, density, and spread from each city center. The question was whether growth filled centers or pushed people outward.

Urban population nearly doubled over the three decades, yet centers lost about 2.5 million residents as edges grew. Average distance from the center rose by about a quarter plus, stated as 28 percent in the study. Center loss plus edge growth drove the spread. The framework lets planners compare sprawl patterns across regions and over time on equal terms.
pmc-13507854:

pmc-13508254:

pmc-13508554:

pmc-13510454:

pmc-13511354:

pmc-13511454:

pmc-13514554:
Pasquale Niscola and six colleagues review, in a 2026 article, how artificial intelligence could personalise the care of acute myeloid leukaemia. pmc-13514854:

pmc-13515454:
Parnapalle Ravi and Jin-Seo Noh review, in a 2026 article, a family of light-absorbing oxides for making hydrogen from sunlight and water. pmc-13517554:

pmc-13518454:

pmc-13520254:

pmc-13520354:
Chul S. Hyun and Sara Soonsik Kim evaluate in 2026 a long-running community hepatitis B programme serving Korean American communities in the northeastern United States. Only about one third of positive cases reached confirmed clinical care, mostly through local private practices. Roughly 42 screenings found one case, while about 104 were needed for one linked case, showing where outreach loses people.
pmc-13521154:
Jinxin Zhang and colleagues present in 2026 a 54-year-old man whose shoulder joint lining stayed blood-stained and swollen for a year after a car crash injury. Repeated bleeding can thicken the lining and deposit iron pigment, mimicking a locally aggressive tumour of the joint lining.

pmc-13521254:

pmc-13521554:

pmc-13521754:

pmc-13521954:
Yanan Hu, Jie Zhong and Zhiming Peng present in 2026 an artificial intelligence framework for redesigning historic street districts that balances foot access, traffic flow, green space and heritage protection. Static master plans adapt poorly as crowds and traffic shift through the day.

pmc-13522354:

pmc-13523154:

pmc-13523454:

pmc-13524554:

pmc-13526854:

pmc-13527054:

pmc-13528154:

pmc-13530554:

pmc-13531754:

pmc-13532854:

pmc-13532954:

pmc-13534454:

pmc-13534854:

pmc-13536554:

pmc-13540854:

pmc-13541554:

pmc-13541854:

pmc-13542954:

pmc-13543354:

pmc-13543554:

pmc-13546554:

pmc-13547154:

pmc-13547754:

One amino acid, glutamine, stood out as essential. Starving lab-grown germ cell precursors of glutamine stalled their formation, tangled their energy balance, and changed a chemical mark on their DNA packaging. Adding back a glutamine-derived fuel, alpha-ketoglutarate, largely rescued the process. The authors link food chemistry, energy, and gene control in germ cell development, with practical value for poultry culture systems.
pmc-13548554:
Yi-mei Du and colleagues translate and validate a sexual health questionnaire for cancer patients in mainland China, in a 2026 two-phase study. The European questionnaire covers sexual satisfaction and pain as part of quality of life, yet no simplified Chinese version had been checked. Phase one followed the official translation procedure, with patient interviews to catch confusing wording about sexual activity.

Phase two surveyed 270 outpatients, with thirty repeating the form two weeks later. Scores held together well inside each scale, stayed steady over the retest gap, and the analysis confirmed the expected two-part structure. The satisfaction and pain sections barely overlapped, supporting that they measure different things. The authors conclude the Chinese version is culturally sound and ready for clinical and research use with Chinese cancer patients.
pmc-13548654:
Majed AL-Mourgi, Anwar Shams, and Shorouq Mohammed report a rare desmoid tumor growing in a young woman's armpit, in a 2026 case report with a literature review. Desmoid tumors invade nearby tissue but never spread to distant organs, and their course is unpredictable. Many are now simply watched, since some shrink on their own, while drug treatments have grown for stubborn cases.

This tumor sat in the right axilla, a crowded crossroads of nerves and vessels where cutting risks arm function. Surgeons removed it completely with no complications during or after the operation. Eighteen months of follow-up showed no return of the tumor on examination or scans, and the patient kept full movement and strength in the arm. The authors argue that for symptomatic tumors in tricky locations, well-planned surgery still earns its place beside watchful waiting.
pmc-13548954:
Jacop Rydén and colleagues use visible light to crack open protected three-membered rings and harvest reactive fragments for building complex molecules, in a 2026 organic chemistry paper. Their starting materials, cyclopropyl silyl ethers, lose an electron under photoredox conditions and split. The radicals form next to a carbonyl group. Such intermediates are hard to catch cleanly, because the usual partner molecules tend to chain-react into sludge.

The freed radicals add across electron-poor double bonds, joining two beta positions. From one shared starting material, the products can branch three ways. Some go on to further ring-closing reactions. Others cross over from radical to polar chemistry, ending in an aldol ring closure. Still others serve directly as advanced intermediates. The team proves the value by reaching two natural product frameworks and completing a first synthesis in a third family.
pmc-13549754:
Martin Ullrich and colleagues test a matched pair of radioactive copper isotopes on antibodies aimed at a myeloma target, in a 2026 preclinical study. Copper-64 suits PET scanning, while its chemical twin copper-67 can both image and deliver therapy, so the same antibody can first map disease and then treat it. Two commercial antibodies against BCMA, a protein on myeloma cells, were fitted with a copper-gripping chelator and tested in mice with myeloma grafts.

Both kept tight binding after modification. One, MAB193, piled into tumors with the cleanest background, reaching a tumor-to-muscle contrast near fifteen within two days. Its copper-67 version delivered tumor doses that shrank tumor mass above a threshold, and dose projections for people stayed within acceptable bounds. The authors champion the copper pair for planning doses by scan before therapy.
pmc-13551754:
Qingyuan Li, leading six colleagues, published a 2026 systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of exercise for core symptoms in children with autism spectrum disorder. Evidence had been inconclusive, so the team searched six databases for randomized trials and rated bias with a standard Cochrane tool. Twenty studies with 874 children qualified for synthesis.

Moderate-certainty evidence showed a significant improvement in core symptoms with exercise in the reported pooled estimate. Evidence for benefits lasting after programs ended was low-certainty and not statistically significant. Child age and the type of comparison condition changed effect sizes, while exercise type, session length, and frequency did not. Neither total volume nor weekly duration showed a dose pattern, leaving open how best to prescribe activity.
pmc-13551854:
Aina Llenas-Bladé, with thirteen colleagues, published a 2026 plan for a weight study in cancer care. The CANOBESE study tests a weight program during curative treatment. Obesity is common in cancer patients and raises the risk of complications. Yet guidelines focus on under-nutrition, not excess weight. Weight loss during treatment is rare over safety fears. The study will recruit fifty adults with a body mass index of 30 or more and new solid tumors.

The program pairs a tailored low-calorie, high-protein diet with home exercise. Sessions mix cardio and strength work under supervision. Behavioral support runs through the program, with added mind care when needed. Follow-up lasts as long as treatment, from three to nine months. The team will judge recruitment, retention, and how well patients stick to the plan.
pmc-13551954:
Eric Pantera, Nicolas Reneaud, Claude Bouscavert, and Didier Pradon published a 2026 study of a robotic exoskeleton for people with complete paraplegia. The device, called Atalante, balances itself as the user walks. Thirteen adults with chronic complete spinal cord injury took part. Training ran six weeks, with sixty supervised sessions. The team scored safety, ease of use, and patient comfort in a clinic setting.

Eleven people finished the full program. One serious event occurred: a shin fracture in a person with severe bone loss. That person left the study. Four near-falls were logged across 651 sessions. Minor events were brief and mild. Walking cost and speed stayed stable across the program. The team supports screened, supervised use of the device as a walking aid.
pmc-13552254:
Judith Wesenberg, with six colleagues, published a 2026 study of a German apathy scale for a motor neuron disease. Apathy is common in such diseases, and it comes in types. The scale splits apathy into executive, emotional, and initiation types. No checked German version existed. The team translated the scale with multi-round back-translation. Seventy-seven healthy controls and thirty-two patients with ALS filled self and caregiver ratings.

The German scale held together well, with strong internal consistency. It matched other apathy and frontal behavior scales as expected. It showed no link to anxiety or depression, which supports its focus. Patients scored higher than matched controls on executive and initiation apathy. Emotional apathy did not differ. Close to half the patients crossed a test threshold for initiation apathy.
pmc-13554254:
Dongsun Chen leads a ten-author team listening to Chinese women who had undergone fetal reduction in a 2026 interview study. The procedure lowers the number of fetuses in a pregnancy, often to protect the mother or remaining babies. Twelve women at a Henan hospital spoke in depth between June and October 2025. Two analysts sorted their accounts into themes independently.

Three themes emerged: tangled emotions, ways of coping, and wide-ranging needs. Emotions ran from regret and guilt to dread for the baby who remained. Women coped by hiding feelings, accepting what came, or leaning on family. Needs spanned clear information, mental health care, reachable services, and money help. The authors urge routine screening and layered support for these mothers.
pmc-13555654:
Muthu and co-authors reported a 2026 method for recovering atom thin MoS2 sheets from gold assisted exfoliation without polymer films. Gold helps peel large, high quality single layers of this two dimensional semiconductor, but the sheets stick so firmly that polymer transfer usually follows, adding contamination, strain, and defects.

Their two step iodine treatment first exposes the sample to iodine vapour and then etches with liquid iodine in sequence. Spectroscopy, time tracked imaging, and first principles calculations showed iodine settling on the gold changes its electronic structure and loosens its grip. Muthu found recovered sheets carried less strain and charge doping and fewer wrinkles than polymer transferred ones. Devices built from them gave stronger photocurrent and better operating stability.
pmc-13555854:
Hao-Chun Liao leads a six-author team detecting hidden anemia from routine chest X-rays in a 2026 Taiwan study. Anemia is usually found by blood tests, yet chest images are taken far more often. Their dataset held more than three hundred thousand adults from one hospital system. A pretrained vision model pulled features from each image, and a simple classifier judged anemia from those features alone.

The approach scored strongly on both internal and outside test sets. It caught about seven in ten cases while clearing more than eight in ten healthy people. Accuracy ran best on certain image types and in middle-aged men, and weakest in younger women. Adding clinical details improved results further. The authors propose opportunistic screening during routine care.
pmc-13558654:
Junko Kuramoto and colleagues compared in 2026 the DNA methylation fingerprints that accumulate as fatty liver disease turns toward cancer in Japanese and American patients. They profiled 220 liver samples across normal tissue, inflamed fatty liver, and cancer arising from it, using a genome-wide array. Chemical methylation marks silence or free genes, and the team asked which marks the cancers inherit from the precancerous stage in each population.

Fatty liver tissue already carried a methylation profile distinct from normal liver, and the two national cohorts differed from each other. Four cancer-related genes showed shared early marks in both countries, marking a common route, while other genes were altered only in Japan or only in the United States. Expression of marked genes shifted accordingly. Lifestyle and ancestry, the authors suggest, write partly different pre-cancer signatures.
pmc-13559454:
Zongxuan Gao and six colleagues published this 2026 analysis of global asthma burden tied to risk factors from 1990 to 2021, split by sex and socioeconomic level. Using Global Burden of Disease 2021 modelled estimates, they tracked disability-adjusted life years, deaths and years of life lost tied to high body-mass index, smoking, workplace asthmagens and nitrogen dioxide pollution. They also measured inequality across countries.

Total asthma disability years attributable to all risk factors rose 8.6 percent over the period, driven by population growth and ageing, even as the age-standardised rate fell steadily. The burden shifted by sex: male totals eased down 2.2 percent while female totals climbed 24.6 percent across the three decades. High body-mass index carried the largest share of burden and grew fastest. Workplace asthmagens caused the most years of life lost per death, and theirs was the one burden where inequality persisted or widened, especially in lower-income settings.
pmc-13560154:
Ridvan Akdogan and Seda Nur Yürük Yucakuş published this 2026 study of neonatal nurses' experiences stabilising newborns straight after birth, the minutes that often decide survival. Nurses lead this work, yet their lived experience of its clinical and emotional weight is little documented. The authors held in-depth interviews with 17 nurses working in delivery and operating theatre units of a large hospital, between August and December 2025, and analysed them with Colaizzi's method.

Five themes emerged: clinical skill and standard practice, structural and rank barriers, team ties and safety culture, emotional labour and moral distress, and protective strategies. Protocols gave nurses confidence and speed in the golden minutes. But limited authority, cramped rooms and communication gaps bred frustration and ethical tension, and fear of irreversible error weighed heavily. Careful records and ongoing training were seen as shields. The authors argue stabilisation support must be organisational and emotional, not merely technical.
pmc-13563754:
Augustine Teye and seven colleagues survey the people who inject sheep and goats around Kumasi, Ghana, about the damage bad injections leave behind. In practice, herders and para-veterinarians give most shots, not the licensed veterinarians alone, and the harm, abscesses, dead tissue, condemned meat, is poorly recognised. Their 2026 study questioned 230 providers: 59 veterinarians, 18 para-veterinarians, 143 herders, and 10 meat handlers. Abattoir records from January to August 2025 added hard evidence from the slaughter line.

Knowledge tracked training closely. Veterinarians knew the complications and chose the neck, the correct site, while para-veterinarians and herders favoured thigh and rump muscles and missed key risks. Inspectors found 100 injection-site lesions among 43,483 slaughtered animals, mostly in the thigh, matching the untrained habit. Formal training also predicted good practice and positive attitudes. The authors push injection-safety training outward to the people actually holding the syringe.
pmc-13569354:
Duo Zhang and co-authors dose, in a 2026 laboratory study, three fungi that live with the mountain pine beetle against eight scent chemicals that pine trees use as defenses. Beetles depend on these fungal partners to overcome tree defenses, so chemical tolerance shapes whether the partnership survives inside a tree.

Every chemical slowed fungal growth except one pairing, and strength varied sharply by fungus and by chemical, including between mirror-image forms of the same compound. One fungus was hit hardest overall, while two chemicals were broadly toxic and one was mildest. The uneven sensitivity helps explain which fungal partners thrive in defended trees and where beetle outbreaks may find their limits.
pmc-13569754:
Lihui Yu and Jingyu Chen review, in a 2026 narrative article, destroyed lung, the end stage of chronic lung infection in which tissue is irreversibly ruined and function collapses. Drugs can quiet active infection but cannot rebuild the damage, so surgery dominates management, and four illustrative transplant cases are discussed.

Removing the whole lung remains the standard operation for carefully chosen patients with one-sided disease, despite substantial risk. Transplantation is reserved for rare cases with both lungs affected, extreme impairment, or no workable removal option, and it carries major risks including infection and bleeding. Surgeons get a sober ordering of options for a condition with no easy answer.
pmc-13571054:
Bulent Diri and co-authors read, in a 2026 study, thirty-seven Akkadian cuneiform medical texts from the second and first millennia BCE against the modern international criteria for migraine without aura. Texts mentioning secondary headache causes or aura symptoms were set aside, and the rest were scored for pain duration, pain character, and accompanying symptoms.

Fifteen texts described continuous or prolonged pain, every text showed some match on pain character such as one-sided, throbbing, or severe pain, and twenty-one mentioned nausea or sensitivity to light or sound. The authors conclude that the core features of migraine without aura were recorded in Mesopotamia nearly three thousand years ago. Headache history gains its earliest documentary anchor.
pmc-13572454:
Meizhou Ding, with seven colleagues, presents a 2026 method for checking how evenly tobacco leaf types are mixed, a factor that shapes cigarette quality. Hand sampling is slow and may miss how the blend looks across a full batch. The team built a real-time image system that first creates more training images, then outlines each leaf type in live pictures.

Three image-making networks were compared, and CycleGAN gave the best leaf images. An attention step was added to a U-Net model so it could stress key features and mute background noise. The tuned model beat four rival models on overlap scores, with gains from 2.77 to 17.46 points. Pixel counts for each leaf type then gave the blend share in each image, a route the authors say could serve other farm goods too.
pmc-13572554:
Debashree Borthakur and colleagues searched an old Assamese food for bacteria that could serve as starter cultures. Napham, made from taro shoots and dried fish by the Bodo people of Assam, owes its taste to tiny life forms that remain poorly studied. Their 2026 study tested 48 germ strains for enzyme action, flavour, and safety.

Four strains passed early safety checks, and one, NAP/4, stood out for living through acid, phenol, and salt, sticking to gut-like cells, and clumping up. In curd and rice-drink tests it raised taste quality and made diverse flavour compounds. Gene tests named it a Staphylococcus species. The authors call it a good candidate, pending genome tests and live-animal checks.
pmc-13573454:
N.O. Savychuk, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 brain scan study of one patient with a painful jaw joint disorder. The cerebellum, at the back of the brain, helps with pain and feeling, not just movement. Jaw position may reshape its links, so the team scanned the patient in three jaw poses.

Scans ran with the jaw in normal bite, in a guided centred pose, and with a stabilising splint in place. In the normal bite, the cerebellar link pattern came out sparse and patchy. The centred pose and the splint pose each gave richer, structured patterns, and the two patterns tracked each other moderately. The authors treat the single case as a hint only. Larger prospective work must test whether jaw pose truly moves brain links in this disorder.
pmc-13574154:
Chenhao Tong and twenty colleagues published this 2026 study on how liver progenitor cells wake up after catastrophic liver damage. In acute liver failure with massive tissue death, these reserve cells must multiply and take on liver-cell functions. The authors used spatial transcriptomics and single-cell sequencing in patients and zebrafish to map the signals reaching the progenitor cells, then tested those signals in cell and mouse models.

One signal, TGF-β, normally holds progenitor cells in resting state by blocking their cell-cycle advance. During liver failure, two growth factors, HGF and EGF, override that brake and drive proliferation. HGF also switched on core liver genes such as Hnf4a in the progenitor cells, pushing them toward mature function. Surprisingly, that maturation step itself required TGF-β signalling. The authors cast TGF-β as a context-dependent switch: it restrains growth in calm conditions, yet enables proper functional maturation during regeneration.
pmc-13576354:
Pırıl Yıldız and four colleagues review five years of cases of children who took too much methylphenidate, a stimulant prescribed for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, in a 2026 single-centre study. Use of the drug has risen fast, and overdoses can affect the heart, blood pressure, and brain. Records came from a large children's emergency department, covering 2020 to 2024.

Thirty-two patients were included; 72 percent were girls, and the overdose was deliberate in 84 percent of cases. The mean dose taken was 5.7 milligrams per kilogram of body weight. Symptoms appeared in 41 percent, led by fast heart rate, mild high blood pressure, agitation, and seizures in 16 percent. Most cases stayed mild and cleared within 12 hours. One toddler needed close watching for brain and mood effects and recovered fully within 48 hours. No link appeared between dose or age and who became ill.
pmc-13578154:
Stine Høvring Godsk leads a 2026 study restoring a silenced immune alarm in soft tissue sarcoma, a rare cancer family with nearly 80 subtypes. Checkpoint inhibitor drugs work poorly in most sarcomas. The alarm in question is STING, a sensor that wakes immune attack when it detects stray DNA inside cells.

In tumour samples from a new patient cohort, higher STING levels matched heavier immune cell presence. The team used fat-based nanoparticles to deliver CRISPR activation parts that switch the STING gene back on in sarcoma cells. Treated cells drew stronger T cell recognition and killing in flat cultures and in three-dimensional patient-derived models. Responses to an anti-PD-1 drug also improved. The authors propose controlled STING activation as a route to make sarcomas answer immunotherapy.
pmc-13578254:
Mohamed Lamine Benmaidi and co-authors propose a 2026 defense for a future style of network that fetches data by name rather than by address. In such networks, attackers can flood routers with fake requests for content, filling their waiting lists and crowding out real users. Older guards either cry wolf too often or send all learning to one central server.

Their shield trains models at the routers themselves and shares only the lessons, keeping raw traffic local. Moving thresholds catch floods early, a fairness step balances uneven traffic across sites, and checks guard against rigged updates while keeping user data private. Trials on a test network of one hundred routers caught most attacks with few false alarms and low delay.
pmc-13579754:
Xiaoli Yang, Peng Fu, and Hui Liu pool past studies on two blood scores that may forecast how cancer patients fare on immune therapy, in a 2026 review. One score blends inflammation cell counts, the other blends a blood protein with white cell counts as a nutrition gauge. Single studies had disagreed, so the team searched three databases to mid February 2026 and merged twenty seven studies covering four thousand patients.

High inflammation scores went with roughly double the risk of death and of disease advance on checkpoint drugs. Low nutrition scores told the same grim story at similar strength. Subgroups held to the same pattern. The authors back both scores as cheap, handy guides for well studied cancers, while asking for fresh proof before they are stretched to rarer tumor types.
pmc-13579854:
Ai-Hua Ye and colleagues trace how a steroid drug blocks bone building in stem cells, in a 2026 study. Long steroid use is the top cause of secondary bone thinning, yet the chain of harm was fuzzy. Stem cells pushed toward bone making were dosed with a strong steroid, and a rat model of the disease backed the dish work.

The steroid lowered bone marker levels and drained the cells of retinoic acid, a signal that feeds bone growth. It did so by raising an enzyme that chews that signal up. Silencing the enzyme restored bone markers, while forcing it high erased the rescue that added signal gave. A master inflammation switch drove the enzyme's rise, and blocking that switch eased the steroid's harm. The chain gives drug hunters three linked targets.
pmc-13579954:
Md Abu Sayem and colleagues review five years of gene test results at a hospital in Chattogram, Bangladesh, to judge how the method serves infection care, in a 2026 study. Just under eight hundred samples with full records, drawn from blood, tissue, fluids, and swabs, were tested by a copying method that reads pathogen genes directly. Testing ran from mid 2019 to mid 2024.

About one in eight samples came back positive. Mycobacteria appeared in a small share, split between the tuberculosis germ and its lesser known cousins, which standard care often misses. Men and airway panel tests showed higher hit rates, while several sample types ran low. The authors praise the method's sharpness, urge smarter sample picking to lift hit rates and trim cost, and ask national TB planning to give the cousin germs their due.
pmc-13582154:
Timo Dräger and colleagues hunted fungal enzyme mixes that can crack open the tough walls of the green microalga Chlorella sorokiniana for food and feed. Microalgae are a sustainable, nutrient-rich crop, but their stubborn cell walls block downstream use. Their 2026 study screened eight fungal strains for enzyme output and wall-breaking power, then optimised the best mixes with designed experiments.

Aspergillus awamori, Aspergillus niger, and Ceratocystis paradoxa led the screen. All mixes peaked at 60 degrees Celsius with a 5 percent enzyme-to-biomass ratio, and A. awamori gave the best sugar-to-protein ratio, with strong glucosidase, mannosidase, and chitinase activity against chitin-like wall sugars. The authors present tailored fungal mixes as a route to greener microalgal bioprocessing.
pmc-13584254:
Ren Liu and colleagues trace how a drug-proof form of the hospital germ Acinetobacter baumannii spread around the world in this 2026 genome study. Some strains carry two strong resistance genes at once, named blaNDM-1 and blaOXA-23, which blunt even last-line antibiotics. The team read the genomes of 1,820 such strains gathered from public collections covering 2001 to 2024.

The double-gene pattern turned up in nearly two thirds of the strains, yet it sat almost wholly inside two bacterial families, called ST2 and ST164. That tight fit suggests the pattern spread by the growth of those families, not by genes jumping freely between strains. Place of origin also shaped a large share of each genome's spare parts, so the authors urge tracking aimed at those two families.
pmc-13587054:
Ubani and Ngole-Jeme publish in 2026 a dataset following what happens inside composting piles where animal manure is mixed with petroleum refinery sludge to break the waste down. The record tracks microbes, chemistry, and contaminants together over a long trial.

Five treatments, cow, pig, poultry, and horse manures plus an unamended control, ran as controlled microcosms for 300 days. Gene sequencing of the bacterial community catalogued 359 genera across 17 phyla before filtering. Diversity patterns depended on which manure was used, with cow manure giving the richest community. Pig and poultry manures selectively enriched hydrocarbon-eating bacteria such as Pseudomonas. Predicted gene functions pointed to pathways for degrading foreign chemicals and aromatic compounds, and culture tests confirmed a key ring-breaking enzyme gene, supporting real biodegradation potential.
pmc-13587454:
Neelima Ventrapragada and colleagues test a fallback drug for advanced GIST at a single center in India. Gastrointestinal stromal tumors that have beaten three or more targeted drugs leave few choices, and the approved fourth-line drug is out of reach in many poorer countries. Cabozantinib, a multi-target drug, might fill that gap. Their 2026 phase II trial gave it daily to 16 patients whose disease had moved on after at least three prior drugs.

At three months, nearly two thirds of patients were free of progression, well past the bar the trial set, with a middle progression-free span of four months. True tumor shrinkage stayed rare by the strict measure, though a looser scan measure counted more responses. Hand-foot skin trouble, high blood pressure, and diarrhea were the main hard side effects, and most patients needed a pause or dose cut. Quality of life held steady overall.
pmc-13587654:
Evelina Jankaitytė and colleagues probe how a toxic Alzheimer's peptide breaks the membrane around brain cells. Clumps of the peptide, called Aβ42 oligomers, are a prime suspect in Alzheimer's disease, yet exactly how they open holes in cell membranes stayed murky. The team built model membranes copying the outer face of a neuron's skin, varying which fats were present, and watched stiffness and leakiness with electric and light-based tools.

Adding either of two special fats let the peptide latch on and stiffen the membrane, but that grip alone did not open leaks. Heavy damage needed the full fat ensemble of the real outer leaflet working together. The lesson is that the peptide's harm depends on the whole lipid team and its layout, not on any single partner fat.
pmc-13589554:
Yuhe Zhao and colleagues read the red spider lily, Lycoris radiata, at full-genome level, opening the history and making of Amaryllidaceae alkaloids. These plant chemicals, counting over 600, include galanthamine, a licensed Alzheimer's drug, but poor genomes had blocked full study of their genes. Their 2026 build showed key downstream enzymes in the galanthamine path and two-way reactions between two key building blocks.

Cross-species gene reads traced several core making genes to early flower plants, while the complete path likely came together in the Amaryllidaceae subgroup through copying and new functions. Chemical-profile and gene-activity reads pointed to roots as active players. The team also rebuilt the galanthamine path in yeast, giving a chem and gene frame for building these plant chemicals.
pmc-13589954:
Sailong Zhang leads a 2026 study of gut injury caused by radiation used to treat cancers of the pelvis or belly. No standard cure exists for this harm, called radiation enteritis. The team tracked a secreted protein named Metrnl, whose levels shifted over time after radiation. Using single cell profiling, they asked which gut cells the protein protects.

Zhang and the team found that Metrnl guards slow, label retaining reserve cells rather than the usual fast stem cells of the gut lining. It switches on a signal path that joins c-KIT and WNT cues, which helps the lining regrow. Giving the protein as a drug eased gut injury in their tests. The authors pitch Metrnl as a fresh route to treat radiation harm.
pmc-13591554:
Minglei Ren and Jianjun Wang study how ocean warming may shrink the genomes of tiny marine archaea that turn ammonia into other nitrogen forms. These microbes drive the first step of nitrogen cycling in the sea. The pair gathered 281 rebuilt genomes from oceans worldwide, spanning the two dominant groups. Genome size fell as water temperature rose in both groups, they report.

The large genome group favors cold water, while the trimmed group prefers warmth. Each group also holds a sub branch leaning the other way, rich in genes for coping with temperature swings. Ren and Wang read the pattern as heat driven trimming paired with fresh branching into new niches. The shift could alter ocean nitrogen cycling as seas warm.
pmc-13591854:
Shengyu Zhou leads a 2026 early trial of eratrectinib, a next generation drug for cancers carrying NTRK gene fusions. Such fusions switch on growth kinases, and first drugs against them work well until resistance blooms. The new drug was built to beat that resistance. Sixteen patients joined dose escalation, and 75 more with fusion positive tumors joined expansion groups at set doses.

Side effects hit most patients yet stayed manageable, with dizziness the most common and no treatment linked deaths. A mid dose was picked for the next phase. At that dose, seven in ten patients saw tumors shrink. Zhou and the team present the drug as a fresh option for this rare tumor group, pending larger trials.
pmc-13595554:
Ni Made Dian Kurniasari and co-authors interviewed nineteen Balinese mothers about pregnancy and childbirth care across four districts of Bali, with data collected in 2017 and 2018. Indonesia has cut maternal deaths sharply since 1990. The quality of the experience still matters. In their 2026 write-up they grouped the women's accounts around one core theme. The theme was mothers' preferences and hopes for birth.

Women wanted care that was easy to reach and restful, and leaned on local midwives for support. Most chose hospitals to give birth because those places felt safer, then told of letdown over staff attitudes and poor communication once there. Many described knowing little about their options and simply taking whatever doctors advised. The authors argue that respecting women's wishes is not a luxury: mothers who felt heard described trust and support, and better talking is the clearest fix.
pmc-13599154:
Jennifer F. Baltzegar leads a seven-author team tracking how a suburban mosquito population in Wake County, North Carolina, gained resistance to common insect sprays. Their 2026 study followed Aedes albopictus, a mosquito that spreads several viral diseases, across the years 2016 to 2024. Spraying around homes there is often arranged by private firms rather than one public program, so pressure on the insects varies from street to street.

Using a new gene test on 2,669 mosquitoes, the group found a resistance change called F1534S first in 2018, in one central neighborhood. By 2023 it had spread across the county and reached a frequency of 0.36 at its peak. Their analysis points to strong selection favoring the change. The authors urge routine resistance checks and better coordination of home spraying before standard sprays lose their effect.
pmc-13602954:
Zihang Zhao leads an eleven-author team mapping a sprawling field: the hormone-like signals exercise releases and their links to diabetes and heart-metabolic disease. These mediators include fat-derived adipokines, muscle-derived myokines, and immune cytokines. The scoping review charted each report by exercise type, mediator, and the kind of link tested, from simple responsiveness to formal mediation.

Screening narrowed 3,388 records to 365 reports covering 363 studies and 103 distinct mediators. Obesity or overweight featured in 78.0 percent of studies. Adiponectin, leptin, IL-6, and irisin were the most studied signals. Most studies showed a mediator responding to exercise or tracking with disease, yet few pinned down where a mediator is secreted, which receptor it uses, or whether it truly mediates benefit. Formal mediation appeared in just 0.3 percent of studies. Long-term training and aerobic exercise dominated. The authors urge studies that follow mediators over time and test mechanisms directly.
pmc-13612154:
Michelle Oberthaler and three colleagues test whether a short video can warm mental health professionals toward AI help. Digital helpers promise relief for overloaded services, yet acceptance among students and therapists was murky. Their online survey drew 317 participants, mostly students, plus trainees and licensed therapists. Before and after watching a demonstration video, respondents rated usefulness, alongside stress, tech affinity, self-efficacy, and data protection worries.

Usefulness ratings rose after the video, with a small overall effect. Trainees moved most, licensed therapists barely at all. Higher work stress went with seeing more usefulness; older age, less. Tech affinity, prior knowledge, self-efficacy, and privacy concerns showed no links. Free-text answers raised data protection, ease of use, time demands, and professional autonomy. Brief demonstrations work as an acceptance lever for students and trainees, the authors suggest, and they flag the stress connection and licensed practitioners' flat response as puzzles worth chasing.
pmc-13614754:
Neşe Arslan and Şule B. Kakil report a 2026 review of outcomes for 970 patients who had upper eyelid surgery at one specialist centre between 2017 and 2023. The operation, called blepharoplasty, trims loose sagging eyelid skin that can block vision and trouble people about their looks. All patients had the same surgeon and the same technique, and all had sagging skin with sight or self-image complaints.

After surgery, patients filled in a structured questionnaire on daily vision, how happy they were with their mirror image, social confidence, and general well-being. Women made up 82.9 percent of the group, and the average age was 54.7 years. Large, patient-reported results like these show whether an operation often classed as cosmetic also restores comfort, sight, and confidence in daily life.
pmc-13614954:
Linda Kalunga and colleagues report a 2026 interview study with 27 leaders in the food industry on why companies hesitate to share food safety data with each other. Pooling private data across firms could speed joint analysis and catch rare contamination events sooner. The authors ran long, structured interviews to learn what actually decides the choice to share.

Four themes stood out: the benefits of sharing, technical barriers, trust, and clear rules for handling shared data. Leaders weighed the gain against the risk of losing control once their figures left the building. Trust in partners, regulators, and customers shaped nearly every answer. Formal data governance, with set rules on who sees what, emerged as the way through the deadlock, offering safety for firms without giving up the shared gain.
pmc-13616754:
Asmaa Sayed Shahin and colleagues study in 2026 whether silver nanoparticles can shield the saliva glands of rats from gamma radiation. This is the kind used against head and neck cancers. Such treatment often dries patients' mouths for good. Forty-five adult male rats were divided into five groups. Two groups served as healthy and sham controls. The rest received a single 15 gray radiation dose. One of those groups got the particles before radiation, and one got them after.

Untreated irradiated glands shrank, filled with empty bubbles and dying nuclei, and showed swollen power plants under fine microscopy, alongside raised markers of immune attack and cell suicide. Comparing tissue structure, immune stains, and cell detail across groups judged how far the particles prevented or repaired that harm. A protectant that survives testing could one day ease dry mouth, a lasting burden for cancer survivors.
pmc-13616854:
Lorenzo Bernardi and seven colleagues examine the learning curve when one surgeon moves from keyhole liver surgery to robot-assisted liver surgery. They reviewed consecutive minimally invasive liver operations in a single program, covering both techniques in the order the surgeon adopted them. Risk adjustment accounted for patient and operation factors that make cases harder or easier.

The series held one hundred ninety-seven operations, split almost evenly between the two approaches. Operating time and blood loss kept improving as robotic cases grew, and robotic performance improved after fewer cases than keyhole performance had, helped by the earlier experience. Complication scores improved later, only in the mastery phase. The authors conclude that a careful, stepwise switch to robotics did not harm results and can shorten the road to proficiency.
pmc-13617854:
Meret Herdick and seven colleagues analyze how patients with myasthenia gravis, a rare disease causing fluctuating muscle weakness, communicate with specialists through a telemedicine app. In a randomized study, forty-five patients were followed for three months; thirty used an app with chat, symptom measures, and device data, while fifteen received standard care. The team counted and categorized every chat contact in both directions.

Patients contacted specialists a median of six times, most often about medical issues, then technical and organizational questions. Specialists contacted patients a median of eight times each, and a large share of their medical messages recommended medication changes. Contact with outside physicians did not differ between groups, but app users rated specialist accessibility higher. The authors say the traffic reveals strong demand for timely treatment advice and suggest testing whether telemedicine can head off symptom worsening.
pmc-13618354:
Ayhan Kocaman and four colleagues test a new nickel borate adsorbent, shortened to NiB, for stripping two sulfonated anionic dyes, Trypan Blue and Ponceau S, from water. Dye wastewater is a stubborn pollution problem, and a reusable high-capacity sorbent would help. The team varied contact time, acidity, dose, stirring speed, temperature, and starting dye concentration, then modeled the results and tried regeneration.

Near neutral acidity, removal topped ninety percent for both dyes within an hour, and measured capacities reached about four hundred sixty-three milligrams per gram at the highest test concentration. No saturation plateau appeared, so the authors treat model capacity figures as apparent estimates. Uptake followed a multi-step path of fast surface attachment, rearrangement, and diffusion, and the process was spontaneous and heat-releasing. Thermal regeneration beat acid washing, keeping seventy percent efficiency by the ninth cycle, which supports NiB as a reusable candidate.
pmc-13621354:
Quang Tam Huynh, Yu-Fang Lin, Quoc Thanh Vo, and Ken-Lin Chang report the first use of a porous crystal-like framework as a catalyst for making a bio-based coating ingredient. The ingredient, IBOMA, comes from pine-derived camphene and serves coatings, glues, and dental materials. Its usual synthesis leans on corrosive liquid acids that cannot be reused and leave messy waste.

Their catalyst carries acid sites on a covalent organic framework and works under light plus microwave heating with no solvent at all. Making the catalyst itself by microwave gave it larger pore volume than the slow oven route. Tuned conditions reached a yield above ninety percent, and the catalyst kept working across five reuse rounds. Waste yardsticks showed the process generating far less residue than three common liquid acids, with a smaller carbon footprint as well.
pmc-13623154:
